title: First projection at a Dalton Kincaid extension with Buffalo Bills
summary: Is it too early to start envisioning what a second contract for Dalton Kincaid could look like? Sure. Maybe a little bit. While he is in the fourth year of his rookie deal with the Buffalo Bills, and the club has already picked up his fifth-year option for 2027, we know Brandon Beane’s history of […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Tight end Dalton Kincaid #86 reacts after scoring a touchdown during the first half of an NFL football game between the Detroit Lions and the Buffalo Billsat Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, New York, USA, on Thursday, September 17, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Is it too early to start envisioning what a second contract for Dalton Kincaid could look like? Sure. Maybe a little bit. While he is in the fourth year of his rookie deal with the Buffalo Bills, and the club has already picked up his fifth-year option for 2027, we know Brandon Beane’s history of signing homegrown talents early. Without a Bills game on Sunday in Week 2, we have time to peer well into the future on Kincaid’s potentially impending extension. After a small-sample season in 2025 in which Kincaid led all tight ends in yards per route run — the ultimate receiving efficiency metric — and his blazing start to 2026, we need to start this projection at the top of the tight end market. Here are the top 3 contracts at tight end right now in the NFL: Years Total Value APY Guaranteed At Signing George Kittle 4 $76.4M $19.1M $33M Trey McBride 4 $76M $19M $32.5M Tucker Kraft 4 $75M $18.75 $26.5M While it’s always relevant to showcase the “top” of the market at a certain position when these type of scenarios arise, it’s simultaneously the perfect time to reference why guaranteed at signing matters more than anything else. Falcons tight end Kyle Pitts, who’s technically fourth in Average Per Year (APY) — which is the default metric used for sorting purposes — at $17.67M, actually has received the most money guaranteed at signing of the group at $36M. With that, let’s get into the ages of these players, which absolutely will play into negotiations with Kincaid. Pitts is almost exactly one year younger than Kincaid. Of course Kittle is much older. Kraft was picked in the same draft as Kincaid but also a year younger, and McBride is a month younger than the Bills star tight end. And let’s stack these tight ends against each other from a production standpoint. I’ll remove Kittle because while he has the highest APY at the position, because of his age, I don’t believe the deal he’s currently playing on will factor as significantly into contract talks with Kincaid: Games Career Yards Per Route Run Regular-season games missed due to injury Career catches Trey McBride 67 1.80 1 356 Tucker Kraft 43 1.67 9 116 Kyle Pitts 79 1.63 8 284 Dalton Kincaid 43 1.91 10 168 In a perfect world for the Bills, the team would’ve gotten ahead of the Kraft contract. But Green Bay didn’t hesitate to hand him the massive extension despite his torn ACL in 2025 while Kincaid’s prolonged injury history likely very much factored into why an extension has yet to be offered to Kincaid. There is some timing precedent for a Kincaid extension — Greg Rousseau. He and the Bills agreed on a second contract after his fourth season. If the Bills ultimately go that route, it’d be sensible, right? Rousseau was a quality player for Buffalo in his first four seasons. And they waited. Kincaid has been quality too, and probably even more productive than Rousseau at his respective position but noticeably less durable. Beane and Co. haven’t historically given out contracts in-season — not many teams do — and this is precisely where the projection gets hazy because we don’t know what’s ahead for Kincaid. Internally, the Bills may know he’s miles ahead on the health front compared to either of the past two seasons. They may finally feel great about that vital element for any player. If that’s the case, they’d subsequently be expecting a monstrous 1,000-plus yard campaign for Kincaid, which would come at the perfect time for the tight end given where he is timeline wise on that rookie deal. And I think a Kincaid extension would look something like this: Years Total Value APY Fully Guaranteed At Signing 4 $76.8 $19.2 Somewhere between $28M – $32M Almost identical to his 2023 draft classmate Tucker Kraft. Essentially a market-setting deal for Kincaid, who was a bit older when he started his NFL career — turned 24 in October of his rookie campaign, but is still distinctly in his professional prime. And right now, I’m projecting lower than truly market-setting on the critical guaranteed-at-signing figure because Beane has regularly gotten these extensions done under that mark. But that could’ve been due to the quality of player he’s signed in the past. It doesn’t feel like the Bills would get into a hold out/hold intype situation with Kincaid — he very much appears to be fully embedded in Buffalo’s team culture — but contract negotiations can certainly alter team-player relationships. Then again, James Cook technically held in last summer. Said hold in lasted like two days, and he signed a very team-friendly deal. Culture can impact the contract-front too. Even if Beane can work his magic to get a Kincaid extension under, say $18M in APY and $32M in guaranteed at signing, we have to be prepared for this to be an expensive deal. But, frankly, it’d be a long time coming for the Bills to have a (homegrown) receiving weapon for Josh Allen worthy of getting a lucrative extension.

(Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Buffalo Bills defensive tackle Deone Walker has gone bananas to begin his second season in the NFL. The former fourth-round pick has been borderline unblockable in the first two games of the season, and his huge splash plays have come on monumentally impressive wins. He has a ridiculous nine quarterback pressures on 59 pass-rush snaps through Week 2, which equates to a high-caliber edge-rusher like pressure rate of 15.9%. The 6’7”, 330-plus pounder also has seven tackles, two tackles for loss, three pass breakups, and a sack — all on 95 snaps thus far in the 2026 season. And he only turned 22 in March (fellow Pisces like yours truly). Given the game-wrecking start to Walker’s sophomore season in the NFL, I believe it’s now appropriate to start workshopping nicknames for Buffalo’s budding star on the interior. Especially with no Bills game this Sunday. We have plenty of time this weekend. He’s a pretty unique cat at his gargantuan size and length with serious juice and veteran like pass-rush moves. But instead of just asking for your suggestions, I’m going to challenge you. Try to “beat” my favorite I got from my friend Matt in a nickname brainstorm group text on this exact topic earlier today: “Swim Diesel.”

title: Buffalo Bills Week 2 rooting interests around the NFL
summary: Rooting interests are easy when it comes to the AFC East: Buffalo wins, everyone else loses. Done.  Unfortunately, the rest of the NFL schedule requires a little more thought — and, this week, at least one rooting interest that might make Bills Mafia feel a little dirty.  Buffalo gets the week started early, hosting the Detroit Lions […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - JANUARY 17: A Buffalo Bills fan yells to players before the AFC Divisional Round game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on January 17, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Rooting interests are easy when it comes to the AFC East: Buffalo wins, everyone else loses. Done. Unfortunately, the rest of the NFL schedule requires a little more thought — and, this week, at least one rooting interest that might make Bills Mafia feel a little dirty. Buffalo gets the week started early, hosting the Detroit Lions on Thursday night in the first regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium. A win gets the Bills to 2-0 and, for at least a couple of days, puts them alone atop the AFC East. After that, we go back to our regularly scheduled program of deciding who Bills Mafia should be cheering for — even when it feels very, very wrong. As we established last week, it is still too early to spend much time trying to predict playoff seeding. Instead, we’re keeping this fairly simple. We want Buffalo’s opponents to win and strengthen the Bills’ strength of schedule. We want teams Buffalo has beaten to keep winning and help with strength of victory. And, whenever possible, we want the rest of the AFC East to lose. Easy enough, right? Well, mostly. _____________________________________________________________________________ AFC EAST Buffalo Bills over Detroit Lions We don’t need to make this complicated. Beat Detroit. Get to 2-0. Open the new stadium with a win. Then we can worry about everybody else. Go Bills! Pittsburgh Steelers over New England Patriots This one doesn’t require math. New England is 0-1. Let’s make it 0-2. Yes, the Patriots are a Buffalo opponent, so a New England win would technically help the Bills’ strength of schedule. We don’t care. Some rules outrank other rules. Green Bay Packers over New York Jets The Jets are the only other AFC East team that escaped Week 1 with a win, beating Tennessee 23-10. Let’s fix that. Green Bay is also on Buffalo’s schedule later this season, so we get the best of both worlds here: a Bills opponent gets a win, and a division rival gets a loss. Go Pack Go. San Francisco 49ers over Miami Dolphins Miami is already 0-1 after losing to Las Vegas. You know the assignment. We could talk about strength of schedule and the fact that Buffalo plays Miami twice. Or we could just root for the Dolphins to start 0-2. We’re choosing the second one. _____________________________________________________________________________ The rest of the AFC Houston Texans over Cincinnati Bengals Welcome to our first strength-of-victory game. Buffalo already has a win over Houston, which means every Texans win from here makes that Week 1 victory look a little better. Cincinnati is also an AFC team that could eventually find itself in the conference playoff picture. There are two reasons to want Houston here. Go Texans. Baltimore Ravens over New Orleans Saints Here’s where things get a little uncomfortable. Baltimore is absolutely a team we may eventually want losing football games. The Ravens are 1-0, they’re an AFC team, and there is a very reasonable chance we’re talking about them when playoff seeding becomes important. But Buffalo also plays Baltimore this season. So, for now, we’re sticking with the rule we established in Week 1: build the strength of schedule and sort out the AFC standings when we actually have AFC standings worth sorting out. So, yes, we’re rooting for Baltimore. For now. Denver Broncos over Jacksonville Jaguars Denver is on Buffalo’s schedule. Jacksonville isn’t. That’s enough for Week 2. A Broncos win strengthens Buffalo’s schedule, and we’re not yet at the point where we’re worried about Denver’s place in the AFC standings. Los Angeles Chargers over Las Vegas Raiders Buffalo plays both teams this season, so there’s no strength-of-schedule advantage either way. That sends us to the AFC standings. Las Vegas is already 1-0, while Los Angeles is 0-1. Let’s spread the wins around rather than let another AFC team get to 2-0. Go Chargers. Kansas City Chiefs over Indianapolis Colts Don’t shoot the messenger. The Bills play Kansas City this season. They don’t play Indianapolis. Therefore, under the rules we established for these early weeks, a Chiefs win is better for Buffalo’s strength of schedule. Yes, I know. Yes, it feels wrong. No, we don’t have to enjoy it. It is what it is. Tampa Bay Buccaneers over Cleveland Browns This one’s easy because Cleveland is AFC. If neither is on Buffalo’s schedule, send the win to the NFC. Philadelphia Eagles over Tennessee Titans Same rule. NFC over AFC. Tennessee falling to 0-2 doesn’t hurt us one bit. _____________________________________________________________________________ NFC vs NFC games Los Angeles Rams over New York Giants Another easy strength-of-schedule choice. The Rams are on Buffalo’s schedule. The Giants aren’t. Go Rams. Minnesota Vikings over Chicago Bears Buffalo gets both of these teams this season, so strength of schedule isn’t going to help us pick a side. That means we get to choose this one for ourselves. Me? I’m going with Minnesota because I’m petty, and all that talk about the Bears’ offense being better than Buffalo’s — hint: it’s not — after Week 1 made me salty. Go Vikings. Atlanta Falcons over Carolina Panthers Carolina was one of last year’s division winners. We said we’re rooting against those teams early and keeping them away from another easy path to the playoffs. Both are 0-1, so give Atlanta the win. Seattle Seahawks over Arizona Cardinals Both are 1-0, so this is mostly about knocking Arizona off the unbeaten list. Seattle already helped us by beating New England in Week 1, so they can have another one. Dallas Cowboys over Washington Commanders Both are irrelevant to Buffalo’s SOS, but Washington made the playoffs last year while Dallas didn’t. Stick with our Week 1 philosophy: knock down last year’s contenders and let the teams that were out of it take the wins. _____________________________________________________________________________ Some of these picks required a little more work than others, but that’s what happens in Week 2. There aren’t playoff scenarios to sort through yet, so we’re working with what we have — strength of schedule, strength of victory, the early AFC standings, and, occasionally, a little pettiness. For now, the formula remains pretty simple: Buffalo wins, the rest of the AFC East loses, and future opponents pile up victories whenever they aren’t playing Buffalo. Even if that means rooting for Kansas City. Again, don’t shoot the messenger.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: 5 takeaways from Bills win over Lions in Week 1
summary: Wheeeew — what a housewarming performance from the Buffalo Bills in their Week 2 victory over the Detroit Lions in the first regular-season contest inside the new Highmark Stadium. Such a glorious night in Orchard Park. These were my five biggest takeaways from Buffalo’s 41-31 victory. The new Highmark Stadium is VERY LOUD The text […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after a touchdown during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Wheeeew — what a housewarming performance from the Buffalo Bills in their Week 2 victory over the Detroit Lions in the first regular-season contest inside the new Highmark Stadium. Such a glorious night in Orchard Park. These were my five biggest takeaways from Buffalo’s 41-31 victory. The new Highmark Stadium is VERY LOUD The text I kept sending friends and family from my initial reaction to the Bills opening touchdown drive, and subsequent three-and-out stop on defense that culminated in a sack of Jared Goff was “it’s so loud in here it’s hurting my ears.” Now, I’m not trying to scare you away from the stadium — it’s unreal. When it comes to the actual football, the crowd noise absolutely matters, and the overall verticality of the stadium along with the canopy — which I think is the real driver here — make this 60,000-seat palatial structure a giant boom box. The Bills scoreboard crew didn’t regularly utilize a decibel meter throughout the entire course of the game. When it was shown, the collective noise in the stadium regularly cleared 120dB. I’m certainly not a sound engineer, but I assume some of the crowd pops probably reached well in the 130dB range, which is well into “the level of sound from a plane taking off nearby.” I couldn’t get over how easily Buffalo scored 41 points Four touchdowns on the first four drives was sensational. Borderline effortless. But as we were reminded of in this contest, teams almost always have to play a full 60 minutes in today’s NFL. And the Bills had a tiny lull in the middle portion of the contest, where it felt like the offense lost a little of its juice. After the DJ Moore injury, really. They got back on track, and still scored 41 points. Sure, the modern NFL is heavily geared toward offense, but that’s absurd. On the way to 41 points, the Bills offense fully demonstrated its real-time adaptability. Moore goes down with an injury? OK, start pounding the rock, and look for Dalton Kincaid off play action. We have seen incredible aerial attacks in the Allen era. Everything Buffalo’s offensive line and James Cook learned from last year’s run-game masterpiece might just be precisely what this Bills team needed to truly become a multi-layered, beat-you-however-we-want offense. Credit where credit is due for Keon Coleman I’ve not had much confidence in Coleman during his time with the Bills. He simply hasn’t produced. Before the season, when it appeared obvious they weren’t going to trade or cut him, I figured whatever statistical output the team could get from Coleman would be a bonus, not anything the Bills should be expecting. Well, in this game, he made a handful of important, even difficult grabs in traffic when things got a little dicey in the second half. Four of his six receptions went for first downs, and his half-dozen grabs were the second-most of his NFL career. Coleman is not at all a separator. But he can win against zone. There’s nuance to that. And maybe he’s finally learning how exactly to find those soft softs, post up and use his size to make himself an available target for Allen. If Coleman can provide the Bills with more six-snag, 63-yard performances throughout the season, that will be a massive development for the passing offense. Deone Walker That’s it. Deone Walker. Each game, it’s looking more and more likely he is a DUDE. The crux of my gameday column before Bills and Lions in Week 2 was Buffalo’s opportunity to see how some of its star players — beyond Allen — stacked-up against the legitimate stars the Lions would trot onto the field. Walker absolutely looked like a superstar on TNF (after an awesome performance in Week 1). Sure, the Lions were down a few offensive linemen, and we can’t forget that regarding this evaluation, but nine pressures on 30 pass-rush snaps from a defensive tackle in the NFL is magnificent regardless of competition. Oh, and there was this absolutely outrageous rep from Walker: Deone Walker (96) rushing from a 5T vs Sewell. Doesn’t get much with the initial swipe but then plants that outside leg into the ground, pins Sewell & gets the arm over to get into the backfield Good PBU from Dorian Williams (42) vs the dig pic.twitter.com/Zh6Ylo3KUt — Anthony Cover 1 (@Pro__Ant) September 18, 2026 That is against PENEI SEWELL, one of the Lions superstars I referenced in the aforementioned article. You know, a three-time first-Team All-Pro the past three seasons. Squarely in the prime of his NFL career. Walker tossed him aside like he had better things to do. One of my friends called him Deone “Mount Mutumbo” Walker last night… I like it. But I’m open to any and all suggestions for Walker nickname ideas. He’s deserving. It’s time. Oh, and in following up my own column, through two games, the Bills have had plenty of other genuine stars beyond Allen, Cook, and Walker. Greg Rousseau was a man possessed again. And Kincaid is Mr. Efficiency as a receiving tight end. That’s the type of makeup I believe a team needs to hoist the trophy. Defensive lowlights and low-key improvement Once again, I’ll write — the Bills secondary is going to take time to gel. Understand where to be in relation to teammates. And against specific pre-snap looks from opposing offenses. All that. Two of their outside corners, Max Hairston and Davison Igbinosun, are 23 and 22, respectively. The defensive line probably isn’t as deep as Jim Leonhard would like it — although I thought DeWayne Carter flashed in this one. When the Bills build big leads, the secondary very well could surrender some big plays. Ironically, I was impressed by the run defense, once again. This week, it was even more impressive given how explosive — and powerful — Jahmyr Gibbs is as a runner. Detroit only had 66 yards on the ground on 20 carries. That is not how they want to play. And they’re typically much more dynamic in the run game, of course. Buffalo’s run defense allowed 3.9 yards per tote against Houston. From an analytics perspective, the Bills run defense was 31st in EPA per run play in 2026. It’s currently 20th in EPA allowed per run before the full slate of Week 2’s action. Very easily could be middle of the pack once Monday Night Football concludes this week. Darn good improvement.

title: DJ Moore injury: Bills WR avoids serious shoulder injury
summary: Buffalo Bills wide receiver DJ Moore headed to the locker room with a shoulder injury Thursday night. He dove for a pass in the back of the end zone and immediately grabbed at the area. On Friday morning, Adam Schefter reported Moore isn’t expected to miss much if any time. That is a big sigh […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: DJ Moore #2 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Houston Texans during the second quarter of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Buffalo Bills wide receiver DJ Moore headed to the locker room with a shoulder injury Thursday night. He dove for a pass in the back of the end zone and immediately grabbed at the area. On Friday morning, Adam Schefter reported Moore isn’t expected to miss much if any time. That is a big sigh of relief. The Bills announced he was questionable to return with a shoulder injury and a stinger, but he was later downgraded to OUT and went for an X-ray. This Schefter report would indicate his collarbone is not broken. Moore was the marquee trade executed by the Bills to open up their pass offense this offseason and he’s delivered through six quarters. In addition to scoring his own touchdown and topping 100 yards, he’s drawn the secondary’s attention away from others. The Bills would move back to an “Everybody Eats” mentality without Moore in the lineup for an extended period of time. With Moore out, the Bills have Skylar Bell as a healthy scratch and he would move into the lineup. Brandin Cooks is a free agent and could return to Buffalo, as well. Trent Sherfield and Greg Dortch are on the practice squad and Dortch has used up two of his three game day elevations. Keon Coleman took the share of Moore’s snaps during the game, stepping up when the Bills needed him most.

title: Keon Coleman steps up for Bills following DJ Moore injury
summary: Earlier this year, there was a lot of talk about the future of Buffalo Bills wide receiver Keon Coleman. He was suspended a few times in 2025 for being late to team meetings, and even Bills owner Terry Pegula had less than flattering things to say about him. But new head coach Joe Brady and […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Keon Coleman #0 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates a reception against the Detroit Lions during the second quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Earlier this year, there was a lot of talk about the future of Buffalo Bills wide receiver Keon Coleman. He was suspended a few times in 2025 for being late to team meetings, and even Bills owner Terry Pegula had less than flattering things to say about him . But new head coach Joe Brady and QB Josh Allen said in February that they believed in him and when it came time to step up against the Detroit Lions, he did just that. Coleman caught six passes on six targets for 63 yards despite playing out of position for a good chunk of the game filling in for DJ Moore. Moore was injured in the first half of the game, and Buffalo didn’t have another speedy receiver. Enter Coleman, who converted on 3rd and 6 and 3rd and 7 during the game on scoring drives, including an impressive catch in front of the Bills sideline. Clutch Keon Coleman catch to keep the drive alive 🦬 #BillsMafia pic.twitter.com/i92MK2Umiu — SleeperBills (@SleeperBills) September 18, 2026 Coleman has faced his problems and spoke to the media when he didn’t have to. He’s taken accountability. On Thursday night he stepped up in a big way when the Bills needed him. With Moore likely to miss time with his injury, they’ll need Coleman more than ever.

title: Panthers Injury Report & Transactions – Week 2
summary: The Carolina Panthers front office is busy throughout the season with transactions, roster moves, and injury updates. Here’s what’s happening at Mint Street this week. Injuries The 0-1 Panthers go on the road to face the Atlanta Falcons in an NFC South rivalry game. Games between the Panthers and the Falcons are almost always bruising, physical affairs, […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 18: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills is tackled by Tyrel Dodson #25 of the Miami Dolphins after sliding in the second half of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 18, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers front office is busy throughout the season with transactions, roster moves, and injury updates. Here’s what’s happening at Mint Street this week. Injuries The 0-1 Panthers go on the road to face the Atlanta Falcons in an NFC South rivalry game. Games between the Panthers and the Falcons are almost always bruising, physical affairs, and player health is at a premium in this one. Fortunately, the Panthers have a fairly clean injury report as of Friday. Young stud wide receiver Jalen Coker was limited in practice on Wednesday and Thursday, but he was a full participant on Friday. Look for him to get behind Atlanta’s secondary for at least one monster touchdown. The injury report is more troubling on the defensive side of the ball. Outside linebacker Patrick Jones II was limited in practice all week and is questionable for Sunday. Veteran defensive tackle Bobby Brown III won’t be playing on Sunday due to a back injury. Transactions The Panthers made three transactions this week, and each of them have ramifications. Signed LB Tyrel Dodson to the active roster Last week I wrote at length about the potential significance of the Panthers signing Dodson to the practice squad . He’s 28 years old with 310 tackles and 9.5 sacks over the last three seasons. He’s not coming off any sort of injury, nor are there off-field concerns. Carolina elevated him to the 53-man roster this week and I wouldn’t be surprised if the coaching staff gives him an opportunity to prove himself with some meaningful defensive snaps against the Falcons. Waived WR Jimmy Horn Jr. In order to sign Dodson to the active roster, somebody had to come off it. That somebody was Jimmy Horn Jr. Horn, a sixth-round pick by the Panthers in the 2025 draft, was waived this week after muffing a punt last week against the Bears. As a rookie last year he had 11 receptions for 108 yards while returning five kickoffs and two punts. The Panthers were looking to utilize him more in the return game this year, but the muffed punt was the final straw for Carolina’s coaching staff. After clearing waivers earlier this week, Horn signed with the Cleveland Browns’ practice squad. Signed WR EJ Williams to the practice squad After elevating Dodson, the Panthers went out and added wide receiver EJ Williams to the practice squad. The 6-foot-3, 205-pound receiver has some familiarity with the Carolinas after playing three seasons at Clemson from 2020-2022. He then transferred to Indiana where he spent the last three seasons. In the Hoosiers’ national championship season last year he contributed 36 receptions for 438 yards and an impressive six touchdowns. While his college career was unspectacular with just 1,210 career receiving yards over 60 games, he has an NFL body and will now have the opportunity to prove he belongs in the league.

title: Brian Answers: Bryce Young, Brad Idzik, Ejiro Evero, Misery and Sadness, and more!
summary: Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! Following a mixed bag (pun intended) on Sunday, the Panthers face their division rival as the entire NFC South started the season 0-1, which is par for the course with this division. We’ll get to see the Panthers offense […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears runs with the ball against Bobby Okereke #58 of the Carolina Panthers during the fourth quarter of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! Following a mixed bag (pun intended) on Sunday, the Panthers face their division rival as the entire NFC South started the season 0-1, which is par for the course with this division. We’ll get to see the Panthers offense try not to come back to Earth, while the defense tries to find its way back into Earth’s orbit. Let’s break down all your questions ahead of this week’s game! sgtx: Brian, where do you fall on “The Big Evero Debate” going on right now. Do you think he’s a good DC that hasn’t had the personnel here, or a poor DC that had his chances and needs to be replaced. I’m still fine with Ejiro Evero. I know a lot of fans still hang onto 2024’s horrific season and then some overall letdown performances in 2025, so I get why many fans are calling for his head. Which is why I am not going to sit here and say anybody is wrong. But let’s look at the facts. The Panthers started at ground zero by trading away a ton of draft capital and DJ Moore to get Bryce Young, and let a premium pass rusher in Brian Burns go all in the same off-season. They have since been trying to rebuild basically the entire team since then. They did spend some money on defense in 2025 and grabbed two edge rushers with day two picks, but ultimately I think this 2026 defense is in the best spot we’ve seen since Evero became defensive coordinator. So that fact does play into the equation for sure. I like Evero’s defenses on many Sundays, but the bad Sundays are truly bad like this past weekend. I attribute a lot of this weekend’s defensive performance to players missing on assignments and making mistakes, but that ultimately does fall somewhere on the coordinators shoulders. I am not ready to fire Evero today, or even mid-season, but if the defense doesn’t improve (and I fully expect it will), there’s certainly a conversation to be had in the off-season of overturning that entire defensive coaching staff. But I am not there yet. Coach_K: Who of our rookies would you buy a jersey of right now? While the defense as a whole wasn’t good on Sunday, I am all in on the Lee Hunter hype train on the defensive line. See: some work here. A big takeaway from watching the CHI OL vs CAR DL is that 'no gloves' Lee Hunter looks like a dude pic.twitter.com/CuyIk4EoRS — Brandon Thorn (@BrandonThornNFL) September 16, 2026 I think the Panthers may have found the perfect compliment to Derrick Brown as a disruptive interior lineman, and he’s only one game into his NFL career. It will be fun to watch him mesh with the rest of that unit as time goes on. e4*: Will the inactive list look notably different this Sunday? I would hope DL Cam Jackson gets a jersey against a Falcons offense that should be heavily run focused this week. I’m hoping Patrick Jones can play on EDGE as well, and maybe we’ll see S Zakee Wheatley make his regular season debut. These are all hopes, but not promises. storybook: How many of Sunday’s defensive problems can we attribute to poor communication among a defense with several new starters going against a very sophisticated offense? I think the 100+ degree weather combined with a lot of new starters playing what I would call an elite tier Chicago offense played major roles in the defensive collapse we saw on Sunday. I cannot imagine it will get that bad even once for the rest of the season. The defense needs to acclimate together and that could take more than just one week. There were several missed tackles and blown assignments that the coaching staff definitely needs to clean up, but I am not hitting the panic button just yet. positivebob: Are there any real conclusions possible from a single game? Especially week 1. Especially when the opponent was such an outlier-great offense, bad defense-when most teams Carolina faces will be more mid on both sides of the ball? Can you predict weekly, extreme mood swings for the next 17 weeks, not just from week to week, but play to play? That’s what makes it fun, right? The biggest conclusion I can take from this game is Carolina has cleared the hurdle of the offense starting extremely sluggishly, it was refreshing to see them come out firing. The game was 31-31 coming out of the 2nd half, and deep into the 3rd quarter the Panthers were very much staying in an offensive shooutout against one of the best offensive starting lineups in the NFL. I think things will definitely regress more to the mean, but I predict the Panthers passing game to at least continue looking locked in. But I think the offensive line could falter somewhat and keep them from putting up huge point production just because teams will figure out this protection scheme and exploit the weak links. On defense, I expect them to improve, but the rushing defense is still a concern outside of runs straight up the middle into the teeth of this defensive line and group of linebackers. But I’m expecting the defense to have a much better game and set people at ease against the Falcons, even if Bijan Robinson still has a 150 yards from scrimmage day. schrodingersblackcat: I loved how aggressive Idzik was in his first game as play caller. Granted, he seized on the weaknesses of a below-average Bears defense. I expect a similar look against a below-average Atlanta team this week. Do you expect Idzik to remain so bullish against better teams? As a regular critic, I gotta say Bryce had an excellent game. He was prepared and dialed in, both pre- and post-snap. It didn’t feel like we were racing the clock to get the play off. The tempo felt good. He stayed in the pocket and trusted his arm. He didn’t shy away from tight window throws. What did you see in Bryce’s performance on Sunday that gives you the most hope that he will make a leap in his fourth season? I liked that OC Brad Idzik really seemed to open up the passing playbook right away. The Panthers often started games trying to establish the run in 2025, in this game they just came out swinging for the fences and I’m not sure Chicago expected it. Having a fully healthy group of offensive weapons helps with that approach, but they really didn’t shy away from attacking down the field and it paid a ton of dividends. I expect Idzik to continue to be aggressive down the field because that will actually help open up the rushing attacks against better rushing defenses than the Bears. What I saw from Bryce was confidence, something we’ve definitely seen but not this early in the season. We all know he can throw with insane anticipation, but we really saw it shine on down field throws that racked up huge chunks of yards, and those explosive plays in the passing game have been what this offense was really missing since Bryce became the starting quarterback. We saw flashes of it over time in many seasons, but for him to open the season letting it loose with the anticipation he did is a huge step forward. What gives me the biggest hope is we don’t have to wait for him to get into full gear mid-way or 75% of the way through the season, at least in theory, following this performance. He has confidence in the scheme, his receivers, and his throws. That could all come crashing down this week, but I’m drinking that Kool-Aid right now. TXPanther: The Panthers are now a 2.5 point favorite after opening as 1.5 point dog. What will the line be before kickoff on Sunday? I think it will probably stay the same. Divisional matchups are weird and the Panthers/Falcons bi-annual Misery and Sadness Bowl is no different. They may put the Panthers at 4.5-5.5 point favorites if Cooper Rush is confirmed to be starting, which I still wouldn’t call a safe bet…
author: Brian Beversluis

title: Panthers vs Falcons: Week 2 matchups to watch
summary: The Carolina Panthers scored 37 points in their home opener. The offense was clicking and picking up yards and scores at will. Unfortunately the defense let up an absurd 59 points in what ended up as a three score loss. In this space, we talked about the importance of Jalen Coker and Tetairoa McMillan beating […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - NOVEMBER 16: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers throws the ball during the NFL 2025 game between Carolina Panthers and Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on November 16, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers scored 37 points in their home opener. The offense was clicking and picking up yards and scores at will. Unfortunately the defense let up an absurd 59 points in what ended up as a three score loss. In this space, we talked about the importance of Jalen Coker and Tetairoa McMillan beating the Bears secondary. They did that. We also talked about the defensive front against a strong Bears offensive line. They lost that battle as badly as they can lose it, and that ultimately decided the game. This week, the Panthers play division rival Falcons who are coming off a game that’s basically the opposite of the one the Panthers just played. Neither they or the Steelers could move the ball against one another, and a defensive touchdown fittingly decided the game in favor of the Steelers. Something has to give in this one. Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke vs Bijan Robinson The Panthers used the offseason to completely revamp their starting linebacker duo. That did not help them in Week 1 against the Bears. Both D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai tallied at least 100 yards rushing, and both found all sorts of space slicing through the middle of the defense. Devin Lloyd had a really rough debut with the Panthers, while Bobby Okereke was largely invisible outside of an early forced fumble. They struggled to do their part to contain the Bears’ one-two punch, and they hardly used their backs in the passing game. Robinson is a much more talented back than either of those two, and he also led the Falcons in catches and receiving yardage in Week 1. If the linebackers play anything like they did in Week 1, it’s going to be another very, very long day for the Panthers defense. Za’Darius Smith vs Monroe Freeling Outside of a sack given up to Montez Sweat in the first quarter, Monroe Freeling held up pretty well in his debut at right tackle. He’ll get tested again in Week 2. Za’Darius Smith is operating on a snap count as he works his way back from his midseason retirement last season. In limited snaps against the Steelers, he registered both of the Falcons’ two sacks. He’ll probably be deployed as a pass rush specialist again against the Panthers, and it’s vital that Freeling hold up to let Bryce Young cook. Tetairoa McMillan vs AJ Terrell AJ Terrell has long been thought of as one of the better corners in the NFL, but he certainly didn’t look it in Week 1. He was called for a couple of pass interference penalties and should have been called for a third on a deep ball to DK Metcalf. He struggled to keep up with both Metcalf and Michael Pittman. McMillan has a chance to catch him while he’s struggling, and there will be opportunities to pick up some big plays if Terrell maintains his Week 1 form. The Falcons have very good safeties, but there should be room for the receivers to win on the outside. Bryce Young vs Mercedes-Benz Stadium Young conquered his Week 1 matchup against Week 1 by having one of the best games of his career in general, and definitely the best game he’s ever had to open a season. Now he’s playing in a stadium that has been home to his best two games in each of the last two seasons. Young closed the 2024 season by accounting for five touchdowns in a 44-38 win to knock the Falcons out of the playoffs. In 2025, Young threw for 448 yards and three touchdowns in another overtime win. Can he make it three straight dominant performances in the ATL?
author: Jonathan DeLong

title: Chicago Bears Week 2 Flashbacks: Grossman, Amukamara, Piñeiro, and more!
summary: Climb aboard the Gridiron Time Machine as we rev the engines up for another season-long trip down memory lane! 1.) 2006, Bears vs. Lions: Rex Grossman has a career day as Chicago rolls. Coming off a 26–0 shutout of Brett Favre and the Packers in Green Bay, the Bears returned to Soldier Field in Week […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - SEPTEMBER 15: Pat O'Donnell #19 holds as Eddy Pineiro #15 of the Chicago Bears celebrate a 40 yard field goal in the second quarter against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on September 15, 2019 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Matthew Stockman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Climb aboard the Gridiron Time Machine as we rev the engines up for another season-long trip down memory lane! 1.) 2006, Bears vs. Lions: Rex Grossman has a career day as Chicago rolls. Coming off a 26–0 shutout of Brett Favre and the Packers in Green Bay, the Bears returned to Soldier Field in Week 2 of the 2006 season looking to prove their dominant opener was no fluke. Rex Grossman made sure of that. After spending much of his first three NFL seasons battling injuries, and even hearing some boos during the preseason, Grossman put together what was easily the best performance of his young career. He completed 20 of 27 passes for 289 yards, four touchdowns and no interceptions, good for a ridiculous 148.0 passer rating. Both his passing yardage and touchdown total were career highs at the time. Chicago wasted almost no time taking control. On Detroit’s opening possession, Tank Johnson sacked Jon Kitna and knocked the ball loose, allowing Brian Urlacher to recover at the Lions’ three-yard line. Grossman immediately cashed in, finding tight end John Gilmore for a touchdown. The defense forced another fumble on Detroit’s next possession, this time with Alex Brown stripping Kevin Jones and recovering it himself. Robbie Gould turned that takeaway into a field goal, and early in the second quarter Grossman found Bernard Berrian for a 41-yard touchdown to put Chicago ahead 17–0. Grossman tossed two touchdowns to Gilmore, while Berrian finished with 89 receiving yards and Desmond Clark added 85 yards and a score. On the other side of the ball, things weren’t any easier for Detroit. The Bears recovered three Lions fumbles, held them to 245 total yards and sacked Kitna six times. The 34–7 win moved Chicago to 2–0 while giving the Bears a staggering 60–7 scoring advantage through the first two games of the season. As it turned out, that start was a pretty good indication of what was coming. The Bears went 13–3, won the NFC North, defeated Seattle and New Orleans in the playoffs, and advanced to Super Bowl XLI. And for at least one afternoon at Soldier Field, the phrase “ Good Rex ” didn’t even begin to cover it. 2.) 2018, Bears vs. Seahawks: The defense finishes the job and gives Matt Nagy his first win. The Matt Nagy era couldn’t have started in much more painful fashion. One week earlier, the Bears had taken a 20–0 lead at Lambeau Field, only to watch Aaron Rodgers lead the Packers all the way back for a crushing 24–23 victory. So when the Bears returned home for a Monday Night Football matchup against Russell Wilson and the Seattle Seahawks, the message was pretty simple: Finish. Chicago opened the game with a 96-yard touchdown drive capped by Mitchell Trubisky’s shovel pass to Trey Burton, but the offense struggled to find much consistency afterward. Fortunately, the Bears defense didn’t need much help. Led by their newly acquired superstar Khalil Mack, Chicago harassed Wilson all night, ultimately sacking him six times. Even after Trubisky threw interceptions on consecutive second-quarter possessions, the defense answered both mistakes by immediately forcing Seattle three-and-outs. Trubisky finally gave the Bears some breathing room early in the fourth quarter when he connected with rookie Anthony Miller for a 10-yard touchdown, making it 17–3. Seattle answered with a touchdown to pull within seven. Then Prince Amukamara made the play of the night. With 6:37 remaining, Amukamara recognized the Seahawks’ formation, jumped a pass intended for Rashaad Penny and took the interception 49 yards to the house. It was Amukamara’s first interception since 2015 and the first pick-six of his NFL career. 20 days till the #NFLdraft Today’s countdown feature is Prince Amukamara, who was solid for the ‘18 #Bears . 66 TOT, 12 PD, 3 INT, 2 FF, 1 INT He was drafted ‘11 by the NYG in the 1st round. 🔥 pic.twitter.com/zPyCaqVJ5s — Just Another Year Chicago: Bears (@JAYChi_Bears) April 5, 2024 One possession later, Danny Trevathan blitzed Wilson, recorded his second sack of the night and forced a fumble that Leonard Floyd recovered. Trevathan finished with a team-high eight tackles, two sacks, two quarterback hits and the forced fumble, earning NFC Defensive Player of the Week honors. Seattle managed one last touchdown with 14 seconds remaining, but Anthony Miller recovered the ensuing onside kick to seal a 24–17 Bears win. More importantly, it gave Nagy his first regular-season victory as an NFL head coach. After spending the previous week hearing about the collapse at Lambeau, the Bears defense finished one. It wouldn’t be the last time that unit carried them in 2018. 3.) 2019, Bears @ Broncos: Fourth-and-15, one second left, and “Steady Eddy” After the excitement of a 12–4 division championship season in 2018, the Bears’ 2019 campaign began with a thud. Chicago managed just three points in a season-opening loss to Green Bay, and things weren’t looking much better offensively a week later in Denver. Eddy Piñeiro provided almost all of Chicago’s early scoring, connecting from 40 and 52 yards to give the Bears a 6–3 halftime lead. The offense had now gone six quarters without scoring a touchdown. That drought finally ended late in the third quarter when David Montgomery punched the ball across the goal line from one yard out, finishing an 80-yard drive in which the Bears ran the ball on all nine plays. Chicago suddenly had a 13–3 lead and appeared to have the game under control. It didn’t last. Denver chipped away with a field goal before Joe Flacco led the Broncos on one final drive. With 31 seconds remaining, he found Emmanuel Sanders for a seven-yard touchdown. After each team traded penalties, Broncos coach, and former Bears defensive coordinator, Vic Fangio elected to go for two. Flacco found Sanders again. Denver 14, Chicago 13. After an offseason dominated by Chicago’s very public search for a kicker following the infamous end to the 2018 season, it looked as though the Bears might not even get Piñeiro a chance. Then came fourth-and-15. September 15th, 2019: The Bears beat the Broncos in a wild finish in Denver #DaBears pic.twitter.com/xfWTNfZ5Nr — Back Then Football (@BackThenFB) September 16, 2026 With nine seconds remaining and Chicago at its own 40, Mitchell Trubisky stepped up in the pocket and found Allen Robinson II over the middle for 25 yards. Robinson went down at the Denver 35 and the Bears managed to call their final timeout. One second remained. Out came Piñeiro. From 53 yards away, he drilled it. Bears win, 16–14. Piñeiro finished the afternoon a perfect 3-for-3 on field goals, hitting from 40, 52 and 53 yards. His game-winner was the longest by a Bears kicker since Paul Edinger hit from 54 yards to beat Detroit in the 2000 season finale. Piñeiro was rewarded a few days later by being named NFC Special Teams Player of the Week. Considering everything that had happened at the kicker position over the previous nine months, you couldn’t have scripted it much better. For one glorious September afternoon in Denver, there was no kicking controversy, and no double doink. There was just Steady Eddy. Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs .

summary: Sure, it’s only Week 2, but this is a pretty big game on Sunday between the Chicago Bears and the Minnesota Vikings. full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 08: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears runs the ball during an NFL football game against the Minnesota Vikings at Solider Field on September 8, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois . (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sure, it’s only Week 2, but this is a pretty big game on Sunday between the Chicago Bears and the Minnesota Vikings. The Bears are one of the most buzzed-about teams after dropping 59 on the Carolina Panthers, while the Vikings came back and scored the final 29 points of the game in their 39-22 win over the Green Bay Packers. And besides, division games are always played with a little more emotion. The Bears and Vikings split last season, but over the last 5 years, Chicago has only two wins. Those two wins were low-scoring games, 12-10 (2023) and 19-17 (2025), but I think we’ll see some points on Sunday. Our partners at FanDuel Sportsbook have the game’s over/under at 47.5, and you can put me down for the over. The Vikings allowed the Packers to rack up 419 yards last week, and Green Bay’s offense was undermanned due to injury and suspension. The Bears’ offense is healthy across the board, and they put up 552 yards on the road in Carolina. Minnesota’s defense is better than it looked last week, but they’re going to be playing a better offense. Caleb Williams and company should be able to move the ball in Soldier Field, which is why I think the Bears win and why I think they cover FanDuels’ spread (Bears -4.5), so let’s call it 34 to 27, good guys. You can get Bill Zimmerman’s three props to play here , but here’s one that I really like. The Bears were already going to run the ball, and with rain likely on Sunday, you may see them really lean on Darnell Wright and Jonah Jackson to clear some room for D’Andre Swift, who seems to have leveled up this year. So give me Swift to score two touchdowns at +420.

title: Bears-Vikings Franchise Connections
summary: The Chicago Bears will look to continue their winning ways and improve to 2-0 on Sunday, when they take on the Minnesota Vikings in Chicago’s home opener at Soldier Field. In an NFC North division where all four teams figure to compete for a playoff spot, every win you can acquire within the division is […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - AUGUST 29: Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears warms up prior to the Week 3 preseason game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on August 29, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears will look to continue their winning ways and improve to 2-0 on Sunday, when they take on the Minnesota Vikings in Chicago’s home opener at Soldier Field. In an NFC North division where all four teams figure to compete for a playoff spot, every win you can acquire within the division is a crucial one. Each week going forward, we’re going to highlight some of the connections that the Bears’ coaching staff and roster each have with the Vikings, as well as Minnesota’s ties to Chicago. As one could expect between two divisional foes, there’s certainly some overlap between the two organizations. Heading into Week 2, the Bears have three players from their 53-man roster who have previously played on the Vikings. The most notable of the three is Case Keenum, who started 14 games at quarterback for the Vikings in 2017. Minnesota went 11-3 with him as their starter and advanced to the NFC Championship Game. To Vikings fans, he’ll forever be remembered as the quarterback who hit Stefon Diggs for that game-winning touchdown against the Saints, dubbed as the “Minneapolis Miracle”. Safety Xavier Woods, who missed Week 1 for the Bears but is anticipated to return, also spent a season with the Vikings. He spent 2021 with Minnesota, starting in all 17 games. He finished the season with 108 tackles, three interceptions, ten pass deflections, and two forced fumbles. That year, Woods ranked No. 33 in the NFL with a 76.7 PFN SAF Impact Score , generally ranking him as an average starter at the position. The two current Bears players to be drafted by the Vikings are center Garrett Bradbury, who was a first-round selection by Minnesota in 2019, and defensive lineman James Lynch, who was a fourth-round pick in 2020. Bradbury spent six seasons with the team as its starting center, having started in all 88 games he played there. Though the Vikings declined his fifth-year option in 2022, they signed Bradbury to a three-year, $15.7 million extension in 2023. He was released before his third and final year of the contract played out. Lynch spent four seasons in Minnesota, appearing in 37 games and starting in three. He missed the entire 2023 season due to a torn ACL, but he served as part of the Vikings’ defensive line rotation, combining for 53 tackles and 2.0 sacks in the games he played. If we want to get technical, practice squad defensive end Marcus Davenport also has ties to the Vikings, having spent his 2023 season with them. He signed a one-year, $13 million deal but only appeared in four games due to injury. The only player currently on the Vikings who has played for the Bears is long snapper Andrew DePaola. He played in 16 games for Chicago in 2017, when Patrick Scales tore his ACL in the preseason of that year. Once Scales returned to the team, DePaola had brief stints with the Raiders and Panthers before signing with Minnesota in 2020. There, he grew into one of the best long snappers in the NFL. He is a four-time All-Pro and a three-time Pro Bowler across his seven seasons with the Vikings. The most notable behind-the-scenes overlap between the Bears and Vikings is Ryan Pace, who currently serves as a football advisor for Minnesota but is best known for his seven seasons as Chicago’s general manager from 2015 to 2021. During that span, the Bears went 48-65 under Pace, making the playoffs twice and winning the NFC North in 2018. Though that 2018 team fielded an incredible defense, the Bears were unable to make it past the Wild Card Round. The less said about that game, the better. Well, I suppose there’s also Chicago team president Kevin Warren, who spent over a decade in the Vikings’ front office, but most Bears fans are tired of hearing about him.

title: Bears-Vikings: Keys to a Chicago victory
summary: The Chicago Bears face the difficult task of following up on their 59-point season debut against one of the league’s most notorious defensive coordinators. If you haven’t heard by now, this Sunday is set to be a chess match between Ben Johnson and Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores. The home crowd inside Soldier Field […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears calls a play from the line of scrimmage during the game against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears face the difficult task of following up on their 59-point season debut against one of the league’s most notorious defensive coordinators. If you haven’t heard by now, this Sunday is set to be a chess match between Ben Johnson and Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores. The home crowd inside Soldier Field is going to be rocking. What will it take for the Bears to keep their offense humming, slow down Carson Wentz and Co. and keep Brian Flores’s unit at bay? Our team of writers weighs in. Sam: Be quick at the line of scrimmage and trust your film study. I know Ben Johnson is going to scheme to neutralize the Vikings’ blitz with short patterns, 13 personnel to disguise who stays to block and who leaks and, of course, the run game. Being quick to the line of scrimmage will keep the defense on its back foot, they like to move around and shift and if you’re snapping the ball with time left on the play clock, they are catching up. Defense, get after Carson Wentz and stay disciplined. He’ll eventually throw one your way. Gary: Seems redundant to say since it’s essentially the Bears’ basic offensive philosophy, but establishing the run game will take a lot of the heat off passing situations and make our already potent play-action passing even more potent. I expect a good dose of 13 personnel in both running and passing situations to out-beef the Vikings’ defense. We’ll most likely see a downtick in explosives but a steadier approach at staying ahead of the chains. Lester: Running the ball, which is a huge part of their identity, will help slow the blitz and keep the Vikings honest. I think some max protect with two-man patterns could give Caleb 2 reads before taking off, but he’ll also need to be cognizant of a check release from a tight end or back. If the pass pro holds up, we might see an over route hit for one of the Bears’ speedy receivers. On defense, stop the run and make whoever is playing QB beat you. Ryan: I am assuming it is going to be Carson Wentz under center for the Vikings. If so, the Bears need to get pressure. In the past, Wentz has been known to panic with any sort of pressure in his face. “Happy feet” has been used to describe him. If the Bears are unable to get pressure, a veteran like Wentz could pick our suspect defense apart. On offense, running the ball will be key in order to prevent the Vikings pinning their ears back and blitzing their tails off at every opportunity. T.J.: Make Flores and the Vikings defense respect the plethora of offensive weapons at Caleb Williams and Ben Johnson’s disposal. If they can make the Minnesota pass rush and blitz slow a step (or stop altogether) that should give the edge to the Bears. Meanwhile, the Chicago defense needs to keep Justin Jefferson and company out of the end zone. We know they’re not likely to be at the top of the league, but let’s see them limit the bleeding to field goals instead of touchdowns in week 2. Josh: The offense needs to pick up where it left off and just continue to use the multitude of weapons they’ve assembled. On defense, they have to get better play out of the secondary. The line is simply not able to get home, so that means the defensive backs have to get burned less to suppress the score and mitigate Jefferson. What are your keys for a Bears’ victory Sunday?

title: Vikings at Bears: 3 Props to Play
summary: The Chicago Bears crushed the Carolina Panthers 59-37 to open the season, and that offensive outburst certainly helped with some success on the props in week one. Last week, we went 2-1 on props. Caleb Williams went over on passing yards and D’Andre Swift went over on rushing yards. Unfortunately, we hung an L with […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after scoring a touchdown with D'Andre Swift #4 during the second half of the game against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears crushed the Carolina Panthers 59-37 to open the season, and that offensive outburst certainly helped with some success on the props in week one. Last week, we went 2-1 on props. Caleb Williams went over on passing yards and D’Andre Swift went over on rushing yards. Unfortunately, we hung an L with Colston Loveland over on his receiving props. That was shocking. This week, the Bears head back to Chicago and welcome in the Minnesota Vikings, and more notably, Brian Flores’ defense. Will Flores be able to slow down Ben Johnson’s offense? How will this chess match play out? Here are the three props to play this week in the Bears- Vikings matchup. As always, odds are courtesy of FanDuel. Colston Loveland OVER 46.5 Receiving Yards -114 Oh, you know we are going back to the well. After the world thought Loveland was going to have a monster game against the Panthers to open the season, Loveland ended up with a giant goose egg on only two targets. Do we really think Ben Johnson is going to have one of his favorite toys be nonexistent for two games in a row? I think the Bears make an effort to get Loveland involved, and probably try to work it to him early in the game. I think he definitely goes over in this one, and we see him consistently more involved in the offense moving forward. Justin Jefferson OVER 77.5 Receiving Yards -114 We usually only do Bears players, but sometimes you see something on the other side that’s just worth considering. We all love the Bears offense, but I think most of us can look at the Bears defense and understand that it has plenty of holes. Jalen Coker had 138 yards receiving last week. Tetairoa McMillan had 75 yards as well. The Panthers’ top two receivers tallied 213 yards mostly against Tyrique Stevenson and Jaylon Johnson. How are those two possibly stopping Justin Jefferson? Whether it’s Carson Wentz or Kyler Murray, I don’t think it matters. I think Jefferson beats the Bears secondary for at least one, probably two explosive plays and tops 100 yards receiving for the game. D’Andre Swift OVER 60.5 Rushing Yards -114 Brian Flores’ defenses always cause problems, especially in the passing game, but they do allow yards in the running game. Last year the Vikings ranked 21st in yards allowed on the ground, and while they didn’t give up much to the Green Bay Packers in week one, the Packers were without Josh Jacobs and largely ran a bunch of RB3s as starters. Swift’s number last week was 63.5, and he smashed the over, so this week his number actually drops three yards, so that’s a wager I will happily come back to and place on Swift to have another strong game. I’m sure it won’t be quite as explosive as it was in week one, but I do think he can comfortably go over 60 yards and push somewhere around 80 to 90 yards on the ground, as the Bears’ offensive line has another strong performance opening holes for Swift.

Mandatory Credit: John Jones-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Chicago Bears have a 16-man practice squad, but the list will be fluid, and we’ll update it throughout the year. UPDATE (9/18): The Bears signed safety Keidron Smith to the practice squad and placed safety Anthony Johnson Jr. on the practice squad injured list. Caden Barnett, OG Kyle Hergel, iOL Christian Jones, OT Salvon Ahmed, RB Zavier Scott, RB Scotty Miller, WR Kaden Davis, WR J.P. Richardson, WR Stephen Carlson, TE Qadir Ismail, TE Miller Moss, QB Wayne Matthews III, LB Buddy Johnson, LB Keidron Smith, S Deantre Prince, CB Marcus Davenport, DE Practice squad injured: Anthony Johnson Jr. (S) Here are the qualifications for practice squad eligibility and some rules to remember. A 17th player is permitted as long as he qualifies for the NFL’s International Pathway Program. Players with no accrued seasons (rookies) and those with fewer than nine regular-season games in their lone accrued season. A maximum of ten players are allowed who have earned no more than two accrued seasons. Up to six players with unlimited accrued seasons are permitted on the practice squad. However, the number of players in the last two categories cannot exceed 10 total players. Teams can elevate up to two practice squad players for each game, but they can still only have 48 players active on game day. After the game, the elevated player(s) will revert to the practice squad. A player can be elevated up to three times, but if he’s needed after that, the team would be required to sign him to the 53-man active roster. Players on practice squads are free agents who can be signed to another team’s active roster. A player’s current club can’t block him from leaving; they can only make a counteroffer to keep him. Ultimately, it’s the player’s decision. If a player is signed away, his new team must keep him on its 53-man roster for three weeks, but if he’s released, he’ll revert to his previous team. Players signed to another active roster are also guaranteed three weeks’ salary. A practice squad player can’t sign with his team’s upcoming opponent unless he does so six days before the upcoming game or ten days prior if his team is on its bye week.

title: Vikings at Bears Q&A: Ben Johnson vs Brian Flores
summary: Hey, I have a little fact for you that you probably hadn’t heard. It really hasn’t been talked about locally in Chicago media, and I haven’t heard it mentioned at all on the national shows. I would have thought it would have gotten more attention, but it’s mostly flown under the radar. In week one, […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 30: Defensive coordinator Brian Flores of Minnesota Vikings looks on against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on November 30, 2025 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hey, I have a little fact for you that you probably hadn’t heard. It really hasn’t been talked about locally in Chicago media, and I haven’t heard it mentioned at all on the national shows. I would have thought it would have gotten more attention, but it’s mostly flown under the radar. In week one, the Chicago Bears scored 59 points! The high-powered offensive attack of the Chicago Bears (I can’t believe I just wrote that) returns to Chicago this week and welcomes in the Minnesota Vikings. The head coach of the Vikings might be Kevin O’Connell, but this matchup is coming down to Ben Johnson vs. Brian Flores. How will the Vikings’ defensive coordinator try to slow down Ben Johnson’s offense? To get that answer, and answers to many other questions surrounding the Vikings, we sat down with Christopher Gates from SB Nation’s Vikings site, The Daily Norseman, to get those answers. Check out our conversation. 1. Let’s start with a question about last week. The Green Bay Packers’ fans are crying (and crying hard) about the officiating in the game. How much do you think officiating played into the Vikings’ win, and what do you think was the biggest reason for the comeback? To be perfectly clear, there is nothing more satisfying than listening to Green Bay fans complaining about officiating. It’s hard to adjust after you’ve gotten pretty much every single call for the better part of four decades, I guess. But while there was one drive where the Vikings may have gotten a couple of calls that went their way and caused a couple of third-down stops by the Green Bay defense to get negated, there were some calls that were missed as well. Aaron Jones had a 56-yard run wiped out because someone, apparently, tapped him on the shoulder or something; Carson Wentz got his facemask grabbed on one play, Justin Jefferson got his grabbed on another. On the other hand, the officials didn’t make Matt Lafleur take a field goal off the board that would have put the Packers ahead by eight points late in the third quarter, nor did they cause the Packers’ offensive line to just basically stop blocking for pretty much the entirety of the fourth quarter. As far as why the comeback happened, Brian Flores just kept his foot on the gas and found the right weak spots up front to exploit. That led to a couple of big turnovers and two very short fields that the Vikings were able to cash in on, and a 22-10 deficit turned into a 39-22 victory in relatively short order. 2. I know the starting QB in this game is currently up in the air; I assume it’s going to be Carson Wentz. But beyond that, what do you make of the QB situation in Minnesota? Can Kyler Murray make a positive impact this season? Has JJ McCarthy played his last game in Minnesota? I’ve never been particularly enamored with Murray, to be honest. I know there was a lot of hype surrounding him from certain outlets online going into the season, but I’ve just never been terribly impressed with him. I understand that he’s a former #1 overall draft pick, but he’s had significant leg injuries in recent years, and that’s never a good thing for someone whose game relies as much on mobility as his does. Maybe I’ll be proven wrong about him if he can make it through more than one quarter of football in a Vikings uniform, but I’m not expecting a Sam Darnold-esque renaissance from him or anything, even if he does. Wentz is reliable enough as long as the Vikings can keep him upright. He’s not going to be spectacular, but he’s not necessarily going to kill you offensively either, I don’t think. I’d be shocked if he wasn’t the starter on Sunday, and with that being the case, the Vikings are going to have to try to lean more on a running game that’s now short-handed with Jordan Mason going on IR on Wednesday. As far as McCarthy… .well, I think I’m close to being the last McCarthy believer on the planet. He’s had injuries and hasn’t been spectacular in his time on the field, but I also don’t know how great the Vikings’ plan for developing him has been. He was expected to step in as, essentially, a rookie and run Kevin O’Connell’s offense like a ten-year vet, but towards the end of the year in 2025, when the Vikings simplified things offensively a bit, he did look significantly better. As of now, McCarthy is the only quarterback on the roster who’s under contract beyond this season, and given the injury history that both Murray and Wentz have, we’re likely going to see him at some point this season, so we may get some more answers on him yet. 3. Bears fans know that a Brian Flores defense is always going to present a challenge, but I know the Vikings had some notable departures this offseason, led by Jonathan Greenard. Will the Vikings defense be as strong as it’s been, or could it take a step back this year? I think the Vikings’ defense is going to continue to be fine, and that’s a testament to what Flores does as far as adapting his scheme to his players. Greenard is gone, but that’s finally opened the door for Dallas Turner to be a full-time starter. Turner took a step toward that last year with Greenard being hurt a bit, but now he’s officially the guy across from Andrew Van Ginkel on the outside, and he’s showing signs of being the guy the Vikings traded up for in 2024. He’s also getting the most out of guys like Levi Drake Rodriguez and Jalen Redmond, who are giving the Vikings’ linebackers the opportunity to make plays and get after quarterbacks the way Flores wants them to. As long as Flores is the Vikings’ defensive coordinator, this defense is going to be dangerous. Having said that, I know that Ben Johnson’s offenses have been a lot more successful against Flores-led defenses than a lot of others during his time in Minnesota. I don’t know if Johnson has all of the answers, but he seems to have a lot more of the answers than most coaches and offensive coordinators seem to have. There’s a reason that’s the matchup everyone is keeping an eye on this Sunday. 4. The Bears defense is, well, let’s just say it’s not the strength of the team. What would be Dennis Allen’s best strategy to attack this Vikings offense? The strategy, as hard as it might be to try to pull off, is to try to take away Justin Jefferson and force Wentz (or Murray, if the Vikings decide to run him out there) to find anyone else to beat you. Jefferson had eight catches for 92 yards and two scores against the Packers last Sunday. The Vikings’ #2 and #3 receivers, Jordan Addison and Jauan Jennings, combined for the same number of catches as you and I combined for. (That would be zero, if you’re scoring at home.) Jefferson is going to get his at some point, in all likelihood, but if you can make the Vikings’ offense look somewhere else first, it will make things a lot more difficult. The Vikings’ offense still relies a lot on longer-developing routes, so if the Bears want to try to bring the heat and try to force Wentz to get rid of the ball more quickly, that could work to their advantage as well. 5. How do you think this one plays out? Want to take a stab at the final score? Well, I don’t think the Bears are going to put up 59 again in this one. I don’t think the Vikings are going to put up 37, either. While I’d love to pick the Vikings to get a seventh consecutive win at Soldier Field… .and that’s still incredibly strange to write… until this offense shows any sort of ability to move the ball consistently, I can’t, in good conscience, pick them to win this game against a team that looks to be firing on all cylinders the way the Bears are right now. I think it’s going to be a close game, but I’ll take the home team in this one by a final score of 27-23.
