title: Lions defense fails to deliver on Kelvin Sheppard’s offseason commitments
summary: The Detroit Lions could not get out of their own way in an embarrassing 41-31 loss to christen the Buffalo Bills’ new Highmark Stadium. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard is very direct with his players and staff when leading his defense. I think he would appreciate fair and respectful directness in return. Dan Campbell did not […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard speaks before OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, June 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions could not get out of their own way in an embarrassing 41-31 loss to christen the Buffalo Bills’ new Highmark Stadium. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard is very direct with his players and staff when leading his defense. I think he would appreciate fair and respectful directness in return. Dan Campbell did not mince words at half time. "The little shit is killing us right now." – Dan Campbell — Pride of Detroit (@PrideOfDetroit) September 18, 2026 The presnap penalties are infuriating for all head coaches. But what is most infuriating to me about Thursday night’s performance was that the Lions defense failed miserably in three distinct areas of the game that second-year defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard put an emphasis on fixing this off season. Explosive plays Run defense Third-and-long situations Three commitments from Sheppard. Three failures against the Bills. 1. Explosive plays: “unacceptable” The first commitment for correction this off season was to reduce the high number of explosive plays the defense gave up in 2025. “It’s the first thing we started self-scout with, and there was overlap because you go to then doing a self-scout and we’re gonna watch it again,” Sheppard said . “And when the players come in Phase Two, Phase Three, guess what? I got 105 plays, and we gonna watch them again, and when we get to training camp and we need general reminders and subtle reminders of what to do in certain situations, we gonna watch them again.” Well, explosive plays were an issue as the Bills generated eleven explosives to the Lions five. Below is a 25-yard pass in the first quarter that simply cannot happen. It appears Sheppard calls a Cover 3 zone, but disguises with split safeties presnap. Thomas Harper, the safety at the top of the screen, sits on the snap and is responsible for the outside-1 wide receiver in-break. We can see this with cornerback Rock Ya-Sin points this communication at the break for Harper. Credit to the Bills, they are in a good concept to attack Cover 3 with tight end Dalton Kincaid attacking the seam. One issue that makes this completion easier for quarterback Josh Allen is that the hook zone player in that seam is defensive end DJ Wonnum while linebacker Jack Campbell replaces with the rush. As a result, Wonnum cannot get enough depth in his drop to make that seam through a tighter window. Now, we do not know Harper’s rules and keys for the play, or whether he should have subtle awareness that the scheme called for Wonnum to drop and play the seam tighter before breaking into his responsibility. But these subtleties may be the difference between having a young Thomas Harper compared to Brian Branch. In the meantime, these are problems the Lions need to clean up on the back end. Dan Campbell: "We've got to clean up a lot of things on defense right now, particularly in the back end." — Jeremy Reisman (@DetroitOnLion) September 18, 2026 2. Run defense: “it starts there” “We have to get back to playing elite run defense here because to me it starts there,” Sheppard said . “So, guys are going to go in and they’ve already been told we will get back to playing elite run defense here. And it starts with the front seven. It starts when the pads come on and it starts there.” This is the area of the game that I was most disappointed in. The Lions run a stunt up front in one of their new looks implemented this offseason . A critical element of this is that while the stunts wipe blocks and change gaps for the offensive line, linebackers must fill and replace the gaps that are moved. Here, we see a stunt left at the snap, with defensive end Aiden Hutchinson angling inside, leaving linebacker Jack Campbell to fill the gap behind him. Again, we don’t know Jack Campbell’s responsibility in this situation per se, but here he gets sealed by the tight end as cornerback D.J. Reed is tight to the line of scrimmage responsible for spill. Should Jack Campbell have attacked the outside shoulder of the tight end to play the gap differently and force the spill? Or did nickel safety Christian Izien fail to play the inside shoulder of his blocker to force the spill? These issues are unacceptable. 3. Third-and-long: “the fixes are simple” Lastly, the Lions need to play better situational football. Blown coverages on third-and-long is the fastest way to lose to an MVP-caliber quarterback. “We were outstanding on third down, but it was actually third-and-10 plus is like, why are we in the bottom tier in the league in that category?” Sheppard said . “Why aren’t we executing? And then you turn on the tape and it’s very eye-opening to what’s happening. It sounds easy, but it is. It’s simple solutions, man.” Simple solutions. The breakdown here is somewhere between safety Avonte Maddox and nickel cornerback Roger McCreary. With trips receivers to the field side, Maddox breaks on the wide receiver-3 when the route breaks inside. McCreary also sits as the wide reciever-2 in the trips set continues with the vertical route. At the end of the game, three off season commitments to fix three glaring issues from the end of the 2025 season failed to take shape. Is there hope for the Lions defense? The solutions are simple.
author: Anthony Balaj

title: The Lions’ defensive problems are growing out of control
summary: Congratulations to the Buffalo Bills and all their fans on what had to have been a magical night. Brand new stadium was rocking, high-scoring offense was undeniable, you couldn’t have storyboarded a more euphoric Thursday night without it coming off as far-fetched. Speaking of far-fetched, how about that defense from the Detroit Lions? Unbelievable, right? […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Tyleik Williams #91 of the Detroit Lions walks off the field after being defeated by the Buffalo Bills after the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images Congratulations to the Buffalo Bills and all their fans on what had to have been a magical night. Brand new stadium was rocking, high-scoring offense was undeniable, you couldn’t have storyboarded a more euphoric Thursday night without it coming off as far-fetched. Speaking of far-fetched, how about that defense from the Detroit Lions? Unbelievable, right? After a 2025 season of poor performance on third-and-long to go, you couldn’t have seen this coming. The pass rush was re-tooled, and the secondary was filled with guys they liked, but what if I told you it’s getting worse? Much worse. Last year’s opponent third-down conversion rate, 36.9%—which ranked ninth, pales in comparison to where the Lions are through two games—58.6%. At one point in the game, the Bills were 8-of-9 on third down, finishing the game 9-of-12 because they took a knee on their final drive. Remove that play and the Bills were converting third down at a 81.1% clip. Set aside their woes on third down, the Lions didn’t even force one of those on Buffalo’s opening drive that spanned 10 plays, 85 yards, and nearly six minutes of the opening stanza. Yikes. And I know, it’s a rather small sample size. It was a short week and they essentially played five quarters against New Orleans. Detroit’s shorthanded at safety with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph still on PUP, and D.J. Reed was playing through a foot injury; all the excuses are baked in for any hopeful fan. But it doesn’t matter what the situation is, it doesn’t matter who your opponent is, your defense cannot look like that, Kelvin Sheppard. It’s inexcusable. The 2024 season feels like it’s fading further and further into the rearview, but remember how banged up that defense was? Of course you do, it was all anyone could talk about. More defenders on injured reserve than you can field on a practice squad. Aaron Glenn drew the ire of many a fan on social media, but Detroit’s opponent third-down conversion rate over the course of that season? 32.5%, first in the NFL. The Lions finished fifth in DVOA on defense, a top-10 run defense and pass defense according to DVOA. With the cupboard as barren as it was, Glenn’s defense still produced results. The time for dismissing these problems as circumstance is over. Something has to give here. Brad Holmes has reimagined this secondary, to varying degrees of success, over four consecutive offseasons. For every Carlton Davis success story, there’s a Cam Sutton-sized reminder of a swing and a miss. Amik Robertson was a fruitful move in 2024, but the team’s top two draft picks from that year are either in Seattle or a healthy inactive on game day. That doesn’t mean Holmes shouldn’t be looking to improve this secondary as soon as before this trade deadline, but if you think Joey Porter Jr. or some other veteran is going to be a magical elixir for what’s going on with Detroit’s defense, you’re kidding yourself. No one player is coming in here to fix everything all at once. These are coaching problems, and coaching problems have to be coached out. And if we’re not laying all the blame at the feet of the guy buying the groceries—and I don’t think we should be—then the chef in charge of putting the meal together needs to accept his role in things. Miscommunication and missed assignments are plaguing this defense. Before this game got completely out of hand, Detroit forced Buffalo into a third-and-11 at the Detroit 43-yard line—essentially no man’s land. All the Lions have to do is keep the Bills short of the line to gain and they’ll either force a punt or a long field goal attempt. Instead, Avonte Maddox and Roger McCreary let Joshua Palmer slip past them, completely uncovered, for a 43-yard touchdown. Detroit is 1-1, and the season is far from over. The Lions have more than a week to regroup and recover before Glenn and the New York Jets come to Ford Field. There is still plenty of time to fix this. But fixing it starts with acknowledging what Thursday night made painfully clear: this isn’t just an injury or personnel problem. It isn’t just defensive philosophy or playcalling. The problems are pervasive. The Lions have a defensive problem, and at this point, Sheppard and his defensive staff have to be the ones to solve it.
author: Ryan Mathews

title: Detroit Lions grades: Defensive meltdown squanders outstanding Jared Goff night
summary: Let’s hand out some Detroit Lions positional grades for their 41-31 loss to the Buffalo Bills on Thursday night. It’s our Week 2 report card. Quarterback: A One of the major tragedies of Thursday night was that Jared Goff was on an absolute heater against the Bills. And this isn’t just box score scouting (327 […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Defensive Coordinator Kelvin Sheppard of the Detroit Lions coaches from the sidelines during an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let’s hand out some Detroit Lions positional grades for their 41-31 loss to the Buffalo Bills on Thursday night. It’s our Week 2 report card. Quarterback: A One of the major tragedies of Thursday night was that Jared Goff was on an absolute heater against the Bills. And this isn’t just box score scouting (327 yards, 4 TDs, 130.0 passer rating). All night, Goff did his best managing pressure in the pocket, throwing under duress, and threading the needle on several passes. His final touchdown pass to Amon-Ra St. Brown was legitimately jaw-dropping. A shame many had already, understandably, turned the television off. A dart from Goff to St. Brown 🙌 pic.twitter.com/f6mM6MG9KJ — Detroit Lions (@Lions) September 18, 2026 At the end of the day, Goff finished with a +6.7% completion percentage above expected while averaging 9.0 air yards per attempt. He did everything he could to make Thursday less embarrassing. Running back: B Jahmyr Gibbs had a tough night running the ball, but it’s hard to fault him when he was often getting hit before reaching the line of scrimmage. He often made the first guy miss, but the Bills were swarming him all night. That said, Gibbs was extremely effective as a receiver against Buffalo. Gibbs finished with six catches for 61 yards and a touchdown. It finally feels like that part of his game is expanding, and it pulled the Lions out of a lot of holes on Thursday night. Sione Vaki was mostly a non-factor, but he turned his two touches into 20 yards and was a better pass protector than last week. Tight ends: B Sam LaPorta continues to look more and more like himself, finishing this game with six catches, 52 yards, and a touchdown. Unfortunately, the rest of the tight end crew drags the position’s grade down. Brock Wright had a tough night, although he certainly wasn’t put in the most advantageous positions (one-on-one vs. Greg Rousseau? What are we doing here?). Wide receivers: A- I have no real complaints about the Lions’ receiving corps. Once the Lions made a concerted effort to get Amon-Ra St. Brown involved, he torched the Bills’ secondary. Jameson Williams caught a pair of 15+ yard gains. Even Isaac TeSlaa got on the stat sheet, finally, including a fourth-and-18 conversion. I’m sure the Lions would’ve liked to get these players even more involved than they were, but unfortunately, Jared Goff didn’t have time. That’s because… Offensive line: D … the offensive line was abysmal on Thursday night. In the run game, the Bills posted a ridiculous 45% stuffed rate—meaning nearly half of Detroit’s runs were stopped for 0 yards or less. In the pass game, the Lions allowed four sacks, 11 quarterback hits, and 22 pressures, per PFF. Backup right tackle Larry Borom was the worst offender, surrendering seven pressures. Detroit’s other backups (Ben Bartch, 4; Juice Scruggs, 2) didn’t fare a ton better. Defensive line: D While he may have lacked some discipline in the run game, Aidan Hutchinson was largely the only player who provided any sort of spark to the Lions’ defense. He was responsible for six of the Lions’ 24 pressures, one of the two sacks, and two of the eight quarterback hits. Outside of that, not much good was happening up front. Rushing lanes were massive for James Cook. There was no gap integrity when it came to keeping Josh Allen in the pocket. When anyone got close to Allen, they failed to make a play. The front is still the haven for most hope for this defense, as they still are producing a fair amount of pressure, but this was not their best day. Linebackers: F The Bills offense puts more stress on the linebackers than any other position, and Detroit was simply not up for the challenge. There were miscommunications in run defense (with multiple players playing single gaps), terrible discipline in zone coverages, and a ton of biting on play-action or misdirection plays. It’s easy to see this reflected in the box score, where the Bills put up 203 rushing yards, 5.6 yards per carry, and the Bills tight ends were responsible for nine catches, 100 yards, and two touchdowns. Secondary: F There were plenty of questions about this secondary going into the season, and yet they are failing to meet even those low expectations. The little bit of optimism came from the fact that they were entrusting veterans Chuck Clark and Avonte Maddox to hold down the safety spots with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph sidelined. These were assignment-sound, experienced players and expert communicators who would ensure there were no coverage busts. To say they failed their job on Thursday night would be a massive understatement. Detroit’s back end rarely seemed on the same page, and when they were, they weren’t making the plays anyways. They had a single pass defended all night. I also think the secondary was largely responsible for the step back in the run game, as well, as their run fits were not particularly clean either. D.J. Reed is doing alright, though. Special teams: C- Special teams was a non-factor in this game, as neither team was much interested in punting or kicking field goals. Detroit did give up a big punt return to Greg Dortch, though. Coaching: D I’ll start by saying that I’m still somewhat encouraged by Drew Petzing and the offense. I see well-designed plays, good route concepts, and a team that has been nearly perfect in the red zone through two weeks (7-of-9). I am extremely annoyed by his tendency to run the ball on second-and-long, and that got the Lions in trouble a couple of times on Thursday night, but—comparatively speaking—he’s doing fine. The defense is an absolute mess. The Lions can’t play zone coverage. They can’t play man coverage. They have trouble disguising coverages, and they can’t beat teams just playing teams straight up. This appears to be a very clear case of trying to do too much when the personnel just isn’t capable of it right now. On one hand, I like the audacity. This defense needed some shaking up and fresh ideas. But it feels like Kelvin Sheppard is throwing everything at this defense, and it’s clearly overwhelming them mentally. He needs to take a long look at the two weeks of tape, find something promising that this team does, and lean into that. Because it feels like they think they are much more dynamic as a defense than they actually are. September football is for making mistakes and fixing them. But the defense is making far more mental mistakes than is acceptable right now, so Detroit better use this mini-bye productively
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Detroit Lions Week 2 snap counts: Shakeup in secondary could be in the future
summary: The Detroit Lions fell to the Buffalo Bills in Week 2, falling behind early and running out of time to catch up in a high-scoring 41-31 game. On a short week, the Lions had a couple of injuries that cost them starting contributors, but make no mistake, they were clearly outmatched in this game. It’s […]
full_text: Buffalo Bills tight end Dalton Kincaid (86) makes a catch for a touchdown against Detroit Lions safety Thomas Harper (12) during the first half at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, NY, on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions fell to the Buffalo Bills in Week 2, falling behind early and running out of time to catch up in a high-scoring 41-31 game. On a short week, the Lions had a couple of injuries that cost them starting contributors, but make no mistake, they were clearly outmatched in this game. It’s still very early in the season, so they’ll have a chance to rebound and correct mistakes moving forward, but they’ll need to do some early-season self-scouting and address some obvious detriments. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can ascertain moving forward. Quarterback Jared Goff: 65 (100%) Josh Dobbs: Did Not Play Bills QB Josh Allen had an MVP-like performance in this game, so it’s easy to overlook that Goff played very well; if the Lions don’t make the mistakes they did in the first quarter, he showed the skills to lead this offense to points. Context matters, but Goff even outperformed Allen on the passing stat sheet, finishing the game with a 130.0 passer rating. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs: 54 (83%) Sione Vaki: 11 (17%) — 18 special teams snaps (62%) Jacob Saylors: 0 (0%) — 18 (62%) In Week 1, Gibbs played 57 snaps (74%) and touched the ball 34 times. Despite the heavy workload and short week of rest, he still managed a higher snap percentage in this game, though the Lions were probably smart to scale his touches back to 22. Vaki continues to get RB2 reps but is only slowly involved in the offense beyond blocking. Of his 11 snaps, he was on the field for nine passing plays, caught one pass for 13 yards, run-blocked on one snap, and carried the ball for 7 yards on his remaining snap. Wide receiver Jameson Williams: 63 (97%) Amon-Ra St. Brown: 62 (95%) Isaac TeSlaa: 49 (75%) Tay Martin: 0 (0%) — 18 (62%) Tom Kennedy: 0 (0%) — 9 (31%) Despite playing nearly the entire game, St. Brown didn’t see his first target until 6:17 remaining in the first half, but he caught fire after that, finishing with nine catches for 142 yards and two scores. Williams, who had similar time on the field, caught two of his four targets for 33 yards, while TeSlaa continues to be used mainly as a blocker, but also made two catches (26 yards). Martin and Kennedy continue to be used only on special teams, for now. Tight end Sam LaPorta: 64 (98%) Brock Wright: 17 (26%) — 12 (41%) Tyler Conklin: 4 (6%) — 7 (24%) Jackson Meeks: 1 (2%) — 14 (48%) LaPorta got a full workload, as expected, but the rest of the reserves saw their snaps scaled back from Week 1, as the Lions appeared to want to deploy more 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, and 3 WR sets). Offensive line LT Penei Sewell: 65 (100%) — 5 (17%) LG Ben Bartch: 65 (100%) — 5 (17%) C Juice Scruggs: 65 (100%) — 5 (17%) RG Tate Ratledge: 65 (100%) — 5 (17%) RT Larry Borom: 65 (100%) — 5 (17%) G/T Miles Frazier: 0 (0%) — 5 (17%) OT Devoin Cochran: 0 (0%) — 5 (17%) C Seth McLaughlin: Did Not Play RT Blake Miller: INJURED (Ruled OUT) LG Christian Mahogany: INJURED (Ruled OUT) With Miller and Mahogany out, the anticipated starting five played every offensive snap. Unfortunately, the replacements struggled, with early PFF stats showing Borom giving up seven pressures and Bartch giving up four—11 pressures from just two players on 46 passing plays is brutal. Interior defensive lin e 3T Alim McNeill: 66 (89%) — 6 (21%) DT Tyleik Williams: 47 (64%) — 6 (21%) 3T Skyler Gill-Howard: 24 (32%) — 6 (21%) DL Levi Onwuzurike: 22 (30%) 3T Mekhi Wingo: DNP (INACTIVE) McNeill continues to rep at a fever pitch rate, while a change in opponent (one that runs the ball more) results in Williams nearly doubling the snaps of the reserves. This is likely a truer representative look at what the interior defensive line’s snaps will look like on an average week. EDGE EDGE Aidan Hutchinson: 63 (85%) Big End Tyler Lacy: 36 (49%) Rush End DJ Wonnum: 27 (36%) — 6 (21%) Rush End Derrick Moore: 17 (23) Rush End Eric O’Neill: 0 (0%) — 17 (59%) Big End Ahmed Hassanein: DNP (INACTIVE) With the Lions running Base defense (four down linemen and three linebackers) on about half their snaps, we see a more balanced snap distribution between the Big End (Lacy) and Rush End (Wonnum and Moore) positions. Linebacker MIKE Jack Campbell: 74 (100%) — 6 (21%) SAM Derrick Barnes: 74 (100%) — 8 (28%) WILL Devin White: 33 (45%) WILL Malcolm Rodriguez: 15 (20%) — 16 (55%) SAM Trevor Nowaske: 5 (7%) — 24 (83%) MIKE Joe Bachie: 0 (0%) — 14 (48%) MIKE Jimmy Rolder: DNP (INACTIVE) After a great Week 1, Barnes earned more snaps in Week 2, while White and Rodriguez continue to split WILL reps depending on the situation. Nowaske was once again deployed situationally (blitzer, spy), but he saw very limited reps on defense. Cornerback CB D.J. Reed: 71 (96%) CB Rock Ya-Sin: 70 (95%) — 1 (3%) NB/CB Roger McCreary: 18 (24%) — 9 (31%) CB Khalil Dorsey: 2 (3%) — 17 (59%) NB Keith Abney: DNP (INACTIVE) CB Ennis Rakestraw: DNP (INACTIVE) Ya-Sin exited briefly after an inadvertent kick to a sensitive area and was replaced by Dorsey on the outside. It was a bit surprising to see Dorsey find the field over McCreary, but McCreary was deployed exclusively in the slot, splitting time with Christian Izien, as the defensive back reacclimates back from injury. Safet y S Chuck Clark: 64 (86%) — 6 (21%) S Thomas Harper: 33 (45%) — 11 (38%) S Avonte Maddox: 27 (36%) — INJURED NB/S Christian Izien: 26 (35%) — 11 (38%) The Lions looked like they planned to continue their three-safety rotation—using Maddox and Clark in Base, then swapping Clark for Harper in subpackages—but Maddox’s injury forced the secondary to lean on Clark and Harper to close out the game. Izien started in the slot, but his snaps were likely limited as he returns from injury. Moving forward, the Lions would probably prefer to increase Izien’s slot reps, but if Maddox ends up missing time, they may need Izien to fill in as the team’s third safety—and if they believe the veteran Clark needs limited reps, that could mean real playing time at safety, not just an emergency role. Regardless, the secondary as a whole could be in line for a shakeup moving forward. Too often (in both games), the secondary found themselves in trail coverage in man concepts or playing too soft in zones. The defensive game plan seems to need tweaking, but the players aren’t living up to their pre-season expectations either. Specialist s K Jake Bates: 10 (34%) P Jack Fox: 9 (31%) LS Hogan Hatten: 9 (31%) This group looked better than in Week 1, and Bates onside kick had potential, but the thing to watch here is if Hatten ends up on the injury report next week, as he was banged up making a tackle defending a return.
author: Erik Schlitt

title: Detroit Lions safety Avonte Maddox injury update: Dan Campbell ‘nervous’ about status
summary: In the midst of the Detroit Lions’ 41-31 butt-whipping at the hands of the Buffalo Bills, they also suffered an injury that they can ill-afford. Early in the second quarter, Avonte Maddox took a friendly-fire shot from teammate Chuck Clark, and eventually had to be carted off with what the Lions called a foot injury. […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Cornerback Avonte Maddox #29 of the Detroit Lions is helped off of the field after being injured during the first half of an NFL football game between the Detroit Lions and the Buffalo Billsat Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, New York, USA, on Thursday, September 17, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images In the midst of the Detroit Lions’ 41-31 butt-whipping at the hands of the Buffalo Bills, they also suffered an injury that they can ill-afford. Early in the second quarter, Avonte Maddox took a friendly-fire shot from teammate Chuck Clark, and eventually had to be carted off with what the Lions called a foot injury. While originally listed as questionable, he was downgraded to out to start the second half. After the game, Maddox was seen in the locker room in crutches. It’s important not to overreact to that, as crutches can sometimes be more precautionary than anything. However, Lions coach Dan Campbell was not optimistic about Maddox’s status, while also admitting there needs to be more testing to find out. “I don’t know. Maddox is pretty tough, so when he doesn’t come back, that makes me nervous,” Campbell said. “But I won’t know until tomorrow for sure.” Detroit is in a tough spot at the safety position. Both starters—Kerby Joseph (knee) and Brian Branch (Achilles)—started the season on the Physically Unable to Perform list and must miss at least another two games. However, both are eligible to return to practice now. And there appears to be optimism at least one of them could be ready relatively soon. But on the 53-man roster, outside of Maddox, the Lions only have two other pure safeties rostered: veteran Chuck Clark and Thomas Harper. Christian Izien is also an option to drop back to safety, but the Lions have recently shifted him into a significant role as the team’s primary nickel cornerback. If Maddox’s injury is serious, another option would be to bring up defensive back Nick Whiteside from the practice squad. While he has thrived mostly as an outside cornerback, he got some late looks at safety in training camp and performed moderately well. For now, let’s just hope for the best, because the last thing the Lions can afford right now is more issues in the secodnary.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: What hope is there in the Detroit Lions defense?
summary: If you were looking for a silver lining in the Detroit Lions’ defensive performance against the Buffalo Bills in their 41-31 loss on Thursday night, you’d have to squint pretty hard to see it. You may have to hallucinate, to be honest. The Bills racked up 446 yards of offense for an average of 6.5 […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills consoles Aidan Hutchinson #97 of the Detroit Lions after the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you were looking for a silver lining in the Detroit Lions’ defensive performance against the Buffalo Bills in their 41-31 loss on Thursday night, you’d have to squint pretty hard to see it. You may have to hallucinate, to be honest. The Bills racked up 446 yards of offense for an average of 6.5 yards per play. For reference, the best offense in the NFL last year averaged 6.2 yards. Josh Allen finished with a 121.4 passer rating, the Bills ran for 203 yards at 5.6 yards per carry, and they punted only twice—once after a dropped third-down conversion and another time after a second-down drop. In the end, the Bills posted an astronomical 0.44 EPA/play (highest of any game so far in 2026) and 59 percent success rate (second). Whatever the Bills wanted to do on Thursday night, they did. “We’ve got to clean up a lot of things on defense right now, particularly on the backend,” coach Dan Campbell said after the game. The understatement of the night. So where does Detroit go from here? Where is there any semblance of hope on defense after following up a disastrous second half against the Saints with an even more futile performance against the Bills? Lions coach Dan Campbell was asked what gives him optimism this can get turned around this early in the season. “I think this front—we’ve got some juice up front, man,” Campbell said. “I think we’ve got a mix of guys that can apply pressure that can stop the run and that relieves a lot of stress on your backend.” The Lions did apply a fair amount of pressure to Allen on Thursday night. They sacked Allen twice, tallied eight quarterback hits, and finished with a pressure percentage 34.2%—comfortably above the league average. But that hardly seemed to take any pressure off the back end, which was plagued by missed assignment, failed communications, and blown coverages. “We had a couple of busts—we had more than a couple of busts on the backend for touchdowns in the pass game that really hurt us,” Campbell said. “We had a couple of busts in the run game, too, our fits. We’re fitting the wrong gaps or not where we’re supposed to be. We’ve got two guys in one gap, and (James) Cook is busting these runs.” Campbell remains hopeful that time on task will help them play cleaner football. “The more those guys play together, the better they’ll get,” Campbell said. “The more that we really digest what we’re trying to do to opponents or what we feel like we need to do any given week, I think will help those guys, and their confidence will grow and we’ll get better.” Another reason Campbell has hope is that they can finally dig into correcting the film. Prior to Thursday, Campbell admitted the short week really prevented them from correcting their errors made against the Saints in Week 1. With another set of data points and a long weekend to digest and self-diagnose, they can really start the big adjustments. “Now we can really digest—okay, this is our two-game snapshot, this is what you are, this says what you are,” Campbell said. “And we can really deep-dive these players, what they do best, what they don’t do or need help in, and we’ll move on from that.” While there is undoubtedly some truth to the Lions’ defensive mistakes being internal and correctable, it is a eerily familiar refrain from the defensive meltdown at the end of last season. It may be early in the season with plenty of time to improve, but Detroit will need to be much more effective at fixing their mistakes than they were in 2025.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Top 5 Packers Comebacks of the 21st Century
summary: Discussions on the Green Bay Packers’ struggles to close out games have understandably resurfaced after the team’s gutting 39-22 loss to the Minnesota Vikings this week that resulted in a 22-10 blown lead in the second half. This has been a theme as of late after the Packers blew multiple leads last season, including one […]
full_text: (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images Discussions on the Green Bay Packers’ struggles to close out games have understandably resurfaced after the team’s gutting 39-22 loss to the Minnesota Vikings this week that resulted in a 22-10 blown lead in the second half. This has been a theme as of late after the Packers blew multiple leads last season, including one against the Bears in the playoffs. While there’s certainly a valid discussion to be had about the team’s issues, I am choosing to cope by remembering happier times when the team was on the other side of a comeback. So, let’s take a look at the top five comebacks from the Packers since the turn of the century and remember the highs we felt during these moments. 5. Packers vs New Orleans Saints – Sep 24, 2023 Deficit: 17 points Final Score: 18-17 Jordan Love’s first start at Lambeau Field was a rollercoaster. The Saints defense hadn’t allowed more than 20 points in ten consecutive games heading into this one, which meant a pretty hefty challenge for Love and the offense just three weeks into his first season as a starter. The defensive line carried the defense with four sacks, including three from Rashan Gary, one of which knocked QB Derek Carr out of the game. The Packers offense struggled early, partially due to poor offensive line play (evergreen sentence) and missing some key starters (WR Christian Watson, RB Aaron Jones, LT David Bakhtiari, and G Elgton Jenkins). The offense went scoreless through three quarters, leading to a 17-point deficit heading into the 4th. The Packers’ first touchdown of the day came with 7 minutes left in the game thanks to a Jordan Love scramble on 4th down followed by a successful 2 point conversion. After a three-and-out from the Saints, the Packers went down and scored a touchdown thanks to an incredible catch by Romeo Doubs, who raised his hands into a heart to show his QB some Love. They made the extra point and took an 18-17 lead over the Saints with under three minutes left. In typical fashion, Joe Berry’s defense let the Saints march down to the Packers’ 29-yard line before making a stop. It looked like the Packers were about to go down 20-18 with a minute left. However, the Saints kicker missed the 46-yard field goal wide right, giving the Packers the ball to kneel out the game in victory formation. It became the Packers’ largest 4th quarter comeback in team history and Jordan Love started his career at Lambeau 1-0. CINEMA! 4. Packers vs New York Jets – Sep 14, 2014 Deficit: 18 points Final Score: 31-24 Week 2, Jets, Geno Smith. No, not this week’s game. The Packers welcomed the Jets to Lambeau Field twelve years ago, and right off the bat the game felt like it was gonna be a long one! On the first play of the game, Aaron Rodgers fumbled the snap, and the Jets recovered, then immediately turned around and scored. Everyone blinked and the Packers were down 21-3 only five minutes into the 2nd quarter. The Packers racked up a few field goals and cut the deficit to 12 points. As the Jets were driving down the field with less than two minutes left in the half, Tramon Williams intercepted Smith at the Packers’ 3-yard line. The Packers then drove 97 yards with 1:53 left on the clock to score a touchdown with seconds left in the half. The Packers took their momentum into the 2nd half and put up two more touchdowns to take the lead, including an 80-yard touchdown pass to Jordy Nelson on the first play of a drive in the 3rd quarter. Those would be the last points scored in the game, as both teams exchanged punts in the 4th. t-2. Packers @ Detroit Lions – Dec 3, 2015 Deficit: 20 points Final Score: 27-23 Now we’re talking! Like the Jets game, this one got out of hand fast. The Lions were up 10-0 in the 1st quarter when Rodgers threw a tipped interception that led to another touchdown. The Lions went up 17-0 in the first quarter, and that score held going into halftime before they eventually made it 20-0 in the 3rd quarter. The Packers finally got some rhythm on offense and scored a touchdown after Randall Cobb hopped on a James Starks fumble that flew into the end zone, just like they drew it up! On the first play of the Lions’ next drive, Julius Peppers knocked the ball out of Matthew Stafford’s hand and Jake Ryan hopped on the fumble, setting up Davante Adams’ first touchdown of the season and cutting into the Lions’ lead, making it 20-14. Rodgers added a rushing touchdown late in the 4th, putting the Packers down by just two points. The Packers started their final drive with 23 seconds left. After two incompletions, Rodgers threw the ball to James Jones, who lateraled to Richard Rodgers, who lateraled back to Aaron Rodgers before he was sacked as the clock ticked down to 0. Flags flew out for a face-mask penalty, and the Packers were given one more play and had no choice but to go for the Hail Mary. You know what happened next. “Rodgers…in trouble…he turned 32 yesterday does he have a vintage moment in him?? In the end zone…IT IS CAUGHT…FOR THE WIN!” Rodgers to Rodgers for the walk-off win in Detroit. This is one of those “where were you when this happened” moments. I was in a Packers bar in Chicago drowning myself in a discounted pitcher of Miller Lite trying to calm my nerves. t-2. Packers vs Chicago Bears – Sep 9, 2018 Deficit: 20 points Final Score: 24-23 The Packers’ 2nd largest comeback in the 21st century was another “where were you when this happened” game…the “ mah knee ” game. I was lucky enough to be in the stands to witness this glory in person. Week 1 in 2018 was none other than Bears-Packers at Lambeau Field on Sunday Night Football, and boy did this game live up to its time slot. The headlines going into the divisional match-up were already massive. Not only was the Bears organization high on their brand-new head coach, Matt Nagy, but they traded for Khalil Mack in the offseason who the Packers also attempted to trade for. The season as a whole was ultimately a success for the Bears, as they won the division and finished with a winning record for the first time since 2012. However, the Packers (Aaron Rodgers, really) stifled that offseason optimism in Week 1. The Packers were down 10-0 early in the 2nd quarter when the worst possible thing happened: Rodgers immediately grabbed at his knee following a sack. The two-time MVP (at the time) had to be carted off the field, and it felt like the Packers’ season was over before it began. To make matters worse, Khalil Mack turned it up a notch. Mack racked up a sack-fumble on the Packers’ next drive, recovering it himself, and followed that up with a pick-six on the one after that. As a result, the Packers went into the half with a 17-0 deficit and a silently stunned crowd. However, as halftime came to an end and the team ran out of the tunnel, Aaron Rodgers jogged out behind them in full uniform to an eruption of cheers from the crowd. The Bears kicked a field goal on their first drive, making it 20-0. The Packers answered with a field goal of their own, making it 20-3 heading into the 4th quarter. The Packers defense forced the Bears to punt on their next two drives while the Packers scored two touchdowns on theirs, pulling within three points. The Packers defense gave up a “bend don’t break” drive, which led to a Bears field goal making it 23-17, Bears. With less than three minutes left, the Packers had the ball on the Bears’ 20-yard line. On the first play, Rodgers nearly threw a pick that was dropped by Bears CB Kyle Fuller, PHEW. Then, Randall “Bear Killer” Cobb happened. On 3rd and 10, Rodgers threaded the needle to Randall Cobb, who ran 75 yards while dodging tackles for a touchdown. With two minutes left, the Packers took the lead, 24-23. The Packers defense wrapped things up with a Nick Perry ( sans clubbed hand ) sack-fumble on QB Mitch Trubisky on 4th down. The Packers kneeled it out to finish off one of their most exciting comebacks of all time. 1. Packers @ Dallas Cowboys – Dec…

title: What the Packers’ game-day roster could look like: Week 2, New York Jets
summary: A couple of weeks ago, we did an exercise on what the Green Bay Packers’ game-day roster would look like, and I want to update that projection for Week 2 based on new information we have. To recap, here was my prediction on how the Packers would drop their 53-man active roster to their 48-man […]
full_text: (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images A couple of weeks ago, we did an exercise on what the Green Bay Packers’ game-day roster would look like , and I want to update that projection for Week 2 based on new information we have. To recap, here was my prediction on how the Packers would drop their 53-man active roster to their 48-man game-day roster: One tight end inactive (WRONG, all four tight ends were active in Week 1) Two offensive linemen inactive (CORRECT, it was Aaron Banks out with injury and Travis Glover being a healthy scratch) At least one defensive lineman inactive (CORRECT, Warren Brinson was out with an injury and Anthony Campbell was a healthy scratch) One choose-your-own-adventure spot between receiver, defensive lineman and off-ball linebacker (WRONG, it was two of these players, not one, because the team kept four tight ends) For the most part, I feel like I was on the right track going into Week 1 (even before that week’s set of practices began), but if you can’t tell…yes, I was surprised they used four tight ends. Maybe that was just a Minnesota Vikings game-planned thing (I think it’s going to be very hard to keep four tight ends when injuries start to pile up), but it’s not like the New York Jets don’t blitz , either, if that was the justification for the volume at tight end. Before we dig into the nuts and bolts of the roster, we should lay out the Packers’ injury report, which was finalized on Friday : DL Warren Brinson (out, calf) DL Javon Hargrave (doubtful, concussion/knee) OL Zach Bako-Bewele (questionable, knee) OL Aaron Banks (questionable, knee) ED Lukas Van Ness (questionable, concussion) CB Benjamin St-Juste (questionable, hamstring) With seven defensive linemen on the roster (Packers used five last week) and ten offensive linemen (Packers used eight last week), Green Bay should be able to handle those positions — at least from a numbers perspective — even in an absolute worst-case scenario where Brinson, Hargrave, Bako-Bewele and Banks don’t play against the Jets. The real pressure points on the roster, injury-wise, this week are with Van Ness and St-Juste. On the edge, the Packers only have four total players at the position — including Van Ness — a pretty low number for them historically. If Van Ness can’t go, they will almost certainly have to call up either Arron Mosby or rookie Nyjalik Kelly from the practice squad. In my opinion, Kelly seems like the more likely candidate, as Mosby is more of a special teamer than a true defender; thus, Mosby doesn’t really fix Green Bay’s “we only have one backup” issue. If the Packers think they’re going to be down Van Ness, they’ll probably let us know by calling up a practice squad player at the position (likely Kelly) on Saturday. In theory, the Packers could keep just four “cornerbacks” if St-Juste’s hamstring injury issue keeps him off the field, but one of the problems there is that Kamal Hadden, officially listed as a cornerback, was actually a full-time slot player for Green Bay this preseason. Hadden worked out with the safeties, not cornerbacks, in individual drills, common for a slot defender. A question I have is how much Hadden has been working with outside cornerbacks in-season, because if Hadden hasn’t been doing that before St-Juste first popped up on the injury report on Friday, will the team really want to rely on Hadden leaning on banked reps from 2024-2025 under a different defensive coordinator to be the “break in case of two injuries emergency” player on Sunday? If not, I could see a second practice squad call-up (rookie sixth-round pick Domani Jackson is the only practice squad cornerback for the Packers) this weekend, depending on St-Juste’s health. So, how do we get to a 48-man gameday roster? First, it’s important to remember that practice squad call-ups aren’t extra players on game day. These players get added to the pool of players who could potentially suit up for game days, almost like the 53-man roster expands up to a 55-man roster, but the game-day roster still has a hard cap at 48 players. For every practice squad player elevated, another inactive must be made. With all that said, here’s my prediction for Sunday: QB: Jordan Love and Tyrod Taylor RB: MarShawn Lloyd, Chris Brooks and Kaleb Johnson WR: Christian Watson, Matthew Golden, Jayden Reed, Bo Melton and Skyy Moore J. Michael Sturdivant healthy scratch (was in Week 1) TE: Tucker Kraft, Jonnu Smith, Mark Redman and Josh Whyle OL: Jordan Morgan, Sean Rhyan, Jacob Monk, Donovan Jennings, Jager Burton and Anthony Belton Two of: Zach Bako-Bewele (questionable), Aaron Banks (questionable), John Williams or Travis Glover (Week 1 healthy scratch) DL: Karl Brooks, Jonathan Ford, Devonte Wyatt and Chris McClellan One of: Javon Hargrave (doubtful) or Anthony Campbell Warren Brinson (calf) out ED: Barryn Sorrell, Brenton Cox Jr. and Dani Dennis-Sutton One of: Lukas Van Ness (concussion) or Nyjalik Kelly (practice squad call-up) LB: Zaire Franklin, Edgerrin Cooper, Isaiah McDuffie, Ty’Ron Hopper and Niemann CB: Keisean Nixon, Brandon Cisse, Carrington Valentine and Kamal Hadden One of: Benjamin St-Juste (questionable) or Domani Jackson (practice squad call-up) S: Xavier McKinney, Evan Williams, Javon Bullard and Kitan Oladapo SPT: Trey Smack (K), Daniel Whelan (P) and Matt Orzech (LS) There might be an outside chance that the team elects to replace the St-Juste spot on the game-day roster with undrafted rookie receiver J. Michael Sturdivant, if the team believes that St-Juste’s special teams contributions are more important to replace than depth at the cornerback position, but that’s really the only alternative path that I can realistically see. For what it’s worth, St-Juste is a special teams ace, something backup cornerbacks Carrington Valentine and Kamal Hadden very much are not. Sturdivant was onboarded to play a lot of special teams in the summer (he was a difference-maker dating back to college), so I don’t want to rule out that option fully. — Let me know what you think about this in the comments section. Tell me how you see it differently. For reference, below is the Packers’ practice squad (they are allowed to, but not required to, call up as many as two players from there): QB: Kedon Slovis RB: Pierre Strong Jr. and Damon Bankston WR: Isaiah Neyor and Quincy Skinner Jr. TE: Drake Dabney OL: Dalton Cooper, Josh Gesky, Dillon Wade and Cordell Volson DL: Eric Johnson II ED: Nyjalik Kelly and Arron Mosby LB: Kristian Welch (called up Week 1, but Ty’Ron Hopper is cleared now) CB: Domani Jackson S: Kahlef Hailassie K: Lenniy Krieg (international exemption) Join the conversation! title: Sunday will be a big opportunity for the Packers’ inexperienced edge rushers
summary: Green Bay Packers edge rusher Lukas Van Ness was officially listed as questionable on Friday after being a limited participant in practice throughout the week. If Van Ness can’t play Sunday against the New York Jets, the Packers won’t have much experience to lean on in his absence. At the moment, there are only three […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Dani Dennis-Sutton #51 of the Green Bay Packers reacts during the fourth quarter of the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Green Bay Packers edge rusher Lukas Van Ness was officially listed as questionable on Friday after being a limited participant in practice throughout the week. If Van Ness can’t play Sunday against the New York Jets, the Packers won’t have much experience to lean on in his absence. At the moment, there are only three other edge rushers on the team’s 53-man roster: Barryn Sorrell (who was cleared for the game after dealing with a foot issue that limited him in practice this week), Brenton Cox Jr. and rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton. For perspective, here were the Packers’ snap counts, among edge defenders, in 2025 — including the playoffs but excluding the Week 18 JV game: Micah Parsons: 707 snaps (on PUP list) Rashan Gary: 697 (traded this offseason) Kingsley Enagbare: 521 (will be on the other sideline in Week 2) Van Ness: 310 (questionable with a concussion) Sorrell: 154 Cox: 39 Yes, if Van Ness doesn’t suit up, the Packers will be out 92 percent of their 2025 edge rusher snaps going into Week 2’s action. Their EDGE5 and EDGE6 from last year could very well make starts on Sunday, including Cox — who played just four snaps in the team’s playoff game against the Chicago Bears last year. Because of the limited experience and numbers, I could see the team pivoting to their packages where linebacker Edgerrin Cooper plays on the edge more than they did in Week 1 (they flashed these sets a lot in the preseason, for what it’s worth). The other thing the team is probably going to do, if they don’t have Van Ness, is call up someone from the practice squad to just give them another body. Arron Mosby has played a lot of games for the Packers, but he’s mostly here to contribute on special teams, not defense. Because of the short numbers, I actually expect rookie Nyjalik Kelly to get a look over Mosby, if push comes to shove, because of what he can do on defense. Hard to know what a unit of Sorrell, Cox, Dennis-Sutton and Kelly could do on Sunday, because we’ve hardly ever seen the projected starters in starting roles, and the rookies have hardly played NFL football yet (Dennis-Sutton missed the first two preseason games with an overheating issue). On paper, though, if Van Ness can’t go, the Packers’ EDGE5 and EDGE6 from last year will be starting, with two rookies being the only other rotational options available. If nothing else, we’ll get a lot more data points on where Green Bay’s young pass-rushers are in their progression.

title: Packers vs. Jets Injury Report: Green Bay gives 6 game statuses on Friday
summary: The Green Bay Packers have officially ruled out defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf), who has yet to practice for the team in the regular season, for their contest against the New York Jets on Sunday. The good news? Brinson was the only player who is absolutely a no-go this week. The only player that the […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have officially ruled out defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf), who has yet to practice for the team in the regular season, for their contest against the New York Jets on Sunday. The good news? Brinson was the only player who is absolutely a no-go this week. The only player that the Packers listed as doubtful on Friday was defensive lineman Javon Hargrave, who, according to head coach Matt LaFleur, is in the concussion protocol as a result of Week 1’s action. Hargrave was a limited participant on Wednesday, but he was a non-participant on Thursday and Friday. Usually, having the two biggest injuries on the team at one position means there needs to be some shuffling going on, but since the Packers oversigned players on the defensive line early in the season, they still have five healthy players in the unit going into their game against the Jets. Devonte Wyatt, Karl Brooks and Jonathan Ford should be the starters in the team’s 3-4 defense, as they were in Week 1, with third-round rookie Chris McClellan being the top backup off the bench — instead of Hargrave — and preseason star Anthony Campbell should make his NFL regular-season debut this week after being a healthy scratch against the Minnesota Vikings. Players listed as limited by Green Bay going into Week 2’s action are right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele (knee), left guard Aaron Banks (knee), edge defender Lukas Van Ness (concussion) and cornerback Benjamin St-Juste (hamstring). St-Juste apparently got hurt in practice, as he was not on the injury report either Wednesday or Thursday, but was added as a limited participant on Friday. The Packers have 10 offensive linemen on their 53-man roster, so they can handle the Bak0-Bewele and Banks injuries internally, at least in terms of numbers, without having to dip into the practice squad. If Van Ness can’t go, there should be a call-up at the position, as the team only is carring Barryn Sorrell, Brenton Cox Jr. and rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton on the 53-man roster. Just to get through the game, it seems like Green Bay is going to have to call up either rookie Nyjalik Kelly or special teams ace Arron Mosby if Van Ness can’t suit up. Usually, practice squad call-ups happen on Saturday, so we should get a better feel for where the Packers stand tomorrow’s travel day. Linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper (Achilles), edge defender Barryn Sorrell (foot) and defensive lineman Devonte Wyatt (ankle) were all cleared for Sunday’s action today. Hopper missed Week 1, which led to Kristian Welch being called up from the practice squad. Assume that an edge rusher and potentially cornerback Domani Jackson, depending on St-Juste’s status, are the prime practice squad call-up candidates this weekend. On the Jets’ end of the injury report, they’ve already ruled out receiver Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle), safety Minkah Fitzpatrick (groin), running back/returner Kene Nwangwu (back) and edge defender Joseph Ossai (foot), which was expected. Nwangwu and Ossai weren’t able to play last week, and Cooper and Fitzpatrick both suffered early Week 1 injuries. Listed as questionable is edge defender Will McDonald IV, who injured his ankle in practice this week. He was a full participant on Wednesday, but the designated pass-rusher was limited on both Thursday and Friday. Interestingly, rookie second-round pick D’Angelo Ponds, who has missed a lot of time recently with a calf injury, has been given no status going into the game. Ponds wasn’t able to play in Week 1, so it’s uncertain how he’ll fit into the Jets’ pecking order in the secondary. #Packers Friday injury report: RT Bako-Bewele (knee) LG Banks (knee) EDGE Lukas Van Ness (concussion) all questionable. DT Hargrave (concussion/knee) doubtful. #Jets WR J. Cooper, S Fitzpatrick, EDGE Ossa all OUT. pic.twitter.com/6xsQXKPDIN — Mike Clemens (@MikeClemensNFL) September 18, 2026

full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - NOVEMBER 16: Green Bay Packers players stand on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on November 16, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Sunday, the Green Bay Packers head to the Meadowlands to try to shake off a rough performance in Week 1. The team heads into MetLife Stadium for a matchup with the New York Jets, who are 1-0 after a 23-10 win over the Tennessee Titans in Week 1. Despite the two teams’ different fortunes in their respective openers and despite home field advantage, the Packers come into week one as the favorites. As of mid-day Friday, the current spread (from FanDuel Sportsbook ) is 3.5 points in favor of the Packers, which is down a point from the -4.5 line that started the week. That line may shift further depending on the teams’ Friday injury report, however. Green Bay will be closely monitoring the status of Lukas Van Ness and Javon Hargrave, both of whom are in the concussion protocol after exhibiting symptoms in the days following last Sunday’s loss. Hargrave was a non-participant in practice on Thursday, though Van Ness was limited and members of the media spotted him in pads. Meanwhile, the Jets have ruled out Minkah Fitzpatrick, rookie receiver Omar Cooper, and a few others already on Friday morning. Despite last week’s ugly results, APC’s writers are confident in the team’s ability to bounce back. It’s a sweep for our writers in picking the Packers straight up in this game, and the majority of our writers also see Green Bay covering the 3.5-point spread: Writer Straight-Up Winner Against the Spread (GB -3.5) O/U Total 44.5 Tex Packers Packers Under Justis Packers Jets Under Rcon14 Packers Packers Over Jon Packers Packers Over Paul Packers Packers Over Zach Packers Packers Over One other consideration for this week is the fact that rain is expected in New Jersey over the weekend. That could make the game a bit more sloppy if it does indeed arrive during game time. The Packers are, of course, 0-1 against the spread so far this season, with Minnesota easily covering last week. The Vikings were just 1.5-point favorites heading into the game. Meanwhile, the over hit last week, with the total points line set at 46.5; Minnesota’s 4th-quarter scoring spree, spurred by their defense overwhelming the Green Bay offensive line, pushed them to within a touchdown of the total all on their own in a 39-22 win.

title: Aaron Rodgers and Jordy Nelson headline Packers’ best performances against Jets
summary: The Packers have a long but not especially rich history of meetings with the New York Jets. The two teams have played 14 times in their shared history, but the Packers have won just five of those matchups. Still, the Packers have put together some pretty impressive performances in that limited and uninspiring history. Here […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - SEPTEMBER 14: Wide receiver Jordy Nelson #87 of the Green Bay Packers during the NFL game against the New York Jets at Lambeau Field on September 14, 2014 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. The Packers defeated the Jets 31-24. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Packers have a long but not especially rich history of meetings with the New York Jets. The two teams have played 14 times in their shared history, but the Packers have won just five of those matchups. Still, the Packers have put together some pretty impressive performances in that limited and uninspiring history. Here are some of the best. Most passing yards – 442 ( Aaron Rodgers ) In a wild game three weeks after Mike McCarthy got fired in 2018, Rodgers led a massive fourth quarter comeback with his arms and his legs. 442 yards is actually the second-best single-game total of his long career, and a lot of it came in an 18-point fourth quarter surge as the Packers rallied to tie the Jets, then win in overtime. We’ll have more from this game a bit later. Rodgers also threw three touchdown passes in a 2014 win over the Jets, which we’ll discuss in more detail throughout this piece. Most rushing yards – 102 ( Ahman Green ) Eric Mangini came into Lambeau Field in 2006 and absolutely nuked the Packers, handing Green Bay a 38-10 beatdown on their home turf. There was very little to get excited about in the game overall, but Ahman Green managed to grind out 102 yards on 14 carries in the losing effort. Most receiving yards – 209 ( Jordy Nelson ) The same 2014 game that featured three touchdown passes from Aaron Rodgers also showcased a career effort from Jordy Nelson, who caught nine passes for 209 yards, a career best. Nelson was so good that day he already had 129 yards before hauling in an 80-yard score to give the Packers the win. Points – 14 ( Aaron Rodgers , Randall Cobb ) Points scored is definitely a more old-school metric, much more common in the days when a kicker wasn’t typically a team’s leading scorer year-in and year-out. But we’ve got a rare instance where the scoring is interesting — especially since it happened twice! In 2018 and 2014, respectively, Aaron Rodgers and Randall Cobb scored 14 points apiece in wins over the Jets, both scoring two touchdowns and adding a two-point conversion. But even more interesting: both Rodgers and Cobb recorded an octopus in their 14-point efforts! An octopus ( a term first popularized by Mitch Goldich of Sports Illustrated ) occurs when a player scores a touchdown then converts the two-point conversion. Cobb scored his after a one-yard touchdown pass, while Rodgers’ octopus was perhaps the craziest of the 13 the Packers have recorded in their history. Rodgers ran in the two-pointer himself after throwing a rare pick-two on the preceding play, which was called back due to a penalty. Sacks – 2 ( Ezra Johnson , Brian Noble ) There haven’t been many noteworthy sack performances by the Packers against the Jets, but both Ezra Johnson and Brian Noble have taken down a New York quarterback twice in a game. Johnson did it in 1982, the first year sacks were an official stat, while Noble did it in 1991. Both performances took place in losses. Tackles – 13 ( Nate Wayne ) Tackles are a bit of a fungible metric, but among the stats we have, Nate Wayne stands tall. He recorded 13 tackles against the Jets in a 2000 loss. I know the Packers and Jets haven’t played a lot, but a 20-16 game with fewer than 60,000 in attendance at Lambeau Field has to rank among the most forgettable matchups, no matter what heroics Wayne may have pulled off. Interceptions – 1 (nine players tied) Nine players have recorded an interception against the New York Jets, but only Tramon Williams and Charles Woodson have done it multiple times, albeit across multiple games. However, on Halloween in 2010 , Williams and Woodson worked together to help shut out the Jets. Their interceptions were key parts of a 9-0 win as the Packers began to build momentum in what would become a Super Bowl season.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers look for a repeat of 2014 (well, mostly)
summary: In 2014, the Green Bay Packers started off the season with an embarrassing defeat on the road. They went into Seattle and got throttled by the Seahawks, losing 36-16 in a game that didn’t even really feel that close. Panic set in among the fan base, and the season felt over when it had barely […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - SEPTEMBER 14: Quarterback Geno Smith #7 of the New York Jets scrambles with the football against the Green Bay Packers during the NFL game at Lambeau Field on September 14, 2014 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. The Packers defeated the Jets 31-24. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images In 2014, the Green Bay Packers started off the season with an embarrassing defeat on the road. They went into Seattle and got throttled by the Seahawks, losing 36-16 in a game that didn’t even really feel that close. Panic set in among the fan base, and the season felt over when it had barely begun. Of course, week one can lie. The very next week, the Packers played the New York Jets, quarterbacked by a young Geno Smith, and got their season back on track. It took a bit — the Jets jumped out to a shocking 21-3 lead in the second quarter — but Green Bay closed the gap in the second and third quarters, getting two touchdowns from Randall Cobb and a big 80-yarder from Jordy Nelson to provide the game-winning score in a 31-24 victory. It was the kind of response to adversity that the 2026 Packers need to channel this week when the team, coming off an embarrassing road loss in week one, plays a New York Jets squad quarterbacked by a much older Geno Smith. The parallels are all there for the taking. The Packers just need to go out and make it happen. (Preferably, without the drama of getting out to a big early deficit.) Here’s a combination of some looks ahead to this week 2 matchup as well as a few last postmortems of the week 1 debacle in Minnesota. 3 things on Packers offense vs Jets: Can O-line rebound vs the blitz? | Packers Wire The Jets won’t blitz as often as the Vikings did — nobody did and nobody can — but they’re still one of the more blitz-happy defenses in the NFL. It’s on the coaching staff and the players to fix the communication issues that plagued the line last Sunday. Go Pack Go—wherever you go! title: Houston Texans Injury Report: Wide Receiver Ruled OUT
summary: The Houston Texans are coming off a last second loss to the Buffalo Bills, in which the offense played well above what we expected, while the defense played well below what we expected. All offseason, the talk around town was how the offense would bounce back, especially quarterback C.J. Stroud, and he delivered in the […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 20: Nico Collins #12 of the Houston Texans looks on during pregame prior to the first quarter of the game against the Las Vegas Raiders at NRG Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Houston Texans are coming off a last second loss to the Buffalo Bills, in which the offense played well above what we expected, while the defense played well below what we expected. All offseason, the talk around town was how the offense would bounce back, especially quarterback C.J. Stroud, and he delivered in the first game of the season. The rushing attack looked good, the wide receivers were getting open, and the offensive line played as well as they could have until the last drive, in which Stroud was sacked multiple times, which was the final nail in the coffin. The defense was torched all day long, which was a huge surprise in general, but specifically against Josh Allen, whom they have had immense success against the last few matchups. The defensive line was not getting home, and the defensive backs were getting beat left and right. This was very uncharacteristic for the defense, and they have too much talent to have this linger. They should be back to themselves soon. Another home matchup coming for the second consecutive week, this time against Joe Burrow and the Cincinnati Bengals. Here is a look at Friday’s injury report: DID NOT PARTICIPATE: -WR Nico Collins (OUT) -RG Ed Ingram (OUT) -DE Jadeveon Clowney (OUT) -LB Jake Hummel (OUT) FULL PARTICIPATION: -LB Wade Woodaz (Thumb) -OT Trent Brown (Hand/Wrist) Houston is dealing with a multitude of injuries this week, but none bigger than Nico Collins, who is far and away their best player on offense. They will lean on Xavier Hutchinson, Kayshon Boutte, and Jaylin Noel in his absence. Former All-Pro guard Wyatt Teller is set to take the place of Ed Ingram. The Texans need to get in the win column, and it starts this weekend.

title: Five good Texans questions with  Cincy Jungle
summary: The Bengals are not as frequent opponent for the Texans as some other teams in the AFC, but whenever they meet you can be sure it is going to be a great game. The recent series has been a little one-sided, but as we saw last week, that guarantees no success for future meetings. The […]
full_text: The Bengals are not as frequent opponent for the Texans as some other teams in the AFC, but whenever they meet you can be sure it is going to be a great game. The recent series has been a little one-sided, but as we saw last week, that guarantees no success for future meetings. The Bengals are always a serious contender with Joe Burrow at the helm. They got off to a great start last week and that is where our conversation got started with Anthony Cosenza of Cincy Jungle . Battle Red Blog: What did you see in the Bengals week one win that you liked? What concerns came up? Anthony Cosenza: What the defense showed against a pretty good Buccaneers offense was inspiring. To force four fumbles, collect multiple other pressures and seeing the players swarm to the ball was a sight for sore eyes. It wasn’t a perfect day on that side of the ball, but basically every “new guy” (those brought in over the offseason and/or players who have ascended upwards in roles) had an impact. The offensive line also held up well. The concerning aspect was on offensive execution. They had to settle for four field goals (including a 56 and 58-yarder), and only won by six points at home while being plus-3 in turnover margin. BRB: Who are some new faces that will make a big impact on Sunday? AC: The interior of the defensive line is making things happen on defense. Dexter Lawrence II and Jonathan Allen are still forces, while rookie Cashius Howell is a spark plug in a rotational role on the edge. Safety Bryan Cook came over from the Chiefs this spring and has steadied the secondary. On offense, keep an eye out for tight end Erick All Jr. and Dohnte Meyers. All has battled injury, but he provides a skill set for the Bengals to run more under center plays, while Meyers is a great training camp story and is budding as a backend receiver corps gadget player. The former CFL wideout had two touches last week (one catch, one rush), and they both converted big first downs. BRB: Joe Burrow is consistently one of the top QBs in football. Make your best MVP case for him. AC: There have already been at least a couple of seasons wherein he could/should have been MVP (he won Comeback Player of the Year in those seasons instead). His leadership is palpable, while his ability to both fit footballs into insanely tight windows and to come back from almost any deficit are some of the best in the game. If the Bengals make the playoffs again, he stays healthy, and puts up stats, he should definitely be on the short list. BRB: Do you have any key concerns about the Texans offense and defense and how will the Bengals attack that? AC: Tackling was still a little sloppy on defense (but better), so David Montgomery may be a tough ask. Tampa Bay also exploited the middle part of the field in mid-range passing to Chris Godwin, while Bucky Irving had a number of catches in the flats to net good yardage. On offense, it’s really about creating more explosive plays, and finishing drives with six points instead of three. Ja’Marr Chase was a non-factor last Sunday, and I don’t expect that to happen again this week, but he does have a tough matchup against the Texans’ secondary. BRB: Fanduel has the Texans as 2.5 point favorites. How do you see the game going on Sunday? Are there any other bets you feel comfortable recommending? AC: I think later in the week it has hovered more around three points, but I understand it. Houston is good, and not everyone is sold on the Bengals’ moves and their traditional early season struggles. This is an extremely tough game, and one wherein I had the Bengals taking one of their only losses towards the beginning of the year. I could see either team winning, but the line feels fair. I’m really interested in the over/under, as it seems low for two teams who combined to score 64 points last week. We want to thank Anthony for taking the time to answer our questions. Keep in mind that if you want up to the minute news and commentary on the Cincinnati Bengals then you can check out his work on Cincy Jungle . We want to wish Anthony and the Bengals the best of luck for the remainder of the season. As usual, we would like that luck to begin on Monday.

full_text: We come to another week of NFL football and the game within the game for millions of sports fans world wide. SB Nation is proud to partner with Fanduel.com for your gaming and betting needs. Obviously, we here at Battle Red Blog remind you that our recommendations are meant for entertainment purposes only and are not meant to be sound financial advice. Please do not wager anything more than you can afford to lose as we are not gambling experts. Furthermore, I have always enjoyed the folks that say they are right 77 percent of the time. If that were really the case you would not be advertising for my money. You would be living the Biff Tanner life with your own high rise hotel and concubine at every stop. All of those caveats out of the way, let’s take a look at this week’s action to see what is in store. The Line: Texans -2.5 This is usually where the gamblers have a weighted system based on games they feel confident about. The secret is not to bet every game. The secret is to pick a handful of games that feel like locks and bet those. I don’t have a good feel for this game because I am not sure which Texans defense is going to show up. Given that, I am leaning Texans based on the homefield advantage and Burrow’s nagging back injury, but I don’t feel good about the line at all. I am predicting another one score game and when those come down, one little bounce of the ball can spell the difference between victory and defeat. The Money line: Texans 1.69x I could talk in circles about the math involved here, but suffice it to say the bean counters in Vegas seem to think the Texans will win the game. Well duh, they are favored by 2.5 points. This is usually where gamblers separate themselves based on their tolerance for risk. If you are risk adverse then you would fade the line and bet on the Bengals. That way, in most instances you would split your bet. If you are more risk adverse then you would double down and bet on the Texans for the money line. Over/Under: Over 45.5 I simply don’t have as much faith in the Texans defense as I once did and no one should have faith in the Bengals defense. I think one of two things happens. Either it is a close game and that means you need both teams to score about 24 points to comfortably get your over. If it is a blowout then both offenses are capable of putting up 30+ points and you still likely get your over. Either way, of the three main bets, this feels like the safest one of the bunch. Prop Bets: Mike Gesicki over 59.5 yards 6.25x I personally love the way Fanduel has this feature. Essentially you can bet on lower yardage for a lower payout or you can bet on higher yardage for higher payouts. It tops out at 89.5 yards, but that feels a little aggressive for me. A 60 yard performance gets you just over 1000 yards in a 17 game schedule, so that feels like a good bet for any tight end facing the Texans. His totals go as low as 14.5 yards, but that pays less than double, so it hardly feels like an effort. Up here a ten dollar bet would net you $62.50 which feels like a worthwhile bet at a position that normally torches the Texans.
