title: 5 Questions with Arrowhead Pride: does Indy stand a chance?
summary: In Week 2 of 2026 our Indianapolis Colts will hit the road to take on the Kansas City Chiefs. Knowing the party was headed to KC, I sat down with Maurice Elston of Arrowhead Pride, SB Nation’s Chiefs blog. You can find him on Twitter @MrMauriceElston. We swapped questions and answers about both the Chiefs […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - NOVEMBER 16: Head Coach Andy Reid and Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs watch a field goal against the Denver Broncos during the NFL 2025 game between Kansas City Chiefs and Denver Broncos at Empower Field At Mile High on November 16, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Jamie Schwaberow/Getty Images) | Getty Images In Week 2 of 2026 our Indianapolis Colts will hit the road to take on the Kansas City Chiefs. Knowing the party was headed to KC, I sat down with Maurice Elston of Arrowhead Pride , SB Nation’s Chiefs blog. You can find him on Twitter @MrMauriceElston . We swapped questions and answers about both the Chiefs and Colts and what follows is what I’ve learned about this week’s opponent. You can find my answers to his questions here. Chris Shepherd: Based on Week 1, if you were an offensive coordinator tasked with creating a game plan to attack the Chiefs’ defense, what would your plan look like? What areas of the field would you attack, what weaknesses would you target and how would you try to beat this Chiefs defense? Maurice Elston: I would do anything possible to force Kansas City’s linebackers—primarily Nick Bolton—to cover in space or match up one-on-one. Bolton is an excellent run defender and the commander of the Chiefs’ defense, but operating in coverage over a large area is not his greatest strength. I would attack the middle of the field with tight ends and running backs, using motion and different formations to create favorable matchups against the linebackers. The Colts have a tight end in Tyler Warren who is capable of presenting that type of problem. Getting Warren matched against Bolton or another linebacker in space could give Indianapolis an opportunity to consistently move the football. Chris Shepherd: In Week 1, Colts fans watched in horror as the Ravens moved Zay Flowers all over the field to exploit favorable matchups that the discombobulated Colts secondary never figured out how to adjust to. Do you think the Chiefs will try to exploit those same issues, and if so, who will Andy Reid and Eric Bieniemy slot into the Zay Flowers role for Kansas City? Maurice Elston: I don’t believe the Chiefs will copy Baltimore’s strategy exactly because Kansas City doesn’t have to lean on one receiver the way the Ravens leaned on Flowers. I absolutely expect Andy Reid and Eric Bieniemy to test the same communication problems Indianapolis experienced in Week 1, but they will likely do it with several different players. The Chiefs can use motion, shifts and formations to create favorable matchups for Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy, Travis Kelce and Kenneth Walker III. Instead of putting one player in the Flowers role, Kansas City can force the Colts to identify and communicate against multiple threats before the snap. That unpredictability could make the assignment even more difficult for Indianapolis’ secondary. Chris Shepherd: In Week 1, Patrick Mahomes made his return after recovering from last season’s torn ACL. He completed 15 of 27 passes for 184 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. Did Mahomes look like the Patrick of old? Was he still the player who can take over games, or will he need some time to regain that form? Maurice Elston: I wouldn’t say Mahomes completely looked like his old self, but he did look healthy—and that was the most important thing Kansas City needed to see. Mahomes demonstrated that his knee is fine, he can still scramble and he remains capable of making plays outside the pocket. From a passing standpoint, however, there was some understandable rust. He opened the game completing only two of his first 12 attempts and missed a few routine throws that we normally see him make. He eventually settled down and completed 13 of his final 15 attempts, including two touchdown passes. Because he couldn’t participate in his normal offseason routine and did not play during the preseason, some early rust should have been expected. He may not be completely back to his old form yet, but the second half showed that he is getting there. Chris Shepherd: Can you give me one player on offense and one on defense whom Colts fans might not be familiar with but who you expect to make an impact Sunday night? Maurice Elston: Offensively, I would watch rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen. He became one of the Chiefs’ most talked-about young players during training camp and the preseason. Allen received only one target and did not record a catch in Week 1, but I expect Kansas City to begin incorporating him into the offense. In my opinion, Allen may already be the best pure route runner in the Chiefs’ wide receiver room. His ability to separate could become especially valuable against the man-to-man coverage Kansas City’s receivers have consistently faced. Defensively, I’ll go with L’Jarius Sneed. It may seem strange to call Sneed an under-the-radar player considering what he has accomplished, but much of the attention surrounding Kansas City’s secondary has focused on young outside cornerbacks Mansoor Delane and Nohl Williams. Sneed’s return to the slot gives Steve Spagnuolo a trusted defender who can cover, blitz and handle several different assignments. Having someone Spagnuolo trusts to lock down the slot changes what the Chiefs can do schematically, making Sneed an important piece of this defense even if he isn’t receiving the most attention . Chris Shepherd: How do you predict this game will play out? What does each team do well, where will they struggle and what is the final score? Maurice Elston : I expect the Chiefs to win, although I don’t anticipate the margin being as large as it was against Denver. Indianapolis’ best path to keeping the game close is through Jonathan Taylor and Tyler Warren. The Colts must remain committed to Taylor, stay ahead of the chains and use Warren to attack Kansas City’s linebackers and safeties in coverage. There is no completely stopping Taylor because he is too talented, but if the Chiefs can contain him enough to force Indianapolis into third-and-long situations, Kansas City’s pass rush and pressure packages can take control. For the Colts defensively, the challenge will be handling Kansas City’s motion, personnel groupings and improved running game without experiencing the communication breakdowns that hurt them against Baltimore. If those problems continue, Reid and Bieniemy will find ways to exploit them. I believe Indianapolis keeps the game competitive for a while, but Kansas City eventually creates some separation and wins 24-14. I can’t thank Maurice enough for answering this week’s questions. Make sure you head over to Arrowhead Pride and @MrMauriceElston on Twitter to check out his work. As always, go Colts.
author: Chris Shepherd

title: Colts at Chiefs SNF Predictions: 5 ‘glass half empty or maybe full’ primetime thoughts
summary: So, I was definitely full of optimism and a “glass half full” approach last weekend ahead of the regular season opener against the Baltimore Ravens. Everything that went wrong on the field, essentially did for Indianapolis, and hardly any of my bold predictions came true. Following that disaster, we’ll be a lot more conservative here: […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - NOVEMBER 23: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs and Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts embrace after the game at Arrowhead Stadium on November 23, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images So, I was definitely full of optimism and a “glass half full” approach last weekend ahead of the regular season opener against the Baltimore Ravens. Everything that went wrong on the field, essentially did for Indianapolis, and hardly any of my bold predictions came true. Following that disaster, we’ll be a lot more conservative here: 1. Daniel Jones Can’t Shake Early Rust As expected, Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones wasn’t particularly sharp last weekend, as he returned from a season-ending torn Achilles that he suffered in Week 14 of the 2025 campaign—and was held out of all of this year’s preseason. Jones completed 19 of 31 pass attempts for 166 total passing yards, a passing touchdown, and an interception during Week 1’s blowout home loss against the Baltimore Ravens. Jones is still looking to regain some of his prior explosion and athleticism, but it’ll be tough sledding against this veteran Steven Spagnuolo coached Chiefs defense, after allowing just 131 total passing yards last week to the Denver Broncos. Jones doesn’t lay a dud, but he’s not the difference maker at starting quarterback needed to match Patrick Mahomes either. 2. Chiefs RB Kenneth Walker Runs Wild After the Colts run defense surrendered 144 total rushing yards (*4th most last week) and 3 rushing touchdowns to future Hall of Famer Derrick Henry and the Ravens last weekend, it doesn’t get any easier again. New Chiefs’ running back Kenneth Walker is one of the hottest running backs in football after Week 1, following gashing the Broncos run defense for 173 total rushing yards (*3rd most last week) and a rushing touchdown. I expect the Colts defense to play with more pride on the road this weekend, and having a linebacker wear the green dot will only help their communication issues, but I don’t have a great feeling about this one with their unit still reeling. 3. Colts Hang in There to Make It At Least Competitive If there’s a silver lining, it’s that the Colts have historically played Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs very well to-date in the NFL superstar quarterback’s future Hall of Fame career. Mahomes is 1-2 against the Colts lifetime, and Indianapolis narrowly fell 23-20 to Kansas City in overtime last year during Week 12. Even after the disastrous showing last weekend by the Colts, I still expect this to be a pretty competitive close football game. 4. Jonathan Taylor Carries Colts Offensively With starting quarterback Daniel Jones still working his way back to his prior form, the Colts expectedly lean heavily on star workhorse Jonathan Taylor and their ground game to carry their offense during this early stretch in a notoriously tough road environment. What happens when the immovable object meets the unstoppable force? We’ll find out, as Taylor ran for 98 total rushing yards and 2 rushing touchdowns last weekend, while the Chiefs run defense limited the Broncos offensively to just 61 total rushing yards collectively in Week 1. Kansas City bottled up Taylor to just 58 total rushing yards on 16 total carries (3.6 ypc. avg.) the last time these two teams met in Week 12 of last year, but it’ll be Taylor with the ‘masterpiece’ this go around, eclipsing 100 total rushing yards with at least one rushing touchdown score—much to the dismay of the Arrowhead faithful. 5. Colts Play with More Pride But Fall Short on Primetime, Causing Early Season Crisis Mode After that Week 1 embarrassment, I expect to see a much more spirited effort from the Colts in all three facets of the game on primetime for Sunday Night Football, but in the end, Kansas City proves to be too much, too early in the season at home on SNF, as Indianapolis falls 31-20. It leaves the Colts at 0-2 to begin the 2026 campaign and firmly in crisis mode, ahead of hosting a Week 3 matchup against their AFC South rival Houston Texans. You’re never as good or as bad as you’ve last played in the NFL, but the Colts will need to turn this around quickly.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Reacts Poll Results: Following Week 1 blowout loss, Colts fans’ confidence dwindles

The game was already over by halftime, as the Ravens led 31-13 at intermission. Despite having months this offseason leading up to their Week 1 matchup to prepare, the […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - SEPTEMBER 13: Indianapolis Colts head coach Shane Steichen during a NFL game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Indianapolis Colts on September 13, 2026 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts (0-1) were dominated during their regular season home opener against the Baltimore Ravens (1-0), as they were bullied to the tune of 41-23. The game was already over by halftime, as the Ravens led 31-13 at intermission. Despite having months this offseason leading up to their Week 1 matchup to prepare, the Colts players and coaching staff were dominated in all three facets of the game: offense, defense, and special teams. In particular, the Colts linebackers and secondary were an abomination defensively, as there was miscommunication, blown coverage assignments, and their defensive unit collectively failed to consistently execute on the field. Offensively, starting quarterback Daniel Jones was one of the most pressured NFL passers last week, as the Ravens blitzed the Colts with reckless abandonment, and the Indianapolis offense couldn’t effectively adjust. As such, only 9% of Colts fans now believe that the team is headed in the right direction: It doesn’t get any easier for Week 2, as Indianapolis will have to regroup quickly from that disaster of a Week 1 showing and travel to Arrowhead Stadium, a notoriously difficult road environment, to take on future Hall of Fame quarterback Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs (1-0)(-6.5) on Sunday Night Football. The already hot seats of longtime general manager Chris Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen only got hotter, and the Colts will want to turn this around quickly or run the risk of easily falling into an 0-3 start to begin 2026—with hosting the Houston Texans on the docket for Week 3.

title: Jaguars vs. Broncos: Predictions, picks, odds
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars (1-0) are back at Mile High to face the Denver Broncos (0-1) after beating them in Week 15 of the 2025 season. The Jags are 2.5-point underdogs, per FanDuel Sportsbook, but I suspect they’ll finally get some respect by the end of the weekend. Let’s get to some predictions. Prediction #1 In […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - DECEMBER 21: Trevor Lawrence #16 celebrates a third quarter touchdown with Brian Thomas Jr. #7 of the Jacksonville Jaguars against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field At Mile High on December 21, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Matthew Stockman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars (1-0) are back at Mile High to face the Denver Broncos (0-1) after beating them in Week 15 of the 2025 season. The Jags are 2.5-point underdogs, per FanDuel Sportsbook , but I suspect they’ll finally get some respect by the end of the weekend. Let’s get to some predictions. Prediction #1 In Week 1 this season, the Broncos allowed 31 points, and the Jaguars scored 34. In Week 15 last season, the Jaguars scored 34 points against the Broncos in Denver. Since the Jags began their nine-game regular season win streak in Week 11 last season, they lead the NFL in wins (9), points per game (33.7), points scored (303), and total touchdowns (36). I don’t care that the Week 1 figures are from a small sample. I don’t care that Jacksonville hasn’t faced an overly difficult schedule during their current win streak. Have you watched the games?! The Jaguars are GOOD! It’s safe to assume that the Jaguars will put up points on Sunday. The question is: how so? Trevor Lawrence and the passing game have been absolutely humming, but there’s suddenly some potential for a breakout game for Bhayshul Tuten and the rushing attack against the Broncos. Kenneth Walker III embarrassed Denver’s defense on national television a few nights ago. In his Kansas City Chiefs debut, he posted 173 rushing yards, the most by a Chief since Jamaal Charles in 2012 (per Ben Solak ). Critically, much of the damage came from under center runs. Walker scooted for 148 yards on such runs because a) he is a difference-making ball-carrier, b) the talents of interior linemen like Creed Humphrey and Trey Smith are maximized on vertical runs, and c) the team got blocking buy-in from skill players like Travis Kelce and Rashee Rice. Having Andy Reid as the play caller helps, too. Offenses across the league are trying to go under center more often. “In the shotgun, running backs line up to the side of the quarterback, which both limits the types of run concepts offenses can run and makes the side to which they’ll ultimately run more predictable,” Bill Barnwell wrote . The quarterback benefits as well. “Pass dropbacks from under center since 2021 have generated 0.11 EPA per play, while pass snaps from shotgun or pistol have generated 0.04 EPA per play. That’s roughly the difference between average plays run by the Bills and Giants in 2025.” So, after Denver was decimated by under center runs in the season opener, Sunday looks like a prime opportunity for Jacksonville’s offense. last week, Liam Coen's #Jaguars posted their highest snap rate (62.5%) and third-highest success rate (51.4%) when lined up under center pic.twitter.com/s6AYp29OB4 — Gus Logue (@gus_logue) September 18, 2026 Tight ends Nate Boerkircher and Quintin Morris were absolute dogs in the run game last week. Rookie guard Emmanuel Pregnon is the early frontrunner for breakout player of 2026. Blindside protector Anton Harrison is playing inspiring football. And Tuten looks really good! Lawrence and Jacksonville’s deep pass-catching unit will keep picking on weak links in opposing secondaries, as they did last week against Cleveland and last season in Denver, but Week 2 feels like Tuten’s time to shine. Walker was the only player with more broken tackles than him in Week 1, per PFF. Now he gets to face off against the same defense. For as often as Liam Coen brought up RBs winning on contact and creating yards on their own he's got to love these carries from Bhayshul Tuten keep stacking these, and he will be undeniable pic.twitter.com/Egxl72Yaph — Josh Norris (@JoshNorris) September 15, 2026 Tuten has done well to avoid negative plays, though it sure would be nice to see more explosive plays. Maybe we’ll finally see them come in bunches on Sunday. I expect Tuten to have a good game. But my PREDICTION is that Chris Rodriguez Jr. will have a GREAT game. This is the type of game he was brought in for. A road matchup against a playoff contender where every inch matters. Lawrence should post strong numbers, and Tuten ought to have a few chunk gains on the perimeter, but the Jaguars will look to Rodriguez to convert in high-leverage situations and keep the offense on the field. Last week, Tuten saw more snaps (28 to 23) and carries (15 to 6) than Rodriguez. However, the latter was the only Jaguar with multiple carries in short-yardage situations, and he was the only Jaguar with a carry in the red zone. Jacksonville is expected to run all over Denver this week, but I think it will be more of a 1-2 punch than a full-blown breakout from Tuten. The prediction: Chris Rodriguez scores 2 touchdowns Rodriguez has +350 odds to score a touchdown and +3500 odds to score two touchdowns on FanDuel. I also like Lawrence to score on the ground (+350). As he said after the Week 1 win, “scrambles lead the league in touchdowns every year,” and a designated QB run near the goal line shouldn’t surprise anyone either. Since he entered the league in 2021, the only quarterbacks with more rushing touchdowns than Lawrence are Jalen Hurts and Josh Allen. He will use his legs in the red zone on Sunday. Prediction #2 Even if you didn’t catch Kenneth Walker III on Monday Night Football, you must’ve heard about Denver’s disaster-class on the other side of the ball. This is some of the craziest slander I’ve ever seen. Bo Nix had an Average Depth of Target of 3.86 yards in week 1. For reference: the average American watches TV from about 3.67 yards away. pic.twitter.com/YBwtJ5Ci39 — Novig (@Novig) September 16, 2026 After egomaniac Sean Payton handed playcalling duties to Davis Webb to prevent him from departing to become a head coach, the Broncos wilted against Steve Spagnuolo’s Chiefs. Bo Nix finished with 131 passing yards and a career-high 4 sacks (avoiding sacks is supposed to be what he’s good at). The vaunted Broncos offensive line was embarrassing. The operation under Webb was slow. The running backs were awful in pass protection. Jaylen Waddle dropped what should’ve been a massive catch-and-run play. Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile only blitzed Nix on 14.3% of dropbacks in their last meeting, the second-lowest rate for Jacksonville in all of 2025, but he may want to turn up the dial after watching Week 1. The Broncos offense is exposed; the Jaguars defense has a window to deliver a knockout punch. The prediction: Sean Payton takes over playcalling at halftime The offseason addition of Waddle looked great on paper, even if it cost Denver a first-round pick. I was a big fan of the move. In theory, his field-stretching presence would be the final piece for an offense with big-bodied wideouts, a complementary backfield, and five solid starters up front. And with Payton still overseeing game plans and pass protection, the Broncos were poised to lean more on their offense in 2026. Super Bowl expectations remained in place. But we live in a different world than we did a week ago. I don’t think Payton can last more than six quarters watching his offense struggle to score points. He’ll give Webb an ultimatum right before kickoff: “If you don’t score a point for every minute that goes off the clock, I’m taking back the call sheet!” Once Webb inevitably fails to meet expectations, Payton will snatch the sheet from his hands and call a flea-flicker the first chance he gets, just to show off. title: 5 Questions with Mile High Report: Broncos Run Defense Is Vulnerable
summary: As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Denver Broncos in Week 2, we exchanged questions with Ian St. Clair of Mile High Report to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: Denver allowed the NFL’s second-most rushing yards last week (220) after allowing the second-fewest rushing yards per game last season (91.1). Are […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY , MO - SEPTEMBER 14: Kenneth Walker III (9) of the Kansas City Chiefs rushes as Nik Bonitto (15) of the Denver Broncos attempts a tackle as Justin Strnad (40) pursues during the first quarter at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri on Monday, September 14, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Denver Broncos in Week 2, we exchanged questions with Ian St. Clair of Mile High Report to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: Denver allowed the NFL’s second-most rushing yards last week (220) after allowing the second- fewest rushing yards per game last season (91.1). Are you expecting the defense to bounce back to its 2025 form, or was the 2026 season opener a sign of things to come? The challenge after the first game of the season is to not let the outcome sway the judgment of a team, one way or the other. It’s one game, and as the cliché goes, one game does not a season make. However, when you look at the last three games for the Broncos’ rush “defense,” it should make Broncos Country cringe. In the last three games, including the two playoff games last season, the Denver defense has allowed 543 yards rushing. That’s a trend, and not a good one. Against a good rushing team in Jacksonville, it may take a miracle for the Broncos to not have this recent nasty streak hit four games. What would help is if the defense remembered how to tackle, though that seems far-fetched at this point, too. Get ready for game day with SB Nation’s new app! SB Nation’s NEW game chat feature in the app is perfect for keeping the latest Jaguars updates and conversations at your fingertips. With a couple of clicks you can visit Dawgs By Nature and learn everything you need to know about this week’s opponent! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Question 2: Bo Nix’s average pass attempt traveled just 4.3 yards in the air in Week 1, which was surprising to see given the offseason addition of Jaylen Waddle. Do you expect the offense to open up more going forward? This is where I think the anomaly enters the equation. The pairing of opening on the road at Arrowhead Stadium against arguably the best defensive coordinator this century, and an offensive coordinator calling plays in his first game, was a recipe for struggles. Now figure it out and do your job. This isn’t rocket science. You trade for Waddle and he has one catch for two yards. Seriously? Against a secondary that had no returning players to it. On third-and-1, Davis Webb calls an empty set. Seriously? The Broncos offense looked and played like this was its first game playing football. While it’ll take a miracle for the Denver defense to stop the run, Nix and the offense should be much better on Sunday. Question 3: Why will this game between Denver and Jacksonville be different than their meeting last season? Athletes have long memories, and when they’re embarrassed, they’re even longer. Not only did the Jaguars embarrass Denver at home, this team was just unmercifully flogged by Kansas City. Pride is a powerful thing, and the Broncos did make it to the AFC Championship Game with this same roster. The other factor is Sean Payton. He will not accept either type of showing this weekend, and he’ll demand this team figure it out and do its job. Whether that leads to success, we’ll see. The game is also being played in Denver, so that can’t hurt. Question 4: What’s a key matchup to watch throughout the game? The Broncos’ front seven against the Jacksonville offensive line. If Denver’s defense doesn’t do a better job of maintaining the edge and fighting off interior blocks on the line of scrimmage, it’ll be a long afternoon. The converse is also true with the Broncos offensive line against the Jacksonville front; run and pass blocking must be better on Sunday than it was in Kansas City. Question 5: Do you expect the Broncos to cover as 2.5-point favorites, and do you have a favorite player prop for the game? This is difficult because, obviously, I’m a Broncos fan. We all witnessed the same thing on Monday night in Kansas City. We also witnessed the same thing last season when these two teams played. But as Nix said after the loss to the Chiefs, this was a “nasty wake-up call.” I think Denver finds a way to cover and get the win on Sunday. As for a prop, I have two: Waddle anytime TD (+185) and 60+ receiving yards (+118). Thanks to Ian for taking the time to answer our questions. title: Patrick Mahomes is no stranger to Colts DC Lou Anarumo
summary: Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes is no stranger to playing against a Lou Anarumo-coached defense. Sunday night’s game will be the eighth meeting between Mahomes and the Indianapolis Colts defensive coordinator. Mahomes and the Chiefs are 4-3 all time against Anarumo. Before coaching in Indianapolis, Anarumo was the defensive coordinator for the Cincinnati Bengals […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - NOVEMBER 23: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs looks to throw the football during the fourth quarter against the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium on November 23, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes is no stranger to playing against a Lou Anarumo-coached defense. Sunday night’s game will be the eighth meeting between Mahomes and the Indianapolis Colts defensive coordinator. Mahomes and the Chiefs are 4-3 all time against Anarumo. Before coaching in Indianapolis, Anarumo was the defensive coordinator for the Cincinnati Bengals from 2019-2024. The most famous of these matchups was the 2022 AFC Championship Game , AKA The “Burrowhead” Game. The Bengals were flying high, coming off a Super Bowl appearance the previous season that came immediately after beat the Chiefs in the AFC Championship at Arrowhead, in what may have been the biggest collapse of the Patrick Mahomes era. This prompted many players on the Bengals team to get big heads and talk out of their backsides, especially defensive back Mike Hilton, who famously referred to Arrowhead Stadium as “Burrowhead,” a reference to Bengals starting quarterback Joe Burrow. The Chiefs went on to defeat the Bengals, 23-20, en route to their third Super Bowl appearance in the Patrick Mahomes era. This also gave us one of the greatest Travis Kelce postgame moments of his career. “Burrowhead, my ass!” pic.twitter.com/vKCt7KSZ84 — Arrowhead Pride (@ArrowheadPride) January 30, 2023 In their seven previous matchups, the Chiefs have scored an average of 24.7 points per game. But the Colts are coming off a Week 1 trouncing, when they gave up over 500 yards of total offense to the Baltimore Ravens ; 202 of those yards came on the ground, with running back Derrick Henry gashing them for 144 yards and three touchdowns. The Colts ranked 31st in passing yards allowed last season. The team did, however, finish seventh in the league in rushing yards allowed. So only time will tell if Week 1 was who the Colts are in 2026 or if the Ravens game was an anomaly. Despite the seemingly favorable matchup for the Chiefs, Mahomes isn’t taking Anarumo or the Colts’ defense lightly, telling reporters on Thursday afternoon that “Coach (Lou) Anarumo is one of the best defensive coordinators I’ve went up against.” “If you look at their defensive line, their safeties, their corners, they have really good football players or linebackers. And so, they’ll have a lot of pride, and they’ll come out with the right mentality.” Patrick Mahomes on #Colts DC Lou Anarumo: “I think what makes him such a great DC is he tailors his scheme to the team. He wants to go with their strengths.” “Something that makes him a great coach is that he’s not stuck in his ways of how he calls a game.” 🎥: @Chiefs pic.twitter.com/oTa1E5hYsM — Noah Compton (@nerlens_) November 21, 2025 Mahomes also highlighted that Anarumo is adept at tailoring his scheme and game plan around the team he is going up against. So wait and see if the Colts come out determined to stop the run, or if Kenneth Walker III will have another field day in Week 2.

title: Madden Simulation Week 2: Chiefs-Colts on Sunday Night Football
summary: On Sunday, the (1-0) Kansas City Chiefs are once again home under the lights at Arrowhead Stadium, taking on the (0-1) Indianapolis Colts. Let’s see how the game plays out in Madden NFL 27. Note: In Week 1, the Madden Simulation predicted the Chiefs to win, and Felix Anudike-Uzomah’s first sack of the season. First […]
full_text: On Sunday, the (1-0) Kansas City Chiefs are once again home under the lights at Arrowhead Stadium , taking on the (0-1) Indianapolis Colts . Let’s see how the game plays out in Madden NFL 2 7. Note: In Week 1, the Madden Simulation predicted the Chiefs to win, and Felix Anudike-Uzomah’s first sack of the season. STOP! If you want to watch the simulation without spoilers, start this video — or if you can’t see it, click here . First quarter The Kansas City Chiefs received the opening kickoff and immediately went to the ground game. The first two plays went to Kenneth Walker, who picked up 13 yards on the first carry and 11 on the second. Patrick Mahomes then connected with Rashee Rice on a slant to get the Chiefs across midfield. Indianapolis Colts linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither went unblocked on a blitz and sacked Mahomes on third down, forcing the Chiefs to settle for a field goal. Kicker Harrison Butker drilled a 35-yard field goal. The Colts would begin their night by going three-and-out. Mahomes felt Davis-Gaither coming on another potential sack, but released the ball in time on a deep crosser to tight end Noah Gray for 30 yards, getting the Chiefs inside the Colts’ 40-yard line. End of first quarter: Chiefs 3, Colts 0 Second quarter Head coach Andy Reid called Walker’s number twice before Mahomes connected with Tyquan Thornton to reach the three-yard line. On a shotgun snap, Mahomes handed the ball off once more to Walker, who broke through the Colts’ defensive line and into the end zone for a touchdown. The Colts tried to convert their first first down of the game on third-and-one. Daniel Jones threw a bubble screen on an RPO, but L’Jarius Sneed stopped the play for a two-yard loss. The Colts ended the drive with a punt. Mahomes scrambled for 10 yards to the Colts’ 19-yard line as the two-minute warning approached. Mahomes scrambled once more to get inside the five-yard line. On the next play, Mahomes found Walker on a screen pass, and Walker waltzed into the end zone for a touchdown. George Karlaftis and Felix Anudike-Uzomah sacked Jones on consecutive plays, resulting in another Colts punt. End of second quarter: Chiefs 17, Colts 0 Third quarter The Colts’ offense continued to be stagnant, but a roughing-the-passer penalty on Chris Jones changed the momentum for Indianapolis. Jonathan Taylor picked up the Colts’ first first down with an 11-yard run. Jones found Josh Downs on an out route, and Downs took it 39 yards upfield to get to the Chiefs’ five-yard line. Deion Burks capped off the drive with a touchdown catch. On the Chiefs’ ensuing drive, Mahomes’ screen pass didn’t have enough air under it and hit Laiatu Latu in the helmet, bouncing right into his arms for an interception. This gave the Colts excellent field position at the Chiefs’ 38-yard line. The Chiefs’ defense stood tall, with major help from Nick Bolton, who recorded a sack. Kicker Spencer Shrader nailed his field goal attempt. The Chiefs answered back with consecutive 19-yard plays: one on a run by Walker and another on a pass to Rashee Rice. End of third quarter: Chiefs 17, Colts 10 Fourth quarter Walker caught his second touchdown pass of the night, giving him three total touchdowns in the game. The Colts reached Chiefs territory and began to stall after Chris Jones recorded a sack to force a third-and-13. Rookie defensive back Jadon Canaday knocked down a potential first-down pass completion. On fourth down, Daniel Jones picked up the first down with his legs. The Colts’ drive drained a major amount of clock as the Chiefs’ defense continued to play sticky coverage. On fourth-and-goal with less than 2:45 remaining, Chris Jones forced a sack-fumble, and the Colts turned the ball over on downs. End of the fourth quarter: Chiefs 24, Colts 10 Notable stats Patrick Mahomes: 15 for 22 passing, 164 yards, 2 touchdowns, 1 interception, 4 rushing attempts, 35 yards. Kenneth Walker: 17 rushing attempts, 143 yards, 1 touchdown, 3 receptions, 21 yards, 2 touchdowns. Rashee Rice: 4 receptions, 61 yards Xavier Worthy: 3 receptions, 22 yards Travis Kelce: 3 receptions, 21 yards Nick Bolton: 1 sack, 6 tackles Chris Jones: 2 sacks, 4 tackles for loss, 1 forced fumble Felix Anudike-Uzomah: 1 sack George Karlaftis: 1 sack Khyiris Tonga: 1 sack Colts Daniel Jones: 18 for 26 passing, 194 yards, 1 touchdown, 1 rushing attempt, 15 yards. Jonathan Taylor: 10 rushing attempts, 39 yards. Tyler Warren: 5 receptions, 63 yards. Alec Pierce: 4 receptions, 48 yards. Josh Downs: 3 receptions, 50 yards Akeem Davis-Gaither: 1 sack, 2 tackles for loss In Week 3, the Chiefs travel to Miami to take on the Miami Dolphins , with kickoff set for noon Arrowhead time. Until then, we will see how it is played out inside the EA Universe!

title: Chiefs-Colts: 5 Questions with the Enemy before Week 2 battle
summary: On Sunday Night the Kansas City Chiefs face the Indianapolis Colts. We welcome Chris Shepherd of Stampede Blue — our sister SBNation site covering the Colts — for Five Questions with the Enemy. 1. The Colts opened the season with a 41-23 home loss in which Baltimore accumulated 506 yards and scored on six of […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - NOVEMBER 23: Rashee Rice #4 of the Kansas City Chiefs runs with the football during the fourth quarter against the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium on November 23, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Sunday Night the Kansas City Chiefs face the Indianapolis Colts. We welcome Chris Shepherd of Stampede Blue — our sister SBNation site covering the Colts — for Five Questions with the Enemy . 1. The Colts opened the season with a 41-23 home loss in which Baltimore accumulated 506 yards and scored on six of its final seven meaningful possessions. Was that simply a rough performance against one of the NFL’s best teams, or did the game expose concerns that could linger throughout the season? The concern is large but there is real hope that many of the problems are correctable. The biggest issue was the defense. Not the line, linebackers or secondary. The entire defense. The general belief was the team expected rookie CJ Allen would be the day one starter at Mike and wear the green dot for the defense. Instead, Allen missed more than a month during training camp and didn’t play a single snap in week one. The backup plan was to put the green dot on Safety Cam Bynum and watching the tape back, it was pretty obvious, that didn’t work at all. The Colts coaches, to their credit (despite an incredibly bad decision to begin with) have recognized this mistake and are at least trying to fix it. Akeem Davis-Gaither will be receiving plays from the sideline and will be tasked with communicating that information to all three levels of the defense. There are still some very real concerns with this Indianapolis defense but the first step to solving all of them is making sure everyone is on the same page. 2. Daniel Jones completed 19 of 31 passes for 166 yards, one touchdown and one interception in his first game back from a torn Achilles. Beyond the box score, how did Jones look physically, and how confident are you that he can regain the form he showed before last season’s injury? Jones wasn’t bad in week one. He wasn’t particularly good either, but certainly not bad. His movement looked good both in and out of the pocket. The biggest problems for Jones were that he started multiple drives with horrible field position and a lot of great Kyle Hamilton blitzes off of the edge. Between the pressure of playing so deep on the wrong side of the field so often and the physical pressure cause by one of the best blitzing defensive backs I’ve ever seen, it was almost impossible for Jones to get into a rhythm. The interception wasn’t good, but ultimately he is Daniel Jones. The offense worked last year because of Shane Steichen’s system and his ability as a play caller. If Steichen can adjust and figure out how to adapt to Jones needing to get the ball out quicker and Jones can execute that plan, I don’t doubt that he can reach his level of play from 2025, though that is a big ask. 3. Jonathan Taylor was Indianapolis’ biggest offensive bright spot in Week 1, rushing for 98 yards and two touchdowns. How heavily must the Colts lean on Taylor to control the game and keep Patrick Mahomes and Kansas City’s offense on the sideline? The running game will always be the main attraction for the Colts offense as long as General Manager Chris Ballard is running the show and Taylor is running the ball. The Colts have consistently reinvested in their offensive line and continue to find very good players across the front five. Handing the ball off will be absolutely critical for the offense getting in rhythm and moving consistently down the field. Taylor is also always a threat to hit one of those long home runs that have become his trademark. At any point Taylor can turn what looks like it will be a four yard gain into a 60 yard run. Potentially, Taylor can not only control the pace of the game, but flip the outcome on what looked like a standard inside zone handout. 4. Indianapolis allowed 506 yards, 7.9 yards per play and did not record a tackle for loss or a pass breakup against Baltimore. The Colts have since moved the defensive communication responsibilities from safety Cam Bynum to linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither. How much of the Week 1 performance resulted from communication problems, and can that adjustment make an immediate difference against Kansas City? This is what I get for not reading all of the questions before I start answering them. Either way, until the communication issues are addressed it’s tough to speculate on where the weaknesses even are. We’re all holding our breath to see if Latu Laiatu has taken that next step as a pass rusher. We’re all curious to see if Arden Key will give Indy the upgrade opposite Laiatu they needed after Kwity Paye left for the Raiders. There are still so many questions that we’re no closer to answers on because it for most of the week one game it sure looked like all 11 guys were playing assignments based almost completely on vibes. They were confused in the back end, their run fits were a mess in the front seven and the only thing that started to work were the backside edge defenders abandoning backside run responsibilities to combat the play action concepts Jackson was killing them with. And even then it wasn’t as if that turned any tides. There is plenty of reason for optimism that fixing the communication will vastly improve the defense, but week one didn’t tell us much of anything beyond putting the dot on Bynum was a mistake. 5. Kansas City rushed for 220 yards against Denver, with Kenneth Walker III producing 191 scrimmage yards and two touchdowns. After facing Derrick Henry in Week 1, how can Indianapolis prevent another elite running back from taking over—and what must the Colts do overall to pull off the upset at Arrowhead? I’m not going to take anything away from Kenneth Walker or his week one performance. He went out there and killed it in week one. No one can take that away from him and no one should every try. He’s a great back, no doubt. But on the other hand the Denver Broncos missed 28 tackles and Walker forced half of those himself. Again, Walker was responsible for forcing at least 14 missed tackles, that’s incredible. But if Indy can fix their communication issues, mitigate the problems they had with their run fits and wrap up, Walker will still probably get his numbers but with any luck at all they might just be able to keep him from taking over the game. This Indy defense was so disorganized I week one, it’s difficult to imagine a scenario where things look worse for them for the remainder of the season.
author: Maurice Elston

title: Are the Chiefs back?
summary: That sound you heard from watching the Kansas City Chiefs stomp out the Denver Broncos on Monday night was a collective sigh of relief. The concerns many of us had about our favorite football team did not come to fruition. Phew. In fact, it was quite the opposite. The fear subsided and gave way to […]
full_text: That sound you heard from watching the Kansas City Chiefs stomp out the Denver Broncos on Monday night was a collective sigh of relief. The concerns many of us had about our favorite football team did not come to fruition. Phew . In fact, it was quite the opposite. The fear subsided and gave way to jubilation. What a night. What a game. What a relief. I can’t speak for anyone else, but I came into Monday night with legitimate concerns. I’ve voiced many of those concerns here on this website in recent weeks: Can the defensive line generate enough pressure? Did the Chiefs put too many of their eggs in the injured veteran cornerback basket? Can these offensive tackles hold up? Will head coach Andy Reid be willing to change the offense… again? It felt like a lot of questions for a team built around Andy Reid, quarterback Patrick Mahomes, tight end Travis Kelce and defensive tackle Chris Jones. It made me nervous. So much so that I picked the Broncos to win. What can I say, I’m a coward. I was quickly willing to acknowledge as much. The team came out with a swagger it had been missing. It didn’t come from anything anyone said. It was acted upon. It showed up when defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo blitzed not one but two cornerbacks on the first play of the game. It showed up as Andy Reid — ANDY REID — gave the ball on a designed run to running back Kenneth Walker on seven of the first nine plays from scrimmage. It showed up when Mahomes scrambled for the first Chiefs touchdown of the season, only for it to get called back for a hold… And then he did it again on the very next play. Those actions spoke louder than any words ever could. Even if only for one night, the Chiefs got their championship swagger back. The credit for that night should be spread around to countless individuals, but I would like to take a moment to credit a few in particular. I wondered aloud last week if Reid would be willing to make the changes necessary to get this team over the top. I think he’s an all-time great coach, but this game passes everyone by eventually. Was this his time? If one game is any indication, Big Red still has some game left in him. The general manager also deserves some kudos for what we witnessed this week. I personally believe Brett Veach gets far too much criticism. That said, one criticism is fair: The lack of star talent added to the roster in recent years has started to show up in bigger ways. The Chiefs seemed to collect B-level players relentlessly. Sure, those players are helpful, but they lack the talent needed to take a team over the top. Blue-chip talents show up in the biggest moments of a game, or the biggest moments of a season. Think about how many times you recall Mahomes, Kelce or Jones putting the team on their back. That’s been missing over the past couple of seasons as Kelce and Jones age into a different era of their respective careers. Veach added a blue-chip talent (or two) this offseason. The first is Kenneth Walker. We’ve talked for a couple of years about how the Chiefs lacked the ability to create explosive plays in the running game, and Walker is among the best in the league at that particular skill. He applied that ability Monday night to generate as many explosive runs in one game as the Chiefs had from their running backs all last season. On the defensive side of the football, Mansoor Delane played just three snaps, but they were all impactful. He looked like a legitimate shutdown corner when he effectively ran Courtland Sutton’s route and forced an interception. Takeaways sure are fun, aren’t they? We didn’t get to see many last year. The Chiefs finished the season 26th with just 14 forced turnovers. Those takeaways can lead to short fields, which ultimately result in points. That’s exactly what happened Monday night as the Chiefs had not one but two different touchdown drives begin on the plus side of the 50-yard line. The Chiefs had only three touchdown drives of 50 or fewer yards over the first 12 weeks of last year’s season. Forgive me if it sounds like I’m waxing poetic. I got to watch my favorite football team open the season this week against a hated rival — a rival many projected to remain atop the division. Not only did the Chiefs beat them, but they also did so with the kind of dominance we rarely saw a year ago. The 21-point win would have tied for the largest margin of victory all season, but those wins came against the (5-12) Commanders and the (3-14) Raiders. The last time the Chiefs beat a team that finished the season at or above .500 by 21 points was 2022, when Kansas City beat the San Francisco 49ers by a final score of 44-23. This team has been living on the razor’s edge of one-score victories in recent seasons, and this very much was not that. This was a relief. With one game, my anxiety for the season was gone. The Chiefs are back.
author: Brandon Kiley

title: Chiefs Market Movers: Who’s trending ahead of Week 2
summary: The last time the Kansas City Chiefs and Indianapolis Colts played, wide receiver Rashee Rice went for 141 yards, and running back Kareem Hunt had 104 yards and a touchdown on 30 carries. But it still took a fourth-quarter comeback to tie, and an overtime field goal for the Chiefs to get to 6-5 and […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY , MO - SEPTEMBER 14: Kenneth Walker III (9) of the Kansas City Chiefs celebrates rushing for a touchdown during the fourth quarter of the Chiefs' 31-10 win over the Denver Broncos at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri on Monday, September 14, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images The last time the Kansas City Chiefs and Indianapolis Colts played, wide receiver Rashee Rice went for 141 yards, and running back Kareem Hunt had 104 yards and a touchdown on 30 carries. But it still took a fourth-quarter comeback to tie, and an overtime field goal for the Chiefs to get to 6-5 and preserve some hope for a competitive run to finish 2025. Unfortunately, it would be the final victory of the season and the last time any player had over 100 yards rushing or receiving. Last week, the Chiefs leaned on a dominant run game and stifling defense to defeat the Denver Broncos while Patrick Mahomes knocked off some rust. Meanwhile, the Colts couldn’t slow down running back Derrick Henry or wide receiver Zay Flowers and lost by three touchdowns. Past performance doesn’t guarantee future results, but we’ll still look for trends that could matter in this week’s game. Bulls: Fullbacks Ben VanSumeren and Khyiris Tonga: A late addition to the roster, Ben VanSumeren was an instant contributor on special teams in Week 1. He saw only three offensive snaps, but the team quickly signed him to a contract to keep him on the 53-man roster. Khyiris Tonga was key to four first downs, including the 60-yard touchdown run on 4th down. Given the new-look Chiefs offense’s success running the ball behind both fullbacks, they should keep Tonga and VanSumeren in creative roles. Especially against a Colts defense that helped make Derrick Henry the NFL’s third-leading rusher (behind Walker and Jahmyr Gibbs). Running back Kenneth Walker III: It’s hard to overstate just how great Walker was in his Chiefs debut. He leads the league in rushing and broken tackles after the first week, and we only saw glimpses of what he can do as a receiver. The Chiefs finally have another star running back, and he’ll likely feast again this week against the aforementioned Colts defense. Walker is already paying dividends, and his stock should keep rising. EDGE R Mason Thomas: He might be the most important piece in a dynamic young defense. RMT was a force against Bo Nix last week, and will likely terrorize Daniel Jones on Sunday. The speed and technique jump off the screen, but it’s Thomas’s effort and motor that could make him a rookie-of-the-year candidate. The way Spagnuolo’s defense can operate with RMT changes everything, including getting home with a four-man rush, attacking at different levels of the backfield, and even taking pressure off Chris Jones (he played only 55% of the snaps last week). To see a speed rusher with “Thomas” on his back is another throwback to the Chiefs teams many of us grew up watching. Others trending in the right direction this week: Running back Emmett Johnson, Cornerbacks Mansoor Delane and Nohl Williams, EDGEs George Karlaftis and Felix Anudike-Uzomah, Defensive Lineman Peter Woods Bears: Running back/returner Brashard Smith: Nikko Remigio was reliable but not dynamic as a returner in Week 1 —which is basically what we’ve come to expect. Brashard Smith didn’t get a chance to contribute on offense given the success of both running backs ahead of him—and he got only three special teams snaps. He’ll keep waiting for his opportunity as a playmaker, but it may not come this week. Wide receiver Xavier Worthy: The opportunity was there for a breakout performance. Worthy got six targets against Denver and may have gotten more if he’d delivered more than 18 yards on three catches. He, head coach Andy Reid and wide receivers coach Chad O’Shea have got to find ways to unlock Worthy’s potential, but he’s off to a rocky start. Left tackle Josh Simmons: It looks like the Chiefs offense will take the field without their starting left tackle again this week. They had some good success in the opener bringing help for Kahlil Benson, and he performed admirably. But to get through the season, they’ll need plenty of depth along the offensive line—and it’d be nice to see Mahomes air things out a little more with better protection. Simmons is a critical piece this season, and the longer he’s out, the more concerns we’ll have. Others trending in the wrong direction this week: Cornerback Jadon Canaday, Wide receiver Tyquan Thornton, Tight end Noah Gray Value (Sleeper) Picks: Wide receiver Cyrus Allen: The rookie saw only one offensive snap in his debut, raising plenty of questions this week. He was targeted on that play, but the pass was tipped at the line. Mahomes and the Chiefs staff have kept insisting they trust Allen and that his time will come. Given the passing-game struggles against Denver, Chiefs fans are likely to be even louder in their calls for Cyrus Allen this week. Don’t be surprised if he gets a couple of plays scripted his way. Quarterback Justin Fields: It was also only one offensive snap, but Reid’s use of Fields as a goal-line decoy was brilliant. It could also be Reid’s way of setting up similar plays he wants to use in the future. Fields is still an electric runner and could be a fun weapon for the Chiefs this season. Watch to see if they draw up some looks where he’s more than a decoy this week.

title: Chiefs expect the Colts to rebound from disappointing Week 1
summary: Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season could not have gone more differently for the Kansas City Chiefs and the Indianapolis Colts. The two teams face off in Week 2’s edition of “Sunday Night Football.” The day before, the Chiefs delivered a dominant 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football,” while the Colts surrendered […]
full_text: Nov 23, 2025; Kansas City, Missouri, USA; Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce (87) talks with Indianapolis Colts safety Nick Cross (20) during the first half at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jay Biggerstaff-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season could not have gone more differently for the Kansas City Chiefs and the Indianapolis Colts . The two teams face off in Week 2’s edition of “Sunday Night Football.” The day before, the Chiefs delivered a dominant 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football,” while the Colts surrendered over 500 yards of offense in a 41-23 loss to the Baltimore Ravens . For their part, the Colts gained only 251 total yards while surrendering two turnovers and two sacks. Even after a showcase performance by his own unit against Denver, Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo does not expect the Colts’ first game to reflect what they can bring. Any time he prepares for the Colts, Spagnuolo is wary of star running back Jonathan Taylor, who gained 121 yards from scrimmage and scored two touchdowns against Baltimore. “He’s really good,” Spagnuolo observed before Thursday’s practice. “One thing we have to do is try to bottle him up. When he gets to the edge…he’s really good. If you remember from the game a year ago, it was a short-yardage play that he popped. He’s tough to catch, so trying to get him bottled up and not let him hit a seam north and south would be really good.” Colts quarterback Daniel Jones was middling in his first game back from an Achilles tear late last season. Spagnuolo expects better from the veteran. “We can’t be deceived by this quarterback, thinking he’s a statue,” the coach remarked. “He’s a really good athlete, too. And they have option football in their game; their coaches do a really good job of it.” Spagnuolo believes Jones makes Taylor a more dangerous back. “When Daniel Jones and Taylor are playing together,” he explained, “Taylor plays really well because you have the threat of the quarterback throwing it, so they’re dual threat in that regard… I’m not deceived by the fact that they didn’t have a great game last week.” The Chiefs also expect the Indianapolis defense’s veterans to rebound after an embarrassing opening week. Their defensive coordinator, Lou Anarumo, also has a long track record of finding creative formations to thwart the Chiefs’ offense. “If you look at their defensive line, their safeties, their corners,” noted quarterback Patrick Mahomes on Wednesday, “they have really good football players or linebackers. So, they’ll have a lot of pride, and they’ll come out with the right mentality. They won a lot of football games last year off their defense, and Coach Anarumo is one of the best defensive coordinators I’ve went up against.”

title: Chargers-Raiders Game Preview: Justin Herbert, Chargers offense must rebound in Week 2
summary: The Chargers are back at home this Sunday to host the Raiders (1-0). Their Week One matchup with the Cardinals unfortunately left us with more questions than answers in regards to what the Chargers are this year and who they’re going to become by the end of the season. Sunday’s game could be a pivotal […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Justin Herbert #10 and offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel of the Los Angeles Chargers celebrate a touchdown against the Arizona Cardinals during the first quarter of the game at SoFi Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chargers are back at home this Sunday to host the Raiders (1-0). Their Week One matchup with the Cardinals unfortunately left us with more questions than answers in regards to what the Chargers are this year and who they’re going to become by the end of the season. Sunday’s game could be a pivotal one. A loss drops them to 0-2 before they face a seven-game slate against numerous reigning MVPs, Super Bowl champs, and other AFC powerhouses. They simply cannot afford to go into it without some semblance of breathing room in case everything starts to hit the fan. The Chargers don’t need to be world-beaters this weekend against the Raiders, but they do have to put a performance out there that at least shows they can execute at a baseline level while proving they can improve with each new week. After that, I’m not sure what to expect after Week One’s harsh and surprising outcome. But if that’s the case, I guess we just have to enjoy it and leave it up to that fickle thing called destiny. That said, here are the three biggest storylines that I’ll be following when these two teams take the field on Sunday afternoon. 1.) How much progress can the Chargers offense make in one week? What we saw from the Chargers offense against the Cardinals was nowhere near what expectations had us believing it would look like. A dynamic run game. An explosive passing attack. Layup plays for Justin Herbert so he wasn’t shouldering the entire offensive load. Outside of the very first drive of the game, we saw none of that. The second drive was promising until Omarion Hampton authored his own rendition of the butt fumble, but that was the only sign of a spark through the final three quarters of the game after the opening period. Jim Harbaugh said he regretted not giving his starters more snaps during the preseason. Mike McDaniel lamented that the preseason expectations he created for himself based on what he saw in practice was completely disconnected from what the product ended up being on the field. The Herbert experience was a mixed bag but overall leaned towards the wrong side of the spectrum. That interception was inexcusable given the situation, period. So, how does this unit essentially make a 180 turn into what we all hoped it would be? And how do they do it without their best and most-dynamic receiver in McConkey? I don’t exactly have the answers, but McDaniel absolutely has to. I think Harbaugh was right, in a way, when he said he and McDaniel needed each other. The commitment to McDaniel as his OC means that Harbaugh’s long-term future with the Chargers hinge on his success as it’s tough to see him here much longer if he’s already failed two different coordinator hires. As for McDaniel, he needs to have success here or else he can kiss his future head coach prospects goodbye. After all, who would want to hire him if he couldn’t make a Justin Herbert offense work? Sunday could be a pivotal day for many in the Chargers organization. 2.) How will Kayode Awosika look without being in a “platoon”? One of the worst decisions made by the Chargers coaching staff against the Cardinals was going through with this “platoon” idea in regards to the left guard spot. They really rotated Awosika and Trey Pipkins throughout the game and as we all expected, it did not work out. Awosika was great when he was in the game. He made far less mistakes and overall was the much better blocker. Pipkins being in the game, whether a coincidence or not, led to two of the biggest blunders on the day by the Chargers offense. During that fourth-and-three play near the goal line, it was Pipkins who allowed that instant pressure and sack on Herbert that not only took away plays, but also led to a surge in momentum for the Cardinals who turned it into three points just before halftime. Later on, Pipkins was in the game during the three-and-out that ended in the blocked punt. The Cardinals scored two plays later. It was night-and-day between Awosika and Pipkins. Awosika deserved to hold the starting job outright before the Cardinals game and I’m still shocked Harbaugh felt differently enough to make the call for a platoon. 3.) Can Chris O’Leary get his defense to come alive? That was not the debut O’Leary had in mind as an NFL coordinator. Not only was his unit seemingly unable to slow down the Cardinals this past Sunday, but even his best players failed to make much of an impact on the game. One of the worst areas for the Chargers, per Pro Football Focus, was their tackling grade as a team. PFF had the Chargers with a 54.4 team tackling grade, the lowest on that side of the ball. What was even more worrisome are the names who authored some of the worst individual tackling grades on the team. Overall there were six different defenders who logged a tackling grade below 50.0 (60.0 is considered “average”). That group includes Derwin James (47.0), Tarheeb Still (37.9), Tuli Tuipulotu (28.1), and Khalil Mack (25.3). Yes, you’re reading those names and numbers right. Of the 99 players who have played at least 20 snaps on defense this year, Tuli Tuipulotu and Khalil Mack rank 89th and 95th, respectively, in individual tackling grade. Taking a step back, Mack enters Week Two ranked 45th among all EDGEs (min. 20 snaps on the year) while Tuli ranks much lower at 80th. As for James, he is currently ranked 58th out of 85 qualifying safeties. It’s just one game thus far, but this is certainly not the direction you need your best players trending out of the gate. O’Leary needs to find his groove and get his players settled in fast to get them playing up to their own standard the rest of the way.
author: Michael Peterson

title: Chargers-Raiders Game Preview: Fernando Mendoza could start sooner rather than later
summary: The Chargers are 0-1 and are set to face a 1-0 Raiders team this Sunday who have upset on their minds, on top of the added motivation to make a divisional rival face an 0-2 start to the year. This week, we were lucky to have Matt Holder of Silver & Black Pride (SB Nation’s […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - SEPTEMBER 13: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders stands on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins at Allegiant Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chargers are 0-1 and are set to face a 1-0 Raiders team this Sunday who have upset on their minds, on top of the added motivation to make a divisional rival face an 0-2 start to the year. This week, we were lucky to have Matt Holder of Silver & Black Pride (SB Nation’s Raiders community) join us for an edition of 5 Question with the Enemy. Holder is always one of the best to do these with, so a big thanks to him for the conversation! Also, if you want to see his side of the interview where I answered questions for him, head over to S&BP (linked above)! Let’s go ahead and dive in! 1.) It’s yet another new era for the Raiders as they welcomed Klink Kubiak this offseason as their next head coach. Kubiak is coming off winning a Super Bowl with the Seahawks as their offensive coordinator and that’s a big reason why Las Vegas seemingly wanted to pair him with first-overall pick Fernando Mendoza. What were the expectations for this year and how have they changed, if at all, from when he was hired to right now in Week Two of the season? In my opinion, the Raiders are playing with house money, and I don’t mean that as a pun to them being located in the gambling capital of the world. This is year one of what will likely be a two-year rebuild, so no one should have high expectations in terms of wins and losses. Instead, this season is about watching a young team grow together and build chemistry for 2027 and beyond. Because of that, I’m okay with a slow start to the campaign, but I do want to see them playing more competent and competitive football down the stretch. Obviously, Mendoza is a big factor in that whenever he hits the field. That being said, last week did inspire some hope that Las Vegas might be a little ahead of schedule. Yes, it was against the Dolphins, who are heavy favorites to land the 2027 No. 1 pick, and the Raiders were favored heading into the matchup. However, they flat-out dominated the game to distance themselves from the bottom of the barrel in the NFL, which is a big step for a club that just had the No. 1 pick and finished 3-14 a year ago. Factor in that one of the team’s best players, Brock Bowers, didn’t play, and the buzz in Vegas after the season opener is further justified. 2.) Despite being selected first overall, the Raiders decided to start veteran Kirk Cousins in Week One and it looks like he’ll hold the reins of the offense for the foreseeable future. What did you and the rest of the Raiders fan base think of that decision at the time and did you agree or disagree with it? Did his performance in Week One change that initial opinion at all? The fanbase is kind of split on the decision, where a lot of people want to see Mendoza on the field immediately. I get that. Most No. 1 overall picks play right away, and fans want to see what the young guy is made of. Others, such as myself, are perfectly fine letting Cousins get a few starts while the NFL’s worst offensive line in 2025 works out the kinks to begin this season, and the rookie gets more time to adjust to life in the league. I subscribe to the notion that organizations fail young quarterbacks more often than young quarterbacks fail organizations, and with this franchise’s history at the position, I’m perfectly okay with keeping the training wheels on Mendoza and playing it safe. Overall, I’d say most of Raider Nation is on board with the club’s plan. As for Cousins’ Week 1 performance, it might have opened the door for Mendoza to start a little earlier than expected. Putting it simply, the 38-year-old’s arm is dead. He was one-of-seven and threw two interceptions on passes 10 (ten!) or more yards past the line of scrimmage against the Dolphins. When facing better competition, not being able to throw the ball past the sticks consistently isn’t going to be a sustainable winning formula. And if the team isn’t winning, there’s no point in continuing to give reps to a quarterback who likely won’t be on the team next year when the future of the franchise is sitting on the sidelines. Of course, Mendoza has to show that he’s ready, too, but the calls for him are going to get louder if Cousins doesn’t pick it up. 3.) If you were Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, how would you go about attacking this Raiders defense? Which players would you specifically try to target? Which matchups would you want to exploit? Normally, I’d say run the ball right down the middle because Las Vegas’ defensive tackles are the weakest part of the defense right now. However, with Los Angeles’ interior offensive line, that’s a battle of incompetencies that nobody wants (or should want) to watch. So, I’d pivot toward Ladd McConkey, assuming he’s healthy enough to play and be effective. McConkey being one of the few (maybe the only) bright spots for the Chargers last week is part of my logic. Diving deeper, I saw he spent about 70 percent of his pass snaps in the slot, which presents an interesting matchup. The Raiders traded with the Bills for nickelback Taron Johnson in the offseason, who was a second-team All-Pro a couple of years ago. Johnson is still a physical defender, but his movement skills haven’t been the same after battling injuries over the last two seasons. That got exposed on a few reps last week, and is something a quick and shifty receiver like McConkey could exploit. Granted, the wideout’s production primarily came on the outside despite spending less time there in the season opener. Still, he should be the focal point because the Raiders have question marks at outside corner, too. Eric Stokes was one of the few bright spots from last year’s team, earning a nice payday in the offseason and returning as the team’s top corner. But Stokes’ change-of-direction skills have always been an issue, and he got beaten on a few out-breakers against Miami. At the other spot, Darien Porter is entering his second season and started about half of the games during his rookie year. So, he’s still young, and Porter is considered “day-to-day” right now after suffering a foot injury last week. Behind the second-year pro is rookie fifth-round pick Hezekiah Masses, who has 10 NFL snaps to his name. Masses had a PBU in relief of Porter last week, but obviously, he’s very much unproven. 4.) Switching sides of the ball, if you were defensive coordinator Chris O’Leary, how would you plan on stopping this Raiders offense? How would you attempt to shut down running back Ashton Jeanty and tight Brock Bowers (if he plays)? This goes back to your question about Cousins: load the box and make Kirk prove he can beat you over the top. It helped that the game was already pretty much over, but the Raiders offense did stall in the fourth quarter last week when the Dolphins started blitzing and selling out to stop the run. Las Vegas’ offensive line also has question marks, with left tackle Kolton Miller and center Tyler Linderbaum being the only sure-fire starters heading into training camp. The unit played well last week, until Miami started sending its linebackers straight downhill. Then, it started to look a lot like last year, where Jeanty had no breathing room and ended up having a lot of negative runs. Honestly, I don’t have a good answer for you on Bowers since we haven’t really seen him in Kubiak’s offense. He only played in 10 snaps and had just two targets during the preseason. So, I’m not entirely sure how Kubiak is going to use his “ football robot from heaven “, especially since Bowers has a versatile skill set. But, at the end of the day, Kubiak wants to run the ball, and a smart strategy is to force Cousins to beat you regardless of which pass-catchers are on the field. 5.) Let’s go ahead and…

title: Chargers LB Daiyan Henley has a lot to prove this season
summary: Los Angeles Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley is entering the final year of his rookie contract after being selected by the team in the third round of the 2023 NFL draft out of Washington State. Henley has started every game for the Chargers in the last two seasons leading up to 2026, but he is still […]
full_text: Los Angeles Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley is entering the final year of his rookie contract after being selected by the team in the third round of the 2023 NFL draft out of Washington State. Henley has started every game for the Chargers in the last two seasons leading up to 2026, but he is still hoping to ink that long-term extension with the franchise. Henley spoke with the team’s website about how he is more motivated now than he ever has in his career. “The reason why I would say more [motivated] than ever is because it’s another year and another opportunity to do better,” Henley said via the team’s website . “Another chance, another showing of who I really am out there on that field, on tape to display to the world. “With opportunities missed in the past, like I said, we don’t dwell on that,” Henley added. “We move forward and that’s all I see right now, opportunities in the future. I see opportunities now. I’m amped, I’m motivated and I can’t wait to go.” Henley was the only player on the Chargers’ defense last season to log more than 100 tackles. His ability to go from sideline to sideline really helped shape Los Angeles’ defense, and his efforts are key to the unit’s overall success. If Henley can channel this motivation into his play on the field, he should be able to get that long contract extension and help the Chargers reach new heights as a team in 2026.

title: Puka Nacua misses Rams’ practice on Friday

full_text: Puka Nacua’s status for Monday’s game against the New York Giants is in doubt, as the L.A. Rams’ star receiver did not practice on Friday due to a hip injury. It is not clear if the injury is the same as the psoas injury that caused Nacua to miss a string of practices in training camp, but it’s obvious that his status for this week is up in the air and that’s another potential problem for the Rams. Both Atwell and Daniels were healthy scratches in Week 1. Nacua missed six games in 2024 and one game in 2025. title: Rams officially put ‘Wolverine’ Myles Garrett on IR: When will he be back?
summary: The Los Angeles Rams put Myles Garrett on the injured reserve list on Thursday, as expected following his recent knee surgery. As a result, he’ll miss at least four games and won’t be eligible to return until Week 6 against the Cardinals. Unfortunately, that stretch of games is probably the toughest four games on their […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams put Myles Garrett on the injured reserve list on Thursday, as expected following his recent knee surgery. As a result, he’ll miss at least four games and won’t be eligible to return until Week 6 against the Cardinals. Unfortunately, that stretch of games is probably the toughest four games on their schedule. Games against the Giants, Denver, Philadelphia, and Buffalo are exactly when the Rams need him most. In the first episode of the Coach McVay show, head coach Sean McVay explained the thought process behind not getting the arthroscopic procedure done sooner: “He had a knee issue that prevented his ability to practice. Thought it could be something that he’d be able to kind of work through. And then once you get into real game-like settings and situations you realize all right, hey, he’s not feeling the way that, you know, he’s accustomed to. And so, let’s get this thing fixed.” He emphasized that it was a collective approach among him, Garrett, and the team’s medical experts. McVay is looking to a variety of players, including rookie Wesley Bailey, to help fill the void in his absence . Sean McVay calls him ‘Wolverine’ Garrett will miss a minimum of four games and the Rams are hesitant to set any expectations for how long it will take to have him back on the field. McVay told Long that the team would not rush him back : “He’s feeling good,” McVay said. “… He had crutches yesterday, and then he was walking without crutches today, so he’s like Wolverine, healing fast. I’m reluctant to put a timeline on it. We’ve kind of talked about it, but we know that he’s going to miss those four weeks at a minimum, and we’re not going to rush him back. We want to make sure that he’s feeling good, (that) he’s able to get out on the practice field and do all the things that are necessary for him to perform at a level that he’s been accustomed to. And so that’ll be something that I’ll kind of keep you guys posted as we have updates as we go.” Aaron Donald could come back from retirement on Monday against the Giants, which would be a needed boost for the defensive line at a time of need. In addition to Bailey, the Rams look to Byron Young, Josiah Stewart, and Desjuan Johnson at the outside linebacker position. Young had 12 sacks last season without Garrett, so he’s proven to be a productive player before this season and latest injury. Stewart was credited with one pressure last week. L.A. defensive coordinator Chris Shula must be hopeful that New York’s offensive line, typically a weak point, isn’t as improved as the Giants hope that it is. The Giants drafted guard/tackle Francis Mauigoa with the 10th overall pick and they allowed Jaxson Dart to be sacked twice in Week 1 against the Cowboys. The Rams look to rebound from a poor defensive performance in Week 1 against the 49ers, especially against the run. They’ll just have to do it without their marquee offseason trade acquisition.
