title: The Vikings’ Path Forward: A Rune Reading
summary: After the Vikings absolutely destroyed Green Bay in the last 20 minutes of last Sunday’s game, I found myself with more questions than answers. The similarity to the week one victory of the 2025 season, against the Chicago Bears, are readily apparent. It was an exciting finish to a game that looked like it was […]
full_text: After the Vikings absolutely destroyed Green Bay in the last 20 minutes of last Sunday’s game, I found myself with more questions than answers. The similarity to the week one victory of the 2025 season, against the Chicago Bears, are readily apparent. It was an exciting finish to a game that looked like it was a lost cause for most of the contest. Last season we saw a team that could not win games when it mattered, as evidenced by the five straight victories after playoff contention was lost. Keeping that in mind, I am asking a question with the intention of giving us insight about what to expect. Who am I asking, you might ask? That’s a great question! I am consulting the Norse gods. I Had Runes Before It Was Cool! My incredible life partner wanted me to get in touch with my Nordic roots. As the son of a full-blooded Norwegian and a descendant of the Germanic people, runes are a part of my heritage. Most, if not all, of us have seen the Minnesota Vikings Nordic inspired jerseys and apparel. It seems fitting that I try to navigate what to expect this season by using the ancient mythology. Although I have had these runes for a while, I am still in the very early stages of learning how they work and what to use them for. I figured asking questions about the Minnesota Vikings was a great way to begin this journey. I am going to begin by explaining how a rune reading works and about the different facets of the practice. Then, I will examine a question using the ancient method. During examination and after, I will draw my conclusions about what I saw. There are many different variations when casting runes. For the purposes here, I am doing a 5-rune cast. Each rune represents a unique facet of the proposed questioned and provides a nuanced picture. The question I asked Odin himself pertains to whether or not the Vikings are legitimate contenders or if they are destined to end the season in mediocrity. The question I posed to encompass the context of the team and the season was a simple one: “Do the Minnesota Vikings have a path to the playoffs?” He Who Cast the First (5) Stone(s) Please, excuse the potato quality of my rune cast photo. I took it in my kitchen with terrible lighting. In a five-rune cast, the first symbol drawn represents the current state of affairs. The first symbol shown is Isa, which translates to ice. It represents challenge, frustration, and psychological blocks. This could encompass many things. For one, Jordan Mason was a surprise add to IR after coming out of Sunday’s win with a sore thumb. There were also a number of miscues on both the offense and the defense in the game against the Packers. Pass blocking was atrocious at times on Sunday and the Vikings’ secondary got torched on multiple occasions by Christian Watson and Tucker Kraft. Even though Minnesota snuck out with a win, I am sure the film room and practice was filled with what I will describe positively as “opportunities for improvement.” Isa also reinforces the runes around it, and you’ll notice that the next rune is blank. This second rune denotes obstacles and challenges. In rune divination, the blank rune—also called the Wyrd rune, Odin’s rune, or Rune of Fate—is a special tile or stone with no inscription. It is not part of the original 24‑rune Elder Futhark but was added by modern practitioners (notably Ralph Blum) to represent the concept of “absence” or “the unknown.” Odin’s rune is telling us that the Vikings will face adversity, as they always do, but it may manifest itself in unforeseen ways. We could potentially see a disconnect between perception of this team and what they actually are. Any given Sunday is the phrase that comes to mind for me here, and the sense I get is that we are in for one chaotic season. Another interpretation I have for this rune is that no matter how much conjecture or reasoning I employ to predict how the Minnesota Vikings’ will fair throughout the rest of the season, I have no idea what is going to happen, which is funny, because predicting what is going to happen is kind of the premise of this piece. The third rune in the cast reveals goals and desires. The third symbol shown is “Jera”, which translates to a year/a good harvest. This is very encouraging as it represents the Vikings organization’s desire to realize the results of earlier efforts. It tells me that Kevin O’Connell and crew are putting in the work and that the team has a clear goal to improve week over week and manifest success. It also represents the cyclical pattern of the universe, which makes sense here because the NFL season happens every year in the same manner, just with different outcomes. The Jera rune is a symbol of change, and I am going to choose to view that change as positive. The goal of this team has to be to overcome the stigma of being the historically best team to never have won a Super Bowl. Anything short of desiring success would be a failure to conceptualize a fruitful path forward. The fourth rune provides guiding insight or advice. This one really resonated with me because of some things that I saw on Sunday. Ansuz translates to As/Odin. It provides insight and represents a few concepts: communication, true vision, truth, wisdom, blessings, the taking of advice. Now, you might be thinking to yourself, “that sounds pretty good.” Unfortunately, what you probably don’t know is that when I “cast” this particular rune, it presented itself as inverted. When a rune presents itself upside down, it is referred to as “Merkstave” or reversed meaning. The inverse of Ansuz is characterized by misunderstanding, delusion, manipulation by others, boredom, and vanity. One word sticks out here, to me, and that word is vanity. There were a couple of occasions where we saw some selfish tendencies. One play in particular, from Dallas Turner, during his strip-sack of Jordan Love. After getting the sack, you can see Turner start to celebrate before the whistle. Instead of keeping his focus on the play, he wanted to look cool after his disruption of the quarterback. I’m not saying that he would have been able to recover the ball, since it took a fortunate Green Bay bounce, but he might have had a chance. Another moment was when Harrison Smith had an interception pass right through his arms. Instead of continuing the play, and maybe he assumed it was an incomplete pass, he had a moment of weakness. He put his head down on the field and just laid there instead of helping block for his teammate James Pierre. The fifth and final rune represents potential outcomes and where the current path the Vikings are on will take them. This is a very promising sign to wrap up this cast. Ehwaz translates to horse and is indicative of change, steady progress, teamwork, loyalty, and trust. All of these characteristics inform the casting as a whole, as the fifth rune is typically viewed individually and as a way to encompass the message communicated in a reading. Kevin O’Connell and his players are always talking about leaning on each other and making each other better. Even when the chips are down, this team will find a way to fight. Now, let’s turn back to the question asked of the Norse deities: “Do the Minnesota Vikings have a path to the playoffs.” In summation, I would say the answer falls somewhere along the lines of, yes, if they are able to stay focused and keep the end goal in mind. Both the offense and defense need to play cohesive units. Players need to hold each other accountable to their roles and assignments. The path to success isn’t built by the individual, but rather by a group of individuals who can lift each other up to achieve something greater than themselves. Is Reality in the Room with Us? As we progress through the season, I hope to do more casts to see if I am able to truly tap into something. Now, do I think Odin is real and that I can actually talk to him? Yes, I do, so deal with it! You might think I’m a little bit Looney Tunes for that, which is…
author: Jesse M

title: Week 2 Preview: The Search for Seven in a Row
summary: The Minnesota Vikings aim to win back-to-back division games this Sunday as they travel to Soldier Field to face the defending NFC North champion Chicago Bears. Dammit, that doesn’t sound right.  It will be the search for seven straight wins at Soldier Field, which also feels weird. Maybe because nothing ever comes easy there. Five […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 08: Aaron Jones Sr. #33 of the Minnesota Vikings runs with the ball against the Chicago Bears during the first quarter in the game at Soldier Field on September 08, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings aim to win back-to-back division games this Sunday as they travel to Soldier Field to face the defending NFC North champion Chicago Bears. Dammit, that doesn’t sound right. It will be the search for seven straight wins at Soldier Field, which also feels weird. Maybe because nothing ever comes easy there. Five of the six wins were one-score games. And the previous 15 trips before that? That would be 3-12. The emotional hangover from the thrilling Week 1 win over the Green Bay Packers had better be in the rearview, because winning this one will require peak focus and execution across all three facets of the game. Let’s break it down. SETTING THE STAGE The Chicago Bears certainly played into the preseason narrative against the Carolina Panthers last week: a high-scoring offense paired with a questionable defense. The result was a 59-37 victory in which Ben Johnson’s squad put up a whopping 552 yards while giving up 478 to a Panthers offense no one will compare to the 1998 Vikings. This one was actually tied 31-31 around the midpoint of the 3rd quarter before the Bears pulled away, so it wasn’t a case of the Panthers putting up a lot of garbage-time points and stats. The Bears’ ridiculous luck forcing turnovers in 2025 carried over into Week 1 of this season, as they forced three turnovers to the Panthers’ one. Even so, the Bears were impressive on offense. I have to call it like it is. With the Vikings playing in the late window, I set up NFL Sunday Ticket to watch both this game and the Lions-Saints game so I could see it for myself. As a Vikings fan, I didn’t feel all that great afterward. VIKINGS ON OFFENSE Let’s start with the positives. Whether it’s Murray, Wentz, McCarthy, or the equipment guy at quarterback, the Vikings should be able to score points in this one. Against the Panthers, the Bears played like the team that lost a bunch of key pieces in the offseason, especially in the secondary. Even Jaylon Johnson got picked on for 127 yards and a 41.5 PFF coverage grade. In the air, Bryce Young had a day with 361 passing yards (9.8 avg.), three passing TDs, and a 110.2 passer rating. Jalen Coker went off for 8 catches, 138 yards, and two TDs. On the ground, running backs Chuba Hubbard and AJ Dillon combined for 5.1 yards per carry and a TD. Murray or Wentz, the Vikings should be able to move the ball on the road. The key will be avoiding turnovers, which seem to follow the Bears like a lost puppy. The weather in Chicago also looks to be overcast and rainy on Sunday, adding to the challenge of playing a clean game. Unlike his struggles against Jonathan Gannon, Kevin O’Connell has performed fairly well against Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen during his tenure with the Vikings. His offenses are 3-1 in games against the Saints (with Allen as head coach) and in his current role on Ben Johnson’s staff. In those games, the Vikings have averaged 25.8 points and 311 yards. These numbers were dragged down by J.J. McCarthy’s first-ever NFL start and a poor Week 11 showing, in which he passed for only 150 yards. The latter was the devastating 19-17 home loss that, in hindsight, cost us the playoffs. VIKINGS ON DEFENSE This is the main event. As the Detroit Lions’ offensive coordinator, Ben Johnson was Brian Flores’ kryptonite. He went 4-0 in those games, never scoring fewer than 30 points and averaging 404 yards per contest. He was especially effective in the running game, averaging 4.6 yards per carry and scoring 10 rushing touchdowns. When he took over as Chicago Bears head coach, with less talent to work with (particularly across the offensive line), things stabilized. Thank goodness. He went 1-1 and was held to a more modest 21.5 points and 318.5 yards per game. This we can live with. Flores also held Caleb Williams in check passing-wise last year within Johnson’s system. In the two games, he went 37/67 (55.2%) for 403 yards, 1 TD, and no interceptions. He was sacked four times for 25 yards. His overall passing rating was a paltry 77.8. The issue stems from Williams’ dual-threat capability, as he rushed 10 times for 84 yards and a touchdown. Some came on third down to extend drives. Watching him last week, he’s a menace to opposing defenses. He’s elusive in a way that’s hard to describe. While most mobile QBs sense danger early in the play and adjust accordingly, Williams can scan the field and then escape at the last second. This, in turn, puts even more pressure on the secondary to hold up for an often unsustainable amount of time. And if the coverage somehow holds, he takes off for a big gain. Putting a spy on him also limits what you can do with coverage variations and pressure packages. As I also noted in the DN’s roundtable on the Bears, Ben Johnson seems uniquely adept at exploiting holes in the 15-20-yard range in the middle of the field within Flores’ system. For some reason, he reads coverage disguises and shifts better than anyone else and consistently gets receivers into vulnerable areas. Granted, it’s only one game, and the Panthers aren’t exactly the 1985 Bears or 2000 Ravens defensively, but it sure looks like Williams has made the expected Year 3 leap under Ben Johnson’s guidance. How Brian Flores approaches this game will be worth watching. The YOLO blitz-here, blitz-there, blitz-everywhere strategy used last week could be a recipe for disaster. Jordan Love is nowhere near as elusive as the dual-threat Williams, and even so, he caught us on quite a few occasions, totaling nearly 400 passing yards. Oh, and the Bears have a more complete array of offensive weapons. Just in the running game, we’re going from no Josh Jacobs to a D’Andre Swift-Kyle Monangai combo that rushed 28 times for 224 yards and four TDs last week. No, that’s not a typo. Whatever the plan is, it almost surely means winning early downs and taking away the chunk plays that hurt us last week. This will force Williams into longer, sustained drives, where his historically low completion percentage can play in our favor. Sound tackling will be more critical than ever, which could be problematic if it is indeed rainy and wet. It also means fewer safeties at the line, then sprinting back before the snap, which Johnson has had success against over the years. You can still be creative with pressure in the Big Nickel while a safety or two play it vanilla on the backend to prevent big plays. Keeping good balance and seeing the plays develop in front of you seem like they’ll be important elements in this one. I also recall the old Mike Zimmer strategy against prime Aaron Rodgers. Getting to Rodgers was secondary to keeping him contained on the edges and bubbled up. The sacks would come when he couldn’t get out of the pocket to extend the play. I dunno, watching Williams last week, that wouldn’t hurt, either. Then again, I’m an idiot who can’t even play defense in Madden. All I know is that I don’t envy Brian Flores in this one. PREDICTION I picked the Bears to beat us on the road in Week 1 last year, and I stepped on a rake (good). I’m a huge Flores guy, and I think he will somehow keep Ben Johnson’s video game offense under 30 points. Wet conditions could also help us, since they benefit defenses (and we have the stronger unit). I think this will come down to whether our offense reaches 30 points. The good news? A so-so Panthers offense just did it, and we have more firepower. The bad news? It will mean winning the turnover battle against a Bears team that rarely loses it, and doing so without Jordan Mason (ugh). My head says the Vikings, but my gut says the Bears. Then again, my gut said the Vikings would go 14-2 in 2010 and win the Super Bowl. When it comes to the Vikings,…
author: Shawn C

title: Five Good Questions with Windy City Gridiron
summary: For the first time this year, we’ve gotten an opportunity to sit down and exchange some questions with the Minnesota Vikings’ opponent for the upcoming week. Yes, it’s the return of Five Good Questions for the 2026 NFL season. This week, yours truly got the opportunity to exchange questions with Windy City Gridiron, the home […]
full_text: For the first time this year, we’ve gotten an opportunity to sit down and exchange some questions with the Minnesota Vikings’ opponent for the upcoming week. Yes, it’s the return of Five Good Questions for the 2026 NFL season. This week, yours truly got the opportunity to exchange questions with Windy City Gridiron, the home of Chicago Bears football here on SB Nation. I sent some questions over to Bill Zimmerman from WCG, and he sent questions my way was well. You can see my responses to his questions right here , and the answers he gave me are below. 1) 59 points. Man, that’s. . .that’s a lot of points. How did the Bears manage to dominate what was thought (prior to Sunday, anyway) to be at least a decent Carolina defense in the fashion that they did? I’m not going to lie, it was a work of art. The Bears offense has been clicking all summer, so I think Bears fans expected a high-powered offense. That being said, I would assume people expected an offense that would put up, you know, 31 or 34 points. Can’t say anyone saw what we watched. It’s a cliché, but let’s just say it starts up front. The Bears offensive line controlled the tempo from the start of the game. They neutralized Derrick Brown, and he didn’t make a major impact in the game. Caleb Williams has grabbed all the headlines, but the running game is what really was the engine. The Bears rushed for 295 yards on a 7.5 yards-per-carry clip. Both D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai rushed for 100 yards or more, and the team had 6 rushing touchdowns. When the running game is rolling like that, it certainly opens up the passing game, and Caleb Williams took full advantage of that. 2) Ben Johnson stated that he wanted the Bears to be the highest-scoring offense in NFL history. That mark is currently held by the 2013 Denver Broncos, who averaged 37.9 points/game. I know it’s only been one week, but do you think the Bears can pull it off? I don’t think the Bears are going to average 38 points per game, but I do think it’s a possible outcome that they break the point-total record (with 1 additional regular-season game) of 606 points. But let’s pull back a little bit. We certainly can’t declare the Bears the greatest offense of all-time after one game, but they certainly look like they have a chance to be the best offense in the NFL this season. The 1985 Bears have the highest-scoring team in franchise history at 456 points. I think the Bears will 100% beat that this season. Heck, they are already 13% of the way there after one game. Beyond that, I will set a bold goal that’s a little lower than Ben Johnson’s. 540 total points would put the Bears in the top 10 in league history. Let’s see if the Bears can keep the offense rolling and see if an output like that is possible. I will say this: Ben Johnson is a total psycho, and I mean that in a good way. He admitted on ESPN Chicago that he considered going for 2 on the final touchdown to hit 60 points. If the Bears are sitting at like 570 points going into the final game of the season against the Vikings and they have a chance to run up the score and get that record, he’s going to do it. 3) A lot of the focus this week is likely going to be on the proverbial chess match between Johnson and Vikings’ defensive coordinator Brian Flores. If you were in Flores’ shoes, how would you go about attempting to attack this Chicago offense? I think the best bet is going to be to try to neutralize the Bears’ rushing attack and make them one-dimensional. Going back to last season, when the offense is really clicking, they are running the football really well. I think if you neutralize the rushing attack, you can try and see if you can make Caleb Williams throw some unforced errors (he hasn’t done it much the last 6 or 7 games). I know Flores is going to blitz, but I will be curious if that gets Caleb on the move where he’s really dangerous. I’m fascinated to see what Flores does to try and neutralize the offense and affect Caleb Williams. 4) While the Bears were impressive offensively, the defense still allowed the Panthers to put up 37 points of their own. The Vikings were a bit sluggish on offense for most of their win over Green Bay, and their quarterback situation is already up in the air, but is the Chicago defense still a potential point of worry in this one? Three questions about the offense- we were getting along so well, and then you had to bring up the… defense? (Vomit emoji) Yes, the defense is a huge point of concern for this team. They are going to allow a lot of points all season long. The Bears defensive line is very weak. They traded Gervon Dexter, who was their 2nd-best defensive lineman, for a draft pick and some secondary help. He wasn’t the perfect fit for Dennis Allen, and he wasn’t going to be re-signed after this season, but a lot of fans thought that was a questionable decision. Montez Sweat is still a strong performer at edge, but the other three DL can easily be controlled. Their linebackers are above average, but with the two major injuries in their secondary (Kyler Gordon and Coby Bryant), their secondary is just as questionable as their defensive line. Jaylon Johnson had a great camp but struggled against Carolina. Tyrique Stevenson is bad. The only positive right now is Dillon Thieneman, who certainly looks the part and will be a plus for their secondary. Hopefully Xavier Woods is back this week and helps stabilize the secondary a little, but I don’t know how Justin Jefferson doesn’t go nuclear this week. 5) How do you see Sunday’s game playing out? I know that weird things have a tendency to happen when these two teams meet at Soldier Field, but can anything weird enough happen to slow down this Chicago offense in their home opener? Well, what is considered slowing down the offense? I don’t expect the Bears to put up another 50-burger, so I guess that’s slowing down. But I’m usually of the opinion that, with the way these NFC North teams are, you just pick the home team to win the game. I think the Bears win the home opener. I think the Bears’ offense scores a lot of points, but I think the Bears’ defense allows a lot of points. I think the 5.5-point spread is too big. I’m not going to bet it, but if I had to, I’d take the Vikings +5.5. I am going to say the Bears win this one 34-30. I do think this is another easy over. I don’t know how the opening total was below 50 points in this one. Thanks again to Bill for taking the time to sit down and answer the questions I sent his way for this week!
author: Christopher Gates

title: Can the Vikings Survive Without Murray and Mason vs Chicago?
summary: Murray or Wentz? Flores vs Caleb? Vikings-Bears keys that decide Sunday. — On The Real Forno Show, Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano mapped Minnesota’s path to 2-0 in the NFC North before Sunday’s noon CT game at Soldier Field. The Vikings 1st & SKOL episode starts with Kyler Murray’s concussion and the NFL protocol, […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 22: Kyler Murray #1 of the Minnesota Vikings looks on after the preseason game against the Baltimore Ravens at U.S. Bank Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Murray or Wentz? Flores vs Caleb? Vikings-Bears keys that decide Sunday. — On The Real Forno Show, Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano mapped Minnesota’s path to 2-0 in the NFC North before Sunday’s noon CT game at Soldier Field. The Vikings 1st & SKOL episode starts with Kyler Murray’s concussion and the NFL protocol, then splits on the only question that matters Friday: if independent doctors clear him, do you play the starter or protect the next 15 weeks with Carson Wentz? Forness would sit him. “I wouldn’t play him,” he said, citing stacked concussions, Christian Darrisaw’s 2022 relapse, and the unofficial three-strikes calendar. “I’d rather him just miss one than miss three or four.” Stefano would play the listed starter. “Kevin O’Connell has said he’s the starter, so if he’s healthy you play the starter.” He added the cold front-office line: “He’s a one-year rental.” Forness pushed back: treat Murray like a rental and you may not get him back if he plays well. Both agreed KOC will follow the neurologists. The on-field fight is where they split again. Forness called Brian Flores vs Caleb Williams “100% the key to the game.” Williams, he said, is “more of an artist than he is a mathematician,” capable of Mahomes-Allen-Lamar throws and tight-end thickness in a 220-pound frame. In four games against Minnesota since Williams arrived, Chicago has scored 82 points (20.5 per game), with about 15 of those in garbage time. Flores’ Week 1 mix vs Green Bay was heavy base (46.3%) and two-high (67.4%). Soldier Field historically cuts the blitz: 44.4% and 40.9% in Chicago the last two visits, versus 60.0% and 77.8% at U.S. Bank. Stefano’s label from last year still fits: “We called him Houdini.” Win condition: collapse the pocket, wrap up, and don’t let the magic act walk out the back door. Darnell Wright (knee), Braxton Jones, Theo Benedet, and Joe Thuney are the pressure points. Stefano’s counter-key is Kevin O’Connell vs Dennis Allen. “When it comes to Kevin O’Connell and how he schemes against that Allen defense, I believe that’s gonna be the key.” Mason is on IR with a thumb fracture. Aaron Jones and DeeJay Dallas have to be impactful, not volume-obsessed. Forness wants Addison featured if Jaylon Johnson camps on Justin Jefferson. Johnson, asked if he enjoys the rivalry, said he does not, “because I don’t like playing against the best.” Forness also flagged Tyrique Stevenson, rookie Dillon Thieneman, and Malik Muhammad as beatable. Minnesota run defense graded first in EPA per rush allowed in Week 1 (−0.43) when the numbers were even. Key points from the episode: Kyler Murray’s status: Practiced in limited capacity Wednesday; Kevin O’Connell said he remains the starter if cleared Caleb Williams’ challenge: Must find quick answers against Flores’ blitzes — something Jared Goff did under Ben Johnson but Williams has yet to prove he can Bears offensive line concerns: Darnell Wright questionable with a knee injury, Braxton Jones replaced by Theo Benedet at left tackle Run game without Jordan Mason: Mason out at least four weeks with a broken thumb; Aaron Jones steps up as RB1, DeeJay Dallas likely fills RB2 Vikings run defense: Ranked first in EPA per rush allowed in Week 1 (negative 0.43) Jordan Addison factor: Tyler identified Addison as a potential X-factor against a weak Bears secondary, calling him “your deep ball receiver on this team” Bears cornerback Jaylon Johnson was asked if he enjoys the Vikings rivalry: “No, because I don’t like playing against the best.” Bright outlook: Tyler noted “there’s a realistic chance that this Vikings team could be 5-0 going into the bye week” Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: This is a can’t-miss matchup. Ben Johnson versus Brian Flores is “gonna be can’t-miss football,” as Tyler said in the opening. Whether Murray or Carson Wentz starts, the Vikings’ path to victory runs through disrupting Caleb Williams — and Flores has the blueprint. For full film breakdown, unfiltered analysis, and weekly Vikings coverage, catch The Real Forno Show on Vikings 1st & SKOL and the Bleav Network. Subscribe, leave an iTunes review, and join the conversation. Fan with Us!!! Tyler Forness @TheRealForno of Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL and A to Z Sports @AtoZSportsNFL , with Dave Stefano @Luft_Krigare producing this Vikings 1st & SKOL production, the @RealFornoShow found at the @BleavNetwork . So here’s two questions, Vikings fans: If Murray is cleared Friday, do you start him at Soldier Field or give Wentz one clean week? Do you trust Brian Flores to contain Caleb Williams, or will Houdini escape at Soldier Field?
author: David Stefano

title: 3-Point Stance: The Patriots most crucial to replacing A.J. Brown
summary: Last week, the New England Patriots experienced what life would be like without A.J. Brown this season. It was far from clean. Brown suffered a high-ankle sprain in the third quarter of New England’s season opener against the Seattle Seahawks on Sept. 9. Once Brown left the field, the Patriots’ offensive production regressed. Despite holding […]
full_text: Last week, the New England Patriots experienced what life would be like without A.J. Brown this season. It was far from clean. Brown suffered a high-ankle sprain in the third quarter of New England’s season opener against the Seattle Seahawks on Sept. 9. Once Brown left the field, the Patriots’ offensive production regressed. Despite holding a 10-0 halftime lead, New England fell after Seattle scored 13 unanswered points . Quarterback Drake Maye struggled to push the ball downfield in the contest. The third-year signal-caller initially threw for 79 yards and one touchdown, completing 11 of his 15 attempts. Then, following Brown’s injury, Maye connected on 12 of his next 18 attempts for 99 yards and gave away three costly fourth-quarter interceptions. Now, with the receiver landing on short-term injured reserve , he’s out for at least four games. And to add salt to the wound, NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport expects Brown to miss about six weeks of the season , which would set him up to return on Nov. 1 against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium. How will the team try to fill that void until then? Moving forward, Maye will have to operate without his No. 1 receiver and, outside of Mack Hollins, a trusted wideout like Stefon Diggs or even Kayshon Boutte. A collective effort from the offense as a whole is necessary to compensate for what will be lost. “Any injury that you get at this point in the offseason, you kind of approach it with an all-hands-on-deck approach,” offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels said on Saturday ( via WEEI ). “We’ve got a lot of different skill guys who can do a lot of different things. “There isn’t one person on our roster who can replace anybody like A.J. Brown in the middle of a game or for a stretch of the season. We’ll band together, we’ll figure out what we can do well and try to get the guys in positions to play to their strengths.” Still, it all starts with who lines up out wide. Romeo Doubs Free-agent addition Romeo Doubs had a quiet opening to his career in New England during Week 1, unable to record a single catch on his three targets. Lining up on 2nd-and-14 at his own squad’s 22-yard line, Maye rolled out to his right with the game tied at 10 apiece early in the fourth quarter. The quarterback found Doubs wide open for a first down, but the receiver turned his head early and dropped the pass. One play later, Maye threw his second turnover, leading to the Seahawks’ go-ahead field goal. “He dropped a pass. You know what I mean? Everybody drops a pass,” head coach Mike Vrabel said about Doubs on Monday. “Everybody misses a tackle. You talk to him the same way you always talk to him. Figure out a way to make a play to help us win, and he did a lot of great things during camp, just like everybody did. And so, I know he’s excited to get back out there, get to work and to find a way to help us win.” In training camp, Doubs also started slowly and didn’t make much of an impact throughout early practices. It wasn’t until his role changed, working the sideline and receiving more 50/50 balls, that he began stacking positive days. But even though Vrabel seems to remain confident in the 26-year-old, another question arises as to whether he can expand his role. In the absence of Brown, Doubs may be asked to work the middle of the field, short and at the intermediate level, which he did a lot of at the start of camp. Nonetheless, while Doubs has struggled with drops in the past, one performance doesn’t change the fact that he can be a reliable jump-ball target for Maye and excel in the red zone. In his second season with Green Bay in 2022, Doubs caught seven red zone touchdowns, ranking fourth in the NFL. Part of the offense’s success for the time being falls on Doubs finding his footing and potentially adjusting to a larger workload. Kyle Williams The same goes for second-year receiver Kyle Williams, who could help replicate Brown’s ability as a deep-ball threat if his chemistry with Maye improves. Although the pair connected on two deep-shot scores in 2025, their chemistry was largely marked by miscommunication. Moving forward, Williams has an opportunity to establish himself and earn a consistent role on the offense. Despite a quiet season opener, Williams had a standout preseason with that responsibility, catching four passes for 129 yards and three touchdowns. “Sure. I mean, we want to get Kyle involved,” Vrabel said on Monday when asked if Williams’ role may expand . “I’m hopeful that Kyle can find a role for us and find a way to help us, using his speed and catch-and-run opportunities like we saw last year at times, or some shot-type plays. The Seahawks’ defense emphasized downfield coverage last week, focusing on preventing Maye’s deep opportunities, which restricted New England to the short passing game. Maye executed that approach efficiently until he “lost patience” and began forcing unnecessary deep throws. But if the Patriots focus on the short passing game, they still need a downfield threat capable of turning any play into a touchdown. Establishing the short game opens that possibility for a deep play, as Seattle’s defense adjusts to New England’s underneath strategy. TreVeyon Henderson An effective run game also draws defenders closer to the line of scrimmage to allow those attempts, and with TreVeyon Henderson close to returning, he’ll be a key part of that. Henderson sustained an ankle injury during a practice on Aug. 24 and was sidelined through the season opener. Since then, however, Henderson has been a full participant in practices this week and said Thursday that he’s “ready to go.” Similar to Williams, Henderson is another explosive playmaker. During his rookie season in 2025, the running back forced 30 missed tackles and totaled four touchdown runs of over 50 scrimmage yards. It’s unknown whether he’ll be more effective running between the tackles or prove reliable at picking up blitzers and earning more third-down snaps. Regardless, Henderson always has a chance to take any touch to the house.
author: Andrew Guindon

title: Trade pickup Jaylen Reed showing positive strides since Patriots arrival
summary: Jaylen Reed’s first game as a member of the New England Patriots was relatively quiet. The team, however, is not concerned about its late-summer trade pickup. As secondary coach Scott Booker explained earlier this week, the team is happy with Reed’s projection since his arrival. “I think he’s doing a good job,” Booker said. “First […]
full_text: Jaylen Reed’s first game as a member of the New England Patriots was relatively quiet . The team, however, is not concerned about its late-summer trade pickup. As secondary coach Scott Booker explained earlier this week, the team is happy with Reed’s projection since his arrival. “I think he’s doing a good job,” Booker said. “First and foremost, it’s always just one of those things where you’re getting to know someone personally. When they come in the room, just trying to figure out where they’re from, where I’m from, and just trying to get a little bit of a personal relationship. Then the next thing is trying to translate what they’re defense were, where they came from, into our defensive language. That takes a couple of days. We got through those times.” Booker went on to outline the Patriots’ developmental plan for Reed. Starting in the classroom, he was later introduced to New England’s new virtual reality room and the in-practice reality. That progression apparently went well so far, even though Reed is still getting used to the intricacies of being with a new team. “He continued to improve and continued to learn,” Booker said. “The details are continuing to come to light every practice, every rep that he gets. So, excited about getting him here first off, and then also just continuing to see his progression. Each program of each 32 NFL teams does things a little bit differently. It goes to stuff in the building. Where’s the training room? How does the training room work? The cafeteria? All that type of stuff. Meetings and then also on the field. “So, just continuing to try and help him acclimate to how we do things, the communication of our safeties, the disguises and all those things that we do. He’s doing a good job and excited about him.” Coming off a four-year career at Penn State, Reed originally entered the NFL as a sixth-round draft pick with the Houston Texans. Knee and arm injuries limited him to nine games during his rookie campaign, but he started both of the Texans’s playoff games while being on the field for a combined 82% of their defensive snaps. The Patriots apparently liked what they saw from the 23-year-old, and brought him aboard in exchange for wide receiver Kayshon Boutte in late August. In his debut with the team, he played eight of 22 kicking game snaps and none on defense. Still, Booker and the Patriots like his potential within their defense. “Like any position and like anybody, the more you can do the better,” he said. “With our safeties and our corners, guys that are on the roster, having the knowledge of multiple positions if you’re able to is best. First of all, it allows you to get onto the field potentially quicker and it also helps you holistically understand, ‘Okay, if this position is doing this, then I have to do this. This is how the puzzle pieces fit.’ “We teach in a holistic way and feel like Jaylen may have some multiple-position ability. And so [we are] teaching him potentially a couple positions.”

title: Patriots defense expects challenge from Steelers’ ‘conflict piece’

[…]
full_text: The Pittsburgh Steelers offense does not lack star power. Aaron Rodgers is a future first-ballot Hall of Famer and one of the best quarterbacks of all time, while his No. 1 wide receiver, DK Metcalf, is a two-time Pro Bowler who has averaged over 1,100 receiving yards in his first seven seasons in the NFL. Add the likes of running back Jaylen Warren, tight end Pat Freiermuth and other highly-drafted players like OT Troy Fautanu and WR Michael Pittman Jr. and you get a competent group of players. All of them will present a challenge to the New England Patriots defense in their own right in this Sunday’s matchup between the two clubs. Only one of them, however, was labeled a “conflict piece” by Patriots defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr: Darnell Washington. So, how big of a challenge is the fourth-year tight end? “A big one,” Kuhr explained. “He’s athletic. Obviously, his size and strength are no joke. He’s great in the run game, like we’ve seen on tape. He did it last year and he did it last week. He gets the ball in his hands, he can make the first one miss if you’re not [playing] great technique taking him down. He is a great piece to have. He is a conflict piece.” Washington joined the Steelers as a third-round draft choice in 2023, and has since appeared in 53 games for the organization. Listed at 6-foot-7, 264 pounds, he is Rodgers’ tallest weapon and one of his favorites: in their one-plus seasons together, the veteran QB has targeted the fourth-year TE a combined 45 times resulting in 33 catches, 382 yards and a touchdown. While those numbers do not necessarily catch the eye over what amounts to a 17-game span, Kuhr and the Patriots are well aware of Washington’s ability to be a problem for their defense. “You have to play him in the run game and he’s not just like a check-down guy,” the second-year play-caller said. “He’ll run vertical, they’ll run any type of route with him. He’s got great hands and he’s a runner after the catch. He’s a piece we’re well aware of [but] as long as we play to our identity and our style, and we play within our scheme, hopefully we’re in a good spot with that.”

title: Newly-retired Stephon Gilmore reflects on Patriots tenure
summary: In terms of games played, the New England Patriots are not the No. 1 team on Stephon Gilmore’s career list. Between the regular season and playoffs, he appeared in 67 contests for the organization — one fewer than he did for the Buffalo Bills. And yet, when it came to choosing a team to retire […]
full_text: In terms of games played, the New England Patriots are not the No. 1 team on Stephon Gilmore’s career list. Between the regular season and playoffs, he appeared in 67 contests for the organization — one fewer than he did for the Buffalo Bills. And yet, when it came to choosing a team to retire with, there was no question which one it would be. “I had great early years in my career, but I think once I came to New England, I really grew into myself, mentally, physically,” Gilmore explained during a ceremony at Gillette Stadium on Friday. “I got so much better as a player. I had great coaches, I was around a lot of great veteran players that really helped me elevate my game. I had my best years here and I learned a lot here. I think I wouldn’t be the person I am today if I didn’t come to this this franchise. So, that’s why I chose New England.” Originally a first-round draft pick by the Bills in 2012, Gilmore joined the Patriots as a free agent in 2017. Over the next four seasons, he developed into one of the best cornerbacks in the game and was twice named first-team All-Pro as well as the NFL’s Defensive Player of the Year in 2019 — one of only seven cornerbacks to win the award since its inception in 1971. Gilmore, however, does not value the individual accolades quite like what he considers the favorite memory of his Patriots tenure. “I think just winning the Super Bowl,” he explained. “My first five years, I didn’t go to the playoffs. Coming here, I go to the Super Bowl the first year and we lose it to Philly. I made that big play in the AFC championship but we still lose the Super Bowl, and then winning — it’s hard. You don’t know if you’re going to go back to the Super Bowl. We were able to go back. I was able to make that play in the Super Bowl to seal the game. That that was a good feeling.” INTERCEPTADOOO!!! Stephon Gilmore intercepta a bola de Jared Goff e acaba com a boa campanha dos Rams! #NFLBrasil #SuperBowl pic.twitter.com/QNv2SF1n6b — NFL Brasil (@NFLBrasil) February 4, 2019 Gilmore’s interception of Jared Goff with less than five minutes to go in Super Bowl LIII helped the Patriots win their sixth Lombardi Trophy and the cornerback to crown himself a champion for the first time. But while that pick would be the shoo-in selection for a lot of players as the best of their careers, the 36-year-old is not so certain. For Gilmore, his pass breakup against the Jacksonville Jaguars in the previous season’s AFC Championship Game ranks right up there with the Super Bowl INT. “I think the AFC Championship play was a harder play to make,” he said. “If I don’t make that play we don’t get to the Super Bowl. But I think for me, winning the Super Bowl was a great feeling and I was able to seal it during that game. It’s hard to pick between those two plays.” Quem aí lembra dessa jogada espetacular de Stephon Gilmore na Final da AFC entre Jaguars e Patiots? 🙋‍♂️👏🏈 #NFLBrasil | #ForeverNE pic.twitter.com/U1sr7hH8MS — NFL Brasil (@NFLBrasil) January 2, 2022 In Gilmore’s opinion, his most complete game was neither the Super Bowl nor that conference championship. Instead, he pointed to a 2019 game against the Dallas Cowboys that saw him keep wideout Amari Cooper without a catch while also registering an interception. It was one of 13 picks he registered in a Patriots uniform, and one of 34 overall in a career that also included stops in Buffalo, Carolina, Indianapolis, Dallas and Minnesota. The final symbolic stop, however, was again Foxborough, Massachusetts.

(Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots will host the Pittsburgh Steelers with uncertainty on the outside. Cornerback Carlton Davis III has been listed as questionable for the 2026 home opener due to a neck injury, as Mike Vrabel previously told reporters during his Friday press conference. “I don’t want to assume, but he’ll be questionable,” New England’s head coach said of the starter, who has remained a non-participant for three consecutive practices. “We’ll have to see how he comes in here tomorrow. We’ll continue to evaluate and if the designation changes, we’ll update everybody.” Interior offensive lineman Ben Brown and outside linebacker Dre’Mont Jones also carry questionable statuses into the weekend, while rookie tackle Dametrious Crownover has been officially ruled out. Here’s the final injury report leading up to Sunday’s 1 p.m. ET kickoff at Gillette Stadium. OUT Patriots OT Dametrious Crownover (knee) Steelers CB Joey Porter Jr. (conditioning, back) Crownover, the No. 196 overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft, stayed sidelined throughout preparations because of a knee injury. The reserve tackle out of Texas A&M saw two snaps on special teams during his Patriots debut last week. And for the Steelers, there will be no Porter in the secondary. The fourth-year cornerback missed the first matchup of September and has since been listed as a partial participant for non-injury reasons, conditioning as well as a back ailment. QUESTIONABLE Patriots C Ben Brown (knee) LB Dre’Mont Jones (foot) CB Carlton Davis III (neck) Steelers WR Michael Pittman Jr. (foot) OT Troy Fautanu (ankle) Brown and Jones logged back-to-back-to-back limited practices in Foxborough before being called questionable. The picture appears less clear for Davis as well as a big-bodied wide receiver across the aisle. In the season opener versus the Seattle Seahawks, the veteran cornerback played 49 out of 50 defensive snaps despite briefly departing after making a tackle for no gain in the first quarter at Lumen Field. He was in attendance for Monday’s bonus practice before missing Wednesday, Thursday and Friday’s sessions. In the event Davis’ questionable status ends up in the inactives, the list of options to join All-Pro Christian Gonzalez on the boundary begin with 2025 waiver claim Charles Woods and team captain Marcus Jones. The depth chart also includes fifth-rounder Karon Prunty and undrafted rookie Channing Canada on the 53-man roster. And Kindle Vildor, now 80 games and 27 starts into his NFL career, resides on the practice squad. Elsewhere, running back TreVeyon Henderson and linebacker Robert Spillane have the green light and will go without game statuses after finishing New England’s work week as full participants.

title: Patriots need ‘competitive stamina’ on point in battle with T.J. Watt
summary: Coming out of the Pittsburgh Steelers’ season opener, T.J. Watt added yet another accolade to his Hall of Fame résumé. For a ninth time in his career, the standout edge rusher was named the AFC’s Defensive Player of the Week. He was effectively guaranteed the award the moment he left Pittsburgh’s Acrisure Stadium field last […]
full_text: Coming out of the Pittsburgh Steelers’ season opener, T.J. Watt added yet another accolade to his Hall of Fame résumé. For a ninth time in his career, the standout edge rusher was named the AFC’s Defensive Player of the Week. He was effectively guaranteed the award the moment he left Pittsburgh’s Acrisure Stadium field last Sunday. Watt notched two sacks in his team’s 20-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons, and scored the decisive points when he returned an interception 35 yards for his first career pick-six. Long story short, the 31-year-old is not showing any signs of slowing down. For the New England Patriots, that very well could be a problem. Entering their Week 2 matchup with the Steelers in an 0-1 hole, the Patriots are under pressure already to earn a victory against a team likely to also battle for a playoff spot in the AFC. Earning that win starts with not letting Watt dictate the game like he did versus the Falcons. The question is how to do that. For Patriots offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels, one key ingredient is fighting fire with fire: matching the intensity he is guaranteed to bring to the table. “It’s difficult to play harder than him,” McDaniels told the media on Thursday. “I think it’s probably one of the greatest compliments a coach could give to an opposing player, just the effort and the competitive nature that he demonstrates on literally every play. And so, when you line up against him, whether you’re the tight end, tackle, whoever it is — and he’ll be on both sides of the ball — you have to do a great job of having great competitive stamina. Because that’s what he’s going to play with. “And the minute you let up, he always seems to capitalize. There are not many players that get as much attention as he does, in terms of the offense trying to limit his production and his impact. The consistency with which he comes through with big plays, week after week, year after year, even though that’s happening is pretty amazing.” Against the Falcons last week, Watt lined up in his usual spot on the defensive left edge on 32 of 38 defensive snaps. The task of matching his competitive stamina on Sunday will therefore primarily fall on veteran Morgan Moses, a player well-familiar with the six-time All-Pro. Last year, Moses and Watt lined up opposite one another 60 times. The Patriots wisely shied away from exclusively trying their luck in 1-on-1 combat, using a variety of blocking structures to limit his impact. And even so, he finished the game with four quarterback pressures, including two sacks. He also forced a fumble and recovered one to help set up Pittsburgh’s game-winning drive. Unsurprisingly, Moses knows the challenge that awaits. “The same T.J. Watt. He never changes,” he said. “Consistent, knack for the ball, great pass rusher. He’s going to play every down full speed. That’s what you get from him.” Moses was beaten for one of Watt’s sacks the last time they faced off in Week 3 of the 2025 season. For him, this latest battle against the star defender will be more than a physical one, however. He knows his mental game also needs to be on point. “It’s a mental appointment,” he explained. “You know what he is, you know what he stands for. He’s been the face of that team for a long time. And so, anytime you have a guy who not just fills the stat sheet on sacks but PBUs, interceptions, forced fumbles, the things that he does that create turnovers for that team, you have to be able to obviously block him to the whistle and be ready for that challenge.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots mailbag: Will the Steelers follow the blueprint against Drake Maye?
summary: It’s been a long wait in between the New England Patriots season-opening loss and their home opener on Sunday, where they will look to get into the win column against the Pittsburgh Steelers. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. What happened to the deep-ball/explosive-play game vs. Seattle? My impression was that Seattle did […]
full_text: It’s been a long wait in between the New England Patriots season-opening loss and their home opener on Sunday, where they will look to get into the win column against the Pittsburgh Steelers. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. What happened to the deep-ball/explosive-play game vs. Seattle? My impression was that Seattle did a really good job taking away the deep ball, and I’ve seen some All-22 guys say the same. Is that what you saw, or was Maye also missing open guys? If so, why? More broadly, I suspect we’ll see a lot more teams try to replicate Seattle’s approach against Maye/Pats. Which upcoming opponents are best equipped to do it? My understanding of Seattle’s formula is four-man pressure/stunts + strong run defense despite the light front, versatile second-level defenders, and especially split-safety/quarters-Cover 6 structures designed to take away explosives, with CBs good enough to hold up. Pittsburgh has the pass rush. Can they replicate the other pieces of Seattle’s formula that gave Maye problems? – Maye The Force Be With You This is now the blueprint against Drake Maye: Take away the deep ball and force him to take the profits underneath in order to string together long drives. In last year’s playoffs, teams played two-high safeties against Maye 51% of the time. Against Seattle on Wednesday night, the quarterback faced split-safety coverages at a 57% clip. For three quarters, Maye played the effective but rather boring brand of football he needed to, living in the underneath area of the field to build a 10-0 lead. Then, he admittedly lost his patience and started throwing downfield, which led to three interceptions and a blown lead. “You can’t get bored taking what they give you, and that goes for everybody,” Mike Vrabel said. As Vrabel said, beating these defenses moving forward will start with Maye being comfortable playing boring football. The Patriots also need to straight-up run the football better against lighter boxes, which would force defenses to move the second safety down into the box and open things up downfield for Maye. They’ll get an immediate test again with the Steelers, as they played every dropback in zone in Week 1 while defensive coordinator Patrick Graham ran a similar strategy against the Patriots last season when he was with the Raiders. Who takes Brown role while he’s out – XGhost-PepperX There isn’t a 1-for-1 replacement when it comes to a player like A.J. Brown. It will be a group effort, with the Patriots utilizing multiple players and their versatility. The biggest two are Romeo Doubs and Mack Hollins. From a production standpoint, Doubs simply needs to be better than his debut in Week 1 (0 catches, 3 targets), while Hollins has already proven his chemistry with Drake Maye. From a skill-set standpoint, both players have the ability to play Brown’s primary X spot, with the other working off of them at the Z spot. Hollins filling in at the X spot could also open the door for Efton Chism III to see the field in a blocking role. Behind them, Kyle Williams will factor more into the mix due to his ability to play on the outside as well. The Patriots’ offense needs an injection of Williams’ speed, especially now in Brown’s absence. When Gonzalez covered JSN, he had 1 catch for 5 yards; not covered by CG? 7 receptions for 117 yards & a TD. Even without the 45 yard TD, it was 6 receptions for 72. Should CG have been on JSN more, especially given that Drew Lock focused on JSN for half of his passes and 2/3rds of his yards? – PatsFanFromNH Having your No. 1 cornerback follow the opposition’s No. 1 wide receiver all game sounds nice in theory. But it’s much more difficult to execute. Beyond tipping your hand when you’re playing man coverage by having Gonzalez follow JSN across the formation, there is a domino effect in zone coverages when moving your secondary around. Gonzalez would then need to know the zone assignments from wherever he ends up on the field, which would force the other defensive backs to play in different spots and then adjust based on the original movement. That creates a tall task for everyone when playing a team like Seattle, which moves JSN around the offense quite a bit. Perhaps it’s more doable against a team like Pittsburgh this week, which largely staples D.K. Metcalf to the outside. Do we think Maye’s shoulder injury is 100% healed? In Week 1, a lot of his deep attempts came out like ducks very similar to how they did in last year’s playoffs. The flea flicker to Brown was particularly egregious – Brown had him beat by a decent margin and that ball was significantly under thrown. Even some of the shorter throws to check downs in the flat came out pretty weak. – Prontocosmo215 Any noticable change to Maye’s throwing mechanics from last year regular season, to post season, to week one this season? Obviously there’s injury claims floating around – Leoa888 I believe he’s healthy and have noticed nothing on the mechanics. I think the biggest issues for the velocity was just Maye playing his first game in seven months and a lack of decisiveness on some of the throws. The flea flicker falls more in the bucket of timing, as Brown takes off downfield before Stevenson flips the ball back to Maye, who then is rushed and does not want to overthrow Brown as the receiver is running out of room vertically. Hey Brian. Do you think we see a more even distribution of snaps with the running backs this week, considering Henderson seems to be trending towards playing and Rhamondre’s heavy workload last week? – Pat In Agawam Yes, I would expect it to be more balanced. Stevenson playing 85 percent of the snaps in unattainable moving forward. The Patriots also could Henderson’s big-play ability and just overall speed on the offense Last year’s team had great chemistry. Why on Earth would they not try harder to resign Gibbens, Chaisson, & Tonga? All 3 positions lacked depth going into the season. You can’t build chemistry with 1 year rentals every season. And every draft pick they made on Day 3 is garbage. That’s why our depth will be our downfall this season. – VinnieBoombatz71 Tonga got priced out in Kansas City for the Patriots liking. Chaisson wasn’t a fit for what they were looking for off of the field. Gibbens was an interesting choice due to his value and history with Mike Vrabel, but did struggle a bit down the stretch. We’ll see if the depth ultimately improves or costs them. What are some of the things to be excited about the next week? – sumeetw Football is back in Foxboro, that’s worthy being excited about. But seriously, a bounce back Drake Maye game would be huge and while A.J. Brown’s injury is a tough loss, I am excited to see who steps up in the wide receiver room (Kyle Williams?). Will we win a single game this season? Some fans think we’re heading towards 0-17! – tsarsyrup1215 I believe they can. In fact, I’m picking them to do just that this Sunday. That’s all for this week’s #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you’d liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post on the Feed. Make sure to follow @iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.

summary: The Saints showed on Sunday that there are still some areas they need to improve. KJ Bolden is […]
full_text: BATON ROUGE, LOUISIANA - SEPTEMBER 5: Ty Benefield #2 of the LSU Tigers celebrates after a play against the Clemson Tigers at Tiger Stadium on September 5, 2026 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. (Photo by Ella Hall/University Images via Getty Images} The Saints showed on Sunday that there are still some areas they need to improve. Here are some college prospects to keep an eye on going into the Week 2 matchup who could be making major strides early this football season. DB is a position where you can never have enough talent. KJ Bolden is a name that should always stay on the radar. This nickel/safety is very versatile and is a key contributor in a Kirby Smart defense, so he should transition into the NFL very well. Bolden and the Bulldogs will be playing against Arkansas at 11 a.m. on Saturday. Tae Johnson is another safety with size and range. Johnson plays for Notre Dame and will be facing off against Michigan State on Saturday night at 6:30 p.m. Ty Benefield is a fast-rising safety at LSU. He is very experienced, but he is also a first-off-the-bus type of defender. Not only does he look the part, but he can play multiple positions across the secondary. He can play down in the box, deep off the ball or even in the slot. Benefield will be in Oxford taking on the Rebels on Saturday at 6:30 p.m. Linebacker is another position group on the defense that needs to be watched as well. Sammy Brown is a name that should be remembered. Brown is a physically gifted linebacker who can cover every single blade of grass and does not have to come off the field on third downs. Brown will be playing against North Carolina on Saturday at 11 a.m. Chris Cole is another name to watch for Georgia. Who wouldn’t want a linebacker coming out of Georgia? Cole has length at the position and can affect the passer in pass-rushing situations, but he’s not just a pass rusher. He can still play traditional linebacker as well. Georgia is playing Arkansas, so you can get a two-for-one by watching this game. We talked about cornerback last week and went over Leonard Moore. Here are two other names to watch out for. Ellis Robinson IV, yes, another Georgia Bulldog. Robinson is a long, rangy, athletic corner. He can hold his own in press-man situations and cover zones very well. Again, he plays in a Kirby Smart defense. Kelley Jones at Mississippi State is probably the best player on the defense, if not the team. His frame and athleticism started to showcase themselves near the end of last season, and if he follows that up with another good year, expect him to shoot up NFL Draft boards. Jones will have a good matchup on Saturday against South Carolina with Nyck Harbor and LaNorris Sellers at 3:15 p.m. The offensive line did not look that good in the game against Detroit, so here are two names to watch for this week. Trevor Goosby and Jordan Seaton are both star tackles with elite size and athleticism who are also great pass protectors. Goosby plays for Texas, and the Longhorns will be playing against UTSA on Saturday at 7 p.m. Seaton plays for LSU and will be with Benefield in Oxford facing off against the Rebels at 6:30 p.m. on Saturday. What are some other names you’re keeping your eyes on this weekend? Share your thoughts in the comments below.

full_text: This Sunday, the New Orleans Saints will head to M&T Bank Stadium to face the Baltimore Ravens for Week 2 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Nikhil Mehta of Baltimore Beatdown joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: Jesse Minter opened his head coaching tenure in Baltimore on a high note with a dominant 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. What were some noticeable and refreshing differences in how he prepared his team and adjusted during the game compared to John Harbaugh? NM: The Ravens had no problem looking like one of the best teams in football for large parts of their games last season. But their offense consistently struggled out of the gate, and their defense struggled to hold leads late. Neither of those issues showed up in Jesse Minter’s head coaching debut. Despite getting punched in the teeth by the Colts’ pass-happy offense to start the game, the Ravens rebounded immediately with an explosive play to Zay Flowers and two quick runs from Derrick Henry and Lamar Jackson to punch in the score. That trio ran their lead up to 18 points by halftime, but Indianapolis got a stop and a score coming out of the half to get back within two possessions. Typically, at this point, John Harbaugh’s Ravens would have started to wilt, surrendering explosive plays on defense and struggling to sustain drives on offense. But Minter and offensive coordinator Declan Doyle kept their foot on their gas and their players’ heads in the game for atll 60 minutes. NJ: Who are some notable names who will be sidelined for the Ravens on Sunday against the Saints? NM: The Ravens could have as many as four Week 1 starters sidelined on Sunday. Wide receiver Zay Flowers has been dealing with a hamstring issue for a few weeks and did not practice on Wednesday or Thursday. It would not be surprising to see Baltimore take a cautious approach with their $140 million investment. Outside linebacker Trey Hendrickson (finger), left tackle Ronnie Stanley (toe), and left guard John Simpson (groin) were also DNPs on both days, making it very possible the Ravens are depleted in the trenches, too. Hendrickson in particular was extremely effective in Week 1, but Baltimore’s depth at edge rusher and the potential return of Nnamdi Madubuike should limit the potential damage from his absence. The offensive line is a different story. Second-year swing tackle Carson Vinson would be in line to start for Stanley, while Andrew Vorhees – who struggled mightily as the starting left guard last year – would step in for Simpson. The former matching up against Chase Young could be a huge problem. NJ: What are some areas that New Orleans could potentially exploit based on what you saw from Baltimore in the season opener? NM: Jesse Minter is a serious film junkie. He is obsessed with studying opposing schemes to crack their protection codes and key in on their tendencies. But Colts head coach Shane Steichen used this against him in Week 1, starting his opening drive with seven straight passes to put the Ravens defense on the back foot. Minter and Roquan Smith admitted after the game that they were expecting Indianapolis to try to establish the run early on. Steichen happily gave them that impression and passed out of under-center and/or play-action looks that got Indianapolis deep in the red zone, where they finally turned to running back Jonathan Taylor to punch it in. Offensively, the Ravens’ passing game cooled significantly without Flowers. With rookie standout Ja’Kobi Lane also sidelined by a fractured wrist, Baltimore’s receiving corps is suddenly a little thin. Rashod Bateman posted career-lows in 2025 and was shut out in Week 1; the pressure will be on him to produce as the WR1 if Flowers is out. NJ: Who is one Ravens player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Sunday—someone who may not receive much national attention but could have a strong performance? NM: Outside linebacker Tavius Robinson was excellent in Week 1, notching four quarterback hits and one sack while leading his positional group in snaps. The 2023 fourth-round pick is entering a contract year without a strong chance at a long-term stay in Baltimore given the Ravens’ investments in Trey Hendrickson, Mike Green, and Zion Young over the past 18 months. But Robinson has been one of the team’s most-praised players by coaches and teammates alike over the past few years. His powerful 6-foot-6 frame helped him set a firm edge against the run to start his career, but he might be blossoming as a pass-rusher at the perfect time for his pocketbook. Robinson’s athleticism was a highlight of his Week 1 play, showing the ability to both contain and pursue Daniel Jones in the backfield. If the Ravens get Shough on the run on Sunday, it will likely be Robinson hunting him down. NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Ravens (-420) are currently 8.5-point favorites over the Saints (+330) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction? NM: The Ravens’ injuries are worrying, but it was clear they were just starting to stretch out their legs in Week 1. From an outside perspective, it is hard to know what to make of the Saints right now. They seem primed for a solid fight in the second year of the Kellen Moore/Tyler Shough era. In the Harbaugh years, this would be a prime trap game for Baltimore – their home opener coming off a strong win to start the season – but Jesse Minter and his staff are less likely to take their eye off the ball. Their players should follow. I think the Ravens win this one 31-20 in a game that feels much closer than the final score suggests. Thank you again to Nikhil Mehta for joining us to preview this week’s matchup! You can check out the rest of his work here .

title: Key matchups: Saints vs. Ravens
summary: The New Orleans Saints are in search of their first win of the season, and their next matchup won’t make it any easier. The Black and Gold are traveling to Maryland to take on Lamar Jackson and the Baltimore Ravens. Despite the loss, New Orleans is entering Week 2 with a bit of momentum, scoring […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: New Orleans Saints running back Travis Etienne Jr. (3) cuts back to gain more yardage and a first down during the Detroit Lions versus New Orleans Saints game on Sunday September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are in search of their first win of the season, and their next matchup won’t make it any easier. The Black and Gold are traveling to Maryland to take on Lamar Jackson and the Baltimore Ravens. Despite the loss, New Orleans is entering Week 2 with a bit of momentum, scoring 30 points in the second half and overtime against the Detroit Lions. The Saints are hoping to bring that momentum early against Baltimore. Saints pass rush vs. QB Lamar Jackson Sometimes you look at a team’s logo and immediately think of one player. For the Ravens, that player has become Lamar Jackson. The ninth-year quarterback is a four-time Pro Bowler, three-time First-Team All-Pro, and, of course, a 2x MVP. What’s so dynamic about Jackson’s game is his versatility. He has the running skills of your favorite running back, yet can throw the deep ball as well as any quarterback in the league. The former MVP will be a problem for the Saints on Sunday, but there are answers. The New Orleans pass rush must get to Jackson. While easier said than done, the best way to beat the veteran quarterback is to force him to attack the short and medium parts of the field. The Saints’ pass rush will have to contain Jackson and shorten his time to throw. The New Orleans pass rush wasn’t successful on that feat in Week 1, however, sacking Jared Goff just once in the loss. But if they want any chance to keep up with the high-powered Ravens offense that put up 41 points last week, making sure their veteran quarterback doesn’t control the game is their first task. Saints run defense vs. RB Derrick Henry Could the Saints’ run defense have been scheduled for a harder first two weeks? First, they tried and failed to limit Jahmyr Gibbs, who ran for 156 yards and 2 touchdowns. Now they must face Derrick Henry, who’s eyeing a chance to move up to ninth on the NFL’s All-Time leading rusher list. Henry was phenomenal in Week 1, rushing for 144 yards and 3 touchdowns against the Indianapolis Colts. If he logs 97 or more yards against the Saints, he’ll pass Hall of Famer Eric Dickerson on the NFL’s All-Time leading rushers list. Henry is a drastically different back from what New Orleans faced in Week 1. Instead of the shiftyness and quick side-steps they experienced with Gibbs, Henry bruises his way through NFL defenses and will be an extremely physical matchup for the Black and Gold. A physical matchup for a run defense that’s likely already exhausted after facing 33 rushing attempts against the Lions. It’s no question the Saints’ run defense will be busy on Sunday. If it’s not Henry, it’ll be Jackson. But their chances of coming out with a win improve drastically if they can hold one of the league’s best under 100 yards. WR Chris Olave vs. Ravens’ secondary The Chris Olave and Tyler Shough connection was everything we hoped for and more in the season debut. Olave ended the day with 10 receptions for 182 yards. The fifth-year wideout is in for a big season, and that continues with the Ravens. But Baltimore is preparing a game plan to slow Olave down, with veteran cornerback Marlon Humphrey saying the Ravens defense’s number one priority is “putting a cap” on the star wide receiver. Other Saints pass catchers have stepped up in place of rookie Jordyn Tyson, who is dealing with an injury. Devaughn Vele was a big winner in his season debut, and Bryce Lance made big plays. While both wideouts stepped up, Olave will need a big game if New Orleans wants to come out with a win. From young stars such as Kyle Hamilton and Nate Wiggins to veterans like Humphrey, the Ravens don’t lack talent in the secondary. But Olave has continued to show the ability to come up big and has the chance to solidify himself as one of the league’s best if he can add to his big season with a strong performance against Baltimore.
author: Kyle Besson

title: Week 2 Film Preview: Highlights from the All 22
summary: Ravens 41 – Colts 23 Inside Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday, the Ravens did not take much time to jump all over the Colts in Week 1 of the regular season. The Colts appeared far less prepared than the Ravens were for the opening week and the disparity was glaring in the first half of […]
full_text: Ravens Wham Ravens 41 – Colts 23 Inside Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday, the Ravens did not take much time to jump all over the Colts in Week 1 of the regular season. The Colts appeared far less prepared than the Ravens were for the opening week and the disparity was glaring in the first half of the ball game. The Ravens jumped out to a 31-13 lead at halftime (Multiple Colts turnovers in their own territory helped) and never looked back on the way to Jesse Minter’s first victory as Head Coach. In this segment we will look at what the Ravens did to get their victory last week and how the Saints can take advantage of what is seen on film to bounce back from their week 1 matchup against the Lions, or what some are calling, the “Best Loss in the NFL”. Pass to Set Up the Run From what is shown in the film, the Ravens coaching staff has a high level of awareness as they clearly knew the Colts would be worried about stopping Derrick Henry (spoiler alert – they didn’t) and took full advantage in the first few drives of the game. Lamar Jackson immediately began attacking the Colts defense with play action to take advantage of the focus on Henry with a 49 yard connection to Zay Flowers on a play action boot variation. Throughout the first half this was a common theme (pictured above) as the Ravens would come out with hard play action fakes to begin drives and find creative ways to get Flowers open to gash the defense, then let Henry and Jackson use their running ability inside the redzone. The Ravens utilized Flowers exceptionally well to create multiple explosive plays in the first half which the Saints must not allow to happen. The boot action by Jackson later in the game was used near perfectly to freeze defenders that should have been worried about run fits once Henry got going. The Zay Flowers Question Flowers has yet to practice this week due to a hamstring injury and this might benefit the Saints tremendously as it was clear that their passing game ran through Zay Flowers. The gameplan in week 1 featured numerous ways the Ravens lined up Flowers to intentionally get him into favorable matchups, the example pictured above led to a 54 yard touchdown as Flowers used that advantage against a Colts linebacker to decisively win an angle or Texas route and utilize good downfield blocking to finish the play in the endzone. If Flowers does not play, the Ravens offense will certainly be missing their biggest weapon from week 1 as Flowers finished with 5 receptions for 150 yards, a touchdown, and the greatest amount of separation created by a player in the NFL for week 1 (pictured below). Creative Runs After a first drive TD and an immediate turnover by Daniel Jones near the Colts own 30 yardline, the floodgates opened. The Ravens kept utilizing the play action pass but the Derrick Henry effect began to weigh on the Colts defense. Though Henry was more of a second option for the Baltimore attack, the Ravens used creative play design combined with motion and the threat of Jackson booting. Seen below is a good example of this as the Ravens used the wham play (tight end or fullback wham blocks defensive tackle) to spring Henry loose for his 32 yard touchdown that put the Ravens up 28-6 in the second quarter. This is quintessential Ravens football as they were able to bleed clock and play solid defense for the rest of the game. As long as the Saints can stay home and have a solid plan for boot action, I am confident this group can muddy the waters enough in the front 7 to not let Henry win this game on his own. Turnover Hungry Defense The Ravens defense took full advantage of the Colts week 1 rust as they intercepted Daniel Jones and stripped Jonathan Taylor on a screen play. Throughout the film it was clear their defense is going to use multiple looks to try and confuse opposing quarterbacks by mixing in zone pressures and man coverage. The Saints must improve their protection issues seen in Detroit to take advantage of the holes in the field that are opened up by an attacking style defense like this. The benefit the Saints have is that the Ravens defensive line was not very impressive versus the Colts and unlike Aidan Hutchinson (who popped up all over the tape), Trey Hendrickson (Ravens top pass rusher) had a very quiet outing, recording just one tackle and no sacks. The Saints must take care of the football if they plan on winning this game. Keys to Victory Limit explosive plays off of play action and boot passes (and expect them early) Take care of the football and correct pass protection issues (starts with Shough) Don’t let Henry get rolling (clog running lanes and make contact as close to line of scrimmage as possible)
