title: Defensive head-to-head preview: Saints vs Ravens
summary: The challenge of the NFL is that every week brings a quality opponent, and this week, it’s not just a quality opponent. The Saints will be lining up against another contender. There are two things that fans think about when they hear the Baltimore Ravens: the running game and defense. No matter the era or […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: New Orleans Saints safety Jonas Sanker (7) and New Orleans Saints defensive end Chase Young (99) wait for the play during a regular season NFL football game between the New Orleans Saints and the Detroit Lions on September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The challenge of the NFL is that every week brings a quality opponent, and this week, it’s not just a quality opponent. The Saints will be lining up against another contender. There are two things that fans think about when they hear the Baltimore Ravens: the running game and defense. No matter the era or the coach, the Ravens organization has consistently been one of the most dominant rushing teams in the NFL while also featuring one of the league’s toughest defenses, and 2026 looks like it will be no different. The Saints faced off with the Lions, and the defense was keeping the game close until the offense started putting them into some tough situations following turnovers. Also, the Saints defense had a very difficult time stopping one of the best running backs in the league in Jahmyr Gibbs. Gibbs accounted for 156 yards on 29 carries. While the Saints struggled against the run, they were able to keep the Lions from beating them through the air. Goff finished the game averaging only 5.3 yards per attempt. He finished 26-of-39 for 206 yards, and the leading receiver was Amon-Ra St. Brown. Brown finished with 10 catches and two touchdowns but only 67 yards. The Saints defense needed to be disruptive, and it was not. The Saints only had one sack and zero turnovers, and of course, there was the fumble that was NOT, which worked against the defense and the overall game. This is a game where the Saints cannot afford to give the offense manageable second and third downs. This Ravens offense will want to stay on schedule, and if the Saints can put them behind the chains and force Lamar Jackson to create from the pocket, it could tilt this game in their favor. Now, all of this is easier said than done, but the defense has to find a way to generate more negative plays and cause more disruption behind the line of scrimmage. The Ravens, on the other hand, were very disruptive, and that’s not something the Saints want to hear coming off a game in which they allowed five sacks. The Colts were only able to manage 251 total yards of offense. The Ravens had two sacks, 10 QB hits, an interception and a fumble recovery. The Colts finished the game with 17 first downs and went 3-of-10 on third-down conversions. While the Ravens had a lot of success against the offense, especially when Jones was dropping back, Jonathan Taylor, on the other hand, was able to have success. Taylor finished the game with 19 carries for 98 yards and two touchdowns. This will be an opportunity for Travis Etienne Jr. and Kendre Miller to make some things happen against a run defense that has shown some vulnerability. The Ravens feature stars at every level of the defense. The addition of Trey Hendrickson at edge during the offseason elevated the pass rush. Roquan Smith, in the middle of the defense, is one of the best linebackers in the game and one of the leaders on the team. Then there’s Kyle Hamilton, the versatile defensive back who can line up just about anywhere in the secondary and cause problems for quarterbacks. This will be a test that shows how much more the Saints need to grow or if they are on the right path toward developing an offense that can push back against some of the best defenses across the league. How do you think the Saints defense will fare against this Ravens offense? Do you think the Saints can find advantages against the Ravens defense and exploit them?
author: Anthony Parker

title: Week 2 Prediction: New Orleans Saints vs. Baltimore Ravens
summary: The New Orleans Saints came painfully close to pulling off a Week 1 upset. Now, the challenge doesn’t get any easier. New Orleans will remain on the road Sunday when it travels to Baltimore to face the Ravens in M&T Bank Stadium, as they look to bounce back from a heartbreaking 31-30 overtime loss to […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints came painfully close to pulling off a Week 1 upset. Now, the challenge doesn’t get any easier. New Orleans will remain on the road Sunday when it travels to Baltimore to face the Ravens in M&T Bank Stadium, as they look to bounce back from a heartbreaking 31-30 overtime loss to the Detroit Lions. Despite the loss, there were plenty of positives for the Saints. After falling behind 21-0, they battled all the way back to force overtime and nearly escaped Ford Field with a victory. Quarterback Tyler Shough delivered an impressive performance, throwing for 410 yards and three touchdowns despite committing three turnovers. Chris Olave was his favorite target, hauling in 10 passes for 182 yards. If nothing else, the comeback showed this Saints team is very capable of responding when things go wrong. But they can’t afford another slow start against Baltimore. The Ravens opened their season with a dominant 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts, piling up 506 yards of total offense. Lamar Jackson threw for 324 yards, while Derrick Henry rushed for 144 yards and three touchdowns. That combination presents a major challenge for a New Orleans defense that struggled early against Detroit before settling in as the game progressed. Containing Jackson is difficult enough, but the Saints will also have to find a way to slow Henry down and keep Baltimore from controlling the game on the ground. There is, however, some uncertainty surrounding the Ravens’ offense. Wide receiver Zay Flowers, who had 150 receiving yards in Week 1, left the game with a hamstring injury, so his status very questionable. For New Orleans, the biggest question may be whether Tyler Shough can build on his Week 1 performance while eliminating the costly mistakes. Throwing for over 400 yards in his first start of the season was impressive, especially after the Saints fell into such a large early hole. But three turnovers against a team as talented as Baltimore could quickly put New Orleans in another situation where it is forced to play from behind. The Saints showed enough in Detroit to make me believe they can keep this game competitive. Shough and Olave showed they can create explosive plays, and the team displayed the kind of resilience that had been missing for a while. Still, Baltimore presents an even tougher challenge. Playing Jackson and Henry on the road is a difficult assignment for any defense, and unless the Saints can force Baltimore into some mistakes of its own, I think the Ravens ultimately make enough plays late to remain undefeated. Prediction: Ravens 31 – Saints 27 New Orleans may leave Baltimore 0-2, but if Shough can clean up the turnovers and the Saints once again go toe-to-toe with one of the NFL’s better teams on the road, there will still be plenty of reason to believe this team is heading in the right direction. title: Our defense vs. their offense: Baltimore Ravens
summary: The New Orleans Saints currently have the 21st ranked defense in the NFL following their 31-30 overtime loss versus the Detroit Lions in week one action. The Saints gave up 369 total yards of offense while 204 of those came through the air (18th in pass yards allowed) and the other 165 were given up […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) drops back to pass during the Detroit Lions versus New Orleans Saints game on Sunday September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints currently have the 21st ranked defense in the NFL following their 31-30 overtime loss versus the Detroit Lions in week one action. The Saints gave up 369 total yards of offense while 204 of those came through the air (18th in pass yards allowed) and the other 165 were given up on the ground (28th in rush yards allowed.) 31 points allowed left the Saints tied for 23rd in defensive scoring with the Denver Broncos and Buffalo Bills. Although New Orleans ultimately lost the turnover battle in week one, they still managed to force one (should have been two?) takeaway against Detroit by way of a forced fumble. Safety Jonas Sanker led the team with ten tackles last weekend while DE Carl Granderson was credited with the lone sack for the black and gold. Vernon Broughton delivered the fumble recovery after a strong punchout on Jahmyr Gibbs. Baltimore’s offense is second in the league in total offense after their 506 yard outburst against the Indianapolis Colts last Sunday. The Ravens put up as astounding 304 passing yards (5th) and 202 rushing (3rd) behind QB Lamar Jackson. The Ravens put up the second most points in the NFL last weekend as they dropped 41 on the Colts. Jackson was responsible for two total touchdowns while RB Derrick Henry rushed for three more. WR Zay Flowers was on the receiving end of Jackson’s lone TD pass and finished his day with 150 yards on just five receptions. TE Mark Andrews added another four catches for 49 yards. Although he did not throw an interception during last week’s contest, Jackson still had one fumble that he lost which led to a four-play TD drive for the Colts. New Orleans will now attempt to avoid an 0-2 start to the season on the road against a top offense in the league. Even with Flowers, one of Lamar’s top pass catching threats, still questionable to go versus New Orleans (hamstring,) Baltimore has deep offensive firepower and will be a challenge for a young Saints defense to contain.

title: New York Giants mailbag: First impressions, retired numbers, penalty reviews
summary: Bob Donnelly asks: It’s great to see the Harbaugh era start with a W and there’s certainly a lot to get excited about. I’m sure there are some in the glass half empty crowd that will say that the W is nice and John is 1 and 0 in one score games, but there remains […]
full_text: Bob Donnelly asks: It’s great to see the Harbaugh era start with a W and there’s certainly a lot to get excited about. I’m sure there are some in the glass half empty crowd that will say that the W is nice and John is 1 and 0 in one score games, but there remains some of the latent issues that often derailed this team last year with ball security (4 fumbles , 2 turnover-worth plays) and penalties (#1 penalty yards) leading the list. As you reflect on the first game performance under Harbaugh what areas concern you most? Ed says: Bob, absolutely nothing has changed from my preseason evaluation of the Giants. The biggest areas of concern entering the season were cornerback play and defensive line depth. Nothing about Sunday changed that. Tae Banks was OK. I thought he got pushed off on the touchdown he surrendered. I didn’t think Greg Newsome was that good against the Cowboys, but he was a lot better than Paulson Adebo. Colton Hood still isn’t ready for full-time duty. DJ Reader and Shelby Harris were fine. When they were replaced by Darius Alexander and C.J. Okoye, Dallas had more success running the ball. If they can find a run-stuffing veteran defensive tackle who can help them get through this season that would be great. Adam Jacobs asks: I have an offbeat question about the taunting penalty by Javonte Williams. Every penalty that occurs in the field of play is marked at the spot of the foul unless it occurs behind the line of scrimmage. Except the Williams penalty. Why was this enforced after the play was finished, and not from the spot of the foul? I am not sure I have ever seen this before. Do you have any idea how this works? Ed says: Adam, taunting is treated as a dead-ball foul. Thus, the result of the play stands. The penalty is assessed after the play. Kölnerbigblue asks: Ed, I know teams can request a review of penalties after the game. Not that it will change any results, can you explain how this process works? Ed says: The NFL audits every snap during the days after games, looking at calls and non-calls. That is both to assess the performance of the offcials, and to determine discipline when it comes to handing out fines. NFL teams can send a maximum of 10 plays to the league office each for review, clarification, explanation. Sometimes, the league will admit that a mistake was made. That, though, will not affect an outcome or result in a do-over. James Pauloski asks: For me, the most amazing statistic from the Cowboys game was that Dallas only had two possessions in the second half. Yes, they scored two touchdowns, but that was it. That seems almost impossible. Did the Giants tie (or set) a record for allowing only two possessions in one half? Ed says: James, I have been unable to find anything to answer that directly. What I can say is that each team had only seven possessions on Sunday, making 14 total (yes, I can do math!). That is an incredibly low total. There was a 2023 game between the Denver Broncos were there were only 12 possessions, six for each team. It speaks to efficiency by both offenses as there were five drives in the game that took more than six minutes, two of those by the Giants lasting more than eight minutes. Todd Kuehn asks: Ed, I really like looking at box scores when the game is over because the information and numbers in them are all objective instead of subjective except for two of them. Maybe I’m wrong about that but when you look at the QBR and the RTG for quarterbacks from the Dallas game it seems to me maybe they are subjective. Dart got a really good RTG 134.2 and Prescott only had 84.8. But when you look at the QBR Dart received 81.5 and Prescott had an 89. How can that be? There is no doubt in almost everyone’s mind that Dart outplayed Prescott. Ed says: Todd, there is no perfect quarterback measuring stick. PFF uses a different methodology than QBR, passer rating, etc. As Tony DelGenio pointed out this week , Pro Football and Sports Network’s ‘Impact Score’ had Dart as the second-highest rated quarterback this week with Prescott 14th. It all depends what they are grading and with they give importance to. Bottom line is that no matter how Dart was graded by any rating system, it was clear that he played very well and did the things needed for the Giants to win a football game against a good team. Martin Hand asks: Hi Ed, I just saw an article about Gronkowski and that his number had not been retired yet… It made me think about our situation with Malik and Abdul… Don’t you think it is a bit self-absorbed for an retired individual to think that the number is his and does not belong to the franchise… Players last a few years, whereas the Giants will last forever… I don’t have my heels dug in over this one, but couldn’t help to think about it and wanted to ask you what you thought. Ed says: Martin, I can’t say I have ever heard that opinion before. Players don’t decide to retire their numbers. Franchises do that in honor of those players. So, yes, the number belongs to the franchise and that is what the franchise has chosen to do with it. To be honest, I vehemently disagree with the whole idea of “unretiring” numbers. I think sometimes well-meaning franchises retire too many numbers. Here is the list of Giants’ retired numbers . I think the Giants allowed Malik Nabers to wear the previously retired No. 1 jersey opened a Pandora’s Box that led to the Abdul Carter mess, and that it won’t be the last time there is a situation like that. Numbers, though, get retired because of a player’s accomplishments. That means something to that player, and to the player’s family. Why should a kid fresh out of college who has done nothing get the number of an all-time franchise great? Because his “brand” revolves around that number? Please. Jeffrey Jacobs asks: Do you see any scenario where the Giants mange to pry Joey Porter Jr. away from the Steelers, and if so what do you think it would take? Ed says: Jeffrey, of course there is a scenario where the Giants try to pry Porter Jr. away from the Steelers. I think it is highly unlikely, but if the Giants believe the player is worth the draft capital they would have to surrender and the big price tag they would have to pay him they would try to make it happen. Spotrac recently posted what their model believes Porter’s price tag would be: Trading CB Joey Porter Jr. New Team Acquires 2026: $3.5M 2027: UFA #Steelers Dead Cap 2026: $1.4M The 26-year-old projects toward a 4-year, $110M extension according to our model. — Spotrac (@spotrac) September 18, 2026 Four years, $110 million would make Porter the seventh-highest paid cornerback in the NFL in terms of average annual value. Is he really worth that kind of money? Also, the Giants are extremely reluctant to give out contracts of that length. Andrew Thomas and Brian Burns, arguably the two best players on the team not currently on four-year rookie contracts, are the only veteran players with deals of longer than three years. Are the Giants really going to go there for Porter? Remember, not too far down the road they will have to negotiate long-term deals with Jaxson Dart, Malik Nabers, and Abdul Carter. As for trade cost in terms of draft capital, I can’t imagine the Steelers being able to drive a hard bargain for Porter if they choose to move him. I am not offering more than an early-Day 3 pick considering the contract I would have to give him. Marcus Mbow bonus I was asked many times during the offseason if I knew whether or not second-year offensive tackle Marcus Mbow has put on weight during the offseason. Until Thursday, I couldn’t answer the question because I had not spoken to him at all. I got a chance to speak with him for a minute in the locker room this week. For all of you obsessed by Mbow’s weight, he put on 15 pounds this offseason and is now around the 320-pound mark. Submit a question Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

title: NY Giants’ DL Chauncey Golston is under-sized, but still plays big role
summary: Chauncey Golston would like to clear something up. The New York Giants veteran defensive lineman is not, and never has been, a stand-up edge defender. “I played the edge, but stand-up? It’s always funny to hear that,” Golston said while sitting at his corner locker in the Giants’ makeshift locker room this week. “I never […]
full_text: Chauncey Golston | Getty Images Chauncey Golston would like to clear something up. The New York Giants veteran defensive lineman is not, and never has been, a stand-up edge defender. “I played the edge, but stand-up? It’s always funny to hear that,” Golston said while sitting at his corner locker in the Giants’ makeshift locker room this week. “I never played stand-up.” Why the misconception? “I’m classified as an edge guy. And you really just go off of what you’re classified as,” Golston said. “It all depends on what defense you’re in. Like, if you’re in a 4-3 and it says defensive end, you’re just an edge guy. But then you go to 3-4, and then it says defensive end, and you can be Cam Hayward. “It’s very multiple. It’s all depending on where you’re playing at. And then for me, being a guy that’s smaller, I guess it just stands out more.” In the second season of a three-year, $18 million free agent deal he signed with the Giants, Golston has emerged as a key part of the Giants’ defensive line. Generally, Golston is playing some form of defensive end when the Giants are aligned with three down linemen. The 28-year-old played 28 snaps in Week 1 vs. the Dallas Cowboys. Via Pro Football Focus, the breakdown was as follows: DLT (9 snaps) DRT (3) LE (8) LEO (1) RE (4) REO (3) Amazingly, Golston is fighting guards, tackles, tight ends, and double teams at just 265 pounds. “I don’t have the ability to be like I can just roll out there and be big and I can take on two people. I can’t do that,” Golston said. “If I don’t come technique first, then I’m going to be out there, and it’s just going to look like Michael Oher in ‘The Blind Side’. I can’t have that.” Golston weighed 285 pounds when he played for the Dallas Cowboys, but lost the weight last season because the Giants were not asking him to play inside. “For what I did last year, I didn’t really ever go inside last year. So it was like, what do I need to be 285 for?,” Golston said. Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson pointed to Golston understanding the physical gifts he does possess, and having consistent technique. “He’s not a big guy, but he plays big,” Wilson said. “He uses his length, his arm length. He plays with good center of gravity. He gets good vertical knockback. When you watch him, his technique is always the same. He plays same foot, same shoulder. He squeezes and constricts blocks. He plays the way that you’re supposed to play when you’re in that position. And he’s done it in the past. It’s not like he hasn’t done it. And Chauncey, man, kudos to him. He’s a guy that’s playing a five-technique in our base front. He moves around. He has a lot on his plate, but he’s doing a great job for this defense.” Golston’s primary physical gift is his long arms. He has 34¾-inch arms that put him in the 87th percentile, and a 96th percentile 84⅜-inch wingspan. “I have longer arms than the guards. I’m quicker than them,” Golston said. “I know how to work off the people around me. Those are some of the things that really help me when I’m in there.” The six-year veteran says it also helps that “I’ve been doing that for a while now.” “The overall amount of reps that I’ve had in my career because I also did that in Dallas … this is familiar territory,” Golston said. “With me playing end, a lot of it is I usually can feel what the scheme is. I can usually feel when it’s power because everything’s going fast this way, but then I see something flashing back that way, usually indicating that it’s something that the run is trying to hit outside of me. It’s little things that I’m able to pick up on because I play on the edge and I also play in there that just help me.” Golston was on some winning teams earlier in his career with the Cowboys, and says “you can always feel the energy” when a team is good. “Winning is contagious,” Golston said. “Not just winning the game, but just having a winning attitude overall, attacking everything, attacking the process. I really feel that. You can feel it, you can see it, and that’s really cool to be a part of. And, to be able to play my own part in it. “And be able to help the people that are coming after me. That are coming up under me. Being able to tell them the little that I do know. And watch them take that and excel.”

title: NY Giants news: CB Paulson Adebo placed on IR, Malik Nabers, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need as the New York Giants get set to fly to Los Angeles to face the Rams on Monday. NFL Week 2 picks, predictions, schedule, odds, fantasy tips | ESPN.com RB Cam Skattebo handled 60% of the Giants’ backfield touches in Week 1, including […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need as the New York Giants get set to fly to Los Angeles to face the Rams on Monday. NFL Week 2 picks, predictions, schedule, odds, fantasy tips | ESPN.com RB Cam Skattebo handled 60% of the Giants’ backfield touches in Week 1, including four red zone carries. New York ranked eighth in run block win rate (78.4%), while Los Angeles allowed 174 rushing yards in Week 1. The Rams’ Myles Garrett (knee) is sidelined, and Donald hasn’t played in over two seasons and could be limited if he returns. Skattebo has a favorable matchup and a substantial workload. Cam Skattebo is a Giants throwback that Brandon Jacobs can appreciate | New York Post Alone inside his hotel room, only 25 minutes away from MetLife Stadium, a jet-lagged Brandon Jacobs started excitedly yelling at the television every time Cam Skattebo crashed into a Cowboys defensive player with purpose. “He definitely doesn’t give a damn,” Jacobs told The Post. “His attitude shows that. Just the way he carries himself. Believe the hype: Giants ’ bully ball | Yahoo! Sports The Giants, too, showed off their bully ball offense in the season opener, completely steamrolling the Cowboys’ defense with heavy personnel and Cam Skattebo treating every tackle attempt like an insult. Pat Ricard led the way on plenty of runs behind the Giants’ talented offensive line. Francis Mauigoa had a good showing in his first NFL action at right guard, along with the strong tackle pairing of Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor. I was impressed by the Giants’ auxiliary blockers at the skill positions, too. Isaiah Likely caught the passes, but the other Giants tight ends showed up to set the edge and create space for the running backs to pick their spots. And rookie Malachi Fields, one of the best blocking prospects in this year’s wide receiver class, picked up where he left off in college, providing several crack blocks on the edge and the willingness and ability to insert inside. The Giants’ Week 2 opponent, the preseason Super Bowl favorite Rams, had issues in 2025 against heavier personnel groupings. L.A. allowed 5.9 yards per play on early downs against offenses with two or fewer wide receivers. The 10 best NFL player matchups to watch in Week 2 | PFF New York Giants WR Malik Nabers vs. Los Angeles Rams CB Trent McDuffie. Monday night’s showdown is sneakily a big one. The Rams hope to play in much greater rhythm against a Giants team with momentum. This game incorporates several fascinating player matchups, but none better than this. Nabers made his return from an early-season torn ACL and was effective. Against Dallas, he caught six of nine targets for 69 yards, compiling a 71.0 overall PFF grade with 2.88 yards per route run. While Los Angeles’ defense experienced a cataclysmic opener, McDuffie was the exception. In his Rams debut, McDuffie made his presence felt against both the pass and run to earn an 83.4 overall PFF grade. Given the Rams’ zone-heavy approach against the 49ers — deploying such looks on 84.6% of defensive snaps — it’s possible we’ll see Nabers rotate against both McDuffie and Jaylen Watson. Nonetheless, the snaps between these two players will be a great war. Giants’ John Harbaugh assures benched player he is not ‘in the doghouse’ | NJ.com Giants coach John Harbaugh benched running back Tyrone Tracy during Sunday’s season-opening win over the Cowboys. But Harbaugh isn’t giving up on Tracy. Or so Harbaugh insists. We’ll see what happens Monday night, when the Giants visit the Rams. It’s entirely possible that Devin Singletary could continue to be the Giants’ secondary back, behind Cam Skattebo. The view from Los Angeles If you think you know how the league views the Giants right now, think again. ​Rams tackle @robhavenstein78 joins tomorrow's @BleavNetwork crossover to set the record straight on #BleavinGiants x #BleavinRams . ​Set your reminder right now—you do NOT want to miss this one: 🚨🏈 pic.twitter.com/vmJHJJ8aAN — Carl Banks (@CarlBanksGIII) September 17, 2026 Giants’ Chris Horton: Dominic Zvada’s kickoffs are strategic, not simple | USAToday.com Horton credited Zvada for his five kickoffs Sunday night against Dallas. The Cowboys often use one returner, and Horton said moving that player with precise placement takes skill. “He came out here, he practiced his butt off for us to put that ball in,” Horton said. “Sunday night, I mean, he was on point, and it was really good.” The same process guides field-goal range. The staff warms Zvada up, picks a line and sticks with it unless weather intervenes. To start a game, the Giants felt good from 58 yards. Of course, he never had to attempt one. “If you’ve got to start the game, we feel good at like 58 yards,” Horton said. “This kid, he has a strong enough leg to get the ball there. But it’s all about the consistency.” Inside the saga around Joey Porter Jr.’s future with Steelers | ESPN.com The two sides have been here because of a significant difference between the Steelers’ view of Porter’s value and how Porter values himself. The core issue is the structure of the contract, sources told ESPN, and the Steelers’ organizational precedent that doesn’t fully guarantee a healthy portion of the contract was considered a sizable hurdle. The sides simply did not get close to bridging that guaranteed gap, which sources say made any talks about a per-year average on a deal moot. “It never even got that far,” a source said. The Steelers could trade Porter, though the team has neither made nor received any serious inquiries about the cornerback. One NFL executive believes the Steelers could get a second-round pick in exchange for Porter and a quality Day 3 draft selection. title: Giants at Rams: Aaron Donald to play, Puka Nacua doesn’t practice
summary: The New York Giants got a mixed bag of news with respect to their opponents on Monday Night Football. Future Hall Of Fame defensive tackle Aaron Donald told reporters on Friday that he plans to play Monday night. At the same time, it was reported that receivers Puka Nacua and Jordan Whittington didn’t practice on […]
full_text: Los Angeles Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald | Getty Images The New York Giants got a mixed bag of news with respect to their opponents on Monday Night Football. Future Hall Of Fame defensive tackle Aaron Donald told reporters on Friday that he plans to play Monday night. At the same time, it was reported that receivers Puka Nacua and Jordan Whittington didn’t practice on Friday. That comes as a bit of good news for the Giants. There has been some question as to how much Donald will be able to contribute in his first game back after two years of retirement. It’s a valid question, however the Giants should prepare for Donald at his best. Donald has always been an athletic freak as well as incredibly skilled. While he declined in the years before retiring, his decline was from “the best to ever do it” to merely “the best doing it right now.” On the flip side, Nacua and Whittington popping up on the injury report is a potential boon for the Giants. Nacua is one of the best receivers in the NFL, while Whittington is a very capable returner. Nacua being limited, or potentially out, would be a boon with starting CB Deonte dealing with calf tightness and Paulson Adebo being placed on injured reserve. The Giants should prepare as though all the Rams’ players will be available and at full strength. However a win is significantly more likely if they catch a break or two on the injury front.
author: Chris Pflum

title: NY Giants place struggling, highly-paid CB on IR with knee injury
summary: The New York Giants are placing cornerback Paulson Adebo on injured reserve with a knee issue, head coach John Harbaugh confirmed to media at practice on Friday. Adebo, in the second year of a three-year, $54 million contract, struggled this spring and summer and did not start in Week 1 against the Dallas Cowboys. Greg […]
full_text: Paulson Adebo | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants are placing cornerback Paulson Adebo on injured reserve with a knee issue, head coach John Harbaugh confirmed to media at practice on Friday. Adebo, in the second year of a three-year, $54 million contract, struggled this spring and summer and did not start in Week 1 against the Dallas Cowboys. Greg Newsome and Deonte Banks did. Adebo played only 10 snaps in that game. Adebo also missed five games last season with a knee injury. Expected to be the Giants’ No. 1 cornerback when he signed in free agency, Adebo has not played up to that expectation. The Giants reportedly signed cornerback Nikko Reed off the Los Angeles Chargers’ practice squad on Monday, meaning he would take Adebo’s roster spot. The Giants also added cornerback Jaden Robinson to the practice squad, dropping offensive tackle Ryan Schernecke. Banks did not practice on Friday. He is dealing with a calf injury. It isn’t injury-related, but Harbaugh confirmed that defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson was not at practice due to a personal matter. title: Todd McShay September mock draft
summary: The New York Giants may be getting ready to travel across the country to take on the Los Angeles Rams, but as the saying goes: It’s always draft season. NFL scouting departments are racing around the country to evaluate every prospect they can, while front offices are constantly evaluating and re-evaluating their squads. For now, […]
full_text: Texas left tackle Trevor Goosby blocks. | Getty Images for ONIT The New York Giants may be getting ready to travel across the country to take on the Los Angeles Rams, but as the saying goes: It’s always draft season. NFL scouting departments are racing around the country to evaluate every prospect they can, while front offices are constantly evaluating and re-evaluating their squads. For now, improvements are limited to picking up street free agents or trading for players. But understanding their strengths and weaknesses is vital to the off-season plan. Draft analyst Todd McShay released his September Mock Draft this week, and this is a good opportunity to take stock of where the Giants are as a team to start the season. 12. New York Giants: OT Trevor Goosby, Texas 6 feet, 7 inches, 325 pounds John Harbaugh wants to rebuild the Giants from the offensive line out, and Goosby fits the physical, heavy-personnel offense that Matt Nagy is installing. Goosby looks the part of an NFL left tackle and could kick over to right tackle for the Giants. His length, mass, and natural power make him difficult to get around or go through, and he can create movement in the running game. Quicker rushers can stress his footwork and change-of-direction ability, but the starting-tackle traits are obvious. Chris’ thoughts As things stand now, Goosby is the top tackle in the draft and a shoe-in for a Top-10 pick most years. But this isn’t most years and McShay has six quarterbacks going in the first 9 picks. That will push blue chip talent down to teams that ordinarily wouldn’t expect to have access to those players. That said, I don’t want to get too caught up in the prospect at this point. Instead, I want to use this in the same way as I use our Saturday college posts; as a different lens through which to look at the state of the Giants. From a philosophic perspective, I do like the approach of finding a long-term bookend for Andrew Thomas and remaining committed to building the biggest, baddest bully on the block. It’s widely expected that Sisi Mauigoa will eventually kick out to right tackle, but after watching him at guard… Why? He played very well against quality opponents in Week 1 and looked like a natural fit at right guard. Leaving him there and finding a new right tackle once Jermaine Eluemunor’s time is done might be the best course of action. However, I also don’t think this is the time to do so. Eluemunor is a solid right tackle and the Giants just re-signed him to a three-year contract. They also have 6th round rookie JC Davis who could develop in the meantime. I could see drafting an offensive tackle high in 2028 if Eluemunor begins to decline or Davis doesn’t develop, but for now the Giants have more pressing long-term needs. As things stand now, I would look at defensive tackle, cornerback, and wide receiver as the positions of greatest need. This also looks like a fantastic year for all three positions. At iDL, McShay has four defensive tackles going in the first round, each after the Giants’ pick at 12 (more on that in a bit). Will Echoles (Ole Miss) – 18th overall – Jacksonville Jaguars A’Mauri Washington (Oregon) – 22nd overall – New England Patriots Bear Alexander (Oregon) – 31st overall – Buffalo Bills David Stone (Oklahoma) – 32nd overall – Cleveland Browns (via Los Angeles Rams) Each of those players would have an immediate impact on the Giants’ defense and could be core pieces as the Giants continue to build their defense. His Top 50 board also has three corners who could be in range for the Giants in the first round: Ellis Robinson IV (Georgia) – 25th overall Vicari Swain (South Carolina) – 27th overall Zach Lutmer (Iowa) – 29th overall The Giants’ starting corners are on one-year contracts and they might find that they need to continue to infuse talent into their secondary. Lutmer, in particular, could be interesting as a multi-faceted Nickel or STAR in Dennard Wilson’s defense if Dru Phillips struggles. And finally there are several wide receivers who could be available depending on where the Giants pick. Charlie Becker (Indiana) – 14th overall Ryan Coleman-Williams (Alabama) – 31st overall T.J. Moore (Clemson) – 40th overall Trey’Dez Green (TE, LSU) – 12th overall Green may be a tight end, but he’s an exceptionally talented pass catcher who can be a nightmare mismatch for a lot of defenses with the ability to be a factor at all levels of the field. Likewise, each of the receivers in the Top 50 that the Giants may realistically be able to draft have the potential to add the kind of explosive deep threat that they lacked in Week 1 against the Cowboys. The big question, of course, is where the Giants will be picking, and the order for this mock draft is based on FanDuel’s Super Bowl odds. That said, McShay and Steve Muench each said in a recent podcast that if the Giants keep playing like they did against the Cowboys, they could be one of the real surprise teams this year. Some have even gone as far as to suggest that the Giants could be a 10 or 11-win season. That would be enough to have them drafting in the late teens or 20’s if they make the playoffs. That would lock them out of the Blue Chip talent, but the glut of quarterbacks could still push some very talented players down the board to them. One of the things to keep an eye on as the year progresses is if the Giants need to continue building their offense around Jaxson Dart or whether they’ll be able to continue to add highly drafted players to their defense. Either way, early mocks like these give us an opportunity to step back and see how the Giants can be most helped as the year unfolds.
author: Chris Pflum

title: NY Giants-Rams matchup: Los Angeles offense will provide stern test
summary: The New York Giants travel to Los Angeles for their second consecutive prime-time game, where they will face the 0-1 Rams. Los Angeles is coming off a disappointing 27-7 loss to the San Francisco 49ers in Australia on Thursday night. The Rams’ decision to travel to Australia just 28 hours before kickoff drew heavy scrutiny […]
full_text: Matthew Stafford | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants travel to Los Angeles for their second consecutive prime-time game, where they will face the 0-1 Rams. Los Angeles is coming off a disappointing 27-7 loss to the San Francisco 49ers in Australia on Thursday night. The Rams’ decision to travel to Australia just 28 hours before kickoff drew heavy scrutiny after San Francisco dominated the game, holding a seven-minute advantage in time of possession and out-gaining Los Angeles by 89 yards. Nevertheless, Los Angeles remains a top team in the NFL, and they’ve had over a week to stew on the loss, but they did lose star defensive end Myles Garrett to a knee injury. Injuries are a factor, of course, but one of the crucial factors in the game will be the trenches, and the Rams offensive line struggled against the 49ers. Battle of the trenches As a weak link system, offensive line play is often about making sure no player blows an assignment and messes up. Perfect Blocks track plays in which no player messes up and blows and assignment. Week 1 Rates & EPA on those Perfectly Blocked plays pic.twitter.com/G30xTahJHp — Jrfortgang (@throwthedamball) September 16, 2026 The Rams blew assignments on the offensive line, and Raheem Morris’ defense was harrassing, although they failed to sack future Hall of Famer Matt Stafford. The Giants have the personnel to be a top-five pass rush in the league, especially if Abdul Carter lives up to his insanely high potential. Dallas focused on Brian Burns in Week 1 — will Sean McVay’s offense do the same? The Rams have a physical and big offensive line that can command the point of attack. Alaric Jackson (LT) and Steve Avila (LG) are a quality tandem on the left side, with Warren McClendon Jr. (RT) and Kevin Dotson (RG) on the right. Coleman Shelton centers the line. One of the biggest matchups in the game, quite possibly, is D.J. Reader against the interior offensive line. Reader was outstanding in Week 1 for the Giants, and he’ll have to be again against a team that will try to run DUO and displace, while marrying its run game to its dynamic passing attack. Overall, the Giants must be on their P’s and Q’s up front. The Rams’ receivers block their back side off, and I expect to see a heavy dose of Kyren Williams and Blake Corum. The Giants’ pass rush can certainly take advantage of the pair of tackles, and the speed of Carter and Burns could look to win against the more power-based line that the Rams possess, but the strength of players like Dotson and Avila could easily give the edge to Los Angeles. The matchup Los Angeles will frequently use 12/13 personnel with a combination of the four tight ends: Colby Parkenson, Tyler Higbee, Terrance Ferguson, and Davis Allen ( if healthy, was concussed in Week 1 ). The Rams were in 13 personnel on 44% of their snaps in Week 1. They took a big deficit and played 11 personnel at a 46% rate, but expect heavier usage in neutral game scripts, which will prompt the Giants to use their five-man front with Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese on the backside. A combination of these players would join Reader up front with the first-team base package: Chauncey Golston, Shelby Harris, Kayvon Thibodeaux, Abdul Carter, and Brian Burns. The Giants did spell Harris and Reader with Darius Alexander and C.J. Okoye — I will be very nervous when that happens against the Rams. Alexander and Okoye were liabilities up front, and McVay will attack them with DUO. Kyren Williams saw 13 carries to Blake Corum’s 10; the former averaged 3.7 yards on the ground with 2.09 yards after contact and a touchdown, while the latter averaged 5.4 yards on the ground with 1.50 yards after contact. This dynamic duo will be a threat in DUO. The rushing attack will set up play-action shots to the Rams’ receivers. McVay will use 11 personnel to get Dru Phillips on the field, where he’ll likely see Davante Adams in the slot — this is a mismatch to exploit. Stretch-zone play-action passes outside the numbers to displace and get the Giants moving away from the throw will be a successful option for McVay if the Giants start to buckle against the run. Then there’s Puka Nacau. He aligned at just a 12.5% rate in the slot, but I can see him moving there for his blocking and the mismatch against Phillips. He only caught five of his nine targets for 74 yards in Week 1. The Giants’ cornerbacks will be tested against Nacua, Adams, and Stafford. Similar to Dak Prescott, I don’t think we’ll see many blitzes, but there will be simulated pressures and twists in defensive passing-favorable situations. Stafford is quick to see the field and still has a cannon attached to him, so the field is his oyster. The third receiver in 11 personnel will likely be a combination of Jordan Whittington, Konata Mumpfield, or Xavier Smith. Tight end Terrance Ferguson, though, is a player to circle and watch when, and if, the Rams start to run the football in their heavy personnel. Ferguson is an athletic tight end who is a threat off play action. Dennard Wilson will likely mix Cover-4 and Cover-3, but may need to rely more on Cover-3 to get the safety closer in the box, depending on how successful the Rams are running the football. Wilson will likely through some curveballs at Stafford, and either Burns or Carter will align across the formation to try and gain a speed advantage, but it all comes down to stopping the run against these Rams — which, of course — is an issue when they have the receiving weapons and quarterback that they possess. Final thoughts The Giants are 7.5-point road underdogs with an Over/Under of 48ish ( depending on the book ). I feel a lot better about this matchup for the Giants after Week 1, but the Rams are a true test. If the Giants pull off this upset, they will vault themselves into the true contender conversation in the NFC. These are bright lights, but this is a different Giants’ team coached by John Harbaugh and led by second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart.
author: Nick Falato

title: ‘Rusty’ Malik Nabers ‘left some yards out there’ vs. Cowboys
summary: Malik Nabers caught six passes on nine targets for 69 yards for the New York Giants against the Dallas Cowboys, a successful return for Nabers from a torn ACL as the Giants won, 28-20. How did the 23-year-old assess his performance? “I’m rusty,” he said. Nabers said he did too much “slipping, falling” while running […]
full_text: Malik Nabers in Week 1. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Malik Nabers caught six passes on nine targets for 69 yards for the New York Giants against the Dallas Cowboys, a successful return for Nabers from a torn ACL as the Giants won, 28-20. How did the 23-year-old assess his performance? “I’m rusty,” he said. Nabers said he did too much “slipping, falling” while running routes during the game. “Just got to get back into more of the football mentality of getting north,” Nabers said. “Just taking a picture of the defense, know where everybody’s at. I left some yards out there, I left some plays out there. I feel like I could’ve scored on probably two of them if I just run straight, get more yards. “So, I kind of think that was just the most frustrating thing about it, was just like I left a lot out there that I could’ve got.” Nabers said he was never required to do anything “crazy” in his return. “Whatever ball is being thrown, I feel like I can make those plays,” Nabers said. “And I feel like just – I never had to go up and make a crazy catch this week or, I mean, last week and do anything like spectacular. So, I mean, I’ll see when the ball is being thrown, I’ve got to make those catches.” Nabers gets another opportunity to shake off the rust on Monday night against the Los Angeles Rams.

title: NY Giants-Rams matchup: Can New York offense keep rolling?
summary: The New York Giants are off to a 1-0 start on the 2026 season after a statement win at home on Sunday Night Football. Now the Giants will have to travel across the country to take on the Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football. Where the Giants were 3-point underdogs at home against the […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart and running back Cam Skattebo | Getty Images The New York Giants are off to a 1-0 start on the 2026 season after a statement win at home on Sunday Night Football. Now the Giants will have to travel across the country to take on the Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football. Where the Giants were 3-point underdogs at home against the Dallas Cowboys to open the season, Las Vegas sees a significantly higher hill to climb for the Giants against the Rams. Despite coming out flat and taking an embarrassing loss in Australia to the San Francisco 49ers, and losing Myles Garrett to a knee injury, the Rams are still 7.5-point favorites over the Giants as of this writing. The Giants’ offense was the big surprise of the night against the Cowboys. It was punishing and methodical, allowing the Giants to utterly dominate the time of possession and allowed just two Dallas possessions in the entire second half. However, as many folks in the national media are quick to point out, Dallas’ defense was terrible in 2025. Can the Giants do it against a good defense? Let’s see what the Giants’ offense is up against in a Los Angeles Rams defense that has to be eager to make up for their week 1 performance Tighten up ball security The Giants’ win over the Cowboys was fantastic. They fielded a punishing run game that was married with a surgical passing attack. Even when the Giants weren’t able to be successful running the ball on early downs, their passing attack was there to pick up the slack and keep offense on the field. That said, the Giants’ methodical offense masked a pretty significant wart: They got lucky with turnovers. Isaiah Likely, Cam Skattebo, Jaxson Dart, and Tyrone Tracy all lost their handle on the ball. The Giants were, frankly, lucky that they were able to recover the ball on three of those fumbles. It was unfortunate that Tracy’s fumble was the one the Giants lost, as he was the least deserving of criticism — he had the ball high and tight with two arms on the ball. It was a great play by Quinnen Williams to punch it out, but it also ended Tracy’s night. In the other cases, the players in question have aspects of their game that need attention. To start, Jaxson Dart needs to be more aware of slot blitzes from his right. Twice he has been caught unaware and hit hard by a blitzing defensive back who walks up to the line late. And while the sack in the preseason could fall on Tracy’s shoulders for a missed blitz pickup, the sack-fumble caused by Caleb Downs’ blitz falls squarely on Dart. Even though the Rams didn’t send these types of blitzes frequently last year, the Giants should expect to see them until Dart proves he can make the defense pay for sending pressure. We could see more passes to the offensive right, throwing into the void created by sending the rusher. We could also see the Giants emphasizing hot routes when they alert to a potential blitz. The fumbles by Likely and Skattebo could both be chalked up to the players trying to do too much. In Likely’s case, he took a hand off the ball to stiff-arm a Dallas defender while a second defender came up to punch the ball out from behind. Likely caught the ball on a quick stick route over the middle, and he was attempting to pick up yards after the catch. Similarly, Skattebo was carrying the ball on a toss play, and picking his way through traffic. Unlike Tracy, Skattebo only had one hand on the ball and was carrying it rather low and away from his body. That made it much more likely that he would lose control as he was bouncing off of hits. The lesson for both Skattebo and Likely is to avoid compromising ball security to pick up extra yardage. The team won’t be nearly so lucky next time. Another Fangio-adjacent defense It was a pleasant surprise that the Giants were able to do pretty much whatever they wanted agaisnt the Cowboys’ defense. Offseason excitement for Caleb Downs and Christian Parker aside, some of the Giants’ worst performances came against Vic Fangio-style defenses last year. Most notably, of course, was the Week 8 game against the Philadelphia Eagles and Fangio himself. As we covered last week, Parker is a Fangio disciple and was expected to bring elements of the Eagles’ defense to the Cowboys. And the scheme was similar, but people perhaps overestimated how quickly it would be up and running. That isn’t the case with Chris Shula and the Rams. Shula is, broadly speaking, a “Fangio-Adjacent” defensive mind. His scheme is an off-shoot of the “Fangio” system that’s taken over the NFL as a way to limit the league’s explosive passing attacks. The general shape of the defense is familiar at this point: A front that’s based in 3-4 principles but frequently uses a 4-2-5 nickel set. The secondary is based on two-deep principles, but consistently rotates coverages to muddy reads, disrupt offenses’ timing, and to change box math in the run game. However, Shula also coached under Wade Phillips and incorporates some of Phillips’ defensive principles into his scheme. For instance, where “Fangio” defenses typically begin in a Cover 4 or Quarters look and rotate to a Cover 3, Cover 6, or Cover 8 look, Shula instead likes to open in a Cover-3 look and rotate to a split-field look (such as Cover 2 or Cover 4). Shula has also mastered using stunts to isolate his rushers and create free runs into the backfield, as well as to improve box math in his favor when playing nickel sets. One of the biggest questions hanging over the game is whether future Hall Of Fame defensive tackle Aaron Donald will play. The Rams are being coy about Donald’s status, but the Giants are expecting the perennial All-Pro to be there. While Donald hasn’t played football in two years, he remains one of the freakiest athletes to ever play the game. The Giants should plan on having to counter his explosiveness and agility, and do so in the context of the Rams’ other talented defensive linemen. Even with Myles Garrett out with a knee injury, the Rams also boast Byron Young on the edge, as well as defensive tackles Braden Fiske, Kobe Turner, and Poona Ford. Young, Fiske, and Turner are all athletic linemen who are downright dangerous in the gap-exchange games that Shula loves to employ. On the outside, we should probably expect that when the Rams rotate out of Cover-3, they’ll be going into more 2-Man or Man-Match Quarters (similar to what Dennard Wilson employs for the Giants), as opposed to Cover-2 or Cover-4 looks. The additions of Trend McDuffie and Jaylen Watson gives the Rams more press-man ability on the outside, and the Giants’ receivers will need to be ready for it. Remaining methodical The Giants didn’t exactly run up the score against the Cowboys, though there was a time (not all that long ago) when cracking 20 points would have been considered a great day. The Giants’ offense was more akin to a freight train than the Top Fuel dragster fielded by the Chicago Bears. But here’s the thing about trains: They’re still the most efficient way to move people and cargo over land. And the Giants’ offense was efficient or, to quote Jaxson Dart, methodical. We saw elements of each of Matt Nagy, Brian Callahan, and Greg Roman’s contributions ot the offense, and they meshed together surprisingly well. But so have the Rams. They’ll have some tape from which to work when preparing for the Giants and the question now becomes whether the Giants can maintain that style of offense as defenses become better able to prepare for it. The good news is that it’s very unlikely that we’ve seen all the wrinkles in the Giants’ scheme. They made use of surprisingly innovative play design against the Cowboys. For instance, they used 20-personnel (two backs, no tight ends, three receivers) on their second play of the day, but aligned fullback Patrick Ricard and wide receivers Malachi Fields and Braxton Berrios to simulate 22-personnel. Later in the game, the Giants motioned from a condensed set to a true spread…
author: Chris Pflum

title: NFL Week 2 picks, predictions: Can the Giants upset the Rams?
summary: The New York Giants seek an improbable 2-0 start when they travel to the West Coast to face the Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football. Can they get it? Here is how the Big Blue View staff is picking that game, and the rest of the Week 2 slate. Chris Pflum Can the Giants […]
full_text: The New York Giants seek an improbable 2-0 start when they travel to the West Coast to face the Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football. Can they get it? Here is how the Big Blue View staff is picking that game, and the rest of the Week 2 slate. Chris Pflum Can the Giants get off to an actual winning streak to start the 2026 season? I think they can. I do think it’s possible for the Giants to go out to LA and come back with a 2-0 record. I just don’t think it’s likely. The way they won against the Cowboys is sustainable and I think both the offense and defense can continue to improve as the players settle into the new schemes. The length and athleticism of the Giants’ defense makes them better equipped than most to counter Sean McVay’s 13-personnel passing attack. The offense has significant untapped potential as players like Darnell Mooney, Odell Beckham Jr., Theo Johnson, and the various running backs become more involved as pass catchers. That, in turn, will make the running game that much more effective. But I don’t know that it’ll happen in time to survive a shootout with Matt Stafford. I don’t necessarily buy that the Rams will be out for blood after being embarrassed by the 49ers, but this is a veteran and extremely well schemed offense. They came out flat in week 1, but this offense led the NFL in yards, points, and touchdowns last year. And despite being worse on 3rd downs than the Giants were last year, they still led the NFL in first downs. The Rams also have a talented and veteran defense with an experienced defensive coordinator. The Rams’ linebackers may be vulnerable the Giants’ passes over the middle, but I’d be surprised if we saw the same level of confusion in the Rams’ back seven as we saw with Dallas. ( As an aside, I find myself shocked at the hubris from Giants’ fans with respect to Aaron Donald. He may have been out of football for two years, but he was still the best defensive tackle in the NFL when he retired, and he has two fewer years of wear and tear on his body than the similarly-aged Shelby Harris. ) Ultimately, I think this game is much closer than the 7.5-point spread and the Giants give the Rams all they can handle. But they don’t have quite enough to stun the NFL and hand LA an 0-2 start to the year. Pick: Rams Tony DelGenio To me, the Rams are one of four NFC teams that could possibly reach the Super Bowl. After sleep-walking through their game in Melbourne and watching the Giants beat up the Cowboys, you can bet they’ll be ready. Some day Matthew Stafford’s NFL clock will hit 12 and he’ll no longer be great. Maybe the the 49ers game was the start of that, maybe not. Against the Giants’ still suspect secondary, and with Puka Nacua and Davante Adams catching passes, I wouldn’t bet on it. Maybe after two years away from the game, Aaron Donald won’t dominate the way he used to. Or maybe he’ll plead with Chris Shula to line him up in the left B-gap where Jon Runyan Jr. will have to deal with him and Andrew Thomas will have to help out. Be alert, Jaxson Dart. That said, any team that played as well as the Giants did Sunday night has a chance. The Rams’ defensive line is less impressive against the run than the pass, and we saw what the Giants’ running game can do in Week 1. The Giants probably want to be run-heavy again and not test LA cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson too often. The Rams’ offensive line is no longer as formidable as it used to be, and perhaps this is a week where the pass rush can get home against a QB who is not especially mobile. Whether the Giants’ IDL can hold up against Kyren Williams and Blake Corum is a different question. I won’t be shocked if the Giants win this game…but I’m not picking them to do so. Pick : Rams Nick Falato The Giants shocked the world with a home upset over the Dallas Cowboys. Conversely, the Rams were upset in Australia against the San Francisco 49ers. The Giants are currently seven-point dogs, and I expect them to cover the spread, but I expect the Rams to win. Sean McVay will run DUO out of 12/13 personnel, and I think it could wear the Giants down, especially when D.J. Reader is not on the field. If the Rams are successful running the ball, the play action with Puka Nacau and Davante Adams will become a big issue for the Giants’ cornerbacks. I’m also concerned about Terrance Ferguson off 13 personnel play-action shots; this is, of course, if Kyren Williams and Blake Corum get going against the run. The upgrade at linebackers for the Giants should make them respectable against the run, but I expect the Rams to lean into it and ultimatley have success. The Giants are not the Giants of old, but I have the Rams here. Pick: Rams by 6 James Hickey A Giants weakness became a much bigger concern this week when three of the top four cornerbacks appeared on the injury report this week— which led the team to sign two cornerbacks this week. This comes on a week the team faces arguably the best passing offense in the NFL — Matt Stafford at the helm, with Puka Nacua or Davante Adams as his two top weapons. If that sounds familiar to last week, well the X-factor is that Sean McVay was not on the other sideline. The headline this week is the expected return of DT Aaron Donald to a defense that gave up the fourth-most rushing yards in the league in Week 1. The Rams allowed 174 yards on the ground and 379 total yards to the 49ers, surrendering 24 unanswered points over the final 35 minutes. On top of that, Myles Garrett, the reigning DPOY, for at least the next four games due to knee surgery. The Rams are the Super Bowl favorites for a reason. In order to win, the Giants will need to do more in their passing game as they build on their physical running was their key to beating Dallas on Sunday night. While the issues in the secondary are a major red flag, John Harbaugh’s Big Blue Bullies find a way to win on Monday night with a late field goal by rookie Dominic Zvada sailing through the upright for the win. Pick: Giants 27, Rams 24 David Hartman Week 1 went just about as well as it could have for John Harbaugh’s Giants, and as terribly as it could have for Sean McVay’s Rams. Much has been made of L.A.’s travel decision for its Australia game, and the team should be rested, and primed for a bounce back in what’s suddenly a very important game for one of the top Super Bowl hopefuls. The Rams are a 7.5-point favorite and I will gladly take the points. In fact, I think Big Blue is going to give them all they want. I don’t want to overreact to Week 1, and maybe the travel was a big factor, but Los Angeles looked old, and the Giants looked hungry, focused, and sharp. Los Angeles has much better personnel on defense than Dallas, even without Myles Garrett. New York’s offense controlled the game (and the clock) on Sunday night and this will be a much sterner test. I think they’re ready for it. I’m taking the upset. I don’t think the top-heavy Rams are as good as advertised, while the Giants might be a little better than people think. New York catches the Rams at the right time, and leaves them in panic mode as they stare down 0-2. Pick: Giants by 4 Valentine’s View The New York Giants got the attention of everyone around the NFL with their Week 1 victory over the Dallas Cowboys. There was nothing fluky about the victory, the Giants were the better team on Sunday night. They deserved to win. The Giants took a huge leap in NFL power rankings, and there are now a lot of bandwagon-jumpers suddenly predicting that John Harbaugh’s team will make the playoffs this season. Conversely, after an embarrassing Week 1 loss to the San Francisco 49ers, there are people wondering if they were too enamored with the still Super Bowl favorite Rams. No one should forget that Week 1 of the NFL season is always rife with overreactions. The Rams are still a very good football team that will win a lot of games, almost certainly go to the playoffs, and perhaps reach the Super Bowl. The Giants, good vibes…

title: Previewing the Jets’ opposition: Green Bay Packers
summary: The New York Jets welcome the Green Bay Packers for their home opener on Sunday afternoon. While New York is seeking to start 2-0 for the first time since 2015, the Packers are under pressure not to drop to 0-2. They gave up 29 unanswered points as they blew a double-digit lead in their opener […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - AUGUST 09: Will McDonald IV #9 of the New York Jets hands a fan a glove during the fourth quarter against the Green Bay Packers during the NFL Preseason 2025 game between New York Jets and Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on August 09, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New York Jets welcome the Green Bay Packers for their home opener on Sunday afternoon. While New York is seeking to start 2-0 for the first time since 2015, the Packers are under pressure not to drop to 0-2. They gave up 29 unanswered points as they blew a double-digit lead in their opener against the Vikings. The Jets won in Green Bay in the last meeting between the teams back in 2022, but that was their first win over the Packers since 2006. However, they lead the all-time series by nine wins to five. Let’s break down the Packers’ roster going position by position: Quarterbacks Packers quarterback Jordan Love is coming off his best season as a full time starter in terms of completion percentage, quarterback rating and touchdown-to-interception ratio. However, he still hasn’t earned pro bowl recognition as he enters his fourth year as a starter. In game one, Love passed for 387 yards; just two less than his career-high. However, he only completed 50 percent of his passes, was sacked four times, fumbled twice and threw an interception. Can the Jets put some pressure on him? In the event Love gets knocked out of the game, their backup is a familiar face: former Jets quarterback Tyrod Taylor. As we’ve seen, he is still capable of being a competent short-term option. Offensive Line As noted, the Packers gave up four sacks on Sunday, and they also averaged just 3.1 yards per rush, but the more alarming number was 15 quarterback hits. The Vikings blitzed more than any other team in the league in week one, though. However, at the same time, Green Bay left more extra blockers in to pass protect. The main issue was probably the fact that undrafted rookie Donovan Jennings was forced to start at left guard due to an injury to Aaron Banks. He was an obvious weak link. Banks is the Packers’ highest-paid player other than Love, but he’s not exactly lived up to that price-point, as he was very inconsistent in his first year in Green Bay last season. His return in place of Jennings will still obviously help matters, but despite his return to practice, he is still bothered by a knee issue and is not certain to play. They listed him as questionable. The Packers’ most reliable lineman is their right tackle, Zach Bako-Bewele (who changed his name from Zach Tom in the offseason). Last year, he didn’t give up a sack in over 600 snaps. However, he already gave up his first sack of 2026 in the opener. Bako-Bewele is also listed as questionable but it seems unfathomable that he wouldn’t play. The current left tackle is former first round pick Jordan Morgan, who started games at four different positions last season. Center Sean Rhyan is also versatile, having started last year as the right guard until Elgton Jenkins’ season-ending injury in November. The fifth starter is another inexperienced player, as Jacob Monk is the current right guard. He started the season finale last season, but otherwise had only played six offensive snaps in his career. Green Bay’s main backup is Anthony Belton, who started eight games last year, including the last six games of the regular season, and the wild card game. The rest of their bench has no starting experience between them. John Williams was a seventh round rookie last year, but did not play. Travis Glover was inactive last week and rookie Jager Burton was in uniform but did not see action. Running Backs Green Bay’s running game suffered a blow when Josh Jacobs was placed on the exempt list due to an arrest in connection with a domestic incident. He looks set to miss 4-6 weeks based on the latest reports. Jacobs rushed for over 900 yards and 13 touchdowns last season, so his absence will be felt. MarShawn Lloyd is currently listed as a starter but was held to 37 yards on 13 carries in the opener. The former third rounder barely played as a rookie in 2024, then missed the entire 2025 season due to injury. Chris Brooks is back in a reserve role, while Kaleb Johnson is also on the roster but didn’t play any offensive snaps in the first game. Pass catchers The Packers’ leading receiver in 2025 was Romeo Doubs, but he signed a free agent deal with New England, so Green Bay will be hoping for one or more of their recent draft picks to step up. Christian Watson and Jayden Reed were day two picks in 2022 and 2023, while Matthew Golden was a first round pick last season. Watson was the one to step up in week one as he had 147 yards and two touchdowns, including an 81-yarder. However, the speedster Golden saw the most targets and was also effective. He put up the most productive game of his career with six catches for 95 yards. Reed, who averaged over 800 yards in his first two seasons, and caught 14 touchdown passes, was limited to just three starts last season. Bo Melton provides depth off the bench, but had just one catch in the opener. Skyy Moore is mostly on the team for special teams duties and undrafted rookie J. Michael Sturdivant was a healthy scratch to start the season. At tight end, Tucker Kraft is a productive pass catcher who had 469 receiving yards and six touchdowns in just eight games last season. They also added another veteran who Jets fans will recognize as a passing game threat in Jonnu Smith, as the Packers will employ plenty of two tight-end personnel packages. Josh Whyle is back in a reserve role and youngster Mark Redman was added via trade in the offseason. Luke Musgrave, who started 10 games last year, is on the PUP list. Defensive Line The Packers operate with a 3-4 base defense and their starting linemen are listed as Karl Brooks, Javon Hargrave and Devonte Wyatt. However, it was a five-deep rotation on Sunday, also including Jonathan Ford, who started in place of Hargrave, and third round rookie Chris McClellan. The 2022 first round pick Wyatt is probably the best known player in this group. He had four sacks in just 10 games last season. The 33-year old Hargrave has been in concussion protocol and did not practice on Thursday, though. He’s listed as doubtful. Green Bay did a decent job against the run in the first game, holding the Vikings to just 3.1 yards per carry. Backups Warren Brinson and Anthony Campbell were both inactive on Sunday and Brinson has been ruled out due to a calf issue. Linebackers The Packers’ defensive star is edge rusher Micah Parsons. However, he got injured with four games to go in the 2025 season and the Packers haven’t won a game since. He remains on the PUP list as Green Bay tries to avoid a seventh straight loss, a stretch which includes last year’s wild card game. With Parsons out, and both Rashan Gary and Kingsley Enagbare having departed during the offseason, the starters are currently former first round pick Lukas Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell, who started just one game as a rookie last year. Van Ness, who has been a disappointment, has also been in concussion protocol this week. He did practice on a limited basis all week, though, and is listed as questionable. Fourth round rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton provides depth off the edge along with Brenton Cox Jr., who has just one career start. The inside linebackers are Edgerrin Cooper and Zaire Franklin, who each played a full time role on Sunday. Cooper had 118 tackles as he played over 1,000 snaps last season. The 30-year old Franklin, who has had 125 or more tackles in each of the past four seasons in Indianapolis, was acquired via trade in March. Ty’Ron Hopper, Isaiah McDuffie and Nick Niemann provide depth off the bench. McDuffie played over 550 snaps last season but only played one defensive snap in the opener. Hopper was inactive in game one. Defensive Backs Packers cornerback Keisean…

title: New York Jets: Stopping the run
summary: We hear it all the time. The NFL is a passing league. You have to pass the ball and defend the pass well to win in this league. Running backs don’t matter. Stopping the run is less important than stopping the pass. That’s the conventional wisdom these days, but is it true? As it happens, […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: Cam Ward #1 of the Tennessee Titans is tackled by Will McDonald IV #9 of the New York Jets during the fourth quarter of the game at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images We hear it all the time. The NFL is a passing league. You have to pass the ball and defend the pass well to win in this league. Running backs don’t matter. Stopping the run is less important than stopping the pass. That’s the conventional wisdom these days, but is it true? As it happens, the league has quietly undergone an extraordinary transformation over the last decade or so. In 2015 the league set an all time record of 244 passing yards per game. Passing offenses seemed unstoppable. 13 NFL teams surpassed 4000 passing yards that year. Even the Jets got in on the fun, passing for 4057 yards. Everybody was trying to figure out how to slow down all the high powered passing offenses. Gradually, over the next 10 years, they largely succeeded. Ten years later in 2025, NFL teams averaged just 210 passing yards per game, the lowest total since 2006. That represented an enormous drop of 34 passing yards per game from the peak of 2015. There has never been another ten year stretch with that level decrease in passing yards in post-merger NFL history. Just six teams surpassed 4000 passing yards in 2025, down more than 50% from a decade earlier. The average team attempted just 32.1 passes per game in 2025, the lowest total since 2006. The last time the NFL had a substantial stretch of years where teams averaged lower than 32.1 passes per game was more than 40 years ago, in the late 1970s through the early 1980s. Back then nobody was calling the NFL a passing league. In fact, there was such a dearth in passing and scoring back then the NFL started a series of rule changes to encourage passing and scoring. Passing efficiency has also been going through a significant decline lately. In 2025 the NFL averaged 6.09 net yards per passing attempt, down .32 net yards per attempt from the all time high of 6.41 set 10 years earlier. That level of decline in a decade has only been surpassed once in post-merger NFL history, from 1989 through 1997. At the same time rushing yards have been increasing. Rushing yards per game hit a 16 year low in 2015 at 108.9 yards per game. There have only been four seasons in all of NFL history with less rushing yards per game. By 2024 that number had risen to 119.8 rushing yards per game, the highest number since 1988. Rushing efficiency has also been on the rise. In 2005 teams averaged 4.0 yards per rushing attempt. By 2025 that number was up to 4.4 yards per attempt, the second highest number in NFL history, just 0.1 yards less than the record of 4.5 set in 2022. All of this suggests that the NFL may not be as much of a passing league as common wisdom suggests. In fact, in an everything old is new again moment, the old fashioned approach of emphasizing stopping the run seems to be back in style. It’s just one week, and cause and effect are a bit tricky here, as losing teams tend to pass more and run less, but for at least one week, the teams that stopped the run excelled this season. The top ten teams in fewest rushing yards allowed have a combined record of 8-2 this season. The 1-0 Jets are one of those teams, ranking fourth in the NFL with just 68 rushing yards allowed. We’ll see what the rest of the 2026 season has in store, but maybe Aaron Glenn and Darren Mougey were on to something in the offseason. The Jets brought in a bunch of guys who excel at stopping the run on defense. They also brought in a number of sure tacklers. Maybe we’re going back to the future. Maybe the NFL is not such a passing league after all. Maybe the Jets are in the process of building the right kind of defense for modern NFL offenses, which increasingly seem determined to run the ball. We’ll find out over the next few months, but maybe this Jets defense is about to surprise a lot of people.

The Jets will be looking to start the season 2-0 for the first time since 2015. Not coincidentally, 2015 was the Jets’ last winning season. Despite the Packers’ superb franchise history, […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - SEPTEMBER 14: Quarterback Geno Smith #7 of the New York Jets rushes for one yard to score against the Green Bay Packers in the first quarter during the NFL game at Lambeau Field on September 14, 2014 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. Despite the Packers’ superb franchise history, the Jets have historically had their way with them. The Jets are 9-5 all time against the Packers, including a 27 -10 thrashing of the Packers the last time these two teams faced each other in 2022. The Packers opened their 2026 campaign with an ugly 39 -22 loss to the Minnesota Vikings. They will be looking to avoid the dreaded 0-2 start, from which few teams recover to make the playoffs. Let’s make a few predictions for the game on Sunday. The Jets revamped run defense held the Tennessee Titans under 70 yards rushing last week. They’ll excel again this week, holding the Packers’ running backs to less than 60 total rushing yards. The Packers are having serious trouble on the offensive line, and they are without Josh Jacobs at running back. The Jets take advantage. The Jets pass defense was excellent against an overmatched Cam Ward last week. Jordan Love is no Cam Ward. The Packers have a ton of weapons for Love to throw to if he gets time. Christian Watson and Matthew Golden have speed the Jets’ defensive backs can’t match.
