(Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images What went wrong for the Green Bay Packers in pass protection in their Week 1 loss to the Minnesota Vikings? You could answer, “Pretty much everything.” Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores blitzed the Packers over 80 percent of the time. The results were 4 sacks and 15 quarterback hits on Jordan Love. We can’t find one simplistic explanation for the success of Minnesota’s attacking defense, but I would like to point out one defensive front in particular that the Packers just could not figure out in the late stages of the fourth quarter. The Vikings showed this front over and over as they tried to close out the game in the final minutes. The front put an edge on a side of the defensive formation with both interior linemen. The other edge was aligned far outside across the field. Next to him were off ball linebackers in the A gap (between center and guard) and B gap (between guard and tackle) to that side. (For the purpose of clarity, bigs are in yellow, while off ball linebackers are in teal. Here the Packers slide four guys to the left. The right tackle is on an island to the outside. And running back Chris Brooks is assigned Blake Cashman if Cashman blitzes through the B gap on the right side of the offensive formation. Brooks starts this play aligned left so this is a lot of ground to cover. As Brooks is scanning, it seems like he fears some of his linemen to his left are beaten so he goes to help, which leaves nobody to pick up Cashman. View Link On the next play the Vikings reprise this front. This time the right guard will have Cashman from the B gap. Brooks will have the A gap linebacker, Eric Wilson. Again, though, he is aligned on the left of the formation, while Brooks is blitzing to the offense’s right. It isn’t quite as much ground to cover as the last play, but it still is a journey. Brooks is slow to get out to block Wilson, and the pressure in Love’s face makes him throw early. View Link Shortly after this, we see a similar Minnesota front. The Packers make an adjustment. Brooks, the running back, moves to the right side of the formation an aligns just behind the offensive line instead of his normal shotgun spot next to Love. He can now pick up Cashman from the B gap off the snap. The Packers at least have the man power to pick this one up. However, Cashman bullies Brooks into Love’s line of sight. Love tries to scramble but runs into a sack. View Link The Packers at least handled this better schematically, but we can insert the requisite cliche that it’s more about Jimmy’s and Joe’s than X’s and O’s. Even with a sounder protection scheme, Love goes down. It’s time for Flores to adjust. The front inverts this time. We still have three defensive linemen to one side and linebackers threatening the A and B gaps. They have merely flipped sides. Safety Harrison Smith also walks down to the line of scrimmage to threaten blitz. These all end up becoming immaterial to the play itself. Brooks is again just behind the offensive line so he can easily take Cashman blitzing out of the B gap. This time Cashman charges up the field, but he isn’t heading for the quarterback. He is aiming for left tackle Jordan Morgan. Cashman charges into Morgan as Brooks is engaged with him. This frees up Dallas Turner to loop around. Morgan is supposed to be blocking him but is now occupied. Turner is able to drill Jordan Love. Love to his credit stands tough in the pocket and delivers a strike to wide receiver Matthew Golden for a 20 yard gain. It’s no thanks to his pass protection, though. Once again they failed to hold up against a blitz from this front. View Link Matt LaFleur is a pretty smart offensive coach. I’m sure he watched the film over and over, and the Packers have spent extensive practice time trying to fix this. With that said, one of the key points of game planning is forcing your opponent to show that they have actually fixed a weakness. After what happened last week, we know the Jets are going to run a heavy diet of blitzes at Green Bay. It’s this defense’s identity anyway. The Jets won’t blitz at an 80 percent rate, but they did have one of the highest blitz rates of Week 1. It figures to up in Week 2. The Packers struggled with it. The Jets surely saw this on the film during the week. This is the sort of front that should be in the game plan on obvious passing downs at least until the Packers prove they can solve it.

title: Film Preview: Eagles should have success against this Titans defense
summary: Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite. I also record a video version for Patreon, where I break down […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - DECEMBER 04: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts (1) during the National Football League game between the Tennessee Titans and Philadelphia Eagles on December 4, 2022 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA (Photo by John Jones/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite . I also record a video version for Patreon , where I break down the plays in greater detail and where you can further support my work. I expected a Robert Saleh defense to be relatively simple to identify. He usually has plenty of zone coverage, four-man rushes, and a front that lets its best players get after the quarterback. That is broadly what Tennessee showed against the Jets. I did not expect so much confusion behind it. The secondary repeatedly lost track of assignments after ordinary motion and shifts, the pass rush barely affected Geno Smith, and the run fits broke down in some surprisingly basic ways. This was a poor defensive performance. The Eagles just have to hope for more of the same this week… Defense Pass Defense Saleh is the head coach and defensive playcaller, and Week 1 looked like his defense on paper. The Titans played zone on 84.6% of their coverage snaps. Cover 3 accounted for 42.3%, and Cover 4 another 34.6%. That is a lot of familiar, four-man-rush zone football. Saleh has called zone on 76% of the dropbacks in the available career sample on Fantasy Points Data as a HC/DC, while blitzing only 20.3% of the time. So Week 1 was what you’d expect. However, I can’t quite believe how poor the defense was at times in Week 1. The Jets used simple motion and late shifts to create chaos in the secondary. Defenders were still sorting out who had whom as the ball was being snapped. At times, a route would open up, and you could see a huge void where a defender should have been. Quick Titans' All22 Defense Thread. 1) They had so many issues with communication in the secondary; it was pretty embarrassing at times. The Jets would use a simple motion or a late shift, which would cause chaos in the secondary. pic.twitter.com/VGDBJwUL45 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 18, 2026 There was very little disguise to compensate for the confusion, either. When a defense is going to show you a fairly standard zone picture, the least it can do is communicate the assignments correctly! This is the first thing I want to see from Sean Mannion’s offense, which we did see in Week 1. Move Makai Lemon and DeVonta Smith around. Use motion, shifts, and different splits to make Tennessee declare its rules and pass routes off properly. The Jets showed that even straightforward movement could disrupt the Titans’ communication. We should find out immediately whether those errors have been corrected. The open space was especially obvious against layered concepts, which the Eagles also used successfully in Week 1. On this under-center three-level stretch, the Jets had an easy completion because nobody accounted for the flat. This is just poor. 4) There appeared to be issues in the secondary on a lot of snaps, to the point where there was just a huge void somewhere. Here, the Jets run a simple 3-level stretch from under center, and no one is in the flat. This is just easy money. Look at the pocket Geno Smith has, too! pic.twitter.com/czo9VUhloa — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 18, 2026 On another one, the outside corner was beaten on a deep comeback despite having outside leverage, and the flat was uncovered yet again. 5) No one in the flat at all, and the outside CB is beat despite having outside leverage on a deep comeback route. Again, look at the pocket that Geno Smith has… The lack of a pass rush was evident. There's not a lot of disguise on the back end either, it's just bad. pic.twitter.com/r6NAkqJtnz — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 18, 2026 The Jets also ran a three-level stretch with a crosser from the opposite side, and the crossing route was wide open. These were not exotic plays. They were basic ways to stretch a zone horizontally and vertically, and Tennessee had no answer on those snaps. They are either playing it wrong or can’t communicate and match these routes effectively. 6) Like, this isn't complicated on offense. Again, it's a 3-level stretch with a crossing route from the other side of the formation, and the Titans have no answer. The crossing route is wide open. You don't see receivers this open consistently very often. Or a QB who has no… pic.twitter.com/9YEvob4F0G — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 18, 2026 That should be encouraging for an Eagles offense that managed only 10 first downs in Week 1 and relied too heavily on isolated explosive plays. Dallas Goedert settling into an open window, Saquon Barkley releasing into the flat, and Smith running the deeper part of a flood concept could produce the kind of easy, repeatable offense that was missing against Washington. I want to see Hurts take those completions when they are available, then punish the Titans if their cornerbacks fail to pass off a crosser or give up a deep comeback. There is no need to hunt a 30-yard throw on every snap when the defense is offering free yards underneath. The Titans allowed 0.88 EPA per play when it finished in a one-high look, the worst mark in the league in Week 1, while its two-high snaps allowed minus-0.18, eighth best. This is largely because of the busts that you can see above. If the Titans are going to play that much Cover 3 or single-high again, they have to show they can handle it better than they did against the Jets. Without pressure, every coverage mistake looked worse. Tennessee generated pressure on only 23.1% of dropbacks, 28th in the league, and took 2.92 seconds on average to generate it. Smith had enormous pockets even on concepts that needed time to develop, as the clips above show. It was startling how rarely the Jets’ quarterback looked uncomfortable. Jeffery Simmons is the obvious exception to any discussion of Tennessee’s defensive talent. He is still an excellent player and can wreck a series by himself. 8) Yeah, they have Jeffery Simmons. He's still very good. But the Eagles should be able to beat this defense. My real concern is that surely they can't be this bad again, right? They can't leave that many open receivers and have so many communication errors. Surely not… pic.twitter.com/m8Y2Jtg6Pk — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 18, 2026 He will test an Eagles interior line missing Landon Dickerson, and the Eagles must know exactly where he is before each snap. John Franklin-Myers can line up inside or outside, while Jermaine Johnson II gives Tennessee an athletic edge presence. Neither the additions around Simmons nor the rotations up front produced enough disruption in Week 1. The blitz numbers are fascinating, although I would be careful with such a tiny sample. Hurts struggled when Washington blitzed in Week 1, but Tennessee allowed an absurd 1.30 EPA per play on its own blitzes against the Jets. They were terrible when bringing pressure. Saleh has never been someone who needs to send five or six constantly, and Tennessee’s non-blitz snaps held up much better. I would expect him to try to manufacture pressure around Simmons while keeping most of his defenders in coverage. If the Titans do blitz, the Eagles need clear hot answers and better protection communication than they showed at times last week. They might try the Eagles occasionally after what happened in Week 1 vs. Washington, but I don’t think they will blitz a lot. Anthony Hill Jr. had a good debut, so he is someone to watch. The rookie linebacker had 16 tackles and two pass breakups in his NFL debut, but the numbers do not fully capture how impressive he…

title: Eagles Film Preview: Titans offense off to a slow start
summary: Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite. I also record a video version for Patreon, where I break down […]
full_text: Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward (1) talks with Offensive Coordinator Brian Daboll during OTAs at Vanderbilt Health Football Center in Nashville, Tenn., Monday, June 8, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite . I also record a video version for Patreon , where I break down the plays in greater detail and where you can further support my work. The Tennessee Titans’ offense was bad in Week 1. They scored 10 points, managed only 195 total yards, and produced almost nothing explosive. However, I came away from the film thinking the structure of Brian Daboll’s offense was better than the final numbers suggest. The offense had some good designs, a surprisingly interesting run game, and enough receiving talent to create opportunities. The problem was that Cam Ward and the protection unit repeatedly failed to capitalize on those opportunities. Let’s talk about it! Pass Game Tennessee did not hide Ward. The Titans used 11 personnel on 73.5% of their snaps and passed on 66.7% of their neutral-situation plays. They also threw on 55.6% of first-and-10s, so this was not an old-fashioned attempt to protect a young quarterback with a conservative, run-heavy game plan. Daboll put the offense in Ward’s hands. It didn’t work. He averaged roughly 5.5 air yards per attempt and never seriously threatened the Jets downfield. I do not think Tennessee’s receivers were the main problem. Wan’Dale Robinson is a useful slot receiver who already understands Daboll’s offense, and Elic Ayomanor is a physical outside target who looks like he can play a bit. Rookie Carnell Tate, the fourth overall pick, is obviously the most interesting player of the group. Tate created separation on several intermediate and downfield routes, but Ward couldn’t get him the ball. This is not an elite group, but it is comfortably good enough for the quarterback to play better than this. The biggest schematic concern was Tennessee’s response to pressure. The Jets repeatedly confused the offensive line with simulated pressures, overloaded one side, and brought second-level defenders. Tennessee either failed to identify the extra rusher or did not build an immediate answer into the concept. 4) Another blitz that the Titans just do not pick up. The Jets send 5, overload one side, and the Titans don't have a plan. No one picks up the blitzing CB, and the routes take too long to develop, so Ward has to bail. You can't win if you can't pick up blitzers. pic.twitter.com/PSioVX4Yxb — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 17, 2026 At times, the Jets brought five and sent a cornerback from the edge, but nobody blocked him, and the routes took too long to develop. Ward had no choice except to escape. Here you can see Tennessee emptied the backfield, and two receivers ran into the same area, leaving Ward without an obvious quick throw. Quick Titans' Offense Thread… 1) Vic Fangio will be very excited about the possibility of confusing Cam Ward and this offensive line. They struggled mightily against simulated pressures this week, and often failed to block up blitzers from the 2nd level. Ward has to get this… pic.twitter.com/eEKh7Sb53K — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 17, 2026 Ward made the situation look considerably worse. Once he felt early pressure, his pocket presence deteriorated. He began seeing ghosts, leaving clean pockets, dropping his eyes, and moving directly into rushers. This sack was almost comical. 2) Some of Cam Ward's pocket presence after early pressure was amusingly bad. He was seeing ghosts and feeling pressure that wasn't there. He basically sprints into this sack. If the Eagles can get into his head, it could get ugly for the Titans. pic.twitter.com/kbLbfzobZk — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 17, 2026 Ward turned away from the defense on fake-reverse play-action, lost his base, put his head down, and ran straight into the back of his own offensive lineman. Tennessee was pressured on 46.2% of its dropbacks, but the offensive line was not responsible for all of it. Ward holds the football and too often turns manageable pressure into a negative play. On several snaps, the Titans blocked the rush, Daboll created an open receiver, and Ward did not make the throw. Tennessee ran a lovely counter play-action concept that pulled the linebackers toward the line of scrimmage and opened a crossing route behind them. Ward saw it but did not pull the trigger. 3) However, there were times when the Titans protected him well, and receivers were open, and Ward just didn't throw it. I thought they did some good things schematically, but you can't do much when your QB doesn't make the throw. This is a lovely counter play action which… pic.twitter.com/2eO2s5v8eR — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 17, 2026 Other examples included Tate breaking open and Ward hesitating, or simple underneath options being ignored. The Titans ranked 28th in EPA from a clean pocket in Week 1, which matches the film. Their quarterback was not taking advantage when the structure worked. Ward’s accuracy was inconsistent, too. He missed simple throws in the flat, sailed boundary passes out of bounds, and failed to give his receivers a chance on several back-shoulder or wheel routes. 5) Again, I quite like the design schematically, but Ward just misses the throw. Rough. The pass protection wasn't great throughout the game, but they did a good job at times, and Ward just didn't take advantage. pic.twitter.com/zpl5kxkL0k — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 17, 2026 The one positive is that he has generally avoided reckless turnover-worthy throws. The problem is that this has become what I would call nothing football. He is not constantly giving the ball away, but he is also creating very little. Safe quarterback play only works if you consistently hit the throws the structure provides. The Titans’ best sequence came when they used tempo at the beginning of the second half. They ran three consecutive plays without allowing the Jets to substitute, forced the defense to simplify its calls, and finally got Ward into some rhythm. I would not be surprised if Daboll uses more tempo against the Eagles for exactly that reason. It could prevent Fangio from changing personnel, reduce the amount of disguise Ward has to process, and make the protection calls easier. Tennessee cannot live in third-and-long against this defense. Their early-down passing designs were reasonable, but once the offense fell behind the chains, the simulated pressures destroyed them. Fangio should be very excited about this matchup. I would combine split-safety looks with simulated pressure rather than blitzing relentlessly. The individual matchup to attack is Dan Moore Jr. at left tackle. 8) However, the offensive line is a concern (despite the fact that I blame Ward and the scheme more than the line itself). Dan Moore had some poor reps at left tackle, and the Eagles' edge defenders should have had success against him. pic.twitter.com/grH0zYbK61 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 17, 2026 I thought JC Latham held up better on the right side, but Moore had several poor reps and remains vulnerable on the edge. Nolan Smith Jr. and Jalyx Hunt should have opportunities there. More importantly, the Eagles should make the entire protection unit communicate. Mugging Zack Baun or Jihaad Campbell in the A-gaps before dropping one of them could be more damaging than simply asking the edge rushers to win one-on-one. The goal should be to make Ward think about pressure before the snap, then force him to confirm the coverage afterward. Based on Week 1, that is a lot to ask of him. Run Game The frustrating part of Tennessee’s Week 1 performance is that I quite liked the run game. The Titans rushed only…

title: Eagles News: Jalen Carter downplays impact of playing with a cast on
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! It would be a shame if Jalen Carter is significantly impacted by this wrist injury after playing in just one game. The Eagles are paying him to be one of the very best defenders in the league. Also wondering if his […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jalen Carter #98 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on against the Washington Commanders during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! It would be a shame if Jalen Carter is significantly impacted by this wrist injury after playing in just one game. The Eagles are paying him to be one of the very best defenders in the league. Also wondering if his injury could impacted his ability to block kicks, which is obviously a big value he provides to the team. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles’ Jalen Carter to wear cast on injured wrist vs. Titans – ESPN Eagles defensive tackle Jalen Carter expects to wear a cast on his injured right wrist for Sunday’s Week 2 matchup against the Tennessee Titans. “Pretty much nothing. It’s just a cast,” Carter said, referring to what adjustments he’ll have to make in-game. “I’m still going to have to strike, grab, play the run and pass rush. That’s pretty much it. I can’t let it affect me.” Carter confirmed he sustained the injury against the Commanders last week while trying to punch the ball out of Terry McLaurin’s hands after a fourth-quarter reception. Carter was sidelined for Wednesday’s practice and was a limited participant Thursday. Carter wore the cast during Thursday’s session. Why Eagles fans shouldn’t panic if Eli Stowers needs more time to develop – BGN Eagles assistant GM, Jon Ferrari, was recently on the New Heights Show with Jason and Travis Kelce to talk about some of the more misunderstood officiating calls — and about how the Michigan game clock got so messed up. But, notably, he ended up talking about how challenging blocking as a tight end, outside the tackle, can be. 3 Titans who absolutely need to be better in Week 2 – Music City Miracles CAM WARD, QB: Titans quarterback Cam Ward finished 19-of-32 in Week 1 for 140 yards and a touchdown. A large portion of his production occurred via a garbage-time possession. Ward recorded 55 passing yards and his lone touchdown late in the fourth quarter once the Jets defense went into a late-game prevent shell. The All-22 tape review wasn’t kind to Ward’s performance . The offensive line was better than the broadcast angles indicated and receivers were creating consistent separation. Ward was hesitant, inefficient, occasionally inaccurate, and even bailed from clean pockets. The sophomore No. 1 overall quarterback needs to get better weekly. How are the Eagles going to replace Landon Dickerson vs. the Titans? – PhillyVoice And the downside to starting Fred Johnson [at left guard]: Johnson didn’t have a very good camp, even at his regular position at OT, while Kendall crushed it and seemed to have satisfied the Eagles’ staff and front office with his progression from Year 1 to Year 2. Kendall is a potential future starter, and Johnson probably is not. I mean, Kendall is just ready. Play him. Conclusion: I can’t recall the Eagles ever screwing around with practice reps to get the media to report it and create confusion for the upcoming opponent. To do that for the first time ahead of a matchup with one of the worst teams in the league would be a weird choice, even if the opponent’s best player is facing the position where the Eagles would be hoping to create confusion. Showing Johnson at LG in front of the media for the purposes of a ruse at the expense of reps for Kendall would be silly, in my opinion. The only thing that makes sense to me is that the team trusts Johnson over Willie Lampkin, who would theoretically be the next-next guy up on the interior. That is far more reasonable. And if so, they are rightfully getting him some reps at LG in case Kendall, Jurgens, or Steen go down. Titans Talk – Iggles Blitz That makes the Eagles look like the 1999 Rams. Ugh. There is a lot of blame to go around. Ward hasn’t shown signs of becoming the player they hoped for when drafted first overall. The OL has been a mess for a few years. They don’t have a great set of playmakers. And now Ward and his teammates are learning a new scheme. That’s not off to the greatest start, as you’ll see below.The Titans didn’t have a single play go for more than 14 yards. If you want to know what the Eagles offense would have looked like without the explosives, there you go. And it wasn’t pretty. Eagles-Titans matchups to watch in Week 2 – NBCSP Eagles interior OL vs. Jeffery Simmons. The Eagles will be without Landon Dickerson (knee) for at least the next four weeks. The good news is that Dickerson expects to be back after missing a month, but the bad news is that the Eagles will have to hold up against one of the best defensive tackles in the NFL without him. Jeffery Simmons is a four-time Pro Bowler and was an All-Pro in 2025 when he had a career-high 11 sacks and 21 QB hits. Simmons this offseason signed a three-year, $105.8 million contract that briefly made him the highest-paid defensive tackle in the NFL. It seems likely that the Eagles will start second-year lineman Drew Kendall in Dickerson’s place, but they have kept their plan close to the vest. No matter what the Eagles do on Sunday, they’ll have to provide some help wherever Simmons lines up. And it’s not just Simmons. The Titans this offseason brought in Jermaine Johnson and John Franklin-Myers, two players who have familiarity with Robert Saleh’s defense from their time together with the Jets. It’ll be fascinating to see how the Titans deploy Simmons. They can put him over the left guard but then that guarantees the center is going to slide that way. If they put him over the right guard, it forces the Eagles to make a decision. Do they help Tyler Steen with Simmons or do they help the weaker spot without Dickerson? NFL Week 2 picks: Upset and score predictions, matchup breakdowns for every game – NFL.com Why Jeremy picked the Eagles: A week after green-clad Yankees stormed Broadway, took over the bars and stadium, and cheered on a dominant win for the away side, Titans fans can expect the same again. Trade out Geno Smith and the Jets for Jalen Hurts and the Eagles, and Robert Saleh’s Titans have another rout on their hands if they’re not careful. No quarterbacks have been better on the road in September than Hurts and Patrick Mahomes (.800 on their careers), and the former is coming off a well-balanced season debut. Losing Landon Dickerson the week before Jeffery Simmons is on the docket isn’t a plus, but replacing the banged-up guard may be addition by subtraction. The even-greater mismatch could come on the other side of the ball, where the worst offense in the league since 2025 is going up against a Vic Fangio-led defense that has paced the NFL in opponent passer rating in the same span. In their last four meetings, Fangio’s Eagles have held Titans OC Brian Daboll’s offenses to a combined 70 points, with a 34-point Giants outburst last year the lone exception to the DC’s dominance in the battle. Wan’Dale Robinson and a mobile quarterback (Jaxson Dart) played key roles in flipping that token tie toward Daboll. Will Ward and Co. deliver a similar result? The odds are not in favor of Nash Vegas. Eagles rookie Makai Lemon says he has ‘lots to improve on’ after quiet Week 1 – Inquirer Makai Lemon used just four words when asked to sum up his first NFL game. “Lots to improve on,” Lemon said from his locker room stall Thursday. He’s not wrong. In the 24-22 win vs. the Commanders last Sunday, the Eagles’ first-round rookie wide receiver caught 3-of-4 targets for minus-5 yards. He did make a key block during Jalen Hurts’ crucial third-and-18 conversion in the fourth quarter, but it’s clear the 22-year-old is kicking himself due to his stat line. What does Lemon need to improve? “Route details,” Lemon said. “Just making sure I define my routes and assignments.”…

title: Eagles opposing player to stop: Titans Week 2 edition
summary: The Eagles had more than their share of offensive line breakdowns in their 24-22 season-opening victory over Washington last Sunday. Now, the Eagles will be facing a true game-wrecker in Tennessee Titans’ All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. With Pro Bowl left guard Landon Dickerson placed on the injured reserve on Monday due to a bruised […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - DECEMBER 04: Jeffery Simmons #98 of the Tennessee Titans pressures Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on December 4, 2022 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles had more than their share of offensive line breakdowns in their 24-22 season-opening victory over Washington last Sunday. Now, the Eagles will be facing a true game-wrecker in Tennessee Titans’ All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. With Pro Bowl left guard Landon Dickerson placed on the injured reserve on Monday due to a bruised right knee, Simmons and Eagles’ quarterback Jalen Hurts may become quite familiar each other Sunday afternoon at 1 p.m. in Tennessee. Simmons has already stirred the drama pot when he blurted out about Hurts this week: “We just need to make Jalen Hurts be a QB. Stop his runs, make sure Hurts doesn’t get out of the pocket and make plays.” Simmons and the Titans’ defense are about the only shot Tennessee has in beating the Eagles. Eagles’ offensive coordinator Sean Mannion addressed the Eagles’ leaky offensive front this week: “Some of it is just execution, some of it’s fundamentals, but I think you kind of hit it. The biggest takeaway for me from the game was just being able to stay on schedule. We got behind the sticks a little bit. If there’s a guy unaccounted for — we had a free safety pressure early. We’ve just got to communicate a little bit better upfront. In large part, we always want to have a hat for a hat. We try to avoid those situations. Some of it is execution, some of it’s fundamentals, but the better we’re able to stay on schedule, the better we’re going to be as an offense. That was the main takeaway from the game. That was some of it. Just a couple instances where it kind of got behind the sticks. The examples you’re speaking to led to at least a couple of them.” In the season-opening win over Washington, Hurts was amazing. He went into “Jordan mode” and saved the day, completing 14 of 25 passes for 203 yards and three touchdowns. He also ran for 46 yards, which included what was the play of the game when he scrambled 22 yards for a critical first down on third-and-18 play in the fourth quarter. It looks as if Drew Kendall, in his second pro season, will start in place of Dickerson at left guard. Kendall is coming off a strong training camp and preseason. Titans’ head coach Robert Saleh has a good history against the Eagles, beating them while he was the head coach of the Jets and again as the defensive coordinator of the San Francisco 49ers in the Wild Card Round of the NFC playoffs. In both cases, the Eagles were favored to win. Saleh changed those percentages by figuring out Hurts. What Saleh will probably do is attack with four and drop seven in a zone, but will come at Hurts from different angles. It has worked with Saleh teams before facing Hurts. With a game-wrecker like Simmons, who will probably have to be double-teamed, expect more of the same from Saleh. “We feel really confident with all of our guys,” Mannion said. “It’s unfortunate with Landon, the guy’s a warrior, and we’ve got to get him healthy. In the meantime, we need guys to step up, but Drew’s had a really nice camp. [C/G] Willie [Lampkin]’s had a nice camp. Really, we have a lot of guys on our offensive line with a lot of position flexibility, versatility. We feel good about all of them. Obviously, Landon will be missed in the meantime, but we feel confident that guys are going to be able to step up and fill the void.”

title: Steelers weren’t willing to give Joey Porter more guaranteed money, per report
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers and their standoff with cornerback Joey Porter Jr have been one of the biggest stories at the start of the NFL season. Porter did not partake at all in training camp, being placed on the PUP list with a back injury. Though as more time goes by, it’s clear that was a […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 02: Joey Porter Jr. #24 of the Pittsburgh Steelers looks on against the Indianapolis Colts during the first quarter in the game at Acrisure Stadium on November 02, 2025 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers and their standoff with cornerback Joey Porter Jr have been one of the biggest stories at the start of the NFL season. Porter did not partake at all in training camp, being placed on the PUP list with a back injury. Though as more time goes by, it’s clear that was a front to avoid the optics of a hold-in. Porter began practicing ahead of the team’s Week 1 game with the Atlanta Falcons, but did not play in Pittsburgh’s 20-13 win. On Wednesday’s injury report, Porter was listed as limited, but not with any injury designation. Rather he was listed as conditioning. On Thursday, however, he left early in practice with the medical staff and his back injury was then added to the injury report on Thursday. As the Steelers get closer to Sunday, it looks less and less likely that Porter will suit up in Week 2, and maybe ever again in a Steelers uniform. According to a report from Jeremy Fowler and Brooke Pryor of ESPN, the biggest cause of this divide and a deal not getting done was the structure of the contract. “The two sides have been here because of a significant difference between the Steelers’ view of Porter’s value and how Porter values himself,” the report reads . “The core issue is the structure of the contract, sources told ESPN, and the Steelers’ organizational precedent that doesn’t fully guarantee a healthy portion of the contract was considered a sizable hurdle.” Specifically, Pryor and Fowler report that Porter wanted more guaranteed money past the first year of his extension. “Many of the Steelers past deals for key players fully guarantee only the first year,” the report states. “That was the case for Porter’s draft mates, Keeanu Benton, Darnell Washington and Nick Herbig, whose four-year extensions this summer guaranteed 2027 for injury only. Porter wants stronger guarantees, sources said. Pittsburgh has broken precedent in the past. For example, Pittsburgh guaranteed $108 million for T.J. Watt in the summer of 2025. While Porter doesn’t have the megastar cachet of Watt, he’s still a high-level cover corner.” Should Porter not suit up on Sunday, a trade seems to be the most likely outcome of this entire saga, should Pittsburgh receive an offer they deem acceptable. title: Steelers-Patriots preview: What to expect from New England’s offense, defense in Week 2
summary: The Steelers are 1-0 but hoping to build off a game against the Cooper Rush-led Falcons last week that was much closer than it needed to be. The Patriots, on the other hand, are still searching for their first win of the season after a low-scoring loss in a Super Bowl rematch to open the […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - SEPTEMBER 09: Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots throws a pass against the Seattle Seahawks during the second quarter in the game at Lumen Field on September 09, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Steelers are 1-0 but hoping to build off a game against the Cooper Rush-led Falcons last week that was much closer than it needed to be. The Patriots, on the other hand, are still searching for their first win of the season after a low-scoring loss in a Super Bowl rematch to open the season. As these two playoff-hopeful teams meet for their first AFC action of the 2026 season, what can Steeler fans expect from New England this week? Read & React takes a look: What to expect from the Patriots’ offense Rushing YPG: 109 (17th) Passing YPG: 168 (25th) PPG: 10 (T-28th) RB: The Patriots entered 2026 with a largely similar offense to the one that helped the team make the Super Bowl last year, with the exception of a reworked wide receiver room. Out are Kayshon Boutte and Stefon Diggs. In are AJ Brown and Romeo Doubs — well, at least to start the season. In a low-scoring, 13-10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks in Week 1 of the 2025 season, the Patriots offense not only sputtered, but lost Brown — the team’s big-ticket addition this offseason — to a high-ankle sprain that eventually landed him on injured reserve. That, paired with a three-interception performance from quarterback Drake Maye on a big stage, led to a disappointing season debut to one of the league’s most up-and-coming teams a year ago. Maye, who was an MVP candidate in 2025, remains a massive threat, and will present a much larger challenge as a quarterback than Cooper Rush was last week against the Steelers. Last season, Maye passed for 4,394 yards with 72% accuracy — partly a product of a short-game-oriented Josh McDaniels scheme, but the young quarterback also showed off one of the league’s best deep balls and excelled despite not having a high-end supporting cast. Maye’s mobility might be the aspect of his game not talked about enough — he managed 47 rushing yards Week 1 — with strong scrambling ability and plenty of highlight reel-worthy plays under pressure in 2025. Drake Maye pic.twitter.com/FjvuzLmd66 — Theo Ash (@TheoAshNFL) December 2, 2025 However, against the Seahawks in Week 1, Maye at times looked like a quarterback trying to do too much, with his final interception being an especially egregious decision that sealed the loss. The final Drake Maye INT is difficult to explain. Just a reckless decision considering the circumstances. pic.twitter.com/RdDllHIi9B https://t.co/KbeLcX2MBk — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) September 10, 2026 Maye will be hoping for a bounce-back performance against Pittsburgh, but he’ll have to do so without the aforementioned AJ Brown. The good news for the Patriots is that Maye made a name for himself last season making the most of a middling wide receiver group. The loss of Brown wouldn’t be as big of a concern if the Patriots’ other big addition at wideout, former Packer Romeo Doubs, hadn’t gotten off to such a slow start Week 1. Doubs had a brutal drop and failed to step up in the offense, even after Brown left with injury. Drake Maye to Romeo Doubs: 3 targets 1 drop 1 interception 0 catches 0 yards https://t.co/YEZ1qBiBTE — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) September 10, 2026 Doubs is a good player who should improve from his season-opening low spot, but it’s still not an encouraging sign for the New England offense. Elsewhere at pass catcher, the Patriots have Mack Hollins, a big-bodied possession receiver, DeMario Douglas, and 2025 draft darling Kyle Williams. At tight end, Hunter Henry is a capable veteran while third-round rookie Eli Raridon caught the team’s first touchdown of the year and could be an underrated name to watch. In the run game Week 1, the Patriots’ offensive line struggled to create lanes against an extremely talented Seahawks front, but it’s worth pointing out that Seattle should once again field an elite defense in 2026. Big-bodied runner Rhamondre Stevenson took the bulk of the carries for New England with speedster TreVeyon Henderson out with injury, but now the second-year runner is healthy entering Week 2, adding another dimension to the New England backfield. It’s not worthwhile to dig too much into trends with only one week of the season in the books, but in Week 1, although the Patriots saw over half their offensive snaps in 11 personnel, another quarter used 12, with another handful of snaps utilizing a fullback. Week 1 offense early down personnel usage and QB alignment (pending MNF) Via @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/QXNOVrYtg2 — Football Insights 📊 (@fball_insights) September 14, 2026 The Patriots had a fairly even run/pass split, trying to establish the run game to set up play action (around a quarter of Maye’s pass attempts Week 1) for downfield shots. However, Stevenson and the Patriots had a hard time finding success on the ground outside of Maye’s scrambling, with Stevenson averaging just 2.8 yards per carry and the team averaging only 0.35 yards before contact per rush, one of the worst marks in the league. Still, both Stevenson and Henderson are capable receivers (the former had five grabs for 44 yards last week) meaning they could still make a big impact even if the run game falters for another week. Odds are that the Steelers will be trying to jar the ball loose on Sunday — a big part of Pittsburgh’s win over New England wast year was a whopping four forced fumbles, including two from Stevenson. And after barely blitzing last week against Atlanta, the Steelers will probably want to dial up the pressure on the line of scrimmage this week to help shut down the Patriots run game, and try to replicate the Seahawks’ success in making Maye uncomfortable and wanting to play hero ball. In an interesting tidbit from Next Gen Stats, New England tackle Will Campbell had one of the best games of his career in terms of pressures allowed last week against Seattle. However, the last time he matched up with Pittsburgh’s Nick Herbig, Campbell allowed a whopping 21.9% pressure rate. It’ll be interesting to see if the Steelers try to bring back that matchup in 2o26. The Patriots should be a good challenge for the Steelers in Week 2 — a Super Bowl contender a year ago and with a dangerous, talented quarterback. That said, after such a dismal outing on offense to start the season, New England is clearly a beatable team that’s still finding its footing in the new season. What to expect from the Patriots’ offense Rushing YPG Allowed: 97.0 (12th) Passing YPG Allowed: 188.0 (16th) PPG Allowed: 13.0 (T-6th) Like the offense, the Patriots’ defense returns most of its core players from last year’s Super Bowl run, but the unit does include four new starters: nose tackle Cory Durden and outside linebacker Elijah Ponder take over as starters after serving as backups in 2025, and offseason acquisitions Dre’Mont Jones and Kevin Byard III are new starters at outside linebacker and free safety, respectively. The Patriots technically have a “new” defensive coordinator this year in Zak Kuhr, but that’s a slightly misleading notion. Kuhr started the 2025 season as New England’s inside linebacker coach, but he took over as defensive playcaller early on in the season when Terrell Williams had to step away from the team while being treated for prostate cancer. Now Kuhr is officially the DC, with Williams taking on another role with the coaching staff. Under Kuhr, the Patriots are a team that uses an even mixture of different coverage schemes. And he’s not one who shies away from sending a high rate of blitzes. Defensive play caller blitz rates vs NFL average by down/distance, neutral field position, removing extreme garbage time over the last decade pic.twitter.com/YQkIWxmBCY — Football Insights 📊 (@fball_insights) August 27, 2026 Defensive coverage rates in Week 1 Via…

title: Steelers mailbag: Will DK Metcalf bounce back vs. Patriots?
summary: Welcome to the Week 2 Pittsburgh Steelers mailbag. I just checked the weather for the next week here in the 412, and it isn’t supposed to reach 80 degrees over the next nine days, most of which will be in the 60’s – I think we’re in the clear (he said hopefully). Pittsburgh will travel […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - SEPTEMBER 21: DK Metcalf #4 of the Pittsburgh Steelers looks on against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on September 21, 2025 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Jordan Bank/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to the Week 2 Pittsburgh Steelers mailbag. I just checked the weather for the next week here in the 412, and it isn’t supposed to reach 80 degrees over the next nine days, most of which will be in the 60’s – I think we’re in the clear (he said hopefully). Pittsburgh will travel to Foxborough to face the New England Patriots, so before then, I’ll dump out all the contents of the mailbag and get your questions answered. Let’s dive in. Q: Last week Roman Wilson was behind the defense on a PI call, DK was behind the defense on an overthrown slot go route on the 3rd play of the game, DK was behind the defense on the non-PI call go route down the left sideline, and DK was behind the defense on the crosser that he dropped. Are you encouraged by the near misses on chunk plays in the passing game enough to outweigh the horrendous run game? – Blkgldtom A: I don’t know if it outweighs how bad the run game was, but I am encouraged about the fact that they are taking shots. They almost certainly won’t go 0-for-9 on them again, and if not for drops and penalties, they would have hit on a handful of the nine deep shots. So that’s encouraging. But the run game needs to figure it out. Q: What are some weaknesses in the Pats’ defense that the Steelers have the personnel to exploit in week two? – SteelerSince73! A: It’s hard to find any glaring weaknesses (mostly because there isn’t one). If there is any tendency that could favor the Steelers, it’s that the Patriots deployed light box looks at the 10th-highest rate in the league last season. Could be a good way to get some chunk runs if their offensive line can win in the trenches. Q: Do you think we will get the run game going a bit more this week? I see Pittman did not practice today. Is this a flare up of what happened to him in camp? How do you think our corner backs look going up against the Patriots top WRs. What is the impact for them to not have AJ Brown playing? How much improvement do you expect in week 2? – steelwoman A: The Patriots have a very good defensive line – much better than that of the Falcons – so I have concerns. I’d start Max Iheanachor at right tackle, Dylan Cook was very bad in Week 1. I’m not sure if Pittman’s injury is related to his camp injury, hopefully being held out of practice is more of a precaution and we see him on Sunday. If not, more snaps for Germie Bernard. I have faith in the secondary, especially in a zone-heavy scheme. I’m going to be going a closer look/keys to victory type piece later on today where I go a bit more in depth on it. Q: Who wins the battle, DK or Gonzalez? And what constitutes a win for you? – RenoSteelersFan A: Gonzalez will win the battle for the majority of the day. If Metcalf can haul in 5+ receptions for 60+ yards, I’d be pleased. Q: What sort of usage are we generally seeing of our 3 edge/outside linebacker sets? What is the benefit of playing Herbig off ball if we also have other off ball backers? – elmango30 A: Alex Highsmith had 41 snaps in Week 1, Nick Herbig had 39. T.J. Watt had 38. They can either drop Herbig into coverage when he’s off-ball, or they can still send him at the quarterback from that spot. It’s a good way to diversify their looks while getting all three guys on the field at one time. Q: How do you keep Steelers fans from jumping off a ledge when things don’t go perfect every game? Sure, winning is the main thing. But the ledgers hover and are a pain in the ass even in a win and ruin every victory weekend. Ledgers, you know who you are, right? – Polamolecules_Dude A: I get the ledgers to an extent because I was (and probably still am) one. Hell, for two years with Kenny Pickett, I came on here and said this isn’t going to work, I don’t care that they beat Will Levis or the Raiders 13-10 – the offense stunk and it wasn’t sustainable. And yeah, that annoys people when you say that after a win, but it doesn’t make it any less reasonable. However, especially early in the season, some games are going to be ugly and discombobulated. On a ledge scale of 1-10 last week, I was probably a 4. The opportunities were there, the defense looked great, and they largely dominated, despite what the final score was. Q: Why Joey Porter Jr? I’m always listening to The Fan, so this isn’t my own question but one that I feel needs an answer. Why was the line drawn on Joey Porter Jr? – Pittsblitz56 A: I wish I knew. I do think Patrick Graham’s zone-heavy scheme has a good bit to do with it, considering Porter is a man-press corner. I’ve come around to the idea of trading him, though, so long as Asante Samuel is kept there long-term (assuming he has a good season). Q: Jarrett, why do you so often use clickbait headlines, cherry-picked stats, and snippets of a larger picture to paint your narratives? This isn’t to say I always disagree with your overall opinion, but the way you often go about it is shoddy at best and unprofessional at worst. – Amperandsteel A: When it comes to headlines, you want to lead the reader in. I’m not perfect and sometimes I’ll make a headline that is too over the top, so that’s a fair critique that I actively try to fix. In terms of the second part, that’s just incorrect, respectfully. There’s nothing unprofessional about how I present an argument, nor is there any difference between how I do it and how everyone else does it. You have an opinion on something and you back it with statistics. For example, a lot of people said the Steelers’ offense looked the same in Week 1 that it did under Tomlin because of the box score. My argument was, no it didn’t look the same. Rodgers attempted nine deep passes in Week 1 – he averaged just three such passes per game in 2025. They also threw the ball far more in Week 1 than they did in all but two games last season, and his average depth of target was north of 10 yards, something he didn’t do once last season. That isn’t me saying the offense doesn’t have room for improvement – it certainly does – but to say it’s somehow unprofessional is just not true. Q: Riley Nowakowski. I didnt notice him at all on Sunday but he had 8 offensive snaps. think his role will increase? – ChippedHam A: If they lean into the run a bit more, I’d expect to see Nowakowski more. If not, his role will stay pretty much the same. Let us know what you think in the comments . Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more! title: Seahawks vs. Cardinals, Week 2 preview: Can Seattle win its 12th straight?
summary: The Seattle Seahawks are heading to Arizona for their first road game of the 2026 season, and if history is any indication, we probably shouldn’t expect a normal afternoon. State Farm Stadium has been the setting for some particularly memorable moments in Seahawks history. It was where Quandre Diggs suffered a gruesome leg injury in […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks are heading to Arizona for their first road game of the 2026 season, and if history is any indication, we probably shouldn’t expect a normal afternoon. State Farm Stadium has been the setting for some particularly memorable moments in Seahawks history. It was where Quandre Diggs suffered a gruesome leg injury in Seattle’s 2021 season finale, a game that also turned out to be Russell Wilson’s final game in a Seahawks uniform. It was also the site of Super Bowl XLIX, one of the most painful games in franchise history. More recently, last year’s meeting in Glendale followed the same general script: Seattle appeared to have control before Arizona made things unnecessarily interesting. The Seahawks led 20-6 in the fourth quarter, only to watch the Cardinals tie the game before Jason Myers hit a 52-yard field goal with 28 seconds remaining. And even that doesn’t tell the whole story. In that 2025 game, Seattle cornerback Coby Bryant intercepted Kyler Murray, only to fumble the ball and have Arizona recover it. So, yeah. Nothing normal. Before the season began, this looked like a game Seattle should win comfortably. The Seahawks are the defending Super Bowl champions, Arizona went 3-14 last season, and Seattle appeared to have the more talented roster. Then Week 1 happened. Seattle lost Sam Darnold on the fifth play of the season before rallying behind Drew Lock and its defense to beat New England 13-10. Arizona, meanwhile, walked into SoFi Stadium and upset the Chargers 26-14. Suddenly, this doesn’t look quite so straightforward. What can Drew Lock show with a full week as the starter? Drew Lock is no longer being thrown into the game with almost no preparation. That’s the biggest difference between Week 1 and Week 2. Against New England, Lock entered after Darnold was injured and initially looked understandably uncomfortable. The offense struggled to find much rhythm, and Seattle remained scoreless until late in the third quarter. But as the game progressed, Lock settled down and helped lead two fourth-quarter scoring drives. He finished 16-of-22 for 187 yards and a touchdown, with no interceptions, while also adding 13 rushing yards. The numbers are encouraging, but the more interesting question is what happens when Arizona takes away the first read. Drew Lock went 3-8 for 35 yards against man coverage against man coverage. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-18T19:52:30.351Z That’s where Lock’s performance against man coverage becomes particularly important. Arizona will have to decide how aggressively it wants to play Seattle’s receivers. With Jaxon Smith-Njigba coming off an eight-catch, 122-yard performance against New England, the Cardinals can’t just sit in soft zone and allow Lock to take easy completions underneath. That should create opportunities for man coverage, especially on third downs and in the red zone. This is where Lock has to show that the Week 1 comeback wasn’t a product of the defense giving him favorable circumstances. Can he identify leverage before the snap? Can he recognize when the Cardinals are playing true man versus a zone structure that initially looks like man? And, most importantly, can he deliver the ball on time when the receiver wins immediately? He’ll have a full week of starting reps to answer those questions. That’s a very different situation from what he faced against New England. The Seahawks cannot afford to beat themselves If there was one obvious problem in Seattle’s season opener, it wasn’t the offense or Drew Lock. It was discipline. The Seahawks were flagged 10 times for 98 yards against the Patriots. But the raw number doesn’t fully explain the problem. Seattle effectively gifted New England all 10 of its points through two separate penalties. The first came when Josh Jobe was flagged for defensive pass interference on an underthrown ball at the goal line, putting the Patriots in position to score a touchdown. Later, a roughing-the-punter penalty on fourth down revived another New England drive that should have ended with Seattle getting the ball back. Those are exactly the kinds of mistakes a team cannot afford on the road, particularly when playing without its starting quarterback. Seattle was already making life difficult for itself offensively. Adding free yards and extra possessions to the equation is asking the defense to do too much. And this becomes even more important in the red zone. The Seahawks committed several penalties in situations where they had forced New England into difficult spots. Against the Patriots, the defense was good enough to overcome those mistakes. The Seahawks need to improve their discipline in keeping the QB inside the pocket. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-18T20:05:50.493Z Discipline also extends beyond penalties. Seattle has to maintain discipline in its pass rush. One thing that showed up at times last season was the defense getting too aggressive trying to hunt the quarterback. The result was an occasional loss of rush-lane integrity, allowing mobile quarterbacks to step through the pocket or escape through an open edge. Drake Maye rushed for 47 yards against Seattle in Week 1, including several scrambles created when the pocket broke down. Jacoby Brissett is not the same type of athlete, but he’s also not a statue. He showed against the Chargers that he can make plays with his legs when necessary, and Arizona’s offense doesn’t need him to become a dual-threat quarterback to make those plays matter. Seattle’s pass rush needs to collapse the pocket without creating escape lanes. The goal isn’t to get pressure; it’s to get pressure while keeping the quarterback contained. Can Seattle find answers for Trey McBride? This might be the most interesting matchup on the other side of the ball. Trey McBride just finished Arizona’s opener with nine receptions for 95 yards and a touchdown. That wasn’t particularly surprising for anyone who has watched him against Seattle. McBride has consistently been a problem for the Seahawks. In eight career games against the Seahawks, he has totaled 36 catches for 579 yards and two touchdowns , averaging 72.4 yards per game. His production has also increased significantly in recent meetings. In 2024, he caught 12 passes for 133 yards in Seattle’s 16-6 win in November, setting a career high in receptions at the time, before following it up with seven catches for 70 yards in the rematch later that season. Then, in the most recent meeting between the teams, McBride caught nine of 13 targets for 127 yards and a touchdown despite Arizona losing 44-22. That’s three games of at least 70 receiving yards in a four-game span against Seattle, including two 100-yard performances. The earlier meetings were much quieter — he had three catches for 29 yards in 2023, three for 34 yards and a touchdown in the 2023 finale, and no catches in either of his two meetings with Seattle as a rookie in 2022. Still, the recent trend is clear enough to make McBride a major problem for a Seattle defense that will have to put significant pressure on its linebackers and a reshuffled safety group to consistently account for him. So this isn’t a theoretical matchup. Seattle has already seen McBride put up big numbers against this defense. And that puts pressure on the linebackers and safeties. The Seahawks’ safety room has undergone significant changes heading into this season, and those depth concerns became even more important when Ty Okada missed the opener with a hamstring injury and Nick Emmanwori was also inactive. With Bud Clark already lost for the season , Seattle entered Week 1 without three players who could have been important pieces in the back end. That matters against a player like McBride because the defense can’t simply assign one player to follow him around the field. Arizona can move McBride around the formation, create matchups against linebackers and use motion to force the defense to communicate after the snap. If…

title: Seahawks injury update: Date for Zach Charbonnet’s return to practice ‘coming soon’
summary: The Seattle Seahawks will definitely not have running back Zach Charbonnet for at least the next three games, but perhaps that will be all he’ll miss while on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald told reporters on Friday that they are working on a date for Charbonnet’s return to […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks will definitely not have running back Zach Charbonnet for at least the next three games, but perhaps that will be all he’ll miss while on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald told reporters on Friday that they are working on a date for Charbonnet’s return to practice. “Zach’s doing great,” Macdonald said. “We’re getting down to him possibly finding a date where he can start practicing again. That’s coming soon. When that exact date is, we haven’t finalized that yet, but it’s coming soon.” Charbonnet started the season on the PUP list after tearing his ACL in the NFC Divisional Round against the San Francisco 49ers. He’s seemingly had no setbacks in his rehab and recovery, and signs point to Charbonnet being back sooner rather than later. The important thing to note for Charbonnet is just how soon he’s eligible to practice. Previously, players who were on PUP couldn’t have their 21-day practice window opened up until after they had missed four games. Now, Charbonnet can return to practice as early as the start of Week 3 against the Washington Commanders , giving him as much as a two-week ramp-up before Week 5 versus, of all teams, the San Francisco 49ers. Charbonnet led the Seahawks in touchdowns scored last regular season, notching a career-high 12 on the ground. His 730 yards was also the best of his career. Jadarian Price may get the headlines as the exciting first-round rookie, but a looming Charbonnet return will be a welcome addition to Seattle’s remade backfield.

title: Seahawks-Cardinals injury designations: Ty Okada out again, Nick Emmanwori questionable
summary: With quarterback Sam Darnold (glute) sidelined, the Seattle Seahawks are expected to heavily rely on their dominant defense once again against the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, but they’ll be left shorthanded for the second consecutive game. Seahawks injury designations Out: Questionable: The team has yet to disclose how or when Okada injured his hamstring, but […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - AUGUST 15: Nick Emmanwori #3 of the Seattle Seahawks tosses the ball before the NFL preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys at Lumen Field on August 15, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images With quarterback Sam Darnold (glute) sidelined, the Seattle Seahawks are expected to heavily rely on their dominant defense once again against the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, but they’ll be left shorthanded for the second consecutive game. Seahawks injury designations Out: S Ty Okada (hamstring) QB Sam Darnold (glute) Questionable: S Nick Emmanwori (ankle, hip) OG Anthony Bradford (knee, hip) The team has yet to disclose how or when Okada injured his hamstring, but after being sidelined from practice for the last two weeks, the level of concern should be starting to rise. Prior to last week’s season opener against the New England Patriots, Seattle activated fellow safety Rodney Thomas II from the practice squad and signed AJ Finley to the active roster, so expect more action on their end. Thomas II was instrumental in the Seahawks’ 13-10 comeback victory against the Patriots after he tipped Drake Maye’s deep shot intended for Romeo Doubs right into the hands of Nehemiah Pritchett for a momentum-altering interception at the beginning of the fourth quarter. He also recorded four total tackles, so it wouldn’t be surprising to see him fill in once again. While Finley did not play any snaps against New England, he could potentially see the field against the Cardinals if Emmanwori remains sidelined, which certainly seems plausible. After entering the week still working his way back from offseason ankle surgery, the second-year safety showed up with a hip injury on Wednesday’s injury report and given his value all over the field, it’d be difficult to picture the Seahawks rushing him back. Emmanwori wasn’t the only play to unexpectedly suffer a hip injury, as Bradford seemingly did as well. The starting right guard was already nursing a knee injury before his hip issue popped up on Thursday’s injury report. Bradford was limited in the team’s Sept. 7 practice before returning in a full capacity the next two days, which subsequently led to him suiting up again New England. However, now navigating through two injuries and not practicing on Friday, it appears he could be trending on the wrong side of questionable ahead of Sunday. Should he be sidelined, backup Christian Haynes would be in line to step in. As for the Cardinals, cornerback Garrett Williams (achilles) was ruled out and OG Isaac Seumalo (shoulder), DT Roy Lopez (groin), OG Isaiah Adams (knee), DT Andrew Billings (knee) as well as CB Max Melton (ankle) are listed as questionable. Both teams will release their official inactives at 11:55 AM P.T. on Sunday.

title: Seahawks vs Cardinals: 4 game predictions for Week 2 showdown
summary: The Seattle Seahawks opened the season with a 13-10 victory at home in a Super Bowl rematch against the New England Patriots. In case you’ve been living under a rock, Sam Darnold was injured on the first drive and Drew Lock led the Seahawks to a comeback victory. Darnold was already ruled out of this […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks opened the season with a 13-10 victory at home in a Super Bowl rematch against the New England Patriots . In case you’ve been living under a rock, Sam Darnold was injured on the first drive and Drew Lock led the Seahawks to a comeback victory. Darnold was already ruled out of this week’s game against the Arizona Cardinals. Even without Sam Darnold, Seattle is currently a 4.5-point favorite according to FanDuel Sportsbook . It will be the first NFC West matchup of the year, so Drew Lock will be counted on to get the division race started off on the right foot. Let’s get to this week’s predictions, starting with one for the tiny beaks in Arizona. Trey McBride 8+ receptions (+140) McBride is one of the best tight ends in the NFL, and arguably the best player on the Cardinals. He began his 2026 campaign with 9 receptions in the opener. The last three times McBride has played the Seahawks, he’s tallied 9, 7, and 12 receptions. I expect Jacoby Brissett to get the ball out quickly to try and mitigate the pass rush with McBride being a main beneficiary. Jadarian Price 100+ yards (+550) Price looked great in his Seahawks debut on limited carries eclipsing 50 yards at over 5.0 YPC. With more opportunities, he should do even better this week. He’ll still be splitting time in the backfield with George Holani and Emmanuel Wilson, but I think Price will get at least 15 carries this week and crack the 100-yard mark for the first time in his NFL career on the back of a few explosives. Drew Lock passing TD under 1.5 (-200) In five of his last seven starts, Lock has only thrown one TD pass. Add in last week’s game where he played all but one drive, and that makes it 75% of the time with just one passing TD. This feels like a game where Seattle will try to pound the rock and might stall out in the red zone. I could be totally wrong and Lock will air it out like crazy. In fact, I would be happy if that was the case…I just don’t think it’s all that likely, and Lock will once again have a lone passing TD. Scoring under 41.5 (-120) Continuing on with my last point, I would take the under for points here. Recent history tells me that the teams would’ve hit the over each of the last three times they played. However, that was without a quarterback for the Seahawks and a potentially more conservative game plan. I also think the Seahawks defense is going to clamp down on the Cardinals offense. This will probably be an uncomfortable game for much of the first three quarters, finishing somewhere around 20-13 for the final score, securely in the under category. title: How Brock Purdy’s story as the 49ers’ starting quarterback began with the Dolphins
summary: The San Francisco 49ers will host the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, and the last time they hosted the Dolphins was a turning point in 49ers history. That was when injuries thrust Brock Purdy into the starting quarterback role. Fans had seen Purdy take the field before, either in mop-up duty (Arizona Cardinals) or when the […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 04: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers drops back to pass against the Miami Dolphins during the second quarter of an NFL football game at Levi's Stadium on December 04, 2022 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers will host the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, and the last time they hosted the Dolphins was a turning point in 49ers history. That was when injuries thrust Brock Purdy into the starting quarterback role. Fans had seen Purdy take the field before, either in mop-up duty (Arizona Cardinals) or when the game was out of reach (Kansas City Chiefs), but they hadn’t seen him when a game was in contention. Many remember the following week’s game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, where Purdy outplayed Buccaneers quarterback Tom Brady. While it wasn’t as flashy as that game, Purdy’s entrance to the field showed one important thing: he belonged. The 49ers already lost their starting quarterback, Trey Lance, two games into the season. Jimmy Garoppolo, who the 49ers replaced Lance with to start that offseason, stepped in without a hitch and things continued. The Dolphins game began with the visitors getting a touchdown from a pass to Trent Sherfield. Garoppolo took the 49ers down the field for their first drive, leading to a field goal after a third-down sack. The sack was Garoppolo’s last play in a 49ers uniform. The next drive, Brock Purdy, a player who began as the No. 3 quarterback at the beginning of the year, was next man up under center. No one knew then, but he wasn’t giving that job back. Not to Lance, not to Garoppolo, not to anybody. On his first drive, Purdy had a few errant passes. Some analysts during the game suggested Kyle Shanahan lacked trust in calling anything sophisticated for the rookie. Regardless, he drove the 49ers down the field and hit Kyle Juszczyk for a touchdown to give the 49ers the lead. It’s a touchdown; there’s nothing bad about that, but there wasn’t anything defining either. Just the same things we’ve seen with Jimmy G. The next 49ers offensive drive ended in an interception. Purdy stared down Brandon Aiyuk, and the Dolphins defense knew where the ball was going. Rookie mistake, the last pick in the draft. It’s hard not to anticipate these mistakes. What is notable is the drive after. That’s the statement. During the two-minute drill, Purdy took the 49ers down the field (with a nice QB sneak on a fourth down) and hit George Kittle just before getting drilled. Brock Purdy uncorked this throw on 3rd and 10 in a two minute drill to keep the drive going at the end of the first half. They capped off the drive with a TD to take the lead, and never gave it back. Easy to see why Kyle likes him so much. Remarkable poise here. pic.twitter.com/RlDJuHrdZu — Brett Kollmann (@BrettKollmann) December 5, 2022 It’s not the play that says Purdy is the starting quarterback, but it is a play to show that this rookie, Mr. Irrelevant, can hang in the NFL. There wouldn’t be any more offensive touchdowns in this game. Purdy would drive the 49ers down to score three field goals to pull the 49ers further away from the Dolphins—a Dre Greenlaw fumble recovery for a touchdown sealed the game. For a season where the 49ers had playoff aspirations and Garoppolo’s fate uncertain, Purdy at least showed he could be a capable backup. His numbers following the game weren’t awful, but not necessarily special either: 25 for 37 (67 percent completion rate with a 5.7-yard average), 210 passing yards, two touchdowns, and one interception for a rating of 88.8. For a rookie playing his first game, it’s not in any way bad, but it’s not something that would put Purdy on the map. After the game, it was evident Garoppolo would be missing time (the rest of the season) with a foot injury. The 49ers were going to be Purdy’s team. It took the following week against the Buccaneers to show that Purdy wasn’t just a capable backup, but the starter of the future. While the Buccaneers game showed the 49ers had something special in Purdy, the Dolphins game showed he belonged. Rather than jitters, errant passes all game, and an opposing defense sending the cavalry to sack him, Purdy hung in the pocket every play and delivered—even when something was being delivered to him. Sunday’s game against the Dolphins marks the first time the teams have met in Levi’s Stadium since that day. They had met in 2024, but at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami. The Dolphins coming to Levi’s always serves as a reminder of the day Mr. Irrelevant became Mr. Relevant.

The other was when the Raiders had two running backs in the backfield, a pony set the 49ers used last week with both Kaelon Black and Deebo Samuel, and Jeanty crossed his face on an angle route for a score.” 49ers starter Connor Colby’s first goal? Making left guard feel right (paywall) “Though he dabbled at left guard at Iowa at the end of the 2022 season, he started on the right side for the vast majority of his college starts. In fact, he’s played right guard since he was a teenager, which made firing out of a right-handed stance second nature. “It’s kind of akin to going to a place like Australia, where you drive on the other side of the road — everything’s kind of flipped over,” Brendel said. “The mechanics are 100 percent the opposite direction.” Brendel said some offensive linemen can switch sides at the snap of a finger. “And there are other guys I’ve played with who have played the same side, the same position their entire careers, and they refuse to play anything else,” he said. He practiced his left-side repetitions at Iowa in the offseason, then took part in a summer competition that included Willis, Robert Jones and Austen Pleasants. His goal was to make left guard feel just as natural as right guard. He admits he’s not there yet. “But I think it’s turning in the right direction,” he said. “Right guard, I’ll always feel, is natural. I’m a right-handed guy. But it doesn’t feel as awkward now.” Five 49ers to watch in home opener vs. Dolphins in Week 2 of 2026 NFL season “There is little doubt the Dolphins will test the middle of the 49ers’ defense on Sunday. But a few big plays and a dominant third quarter should be enough to pull away from one of the least talented teams in the league. Lombardi: 49ers 24, Dolphins 17. I actually think Miami will give the 49ers a sweat, simply because I’m still worn out from the Australia trip and I did spy some tired players in the Levi’s Stadium locker room this week. It’ll be a sluggish game and the Dolphins, coached by former 49ers assistant Jeff Hafley, will put on a scrappy performance reminiscent of the early-Shanahan era.” Kyle Shanahan shares final updates ahead of 49ers-Dolphins “I understand what questionable means, but do you have a level of optimism regarding Kaelon Black and his availability? “A questionable amount of optimism.” Is it the same groin injury he dealt with earlier in the season? “I didn’t ask him.”
