title: 49ers vs. Dolphins preview: Trap games don’t exist in September
summary: The San Francisco 49ers “upset” the Los Angeles Rams in Week 1. If you’ve watched sports long enough, you know that when the talk is so one-sided about one team, the other team usually prevails. That was true in Australia in Week 1, but the Niners find themselves on the other side of the talking […]
full_text: San Francisco 49ers' head coach Kyle Shanahan speaks to the media at AAMI Park in Melbourne on September 7, 2026. (Photo by Martin KEEP / AFP via Getty Images) / -- IMAGE RESTRICTED TO EDITORIAL USE - STRICTLY NO COMMERCIAL USE -- | AFP via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers “upset” the Los Angeles Rams in Week 1. If you’ve watched sports long enough, you know that when the talk is so one-sided about one team, the other team usually prevails. That was true in Australia in Week 1, but the Niners find themselves on the other side of the talking points in Week 1. After all, the Miami Dolphins couldn’t muster much of anything offensively against a Las Vegas Raiders defense that nobody would confuse with the top teams in the league. The 49ers enter Sunday as nearly two-touchdown favorites. Double-digit spreads are abnormal in the NFL. And while this one might feel like it’s warranted after the 49ers’ convincing 20-point win over the Rams, history suggests the Niners’ home opener will be a lot closer than the line suggests. Here’s an uncomfortable stat that applies to the Dolphins: Week 2 road underdogs off a double-digit loss have gone 24-5 against the spread. Perhaps that means the 49ers only win by 10. Maybe it’s a surprising nail-biter decided by one possession. Let’s let the data lead us to the right answer. 49ers’ pass offense vs. the Dolphins’ pass defense 49ers passing offense Using a one-week sample size when said week was historically high-scoring can get you in trouble. The only quarterback with a higher passer rating through 50 career games than Brock Purdy, provided they’ve thrown at least 100 passes, is Patrick Mahomes. Purdy had 34 attempts against the Rams, with 12 of those coming behind the line of scrimmage and another 16 taking place within 10 yards. Kyle Shanahan was not going to let Myles Garrett beat him. The game plan seemed to anticipate Aaron Donald playing. What fascinates me is how different the passing attack looks in Week 2, especially if Miami is without their top pass rusher, Chop Robinson . A short passing attack shouldn’t be viewed as an indictment on the quarterback. There’s absolutely zero shame in being efficient and staying out of longer down-and-distances, which is precisely what the offense accomplished: Average distance to gain on third down in Week 1: 1. 49ers – 3.17 yds (12 plays) 2. Chiefs – 4.53 yds (17 plays) 3. Bengals – 4.93 yds (14 plays) 4. Bears – 5.21 yds (14 plays) 5. Buccaneers – 5.50 yds (10 plays) ^^Signs you're efficient on early downs — Kyle Posey (@KP_Show) September 17, 2026 The Dolphins just faced a quarterback who had no interest in pushing the ball down the field. Kirk Cousins was 21-for-30, but only 1-for-7 on passes 10+ yards downfield, including two interceptions. The Raiders are running into a different beast Sunday. Purdy’s Week 1 passer rating (105.6) was on par with his career number (104.0), as we mentioned above. As noted, Purdy’s yards per attempt was on the lower side, but he still managed to finish 12th in EPA per dropback and fourth in passing success rate. Those short-yardage third downs allowed Purdy to lean on Mike Evans on obvious passing downs. All six of Evans’ receptions resulted in a first down or a touchdown. But if Week 1 is any indication, this will be a Christian McCaffrey, Deebo Samuel, and Kaelon Black game. Dolphins passing defense Why will the 49ers be more aggressive through the air this week? The Dolphins had the most total snaps played by rookies in Week 1, logging 439—158 more than any other team. Cornerback Chris Johnson, free safety Michael Taaffe, and linebacker Jacob Rodriguez were all rookie starters for the Dolphins. Rodriguez is a fun player with instincts that have some pundits comparing him to a certain 49ers linebacker. While Rodriguez racked up 10 tops, he allowed both of his targets to be completed, including one for a touchdown. He’s better in zone when Rodriguez can get his eyes on the quarterback. He’s a great athlete, but McCaffrey on a choice route with a two-way go is an advantage for CMC against anybody, especially a rookie. Eye candy. Much like in Week 1, messing with the defender’s keys will put the 49ers in advantageous situations. The touchdown Rodriguez allowed was on a play-action, and Jeanty leaked out of the backfield and past Rodriguez for a touchdown. Johnson was targeted 9 times and held up well. Johnson limited the damage to five receptions for 48 yards. A couple of those came underneath against Michael Mayer. Don’t be surprised if we see George Kittle isolated underneath against one of the rookies, too. What those stats don’t tell you are the touchdowns Johnson allowed. One came on a simple red-zone slant route from the slot. Hello, Mike Evans. The other was when the Raiders had two running backs in the backfield, a pony set the 49ers used last week with both Kaelon Black and Deebo Samuel, and Jeanty crossed his face on an angle route for a score. Miami finished 12th in Week 1 in EPA per pass allowed. On average, Cousins had 2.9 seconds to throw. Cousins was pressured 32.3% of the time, about five percentage points below last year’s league average. The quality of quarterback is drastically different, making it difficult to dig into the numbers. Cousins has a passing success rate of 46.3. Purdy has the sixth-best passing success rate and was second in catchable target rate. The Dolphins should be stressed on the back end far more than they were in Week 1. Jeff Hafley blitzed Cousins 29% of the time but generated pressure only 29% of the time. Purdy should be comfortable and have time to throw. Purdy will probably see a little more man coverage than he did a week ago. Player to watch: LB Jordyn Brooks The former Seahawks linebacker has blossomed into one of the league’s best. He allowed all four of his targets to be completed, but only for an average of 4.8 yards. He reads the field well and has instincts to step in front of a Purdy throw — especially in that hook/curl zone. Steer clear of Brooks and any potential mishaps, and the 49ers should stay on schedule in the same manner they did a week ago. Advantage: 49ers +1 49ers rush offense vs. Dolphins run defense The uptick in dash motion led Kittle to coin a new nickname for the 49ers . The run game looked like 2023, which might be the biggest compliment you can give. No team had a higher success rate or more yards before contact than the Niners in Week 1. The personnel didn’t change. The 49ers used a fullback on 42.2% of the time. For whatever reason, the league still refuses to steal that part of Shanahan’s playbook, as that figure was 36$ above league average.Going from 0.93 yards before contact to 2.79 on running back carries had to bring a smile to the coaching staff’s face. Motioning at the snap on nearly two-thirds of the snaps led to hesitation, and the Rams were all but blocking themselves. That was against an experienced team with ample playoff experience. The 49ers had five 10+ yard carries. The Raiders had four. The 49ers only had 6.7% of their runs stuffed — a gain of zero or negative. Nearly a quarter of the Raiders’ runs were stuffed. That’s how Las Vegas ended up with a success rate of only 40%. The Dolphins missed 20 tackles against the Raiders. McCaffrey and Black forced five missed tackles. Deebo ran through a tackle on his lone carry. More importantly, the trio combined for 97 yards after contact. The Dolphins matched up with the Raiders’ heavy personnel, which plays into the 49ers’ hands. Miami used base personnel on over 68% of their snaps, which was almost 39% above league average. It’s easy to see why this game is being treated as a potential blowout when you look at how each team performed on this side of the ball a week ago. Player to watch: DT Zach Sieler Even on plays where the Raiders gained positive yards, Sieler can be seen doing his job and handling his man. He’s somebody the Niners need to be aware of. He lives on the other side of the line of…

title: 3 things to watch for in 49ers-Dolphins: The under center movement will continue
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are home again, and the Miami Dolphins are in town for the home opener at Levi’s Stadium. The performance from the 49ers in Australia has reminded some folks about how loaded the team still is, and somehow, the team was overlooked. Now, the team looks to remain undefeated and build on […]
full_text: (Photo by Quinn Rooney/Getty Images) The San Francisco 49ers are home again, and the Miami Dolphins are in town for the home opener at Levi’s Stadium. The performance from the 49ers in Australia has reminded some folks about how loaded the team still is, and somehow, the team was overlooked. Now, the team looks to remain undefeated and build on their Week 1 performance. Here are three things to watch for on Sunday: The under center revolution The 49ers revealed one of their newest wrinkles going under center and used it in the drop-back passing game. With the fourth-highest rate in the NFL, which is seeing a huge bump in under-center percentage, the 49ers finished with the third-highest EPA per play under center at 0.20. On the flip side, Miami faced the second-highest rate, as the Raiders went under center 63.5% of the time. The Dolphins did well against it and posted a defensive EPA of -0.04. You can expect this to continue, along with the winding motion to create angles and force defenses to react a second too late. Miami’s defensive strategy The 49ers took advantage of the lighter personnel on the Rams’ defense and ran the ball right at their nickel and dime packages. Los Angeles came out in base defense on 28.1% of their defensive snaps. Miami led the NFL with a 68.3 base defense percentage. Also, the Dolphins were in nickel at the lowest mark in the league at 31.7%. If Miami continues this trend, the 49ers will attack their base looks with more passing on early downs. Expect a big game from Mike Evans on Sunday if the Dolphins want to stay in base all game. Generating pressure on Malik Willis The 49ers blitzed at the second-lowest rate in the NFL at 10.3%, but generated pressure at 37.9%. Miami allowed the highest pressure percentage last week, with Malik Willis feeling pressure on 56.8% of his dropbacks. The Dolphins offense took a ton of shots downfield with the highest deep throw percentage of 29,6%. Not allowing routes to develop downfield, keeping Willis in the pocket, and generating pressure is the key to slowing down the mobile quarterback
author: Jason Aponte

title: George Kittle coins a new nickname for the 49ers after a dominant performance against the Rams
summary: The YAC bros are so 2020. That’s a thing of the past. The San Francisco 49ers had the Rams chasing their tails in Week 1 against the Los Angeles Rams because of their overdose of “dash” motion, when a player is still going in motion at the snap. The 49ers offense featured motion at the […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The YAC bros are so 2020. That’s a thing of the past. The San Francisco 49ers had the Rams chasing their tails in Week 1 against the Los Angeles Rams because of their overdose of “dash” motion, when a player is still going in motion at the snap. The 49ers offense featured motion at the snap on 65.6% of plays against the Rams, their highest rate in a game in the Kyle Shanahan era. Kyle Juszczyk was in motion at the snap on over half of snaps (17 of 33). No other 49ers player had more than five such snaps. The player closest to Juszczyk was George Kittle. On Thursday, Kittle coined the nickname “Dash Bros.” He said, They’re not my favorite, but they’re very effective. So I just put my pride aside and just do them. I just don’t like cutting and running that much. I like lining up and hitting people in the face. That’s kind of what I do.” There are several advantages to using motion at the snap. Football is a numbers game. Whenever the 49ers used dash motion, they were either +1 or +2 from a blocking perspective to the side of the ball they ran it to. So it’s no surprise the Niners averaged over six yards per carry on runs with motion in Week 1. Another advantage that showed as the game went on was that you never know where the person in motion will insert as a blocker. Juszczyk blocked the backside defensive end several times. The change-up came in the third quarter. After 2.5 quarters of Juszczyk working to the other side of the formation, which caused everybody from the edge defenders to the linebackers to overadjust, Juszczyk ran back-to-back plays late in the third quarter where he went in dash motion into the backfield, only to return to the side he started. That allowed Deebo Samuel to block the defensive end twice. It gave the right side of the offensive line the angles they needed to secure their blocks. Shanahan’s play-calling sequencing was superb. That’s because everything looked the same. The 49ers ran inside zone about 27% of the time, compared to outside zone roughly 37%. They sprinkled in enough man concepts (16.7%) to keep the defense off balance. The execution provided better results than essentially any game from a year ago: Counter: 1 carry, 4 yards → 4.0 YPC — 0% success rate Outside Zone: 11 carries, 67 yards → 6.09 YPC — 60% success rate Man: 5 carries, 33 yards → 6.6 YPC — 54.55% success rate Inside Zone: 7 carries, 29 yards → 4.14 YPC — 42.86% success rate Even into the fourth quarter, with the dash motion, Juszczyk still hadn’t inserted up the middle to block a linebacker. Sure enough, that’s what he did, leading to a seven-yard gain for Christian McCaffrey. So Juszczyk went in motion all game, but with multiple insert points, it forced the Rams to hesitate, so much so that they blocked themselves. It’s part of why the 49ers’ running backs averaged 2.79 yards before contact — the highest stat in Week 1. Generating yards before contact was one of the biggest issues for the 49ers’ run game in 2025. They were 29th in the NFL, at 0.93. So Week 1 was quite the jump in production for the offensive line. Part of that goes to the motion, but you can’t ignore how dominant the offensive line performed. Dominick Puni no longer playing on one leg helps. Having a Hall of Fame left tackle doesn’t hurt. Jake Brendel and Connor Colby exceeded expectations, while Colton McKivitz looked like his usual self as a run blocker. The biggest surprise may have been Luke Farrell. After an inconsistent season in 2025, Farrell looked comfortable executing the blocks he was tasked with, and they were not easy. We know what Kittle is capable of, but if Farrell can play as he did in Week 1 for the rest of the season, the 49ers’ running game should look more like 2023 than it did in the previous two seasons. One thing we can bank on: The Dash Bros are here to stay.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Dolphins could be without a key contributor against the 49ers in Week 2
summary: There may have been some cause for concern when the San Francisco 49ers added running back Kaelon Black to the injury report with a groin injury on Thursday, but head coach Kyle Shanahan said the team was just being smart with their rookie. The injuries to the Miami Dolphins do not seem precautionary. Linebacker Ronine […]
full_text: (Photo by Jordon Kelly/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images There may have been some cause for concern when the San Francisco 49ers added running back Kaelon Black to the injury report with a groin injury on Thursday, but head coach Kyle Shanahan said the team was just being smart with their rookie. The injuries to the Miami Dolphins do not seem precautionary. Linebacker Ronine Harrison has not practiced this week with a hamstring injury. He didn’t play a defensive snap in Week 1, but was a mainstay on special teams. As we’ve seen firsthand in the past, shuffling bodies on special teams leads to mistakes and big plays for the opponent. That bodes well for Deebo Samuel and Jacob Cowing. The big one is Chop Robinson. The Dolphins’ first-round pick from 2024 is projected to be the team’s top pass rusher. Robinson had a quarterback hit in Week 1. But he’s currently in the concussion protocol. After being a limited participant on Wednesday, Robinson was downgraded on Thursday to not practicing, suggesting his status for Sunday’s game is in question. Robinson played 62% of snaps in Week 1 and was the only edge defender to surpass 40 snaps for the Dolphins. Robinson’s backup is an old friend, Rob Beal Jr. After him, the edge rushers on the roster are Josh Uche and Malik Herring. So, if Robinson is out, an already thin pass rush will be even more depleted.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 49ers-Dolphins numbers to know: Sacks are in store for Sunday
summary: While the San Francisco 49ers have a quicker turnaround than the Los Angeles Rams in returning from Australia, the NFL certainly did the 49ers a favor with the Week 2 opponent choice. The 49ers open Levi’s Stadium for the 2026 season against the Miami Dolphins, who compete to be one of the worst teams in […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect While the San Francisco 49ers have a quicker turnaround than the Los Angeles Rams in returning from Australia, the NFL certainly did the 49ers a favor with the Week 2 opponent choice. The 49ers open Levi’s Stadium for the 2026 season against the Miami Dolphins, who compete to be one of the worst teams in the league. Miami had a chance to separate itself from the bottom of the league in Week 1, but instead put up a hapless fight against the Las Vegas Raiders and dropped the season opener 27-13. For as exciting of a Week 1 victory the 49ers had, the air would be sucked out with a Week 2 loss to Miami. These are the numbers to know before San Francisco’s home opener: 46.2 Yards. The Dolphins rushed for 74 yards in their Week 1 loss to the Las Vegas Raiders, 46.2 rushing yards fewer than their 202 per-game average. The 2025 Miami Dolphins were predicated on the run game. While Tua Tagovailoa struggled, De’Von Achane kept the pedestrian Miami offense afloat, finishing fifth in total rushing yards (1,350) and first in yards per attempt (5.7). The idea was that with the addition of Malik Willis, the Miami run game would be even more fearsome. That simply wasn’t the case for the Dolphins against the Raiders in Week 1. While Miami likely had to abandon the run game much earlier than planned after falling behind 17-3 in the first half, there was not a lot of production from Achane. He totaled 36 yards on 11 carries, good for a 3.3 average gain per attempt. Only in two games last season did Achane average less than three yards per attempt, and in both he had 11 or fewer carries. The key to stopping Achane is to prevent him from getting the ball, and the easiest way to do so is to jump out to an early lead like the Raiders did last week. Willis’ legs will create an interesting matchup as the 49ers traditionally struggle against mobile quarterbacks, and Sunday will be Raheem Morris’ first crack against one as San Francisco’s defensive coordinator. Achane will be the main source of the Miami rushing attack, but a struggling 49ers run defense will also have to account for Willis and his legs. 5 Sacks. Malik Willis was sacked five times in Week 1, tied for the most allowed in the league last week. The downside to having a mobile quarterback is that sometimes they’ll take silly sacks, and that’s what happened to Willis in his Miami debut. Willis had plenty of time to operate in Week 1 because of his legs. His average time to throw against the Raiders was 3.47 seconds, tied with Caleb Williams for the second-longest time to throw among starting quarterbacks and only behind Jayden Daniels. Unfortunately for Willis, Williams was sacked only twice and Daniels just once, while Willis was sacked five times. And it’s not like Willis wasn’t getting time to operate. The Miami quarterback had more than 2.5 seconds to throw on 73 percent of his dropbacks, the sixth-highest rate of all quarterbacks in Week 1. But all five sacks came on the plays where Willis had the most time, meaning his decision-making must be quicker in Week 2 against San Francisco. It’ll be a tricky matchup for a 49ers defensive line that doesn’t have the firepower to get after the quarterback outside of Nick Bosa. The 49ers create pressure on 40 percent of Matthew Stafford’s dropbacks in Week 1, but Willis is obviously more mobile than Stafford, so escaping the pressure should be easier for him. The 49ers pass rush against the Miami offensive line is a “moveable force versus stoppable object” matchup, and Willis’ legs alone could keep the Dolphins close. It’ll be up to Morris and the San Francisco pass rush to keep Willis at bay. 6 First downs. The 49ers defense allowed six first downs through the air in Week 1, tied for the second-fewest allowed. The 49ers secondary held the coveted Los Angeles pass ga, featuringed Puka Nacua and Davante Adams to a measly 168 yards. If they could do that to the Rams, imagine what they can do to an offense featuring the less-intimidating Caleb Douglas and Malik Washington. San Francisco’s secondary is what played a large role in holding the Rams offense to such a low mark. Deommodore Lenoir, Renardo Green, Upton Stout, and Jack Jones were targeted by the Rams a combined 19 times, allowing just 10 receptions, with the longest being a 23-yard catch allowed by Lenoir. Unsurprisingly, Miami’s pass offense was just about on par with the Rams in Week 1. The Dolphins might have outgained Los Angeles, but the productivity was the same. Miami could only muster seven passing first downs, with Willis held without a touchdown and one interception. One could hope the 49ers’ defense can carry its Week 1 momentum into Week 2 against a far inferior Dolphins passing offense.
author: Andrew Pasquini

title: Buccaneers vs. Browns: Final injury report for Week 2

The good news for Tampa Bay is that all three were full participants in the team’s final practice of the week. title: 3 Titans who absolutely need to be better in Week 2
summary: The Tennessee Titans have a difficult matchup with the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 2. They’ll need to be significantly better than they were versus the New York Jets. We’ve identified three Titans players in particular who need to be way more productive against the Eagles. Cam Ward, QB Titans quarterback Cam Ward finished 19-of-32 in […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: Cam Ward #1 of the Tennessee Titans warms up prior to the game against the New York Jets at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tennessee Titans have a difficult matchup with the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 2. They’ll need to be significantly better than they were versus the New York Jets. We’ve identified three Titans players in particular who need to be way more productive against the Eagles. Cam Ward, QB Titans quarterback Cam Ward finished 19-of-32 in Week 1 for 140 yards and a touchdown. A large portion of his production occurred via a garbage-time possession. Ward recorded 55 passing yards and his lone touchdown late in the fourth quarter once the Jets defense went into a late-game prevent shell. The All-22 tape review wasn’t kind to Ward’s performance . The offensive line was better than the broadcast angles indicated and receivers were creating consistent separation. Ward was hesitant, inefficient, occasionally inaccurate, and even bailed from clean pockets. The sophomore No. 1 overall quarterback needs to get better weekly. Calvin Ridley, WR Calvin Ridley doesn’t necessarily need to be “better.” Ward and Brian Daboll need to do a better job getting him involved. The multi-time 1,000-yard receiver wasn’t targeted in Week 1. That’s despite Ridley running 25 routes on 26 passing-down snaps, per Pro Football Focus. Ridley’s route-participation rate was 96.2%. The aging wideout still possesses enough juice to create explosive plays. Ward and Daboll need to get Ridley involved versus the Eagles to take some pressure off Carnell Tate and Wan’Dale Robinson. Jermaine Johnson II, EDGE The Titans traded T’Vondre Sweat to the Jets for Jermaine Johnson II. The former Florida State standout had previously played for Saleh in East Rutherford. That was supposed to make Johnson an effective pass rusher in Saleh’s system, but that wasn’t the case in Week 1. PFF credited Johnson with registering one pathetic quarterback pressure versus the Jets. The former first-round pick earned a brutal grade of 41.8 as a pass rusher, as he did not impact Geno Smith in the pocket at all. The challenge versus Jalen Hurts will be way bigger.

Hogs Haven: I think the first thing almost any Commanders fan would say is the performance of the defense. Last year, the Commanders had one of the worst defenses in the NFL, so they completely overhauled it in the offseason, with a new DC in Daronte Jones (who brings an attacking Flores-like scheme) and replacing over half of the starters on defense. Early returns indicate the overhaul has paid off. The defense was living in the Eagles backfield last Sunday, generating a 48.48% pressure rate on Jalen Hurts and a 24% TFL rate, both notably higher than NFL average. BTB: Give us a rundown on a few of the new players in Washington who could make a big impact this season. On defense, as mentioned before, over half the defensive starters this year are new to the team. I won’t go through all of them, but the standouts are LB Sonny Styles, S Nick Cross, and EDGE Odafe Oweh.Styles was drafted 7th overall and has lived up to his billing. He was all over the field on Sunday making plays and even steamrolled Saquon Barkley to get a big hit on Jalen Hurts on a blitz. Nick Cross was a physical presence flying all over the field, showing well in coverage while also getting tackles and limiting yardage to the line of scrimmage. Odafe Oweh was the team’s biggest FA signing with a 4-year, $96 million contract. He didn’t have a huge impact in week 1 against the Eagles elite OTs, ending the game with 1 sack, 3 total tackles and a tackle for loss. I would also be remiss if I didn’t mention standout gunner Tyler Owens, who was a maven on special teams and had an angry run that went viral after the game. Sports Illustrated Washington May Need Treylon Burks One Week After Making Him Inactive Treylon Burks was among the five players on the 53-man active roster who did not dress against the Philadelphia Eagles, as the team dressed four tight ends and five wide receivers instead . What made the inactive status odd was that Burks was featured among the starters in the Week 1 depth chart. Now with TE Chig Okonkwo out this week , the roster math has shifted completely. While he is not a tight end, Burks brings his 6-foot-2, 225-pound frame with him every snap, works well over the middle, and has a bigger catch radius than most of Washington’s receiving room. Quinn talked about those traits during camp: “But at the Z position, we really feel his impact, you know? Deep routes, in-breaking routes, he’s got a long catch radius, and so that’s the thing that you feel on a regular basis.” Ben Sinnott is another player the team would like to see step into a larger role with Okonkwo out. The Sunday night showing marked the fewest yards gained since week nine during the Cowboys’ 2024 season, giving Dallas fuel to turn the tide in their home opener. Both Ceedee Lamb and George Pickens combined to register 43 catches of at least 20 yards in 2025 as the duo ranked among the top 14 across the NFL in the category last season. Yet they will also look to turn the page after combining for six drops and 72 yards while Lamb found the endzone for Dallas’ first touchdown of the season. Add in the fact that the Cowboys had just two possessions through the second half, how defensive coordinator Daronte Jones and the Commanders’ defense can extend the Cowboys’ slowly developing passing attack again may be the biggest question mark . Both Pickens and Lamb recorded at least four receptions and 45 yards each in both of the meetings in 2025, and it’s a debate whether the unit is upgraded one season later. With Amos sidelined for at least another three weeks and uncertainty whether he’ll be available in week five, Rasul Douglas, who Daronte Jones called a “savvy vet,” has been able to step into an impact role with Amik Robertson and Mike Sainristil rounding out the top of the room. Though Douglas allowed a 31 yard completion on third down, the veteran showed why he can at least be a stopgap at the position. Yet the test goes beyond Douglas with Sainristil looking to bounceback as Jones pointed to “urgency” from his third year cornerback. Dallas failed to get much pressure on Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart and, unlike the Philadelphia Eagles, only generated two pressures on four-man rushes during the evening. Blough should have plenty of opportunities to get his offense on the right track, as the Cowboys’ defense also lost safety Malik Hooker and linebacker DeMarvion Overshown to injuries this week. full_text: Frankie Luvu is the Commanders defensive field general. The veteran linebacker’s a team captain and wears the green dot, relaying defensive play calls to the rest of the group. Washington will operate without Luvu in a Week 2 contest against the Dallas Cowboys. He has been ruled out with a hamstring strain, head coach Dan Quinn told on-site reporters in a Friday press conference. Quinn also said that tight end Chig Okonkwo (groin) will be out against the Cowboys. That information was confirmed on the official Commanders injury report, which was release on Friday afternoon. Defensive lineman Javon Kinlaw was also listed as questionable. He showed up on the participation report Thursday dealing with a back injury. He missed that day and was limited on Friday. Here’s the full injury report for the Commanders and Cowboys: Injury Report: pic.twitter.com/131TD3o3mf — Commanders PR (@Wash_PR) September 18, 2026 Leo Chenal should start for Luvu in the linebacker corps, but rookie Sonny Styles will assume green dot responsibilities, as he did after Luvu got hurt in the regular season opener at Philadelphia. Okonkwo’s absence should mean more time for John Bates and Ben Sinnott, depending on what’s needed from a tight end on a specific play. Sinnott will certainly be more active overall, and as a receiver, after taking 18 offensive snaps versus the Eagles. Out LB Frankie Luvu – Suffered a groin injury near the end of the first half vs. Philly TE Chig Okonkwo – A hamstring injury took him out of the Eagles game Questionable DL Javon Kinlaw — Showed up Thursday’s participation report with a back issue

Commanders links Articles The Athletic (paywall) Why Commanders rookie receiver Antonio Williams is already capturing attention The team’s top receivers, Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs, combined for only six catches, 69 receiving yards and a touchdown — to go with three drops and one costly unsportsmanlike conduct penalty . The spacing of the receivers and their timing with quarterback Jayden Daniels seemed off for much of the game, and the team gained only 4.8 yards per pass attempt, the third fewest in the league in Week 1. But Williams’ 1-yard score with a little more than a minute left capped an impressive debut that included four targets, four catches, a team-high 64 receiving yards and the NFL’s rookie of the week honors — a feat made all the more notable considering he played only 11 passing snaps. Williams’ 2.36 expected points added per target led the league in the first week. He had a hand in all three of the Commanders’ touchdown drives: His 16-yard grab on a post route against Eagles cornerback Cooper DeJean set up Jacory Croskey-Merritt’s 1-yard touchdown run in the second quarter; his 33-yard catch on a third-and-14 helped set up Diggs’ touchdown in the fourth; and his 14-yard catch on a crosser started the Commanders’ final drive, which ended with his score. “In the biggest moments, guys make plays like that,” Daniels said. “He showed us all the work that he put in and the type of player that he is and how they scouted him throughout the draft.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Pro Football Focus NFL rookie rankings: Highest-graded players after Week 1 1. WR Antonio Williams , Washington Commanders , 91.2 Williams was impressively productive despite playing just 11 receiving snaps in his first regular-season action. He caught four passes for 64 yards and averaged 5.82 yards per route run, a mark bettered only by Zay Flowers of the Baltimore Ravens among wide receivers with at least 10 receiving snaps in Week 1. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Bonus Wallpaper – The Rookie of the Week #raisehail pic.twitter.com/Yf7HdKlUcj — Dullah (@Dullah_vision) September 18, 2026 Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders Film Review: David Blough’s Offense [T]here were some positives to take away from this game when evaluating David Blough. The one that stands out the most to me was the clear plan to target Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean. DeJean has been developing into a very strong defensive back in the Eagles secondary, where he plays a hybrid role splitting time between playing safety and nickel. He’s been one of the Eagles better players on defense over the past two years, but Blough found a way to attack him. It was pretty clear to see the Commanders went after DeJean when he was playing in the slot, and Blough targeted him with a specific type of receiver. DeJean struggles a little bit with short area quickness, so Blough looked to get the likes of Stefon Diggs and rookie receiver Antonio Williams matched up on DeJean, where they could use their short area quickness to beat him. Diggs had multiple catches against him, including his touchdown pass. [ The following analysis covers the play that is embedded in the tweet from Mark Bullock below ] On this play, the Commanders align in a bunch set to the left with tight end Ben Sinnott joining Diggs and Williams in the bunch. Sinnott runs a shallow cross that is designed to drag inside coverage across the field. Williams runs an out route, designed to drag the outside corner towards the sideline. Those two routes combine to help isolate Diggs against DeJean in space. Diggs aligns as the inside receiver, but at the snap he releases into the trail of Sinnott and Williams. You can see how Diggs sets up this route and it’s very crafty. It’s gives strong vibes of what Zach Ertz brought to the Commanders offense the past two years. Diggs gets himself into the seam at the snap but takes it nice and slow. He gets DeJean to attach to him and then goes to work. He gives DeJean a nice crossover move, stuttering and giving a jab step outside before crossing over and working back inside. DeJean bites hard on the move and Diggs crosses his face to get inside, where Jayden Daniels finds him for a touchdown. Diggs had a lot of success against DeJean in this game but he wasn’t the only one. Antonio Williams also had some success. We finally got our first look at David Blough's new Commanders offense. It was his first game as an NFL play-caller, so ups and downs were to be expected, but how did he fare? Against the Giants, Dallas not only struggled to defend the run (165 rushing yards allowed) but also couldn’t get their own ground game going against the Giants’ defense (No. 5; 69 rushing yards allowed). Cam Skattebo put up 81 yards and a touchdown with 18 carries against the Cowboys’ defense, which is a good sign for the Commanders run game. Commanders RB1 Jacory “Bill” Croskey-Merrit finished with similar numbers (63 yards and a touchdown on 16 carries) to Skattebo against a No. 24 Eagles rushing defense that allowed 132 rushing yards. title: What advanced NFL stats tell us following Commanders loss to Eagles — Stats and Snaps
summary: Much has been made about the Commanders’ opening road loss to the 5.5-point favorite Philadelphia Eagles. While they did leave ample winning opportunities on the field, when the final whistle blew, the Commanders had held their top-ranked division rival to just 24 points and 318 total yards on offense. And, perhaps most importantly, they beat […]
full_text: Much has been made about the Commanders’ opening road loss to the 5.5-point favorite Philadelphia Eagles. While they did leave ample winning opportunities on the field, when the final whistle blew, the Commanders had held their top-ranked division rival to just 24 points and 318 total yards on offense. And, perhaps most importantly, they beat the spread. While the opening day performance left plenty of room for improvement, their first game with new offensive and defensive schemes went better than might have been expected based on some of the doom and gloom prognostications making the rounds. Against one of the better teams in the league, on the road, the Commanders offense ranked 17 th in yardage gained and 20 th in scoring; while the defense ranked 17 th in yardage and 16 th in score containment. Not top of the league table, but a fair bit better than the bottom of the league Week 1 power rankings might have suggested. In terms of offensive and defensive efficiency, as quantified by EPA/play , the Commanders and their opponents started their seasons right in the middle of the pack: Graphic courtesy of RBSDM.com Those looking for signs of hope for improvement this season might take inspiration from standout performances and flashes of potential by Pepsi Rookie of the Week winner WR Antonio Williams, LB Sonny Styles, 2026 FA additions Amik Robertson and Nick Cross, and special teams demon Tyler Owens, among others. Now, let’s take an in-depth look at who stood out, who stood down, and who just stood around in the 22-24 road loss to the Eagles Stats in this article were obtained from three main sources. Official stats from the NFL gamebook, are treated as a source of truth. Advanced stats (eg. pressures, yards before contact, yards allowed in coverage) were sourced from Pro Football Focus (PFF) and Pro Football Reference (PFR). Advanced stats rely on tape analysts’ judgement and often differ between services. Where there were differences, data from both sources is cited. When there was consensus, sources are not cited. OFFENSE Jayden Daniels’ stat line as a passer was an unimpressive 18 comp/34 att (52.9%) for 164 yds, 2 TDs and 0 INT. But there were really two parts to his game. Through the first three quarters he looked off, as did his receivers. His stat line at the end of the third quarter was 9 comp/23 att (39.1%) for 50 yds and 0 TD. In the fourth quarter, he locked in, throwing for 9/11 (81.8%) for 99 yds and 2 TDs. According to PFR , his incompletions included 5 throw aways and 4 drops by receivers. PFR counted pressure on 18.4% of dropbacks (NFL rank 23 rd ), which might have contributed to his 17.2% bad throw rate on passes which were not throw aways. PFF has a lower threshold for recording pressures, making their pressure stats not comparable to PFR. PFF counted 16 pressures (NFL rank 6; 42% of dropbacks). His 1 sack taken gave him a respectable 6.3% pressure to sack rate. PFF counted 3 drops and 0 turnover-worthy passes. On the ground, JD5 rushed 5 times for 31 yds (6.2 Y/A), including 3 scrambles, with 1 broken tackle, and 21 YAC per PFR (37 per PFF). He was charged with delay of game penalties in the 2 nd and 3 rd quarters for 10 total yards. Daniels’ 66.4 Total QBR ranked 14 th in the NFL in Week 1. Not terrible given the heavy pressure rate and all the drops by receivers. Hopefully the slow start was Jayden shaking off the rust of an injury-plagued 2025 season and lack of preseason snaps. If the fourth quarter was indicative of his performance in the new offense, or Blough adjusting the scheme to suit his QB, then the Cowboys could have their hands full. Bill Croskey-Merritt led the Commanders’ rushing attack with 16 attempts for 63 yds (3.9 Y/A), 7 first downs, and 1 TD. His 50.0% rushing success rate ranked second on the team. PFF counted one forced missed tackle, but PFR did not. Bill had one fumble, fortunately recovered by teammate Josh Conerly. He caught one screen pass and was tackled 7 yards behind the line. PFF recorded 1.25 YBC/att, just slightly below league average for RBs using 2025 stats. Like pressures, PFR uses a higher threshold for recording contact, making their numbers not comparable to PFF. According to PFR, Bill averaged 2.6 YBC/att, which is just below the 75 th percentile for RBs based on 2025 figures. His room to run was therefore somewhere between league average and a little above average, depending on which stat service you believe. Bill recorded his first career penalty, a 10 yd infraction for holding in pass protection. Rachaad White rushed 7 times for 22 yds (3.1 Y/A) and 1 first down, with 1 broken tackle. His 42.9% success rate was the lowest on the team. He caught 2/2 passes for 5 total yds. PFF gave him more YBC/att (1.57 yds) than Bill, while PFR gave him fewer (2.0 yds), so it is difficult to know which to believe. Rookie Kaytron Allen had 4 carries for 16 yds (4.0 Y/A) in his NFL debut. He led the team with a 100% rushing success rate. He should be given more carries to see if he can keep that up. In his NFL debut, Antonio Williams led Commanders’ receivers with 64 receiving yards, despite getting less than half the playing time of starter Terry McLaurin. He caught 4/4 targets for 64 yds, 1 TD and 4 first downs (100% success rate) at an ADOT of 13.8 yds. His receiving productivity was in the elite range at 5.82 Y/RR, albeit on a very small sample of receiving snaps. There was some question before the game about how David Blough might deploy the rookie receiver. Williams took 15 snaps out wide and 11 in the slot. There is little question that he should get more playing time against the Cowboys. He was clearly Washington’s best receiver. Stefon Diggs was second on the team with 55 receiving yds and 1 TD. He had the same number of receptions as Williams (4), but more than twice as many targets, giving him the lowest reception rate on the team (44.4%). PFR credited Diggs with 3 drops in the game, equalling his season totals in 2025 and 2024. Even so, he was the Commanders’ second-most productive receiver at a respectable 2.2 Y/RR. Diggs’ game mirrored that of his QB to some extent. Through the first three quarters he caught 2/7 passes for 28 yds. In the fourth quarter, he caught 2/2 for 27 yds and a TD. Compounding the slow start, Diggs’ game was also marred by an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty for 15 yards, following his 4 th quarter TD to bring the score to 15 to 17. The gaffe moved the Commanders out of position to attempt a 2 pt conversion to tie the game. Terry McLaurin caught 2/4 targets for 14 yds. Jaylin Lane caught 1/1 targets for 4 yds. Dyami Brown failed to catch either of his two targets, albeit at a challenging ADOT of 31 yds. Chig Okonkwo ushered in his Commanders’ tenure by catching 2/3 targets for 16 yards, including 1 contested catch. John Bates also caught 2/3 targets, for a total of 13 yds. Bates got the lions’ share of snaps at FB. Ben Sinnott ran 10 routes without being targeted and mainly contributed as a run blocker. Pressure counts were sourced from PFF. PFF and PFR use different thresholds for scoring pressures, making their counts not directly comparable, despite being correlated. The higher total pressure counts from PFF provide larger samples for statistical comparisons. LT Brandon Coleman took the brunt of the Eagles’ pass rush to the tune of 6 pressures in 37 pressure opportunities, including 1 sack. His 13.5% pressure rate is a bottom of the league figure for starting OTs, based on 2025 figures. His 64.3 run blocking grade was a little below median for OTs. Coleman committed one false start for 5 yards. RT Josh Conerly fared slightly better, allowing 4 QB hurries in 37 opportunities. His 10.8% pressure rate is a bottom-10% figure based on 2025 numbers. Conerly’s 71.5 run block grade was above median for starting OTs. Conerly committed one false start for 5 yards. LG Chris Paul allowed just 1 pressure in pass protection (pressure rate). His 56.6 run blocking grade was a…

title: Commanders’ Adam Peters discusses Terry McLaurin, Mike Sainristil and more
summary: Commanders general manager Adam Peters held his first weekly Friday morning interview with the Junkies on 106.7 the Fan in Washington D.C., detailing what went wrong in a 24-22 loss to the Phliladelphia Eagles in Week 1 and what must be better on Sunday afternoon against the Dallas Cowboys. He addressed the hot-button issues of […]
full_text: Commanders general manager Adam Peters held his first weekly Friday morning interview with the Junkies on 106.7 the Fan in Washington D.C., detailing what went wrong in a 24-22 loss to the Phliladelphia Eagles in Week 1 and what must be better on Sunday afternoon against the Dallas Cowboys. He addressed the hot-button issues of the week, including Terry McLaurin’s target share, Mike Sainristil’s lapses in coverage, Dorance Armstrong’s return and more. We’ve pulled the best quotes for you, with a link to the full interview at the bottom. Why Terry McLaurin’s targets were down Terry’s a true No. 1 receiver and they didn’t want him to beat them. You saw a lot of cloud coverage, what you could call double coverage, on Terry. They rolled the coverage to him. He’s a huge part of our offense, and they did a really good job of trying to take him away as much as possible. That’s what this offense is, trying to find the open guy if they’re going to roll coverage to Terry. We have to beat them in other ways. There are going to be games where he doesn’t get as many balls, but we know that in gotta-have-it moments, he’s gonna make that play. He’s gonna make plays in double coverage, too. They did a good job taking him away, and we still have to find ways to move the ball. Terry’s going to get his. He had an incredible camp. I have no worries that he’s going to have a really good year. Drafting Antonio Williams in the third round He was definitely someone that we were targeting. Those guys were coming off the board pretty quick. Even De’Zhaun Stribling, that the Niners took with the first pick of the second round, those guys were coming off pretty quick. The board got thin. We had targeted Antonio and thought he would probably be a second-round pick. We were at the top of the third. We were kind of holding our breath for him. There were a couple of guys we would’ve taken – not necessarily receivers but other guys. But, with Antonio, the reason he lasted until the third round was because he had a fantastic 2024 season, playing all over the field – outside, inside and beating a lot of really good corners – and in 2025 him and Clemson didn’t really have a great year. He battled through a hamstring all year. To his credit, he played through. The whole year, but he wasn’t as productive. That’s ultimately what put him down into the third round, because he was predicted sometimes, at the beginning of the year, to be a first-rounder. For him to be there and seeing what we saw on tape – you look over both years with his ability to win inside and outside – he has a great feel for the game. He knows how to change up the tempo of his routes and get open. He’s a friendly target. He catches everything. He’s a guy we targeted and were thrilled was there in the third round. Honestly, he really shouldn’t have been. Mike Sainristil He didn’t have a good game. Mikey knows that. We all know that. At the same time, we have a lot of confidence in Mikey and his resilience and his ability to bounce back. He knows what he did and what he needs to work on. I have all the confidence in the world that he’s going to do that. He is who we think he is and we know he’s going to bounce back. Adding Dorance Armstrong to the pass rush He was on pace last year to be one of the league leaders in sacks, before he got hurt, which actually happened in Dallas. He was playing great, great ball. He was ascending. Having him back and getting him on the field with Odafe (Oweh), getting him on the field with (K’Lavon Chaisson), that adds another high-end rusher and someone they have to account for. That’s a package that is going to be even more robust this week in terms of having him on the field. He looks great. He really does. He has been rehabbing his tail off and really looks like he’s ready to go. He played in Dallas. He’s from Dallas. It’s going to be a big game for him. I think having an extra, high-end rusher really makes it harder on the offense. You’ll see some of those packages where it’s going to be hard to account for everybody. Offensive struggles vs. Eagles You’ve got to tip your cap to them and their scheme, but we were a little lost, too. That was the first time Jayden’s played a game in a while and it’s the first time he has called a game with all those guys in it. It wasn’t one player on offense. It was kind of everybody. Someone was off on this play and someone else was off on that play. The stats weren’t really good for Jayden but I thought he managed the game well in the first half and didn’t get us into a ton of negative plays. We weren’t just hitting on all cylinders until the second half.

title: Washington Commanders vs Dallas Cowboys Week 2: Five Questions with Blogging the Boys
summary: It’s week 2 of the NFL season and the 0-1 Washington Commanders will be facing an 0-1 Dallas Cowboys team on the road at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, TX this Sunday at 4:25 p.m. EDT. The Cowboys had a very disappointing week 1, getting beat in very physical fashion by the Giants on Sunday Night […]
full_text: Dec 25, 2025; Landover, Maryland, USA; Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott (4) is sacked by Washington Commanders defensive tackle Jer’Zhan Newton (95) during the second half at Northwest Stadium. | Geoff Burke-Imagn Images It’s week 2 of the NFL season and the 0-1 Washington Commanders will be facing an 0-1 Dallas Cowboys team on the road at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, TX this Sunday at 4:25 p.m. EDT. The Cowboys had a very disappointing week 1, getting beat in very physical fashion by the Giants on Sunday Night Football. On offense, the Cowboys are coached by OC and run-game designer Klayton Adams, as well as HC and playcaller Brian Schottenheimer; having preserved the 2025 offensive coaching staff that created the 2nd-best offense in the NFL in terms of yards gained, and the 7th-best offense by points gained. The combo of Adams and Schottenheimer have designed an offense in Dallas that utilizes a lot of play-action, a lot of pre-snap motion, heavy use of tempo, and a very conscious effort to ensure run and pass plays start with the same looks. On defense, the Cowboys have had a lot more turnover. After fielding the 3rd-worst unit in yards allowed and the NFL’s worst unit in points allowed, the Cowboys made major changes in their defensive unit, headlined by the change at DC from Matt Eberflus to Vic Fangio-disciple Christian Parker, who was formerly the Eagles passing-game coordinator and DBs coach. Parker was expected to run a Fangio-style defense that emphasizes rushing four and dropping the rest back in coverage to limit explosive plays. Perhaps that style of defense works better with the personnel of the Eagles compared to the Cowboys, because the Cowboys only managed two pressures on 20 four-man rushes in week 1. I asked David Halprin of Blogging the Boys five questions to better understand the state of the Cowboys and what to look for in this game. 1) The Cowboys defense was one of the worst in the NFL last year by most metrics (right up there with the Commanders). What has been done to overhaul it this year and what have you seen from it so far? A lot was done to overhaul the defense. First was hiring Christian Parker away from the Eagles staff as the new coordinator. With him comes a new scheme that is a base 3-4 but incorporates a lot of 4-3 looks and tries to disguise between the two. So Dallas is incorporating a new scheme, but also a lot of new players. The turnover on the defense had easily over half of last year’s starters gone from the roster on that side of the ball. They also invested heavily in the defense during the draft by using two first-round picks on safety Caleb Downs and OLB Malachi Lawrence. So the Cowboys did a lot to change their defense, but the results in Week 1 looked eerily like last year’s team. They were blowing assignments, busting coverages and allowing the Giants offense to dictate the game. They couldn’t stop the run so the Giants just pounded them in time of possession and only allowed the Cowboys offense two possessions in the second half. Parker has a lot of work to do to make this unit serviceable. 2) What are your thoughts about the Dallas offensive line and what is your assessment of it as a unit? If the Cowboys were at full strength I would be confident that they could make it work much as they did last year. It’s basically the same cast of characters that were there last year, and the offense was really good in 2025. They are missing their best lineman, guard Tyler Smith, so that hurts them some. Right tackle Terence Steele still seems to be the weak link, especially in pass protection. Left tackle Tyler Guyton had also caused some concern in the past, but he had a strong training camp and held up well against the Giants’ talented pass rush. The running game was an issue last week, so that is also a little bit of a concern this season. Overall, I don’t think the offensive line will be an issue as long as Guyton’s improvements are real and Smith returns healthy after his four-game IR trip. 3) What are your thoughts on how the Cowboys have been drafting the last few years? As part of this, do you think they’ve been reaching for positions of need in the draft due to being tight on salary cap space? No, I don’t think the Cowboys are drafting based on need because of salary cap space. They currently have over $20 million in cap space which is among the Top 10 in the NFL. The Cowboys actually do a pretty good job of drafting, that is how they stay competitive while basically eschewing high-priced free agents. Recently, they have had some uneven drafts compared to before when they were on a run of doing very well in the draft. But they are just like any other team, they draft based on a combination of talent, need, scouting reports, etc. There is nothing unusual going on with the Cowboys drafts and overall they do a good job of it, but not quite as good as they were doing for a while. 4) Who is one Cowboys player on offense and one player on defense that Washington fans probably don’t know much about, but should? I’m assuming most people know about Caleb Downs, our first-round pick. So on defense, we’ll go with Jaishawn Barham at inside linebacker. A third-round pick this year, he had an outstanding preseason/training camp. Now, with an injury to DeMarvion Overshown, Barham is about to get a lot more playing time. He is a violent player that is a missile heading to the ball. His first week in New York was decent. He did make a few mistakes, but he also showed the talent that should make him a serious player on the Cowboys defense. On offense, it is tougher because we are basically running out the same unit that played last year, so people probably know many of them. Let’s talk about our TE2 in Brevyn Spann-Ford. He is a big man who definitely helps in blocking, but he has started to show he can be a receiving target, too. Cowboys fans are hoping he breaks out this season. He didn’t do much versus the Giants, but the potential is there. 5) How should Washington go about gameplanning this matchup on both sides of the ball? On offense, use RPOs and other misdirection that utilizes Jayden Daniels’ legs to confuse the defense. The Giants did this repeatedly. They also just physically smashed the ball into the line and moved the Cowboys defense. Basically run the ball, then take shots downfield when you can. The Cowboys defense is still trying to get things sorted out, but they just couldn’t stop the run last week. On defense, try and take away the run. When the Cowboys can effectively run the ball with Javonte Williams, their offense just opens up and the wide receivers can then get loose and really cause damage. The Cowboys like to stick with the run, so they will continue even if it is not working well. Their offense can then get bogged down and their passing game is lethal, but also susceptible to mistakes. I’m not saying you want the game to be in CeeDee Lamb’s and George Pickens’ hands as a defense, but when the Cowboys can’t run effectively their offense is a different animal. A companion article to this with my answers to David’s questions is linked here . Thanks again to David Halprin for taking time out of his day to answer our questions about the Cowboys.

title: NFL Week 2 uniforms: Rams debut 'Classic Sol,' Ravens go all-white
summary: Here's a look at what each NFL team is wearing in Week 2, led by a new alternate look from the Los Angeles Rams.
full_text:
Uniforms revealed in the offseason will make their respective debuts in Week 2. Fresh from their trip Down Under, the Los Angeles Rams look to win their first game of the season with a design rooted in its history.

 

 Los Angeles will wear its "Classic Sol" alternate threads against the New York Giants on "Monday Night Football." The uniform honors the Rams' championship in 1951, with this season marking the 75th anniversary. A sol-colored jersey includes royal blue stitched and colored numbers. The three-stripe royal blue sleeve design is a direct nod to the uniforms worn in the 1951 season. The Giants will counter by going all-white.

 The Baltimore Ravens underwent  a closet redesign in the offseason , and with it came a new helmet and combination. Nicknamed "White Noise," Baltimore will pair all-white threads with the "Purple Rising" helmet against the New Orleans Saints . Baltimore originally revealed the purple lids in 2024, but tweaked them in April with a logo change, maintaining the metallic purple. It tops off a sleek new all-white look. 

 It's an all-white look for the New York Jets as well, but from head-to-toe. New York unveiled new white helmets in July that differ from the throwback ones it typically wears with its classic uniforms. The Jets will pair it together with all-white jerseys and pants against the Green Bay Packers , who will wear their traditional home green on the road.

 In the NFL "Rivalries" space, the Arizona Cardinals are the first to wear their design this season. Revealed last year, Arizona will rock it versus the Seattle Seahawks -- the same team they debuted it against in the previous campaign.

title: NFL Week 2 picks, predictions, schedule, odds, fantasy tips
summary: Minnesota vs. Chicago? Trevor Lawrence vs. Bo Nix? There are more games left in Week 2, and we have picks, predictions, key stats, watchability ratings and more.
full_text:
Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season is here! There are a lot of tough division matchups happening: the Vikings visiting the Bears, the Panthers and Falcons facing off, the Raiders against the Chargers and the Seahawks versus the Cardinals. You can also expect an exciting quarterback duel between Jacksonville's  Trevor Lawrence and Denver's  Bo Nix . 

 We're here to get you ready for the action. First, our NFL Nation reporters take you inside the locker room with the best thing they heard this week, and ESPN Research provides a key stat to know. Then, analytics writer Seth Walder makes a bold prediction for each matchup, NFL analyst Ben Solak gives one reason to tune in to each game (and rates the watchability of the matchup), fantasy analyst Eric Moody shares fantasy football intel and betting analyst Pamela Maldonado hits betting insights for each contest. We also have Football Power Index (FPI) game projections, and Maldonado, Moody and Walder give us final score picks for every game.

 Let's get into the full Week 2 slate, which culminates with a "Monday Night Football" matchup between the Giants and Rams on ESPN . (Game times are Sunday unless otherwise noted, and all odds are via DraftKings.)

 
 Jump to a matchup: 
 MIN-CHI | CIN-HOU | NO-BAL 
 PIT-NE | GB-NYJ | PHI-TEN 
 CAR-ATL | CLE-TB | JAX-DEN 
 LV-LAC | WSH-DAL | SEA-ARI 
 MIA-SF | IND-KC | NYG-LAR 

 
 

 What ESPN Analytics says ... 
 

 

 
 

 Vikings (1-0) at Bears (1-0) 
 1 p.m. ET | Fox | CHI -4.5 (47.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Vikings: DC Brian Flores posted an 83% blitz rate in the first half against the Packers and -- even after throttling down in the second half -- finished with a 71.7% rate that nearly tripled the NFL average in Week 1. Flores has always favored the blitz, but would he dare repeat that aggression level against the Bears? Flores considers the opening weeks of a season to be about improvement and experimentation. "What are the best groups of players who are out on the field? Who plays well with who?" he said. "That's what we're working through as a staff right now." -- Kevin Seifert 

 What we're hearing on the Bears: Chicago is preparing for the "King of the Cover 0 blitz," the nickname QB Caleb Williams gave Flores as a rookie. In 2025, Williams was blitzed 37.2% in his first meeting against Minnesota and 66.7% the second time. Trying to anticipate which strategy Flores will deploy is an ineffective plan. "You try to have answers for everything," coach Ben Johnson said. "He's been in this division three years now, and yeah, I mean you'd like to think he's put everything he could possibly do on tape until you play him next and you realize he hasn't yet. ... There always is with him and that's what makes him such a good coordinator." -- Courtney Cronin 

 

 Stat to know: The Bears need 37 points to break the NFL record for most points in a team's opening two games, currently held by the 1968 Raiders (95). -- ESPN Research 

 Bold prediction: Vikings QB Carson Wentz will throw multiple interceptions. I know he had some impressive moments and didn't throw any picks in Minnesota's Week 1 win. But this is still Wentz, and I assume he's still prone to a mistake or four. -- Walder 

 Viewers rating (out of 10): 9.0. There isn't a more fun schematic matchup in the entire league than Johnson versus Flores. This is Round 7 of their showdown. With a bad Bears defense on the other side of the ball, there should be explosive plays everywhere. -- Solak 

 Injuries: Vikings | Bears 

 Fantasy nugget: Bears WR Luther Burden III finished with just five targets and 9.5 fantasy points against Carolina last week. However, he led Chicago's receivers in routes run and now faces a Vikings secondary that allowed the Packers' Christian Watson and Matthew Golden to combine for 48.2 fantasy points last week. Burden is in a good spot to bounce back. See Week 2 rankings . -- Moody 

 Betting insight: All five of Wentz's starts went over the total last season for the Vikings. Chicago just scored 59 points but also allowed Carolina to produce 478 yards and 37 points. Minnesota's defense now faces an explosive Bears offense, while Wentz and WR  Justin Jefferson get a vulnerable Chicago defense. Read more . -- Maldonado 

 Maldonado's pick: Bears 31, Vikings 24 
 Moody's pick: Bears 35, Vikings 26 
 Walder's pick: Bears 34, Vikings 17 
 FPI prediction: CHI, 65.6% (by an average of 4.5 points)

 

 Matchup must-reads: Mason put on IR after having surgery on thumb ... Bears anticipate 'great challenge' vs. Vikings defense  ... No block, no rock' is not just a mantra for Bears' offense 

 
 

 Bengals (1-0) at Texans (0-1) 
 1 p.m. ET | CBS | HOU -2.5 (46.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Bengals:  QB Joe Burrow will be managing back tightness this week. And he'll be doing so against one of the NFL's best defenses. OC Dan Pitcher compared the combination of edge rushers Danielle Hunter and Will Anderson Jr . to Cincinnati's WR tandem of Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins . Keeping Burrow upright and intact this week will be paramount for Cincinnati's chances against Houston and for the rest of the season. -- Ben Baby 

 What we're hearing on the Texans: Houston is staring at another potential 0-2 start. If the Texans lose this week, it'll be the third such time under coach DeMeco Ryans since he was hired in 2023. But Hunter said "last year is last year," in response to being asked about their confidence level to dig themselves out of a hole to start the season. Houston may have to play without Pro Bowl wideout Nico Collins ( hamstring ), who was injured in practice Wednesday. -- DJ Bien-Aime 

 Stat to know: The Bengals posted a 54% pass rush win rate in Week 1, the team's highest since November 2024. They had the worst pass rush win rate in the NFL last season (28.8%). -- ESPN Research 

 Bold prediction: Texans RB David Montgomery will average 5.0 yards per carry. Montgomery scored three touchdowns in his debut but only averaged 3.0 yards per carry. The Bengals' defense, for all its turnover success in Week 1, did allow .09 EPA per opponent carry in Week 1 -- the fifth-worst mark. -- Walder 

 Viewers rating (out of 10): 8.8. There are high stakes in this one for the Texans, who are trying to avoid 0-2 (against two AFC contenders!). This is one I'm going to keep a close eye on especially because Burrow and Collins are entering the week banged up. -- Solak 

 

 Injuries: Bengals | Texans 

 Fantasy nugget: Montgomery finished Week 1 with 23 touches and 28.9 fantasy points, while handling every Houston rushing attempt inside the red zone. He now faces a Bengals defense that ranked 21st in run stop win rate (25.8%) last week and allowed the Bucs' Bucky Irving to score 20.3 fantasy points. See Week 2 rankings . -- Moody 

 Betting insight: The Texans are 1-8 ATS (against the spread) in September under Ryans for the past three seasons, and their September struggles could continue against an offense built to attack Houston's Week 1 weakness. The Bills averaged 10.4 yards per pass against the Texans, and they now get Burrow, Chase and Higgins. If Cincinnati protects Burrow, it has enough offense to contend. Read more . -- Maldonado 

 Maldonado's pick: Bengals 27, Texans 24 
 Moody's pick: Bengals 24, Texans 21 
 Walder's pick: Texans 23, Bengals 20 
 FPI prediction: HOU, 55.9% (by an average of 1.6 points)

 

 Matchup must-reads: Burrow: 'Ridiculous' that tight back would keep me out ... To'oTo'o to miss some time with shoulder injury ... Cashing in: Bengals rookie Howell impacts pass rush ... Could Montgomery be key to unlock offense? 

 
 

 Saints (0-1) at Ravens (1-0) 
 1 p.m. ET | CBS | BAL -8.5 (46.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Saints: The Saints will be without long-snapper Zach Wood for several weeks because of a calf strain , according to a source. This is a very underrated loss for New Orleans, which hasn't had to deal with this problem for the 10 seasons Wood has been with the…

title: NFL Week 2 predictions: Upsets, fantasy sleepers, stat lines
summary: Will Ashton Jeanty pile up the scrimmage yards? Could the Bengals upset the Texans? And can George Pickens find the end zone?
full_text:
Week 2 of the  2026 NFL season is off to an exciting start, as the Bills defeated the Lions 41-31 in the first game at Highmark Stadium . But what will happen in the remaining 15 games? We have 15 predictions from our NFL experts.

 First, betting analyst Pamela Maldonado picks two underdogs who could win outright. Then, analytics writer Seth Walder projected out stat lines for three players. Fantasy football writer Eric Moody gives three sleepers, and analyst Matt Bowen suggests three players who will find the end zone. Finally, analyst Ben Solak lays out four wild-card predictions.

 Could the Bengals upset the Texans? Will we see big receiving days for the Dolphins' Malik Washington and Caleb Douglas ? Can Eagles running back Saquon Barkley find the end zone? And is it finally time for the Jets to snag an interception? Let's make 15 big predictions for all of Sunday and Monday's action.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Upset picks | Projected stat lines 
 Fantasy sleepers, surprises 
 TD scorers | Other predictions 

 
 

 Maldonado predicts two upsets 
 

 Jacksonville Jaguars +2.5 at Denver Broncos (+124) 

 Denver's offense hasn't shown enough to justify laying points. The Broncos produced only 176 yards and 3.7 yards per play in their Week 1 loss to the Chiefs, with quarterback  Bo Nix turning it over twice. Jacksonville is bringing a pass rush that generated five sacks against Cleveland, while QB  Trevor Lawrence  threw four touchdown passes. Defense makes the Broncos the favorite, but the Jaguars have the more trustworthy offense to win outright.

 
 

 

 Cincinnati Bengals +2.5   at Houston Texans  (+120) 

 The Bengals' biggest weakness looked better against the Bucs , as quarterback  Joe Burrow was sacked only once. If that holds, he gets a Houston defense that just allowed 10.4 yards per pass to Buffalo in Week 1 . Houston can obviously pressure Burrow, but if Cincinnati's offensive line continues to improve, it should have enough through the air with  Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins .

 

 

 Walder predicts three stat lines 
 

 Rhamondre Stevenson , RB, New England Patriots : 16 carries, 63 rushing yards; 5 receptions, 42 receiving yards, 1 receiving touchdown

 Since 2023, running backs catch passes on 8% of dropbacks against man coverage but 15%  against zone coverage. Why does that matter here? Because in Week 1  against the Falcons, the Steelers ran zone coverage 89% of the time under new defensive coordinator Patrick Graham. So I expect Stevenson to have a big day in the receiving game.

 And while I don't expect the Patriots will be as run-heavy as they were in Week 1  -- which certainly didn't work out for them! -- New England should be ahead by enough early to run the ball late in the game. All in all, it should be a healthy workload for Stevenson.

 
 

 Riq Woolen , CB, Philadelphia Eagles : 34 coverage snaps, 1 reception allowed for 7 yards on four targets, 1 interception

 Woolen had a strong Week 1 against the Commanders, allowing just one reception for 1 yard. Granted, that one reception was a touchdown to WR  Stefon Diggs , but I'm not sure that play was entirely on him. Either way, it was a strong game for Woolen, who also scored highly in my cornerback metric . Now, he gets to face second-year Titans QB  Cam Ward , who struggled against the Jets in Week 1 . Woolen should have the advantage against  Carnell Tate , Calvin Ridley or Elic Ayomanor .

 
 

 Malik Washington , WR, Miami Dolphins : 7 receptions, 77 receiving yards, 1 touchdown

 Washington ran a route on 84% of Miami's dropbacks in Week 1 , the highest rate on the Dolphins. He was also targeted eight times but had just three receptions. His 99 incomplete air yards was tied for second among all players, a number that indicates some positive regression could be coming in Week 2.

 The Dolphins threw a little more than expected versus the Raiders, and they'll have to pass plenty against the 49ers since this looks likely to be a blowout loss. Washington, who frequently plays out of the slot, historically runs shorter routes and could be an option underneath in garbage time.

 

 

 Moody predicts three fantasy sleepers 
 

 Jordan Love , QB, Green Bay Packers (rostered in 43.9% of ESPN leagues) 

 Love threw for 387 yards in Week 1 against the Vikings, the second-highest total of his career, and scored 19.4 fantasy points on 42 pass attempts. Green Bay struggled to run the ball without Josh Jacobs , and its offensive line will still be banged up in Week 2 against the Jets. But with Christian Watson and Matthew Golden combining for 48.2 fantasy points last week, Love should be an appealing streaming option.

 

 
 

 Caleb Douglas , WR, Miami Dolphins (34.9%) 

 Douglas caught five of seven targets for 94 yards, scoring 14.4 fantasy points in his NFL debut against the Raiders. He played more than 90% of Miami's offensive snaps and led all rookies in targets, receptions and receiving yards. The Dolphins enter Week 2 as double-digit underdogs against the 49ers , so Douglas could benefit from a pass-heavy game script.

 
 

 Mack Hollins , WR, New England Patriots (5.2%) 

 Hollins outsnapped Romeo Doubs in the first half against the Seahawks in Week 1 , and he led the Patriots receivers in snaps after A.J. Brown exited with an ankle injury. Hollins should continue to see significant playing time against Pittsburgh now that Brown is on injured reserve .

 Holins received at least six targets in four games last season, averaging 12.8 fantasy points in those contests. He finished with five targets and 9.1 fantasy points in Week 1.

 

 

 Bowen predicts three touchdown scorers 
 

 Derrick Henry , RB, Baltimore Ravens 

 Henry rushed for three touchdowns in the Ravens' Week 1 win over the Colts -- including two on carries inside the 5-yard line. Under new coordinator Declan Doyle, the Ravens used schemed zone concepts and creative tight end movement to put Henry on a north/south track. That should work versus a Saints defense that allowed two rushing scores in New Orleans'  Week 1 loss to the Lions.

 
 

 George Pickens , WR, Dallas Cowboys 

 Pickens caught just three of six targets for 28 yards in the Cowboys' Week 1 loss to the Giants, including two drops. But that doesn't mean quarterback Dak Prescott will stop going to Pickens for big plays. The vertical pass game is a key element of Dallas' offense, and it could lead Pickens into the end zone.

 

 
 

 Saquon Barkley , RB, Philadelphia Eagles 

 Barkley did have 15 carries in the Week 1 win over the Commanders, with two goal-to-go attempts, so we can bet on him seeing the ball in scoring position. Plus, he has home run ability to score from outside the red zone. Yes, the Eagles need more up front to create consistent daylight for Barkley, but he gets a matchup against a Titans defense that gave up just 152 rushing yards to the Jets.

 

 

 Solak makes four more predictions 
 

 Raiders RB Ashton Jeanty will lead the league in scrimmage yards 

 Jeanty led the Raiders in both rushing yards (102) and receiving yards (45) last week in the Raiders' win over the Dolphins. Without Brock Bowers  ( meniscus trim ) for another week and facing another light box defense from the Chargers , I expect Jeanty to once again thrive on the ground and in the air. Jeanty was seventh last week with 147 scrimmage yards, but his longest play was only 15 yards. With a couple home run plays on Sunday, he could knock on the door for 200.

 
 

 The Jets will get their first interception 

 The last Jets pick was on Jan. 5, 2025 -- 623 days from their matchup with the Packers on Sunday . Green Bay's pass protection is a glaring issue, and while quarterback  Jordan Love is around league-average in his interception rate, the 16 hits he took in Week 1 could have him looking to get rid of the ball faster in Week 2. I'm banking on safety Minkah Fitzpatrick to track down a deep heave and end the drought.

 Did I predict the Jets to break the drought last…
