title: NFL Week 2 betting guide: Top plays for Sunday afternoon's games
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 2 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: finding betting value.

 Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league.

 From spreads and money lines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. With that, let's dive into our best bets, favorite defensive props and the top game to bet in Week 1.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Jump to: 
 Bowen's Game of the Week  | Solak's plays  | Walder's props 

 

 

 Bowen's Game of the Week 

 Cincinnati Bengals at Houston Texans (-2.5, 46.5) 
1 p.m. ET on CBS, Reliant Stadium, Houston

 

 This line has fluctuated but at -2.5, I am all-in. Would I feel the same at -3? I wouldn't love it, but I'd be willing to bet Houston at home in a bounce-back game after the Week 1 loss to Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills . Let's get into what to look for on both sides of the ball, and we'll finish with some props bets to play.

 

 When Houston has the ball: Houston spent the offseason working on its run game, trading for David Montgomery and adding to the offensive front. And we saw a dedicated effort to run the football in Week 1, as Montgomery had 20 carries, with Woody Marks chipping in with nine. Now, was it super efficient? No. Montgomery averaged just 3.0 YPC, and the Texans registered a run block win rate of 74% (17th in the league). But it's clear that Houston wants the run game to be a foundational element of its offense. This can boost the passing opportunities for quarterback C.J. Stroud , who will see a Bengals defense featuring a rebuilt front anchored by defensive tackle  Dexter Lawrence II and an underrated secondary that can mix both zone and man looks. I would look for play-action concepts (which mirror the run game) to attack the Bengals' two-deep zone shells while also scheming up some shot plays. With Nico Collins out, the scheme won't change in Houston.  Xavier Hutchinson and Kayshon Boutte can work the interior in-breakers while Jaylin Noel operates out of the slot. I truly think Houston looks to control the tempo on offense in this one, but let's keep an eye on third downs because the Texans need to beat man coverage from the Bengals there.

 When Cincinnati has the ball: I want to see this matchup against the Texans' defense. Though the Bengals looked flat in a Week 1 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers ( Joe Burrow finished with 254 yards passing, and Ja'Marr Chase had two receptions for 12 yards), they create conflict because of scheme and talent. The Texans have been a zone-heavy defense under DeMeco Ryans, but they will mix in man coverage (based on game situations), which creates must-see TV when corners Derek Stingley Jr . and Kamari Lassiter match against Chase and Tee Higgins . Tight end Mike Gesicki (78 yards receiving in Week 1) could find room to operate against Houston's split-safety and single-high zone schemes to attack the voids there. But, my main question is will the Bengals' offensive line keep the pocket firm for Burrow and generate movement up front in the run game? The Bengals held a pass block win rate of 53.8% in Week 1 against the Bucs (13th in the league), while Chase Brown averaged only 3.5 YPC. It's a different matchup this week against Houston edge rushers Will Anderson Jr . and Danielle Hunter . Burrow will need to hit some explosive play throws to win this one.

 Leans: Texans -2.5 (-118), Texans moneyline (-142), Over 46.5 (-105)

 Now, let's get to some prop bets ...

 Ja'Marr Chase receptions OVER 6.5 (-109) 

 I expect a dedicated effort to get Chase the ball after he caught only two of four targets in the Week 1 win over the Bucs -- screens, unders and quicks that cater to Chase's explosive catch-and-run ability. Look for Chase to be involved early in this game plan.

 Mike Gesicki anytime TD (+280) 

 Gesicki caught a Week 1 touchdown on a schemed throw to beat man coverage. Plus, the Bengals can set up Gesicki on zone beaters in the high red zone (seams, corners) to counter the Houston defensive tendencies.

 Chase Brown receiving yards OVER 20.5 (-113) 

 Brown caught five of six targets for 22 yards last week versus Tampa, and the screen game/swing routes could be an early answer to counter the Texans' pass rush.

 

 

 
 Solak's plays 
 

 Green Bay Packers -3.5 (-112) at New York Jets 

 I'm grabbing a quick buy-low spot on the Packers, who were much better Sunday than the box score would indicate. The Minnesota Vikings scored 14 late points on defensive takeaways deep in Green Bay territory in their 39-22 victory. But the Packers had a better success rate (38.8%) than the Vikings (34.5%) and struggled only in situational spots. They were 3-for-12 on third down. On four red zone trips, they scored only one touchdown and one field goal. Those are the little execution problems that hurt a box score.

 

 Going from facing a Brian Flores-coached Vikings defense to the Jets should make things far easier. Matt LaFleur has experience facing Aaron Glenn from when Glenn was the defensive coordinator of the Detroit Lions and generally has found success (46% offensive success rate, 0.04 EPA per play, 2.2 points per drive).

 I thought about taking the Packers' team total, currently priced at 23.5 and juiced -135 to the over. I think the Jets' offense will be a functional group this season, but they need to run the ball and play clock control to win games against superior opponents -- and that might limit the Packers' total drives. As such, I'll go instead for the full-game spread at -3.5. I would play this no further than -120.

 Tennessee Titans team total UNDER 15.5 (-105) 

 The Titans' offensive operation was the worst I saw in Week 1: play designs that were dead in the water, offensive linemen uncertain of their assignments, easy drops and bad routes from receivers and poor accuracy and timing from Cam Ward at quarterback. It's tough to find anything to hang their hat on from a 23-10 loss to the Jets.

 

 It's worth remarking that Brian Daboll's offenses have been poor in Week 1 -- six, six and and zero points in the three seasons previous -- and then stronger in Week 2. But against this Philadelphia Eagles  defense, it's tough to have much faith. Philadelphia's defensive front looked as deep and disruptive as ever against an average Washington Commanders front, and the Titans are comfortably one of the eight worst lines in football. Though defensive back Cooper DeJean was banged up in the Week 1 game and sat out practice Wednesday, the Eagles' outside corner duo of Quinyon Mitchell and Riq Woolen still poses a huge problem for the Titans' ability to create explosive plays through the air.

 The talent difference here feels simply insurmountable. The Titans will need defensive takeaways or big special teams outputs to get into scoring range. I don't see them getting enough. I would play this up to -115.

 New England Patriots -5.5 (-105) vs. Pittsburgh Steelers 

 The past four defenses the Patriots have faced are as follows: Seattle Seahawks (Week 1), Seahawks (Super Bowl), Denver Broncos (AFC Championship Game), Houston Texans (AFC divisional round). Even their wild-card opponent had a near-elite defense ( Los Angeles Chargers ). We are finally at a point at which we can buy low on the Patriots against an imperfect defense.

 The  Pittsburgh Steelers ' defense was hardly tested in Week 1 against the Cooper Rush -led Atlanta Falcons . Drake Maye and the Patriots' offense --…

title: Ranking all 32 backup NFL quarterbacks for the 2026 season
summary: We stacked the best No. 2 quarterbacks across the league, including Mac Jones and even a few backups who have already been forced to play in 2026.
full_text:
The very first game of the 2026 NFL season provided an important reminder about backup quarterbacks: They don't really impact a team's chance to win ... until they do. And then they suddenly  really do.

 Sam Darnold getting injured early in the Seahawks' season opener against the Patriots forced Drew Lock into action. When Kyler Murray suffered a  concussion   against the Packers  later in Week 1, the Vikings turned to Carson Wentz . Both teams went on to win with their respective second-stringers. In both instances, the defense likely carried the winners more than anything else, but had the offense collapsed with the backup QB, there would have been no hope. The Falcons, who started QB3  Cooper Rush   against the Steelers last Sunday with both  Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr . out , can attest to that.

 With backups already playing a big role early in the season, I've decided to rank each team's No. 2 QB. It's a tricky exercise because we're operating on severely limited information in many cases. Some of these players haven't played in a meaningful pro game in years. Some of the younger backups don't have much regular-season experience at all -- if any. So the margin for error is large. But that shouldn't prevent us from doing these rankings -- after all, teams must make choices about their backups with similarly scarce information.

 So, here is my ranking of every team's No. 2 quarterback. I included Wentz and Lock, but I used Penix as the Falcons' backup for the purpose of this exercise (though I also noted where Rush would land if he were the true No. 2).

 

 

 1. Fernando Mendoza , Las Vegas Raiders 
 This was the easiest decision. Sure, we haven't seen Mendoza take a snap in a regular-season game, but being the No. 1 draft pick is worth enough to easily put him at the top. He has the highest upside of any QB on this list. And if I had to ask any backup to win a few games right now , I would take Mendoza. Drake Maye was in this spot in this exercise two years ago ; it's fair to say that the Raiders would be thrilled if Mendoza took Maye's track. Funny enough, the player who was No. 1 in last year's version of these rankings is Kirk Cousins , the man in front of Mendoza on the Las Vegas depth chart.

 
 

 

 2. Marcus Mariota , Washington Commanders 
 If a team needs to get through a couple games while their starter is out, there is probably no more reliable veteran backup than Mariota. He started eight games (and played in 11) for the Commanders last season when Jayden Daniels was hurt . Mariota recorded a 50.4 QBR and has posted a 57.4 QBR since 2022. That's about as good as it gets for a non-starter, and I thought the Commanders got a steal when they re-signed Mariota to a one-year, $7 million contract this offseason. He's still only 32, too.

 
 

 3. Mac Jones , San Francisco 49ers 
 Currently enrolled in the Kyle Shanahan School of Quarterback Development, of which Darnold is a notable alum, Jones raised his stock last season while filling in for Brock Purdy for eight games. He recorded a 62.7 QBR and a plus-3% completion percentage over expected (per NFL Next Gen Stats). Those are incredibly strong numbers and, taken on their own, would indicate a surefire starter. But he is not one currently because of his previous track record -- Jones recorded a 37.6 QBR from 2022-24 for the Patriots and Jaguars after a strong rookie year with New England in 2021 -- and the assumption that a large portion of his improvement can be directly attributed to Shanahan.

 
 

 4. Spencer Rattler , New Orleans Saints 
 Even though the Saints were 1-7 in games he started last season, Rattler showed significant growth from his 2024 rookie campaign. He sported a 50.8 QBR (up from 37.1 in 2024), a plus-3% completion percentage over expected (up from minus-10%, per Next Gen Stats) and a 9% off-target rate (down from 20%). Considering his youth, Rattler still has upside. I wouldn't be surprised if he gets a shot to compete to be a starter -- even if it's not in New Orleans -- in the next year or two.

 
 

 5. Michael Penix Jr ., Atlanta Falcons 
 Penix could be Atlanta's starter over Tua Tagovailoa after both return from injuries , but he would be very high if he ended up as Atlanta's No. 2. He has had his ups and downs in the NFL but has started only 12 games and is a mere two years removed from being a top-10 draft pick. So, there's potential. And there are things to like about his numbers -- a 55.7 career QBR along with a low 4.1% sack rate. The accuracy hasn't been there (21% off-target rate and a minus-4% completion percentage over expected), but his youth gives him time to improve if he can recover from a  torn ACL suffered last November, his third dating to college.

 
 

 6. Jameis Winston , New York Giants 
 Winston is well into the second phase of his career as a high-end backup. His results have been solid in aggregate, though his play style ensures a roller-coaster ride. Over the past four seasons, Winston has recorded a very high 3.9% turnover rate but still managed a 49.7 QBR in that span. This is because he's willing to push the ball downfield. Winston's 9.6 air yards per attempt since 2022 is higher than any qualifying quarterback registered last season.

 
 

 

 7. Jalon Daniels , Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
 Is this a reach? Maybe. But undrafted rookies face serious headwinds making rosters, much less being in potentially important roles . So, the fact that Daniels beat out Jake Browning (my No. 2 backup last year ) is a major point in his favor. It's a far stronger signal than a middle-round pick landing a backup job partially due to the draft capital used on him.

 The preseason tape is incredibly enticing, too, with Daniels spinning out of pressures like Russell Wilson , making throws on the run and ripping the ball downfield between defenders. His value is team-dependent. He is a less helpful backup for a Super Bowl contender because he's riskier than many of the players below. But he also has a lot more upside.

 
 

 8. Mitchell Trubisky , Tennessee Titans 
 He had a very limited run of playing behind Josh Allen in Buffalo the past two seasons, but Trubisky had seven starts the two seasons before. Over the past four seasons, he recorded a 54.7 QBR and a plus-4% completion percentage over expected. Those numbers, plus Cam Ward 's struggles in his first season-plus, would actually  raise the Titans' Football Power Index ranking if the team announced Trubisky as the starter for an upcoming game.

 
 

 9. Tyrod Taylor , Green Bay Packers 
 We must bake in some aging downside for the 37-year-old Taylor, but if a team has to get away with playing a backup for a few games, it could do much worse. Over the past four seasons, Taylor's 49.9 QBR and plus-2% completion percentage over expected are pretty good. And his willingness to throw the ball downfield (13% of his attempts go 20-plus air yards, a high rate) and scramble frequently gives him some variance that is useful for backups.

 
 

 10. Tyler Huntley , Baltimore Ravens 
 I've always liked Huntley, but his stock dropped precipitously in 2024 when he bounced among several teams. But he returned to the Ravens in 2025 and saw action in a few games, including two starts. He played very well in that limited span, recording an 81.1 QBR -- good enough to earn a  new contract  from Baltimore with $3.5 million fully guaranteed.

 
 

 11. Mason Rudolph , Pittsburgh Steelers 
 Rudolph originally won the Steelers' backup QB job seven years ago . Since then, he left Pittsburgh before returning last season. And even though the Steelers have changed coaches, Rudolph is their backup yet again. His 53.6 QBR over the past four seasons ranks fourth among players on this list. He throws short -- 6.5 air yards per attempt and past the sticks only 36% of the time -- but the aggregate results are solid.

title: Week 2 fix for Cowboys' D vs. Commanders: Communication
summary: The Week 1 loss to the Giants was an inauspicious start for new coordinator Christian Parker's defense.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas -- One word has spread throughout the  Dallas Cowboys ' defense this week as they get ready to play the Washington Commanders Sunday at AT&T Stadium: communication.

 There were many things the defense did not do well in Dallas'  28-20 season-opening loss to the New York Giants that made the debut of new coordinator Christian Parker less than desirable.

 The Cowboys allowed 165 rushing yards. They gave up three touchdown passes, allowed Jaxson Dart to complete 79.3% of his passes, and sacked him twice. New York converted 9 of 11 third-down opportunities, which was the largest reason the Dallas offense had only two drives in the second half.

 According to coach Brian Schottenheimer and Parker, it all came down to a lack of communication.

 "The first part is being decisive and loud -- that's the person that's giving it. And then the receiving is where we were off on a few things," Schottenheimer said. "Calls were being made, they have to be louder, they have to be more decisive, but they have to be received.

 "And to cosign that, we signal all the time based on different things. So you can't hear what they're saying on the film, so there should be hand signals that show information being received, and we need to be better and it wasn't good enough."

 

 So ahead of this week's game against the Commanders ( 4:25 ET, Fox ), Parker said the defense retooled some walkthroughs and formation adjustment periods. The players focused on verbal and nonverbal situations, especially with the amount of noise expected from the home crowd.

 "Making sure that we're on the same page and making sure we can execute because it's certainly unacceptable what happened in the fourth quarter [against the Giants]," Parker said.

 For Parker, his first game as a playcaller was not what he had envisioned.

 "Getting back to work, it's one poor performance. It's one loss that does not equal two," he said. "At the end of the day, our thing was when we got back here -- and it started on the plane -- was watching the tape, being critical of the mistakes, finding substance in the failure.

 "I think we're not trying to make excuses for anything. We're not trying to act like it didn't happen. We've got to look in the mirror. We've got to be accountable for what we did wrong and what we did right, correct it and then move on to the next opponent because it can't be a hangover and it can't linger."

 In training camp, Schottenheimer referenced how loud the defensive meeting room was because of Parker's emphasis on communication. Quarterback  Dak Prescott joked that the offense had to go to a silent count next door just to get through its work during camp.

 "The things that we messed up on is easily fixed," defensive tackle Quinnen Williams said. "The communication that we messed up on, we did that communication in training camp week after week, days after days. And it's one of those things you kind of watch the film and be like, 'Oh, man, I wish I had that back immediately.'

 "You just learn from it and take it on to the next week and get better. We've got 16 games left, continue to do what we're doing and learn from it and grow from it."

 

 The outing against the Giants had fans wondering if the defense will look the same as it did in 2025, when Dallas allowed a franchise-record 511 points and finished 30th in yards allowed per game.

 The Giants' 165 rushing yards would have ranked third most by a Cowboys opponent in 2025. The 81.8% third-down rate would have been the highest rate allowed last season. The two sacks Sunday continued a trend from last season, when the Cowboys had two sacks or fewer in 10 games. Six times last season, they allowed three or more touchdown passes.

 "That's not our business. We weren't here," Parker said. "This is the 2026 defense and it's our responsibility to fix our performance on Sunday and not performances from 2024, 2025. It's for us to fix our performance from Sunday. And I think everybody has been accountable and responsible for that."

 Defensive tackle Kenny Clark , a captain like Williams, had a word to make sure the Cowboys don't go down the 2025 path.

 "Urgency," he said. "Leaning on our work, come in and attacking the week the right way. Having a great week and playing ball like we know how when we get there Sunday."

title: First impressions of Raiders' defense under Rob Leonard
summary: After a Week 1 win, players praised how the new DC called the defense against Miami.
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- Throughout the offseason, first-time defensive coordinator Rob Leonard didn't want to dive too much into how the Las Vegas Raiders ' defense would look under his guidance.

 It was obvious that the Raiders wanted to be versatile, given the handful of players who can line up at different spots on the field, and they wanted to be aggressive when pursuing the quarterback. But Leonard steered away from revealing his full plans, especially during preseason games, by keeping things basic until the Raiders were in matchups that counted.

 In the Raiders' Week 1 win over the Miami Dolphins , Leonard didn't hold back in his playcalling, and the results were good. Las Vegas put together a promising defensive performance by containing Miami's run game and making quarterback  Malik Willis ' life uncomfortable in the pocket. More importantly, the Raiders' 27-13 victory  showed that they have a solid supporting cast around All-Pro defensive end Maxx Crosby .

 

 "I think he called a great game, and we just got to keep getting better because there's definitely some things we can improve on," Crosby said.

 The numbers were impressive. Everything that was an issue for the unit last season became a strength. The Dolphins were held to 74 rushing yards despite having the upper hand in this category going into the season opener because of running back  De'Von Achane . And even he had only 36 yards on 11 carries.

 The Raiders limited Miami to converting 3 of 10 attempts on third down. On top of that, the Dolphins scored just one touchdown on three red zone trips. The Raiders also forced two turnovers.

 The biggest takeaway, however, was being able to pressure Willis. In Week 1, the Raiders tied for the most sacks (five) in the league, had the fifth-most pressures (15) and had the sixth-best pressure rate at 44.4%.

 "[Leonard] emphasizes allowing us to have a lot of confidence with the calls and be able to execute at a high level," defensive lineman Thomas Booker IV told ESPN. "Violence is speed. I think that's the big calling card of the defense."

 Eight players recorded a pressure, including Crosby and Kwity Paye  -- who combined for 3.5 sacks, 11 pressures and 10 quarterback hits. One play in the fourth quarter showcased a good playcall from Leonard and how strong Las Vegas' defense can be with Paye and Crosby lining up on opposite sides.

 With the Dolphins facing a third-and-10 at the 11-minute mark of the quarter, Las Vegas rushed five defenders. When Achane attempted to block linebacker Quay Walker , Paye looped inside while Crosby forcefully pushed off offensive tackle Austin Jackson . Paye and Crosby then combined to take down Willis for a sack.

 

 Paye's performance alone was a breath of fresh air. The Raiders needed a secondary pass rusher. They spent last season relying heavily on Crosby to be the anchor in stopping the pass and run game.

 Paye, who had two sacks, five pressures and five quarterback hits, showed the potential to be a strong running mate. It helps that he is versatile and can line up at multiple spots on the field. Paye played 23 defensive snaps on the edge and nine snaps at defensive tackle.

 "He played physical," Leonard said. "The style of play was right on par with what we're looking for. I was proud of him. You know, I was proud of him trusting me and the vision that we had bringing him here and sticking with it."

 Paye developing into a reliable secondary rusher moving forward will be essential since it appears the Raiders could be load-managing Crosby, who played in 46 defensive snaps (82%). It was the fourth game since 2023 that Crosby has played in 82% or fewer defensive snaps.

 

 Coach Klint Kubiak's decision to sit Crosby for three straight drives was understandable. Crosby underwent offseason knee surgery , and the Raiders need to be mindful of the 29-year-old All-Pro edge rusher's longevity so that he can continue to produce outings like last week's.

 That's why it was so important for the Raiders to strengthen their front seven in free agency by adding Paye and inside linebackers Walker and  Nakobe Dean , all of whom can attack the quarterback.

 And when Crosby is on the field, opportunities arise for those players to create plays.

 "I got more one-on-ones today, for sure," Paye said. "The slide was away from me, but I feel like [Leonard] schemed it up pretty well."

 Leonard was given the game ball in the Raiders' locker room after the game. It was uncertain how he would handle the duties of defensive playcalling, incorporating ideas he had developed working under Mike MacDonald, Brian Flores and Patrick Graham. But Leonard's ability to have the Raiders look dominant in the trenches with stunts and simulated pressures while taking advantage of the new faces on defense has provided optimism in the unit moving forward.

 "[Leonard] is aggressive and emphasizes style of play over everything else," Booker said. "Scheme is obviously important in this league, but at the end of the day, when you have players that are being physical, running to the ball, swarming, and can play fast, that's going to be a pretty good formula more times than not."

title: Dolphins not discouraged by Chris Johnson's rough stat sheet
summary: Coach Jeff Hafley found positives for first-round cornerback Chris Johnson despite a hard day at the office.
full_text:
NAPA, Calif. -- According to The Associated Press, Miami Dolphins rookies played more snaps in Week 1 than any team since at least 2006; unsurprising for the league's youngest team.

 While linebacker Jacob Rodriguez and wide receiver Caleb Douglas were among Miami's standout performers in Sunday's loss to the Las Vegas Raiders , cornerback  Chris Johnson 's day wasn't as smooth -- at least on paper.

 The first-round pick was targeted 11 times, according to NextGen Stats, allowing six catches for 62 yards. He was also the nearest defender on two of Kirk Cousins' touchdown passes.

 But teammates and coaches say Johnson's performance was more than what the stat sheet suggested, and they know the rookie's confidence won't waver going into this week's matchup with the San Francisco 49ers (4:25 p.m. ET on Fox).

 "I think Chris, when you watch the tape and you look at the scheme and you don't just point fingers at a guy who you think was at fault -- I think there's certainly some plays that Chris wants back," Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said. "I think Chris showed a lot of flashes and played a solid game. He was good against a run at his nickel position. ... He's hard on himself, too, because he's the one that it's showing up on. Chris did a lot of good things [Sunday] and Chris should be confident that he can do a lot of good things in this league."

 Johnson was in coverage on Cousins' touchdown passes to Jack Bech and Ashton Jeanty , but Hafley said neither score was actually his fault based on scheme responsibilities.

 Miami was in Cover 1 on Bech's touchdown catch, which features a deep safety and sometimes a "robber," where either the other safety or a linebacker covers shorter routes over the middle of the field. Safety Zayne Anderson and linebacker Jordyn Brooks both covered Raiders tight end Michael Mayer , and Bech scored on a slant route directly to the area of the field Anderson vacated.

 The Dolphins were also in Cover 1 on Jeanty's touchdown and the Raiders took advantage of a similar mistake -- this time, Brooks and rookie safety Michael Taaffe both covered Mayer, and Cousins found Jeanty in the space that Taaffe vacated.

 "Really just have to clean up some of my techniques," Johnson said after the game. "I feel like I was responsible for a few touchdowns but at the end of the day, I've got to be cleaner in my coverage. The team is relying on me to do that."

 Taaffe told reporters that he was responsible for one of the touchdowns attributed to Johnson but didn't clarify which one. Hafley said the players who missed their assignments immediately owned up to it on the sideline after each play.

 Johnson did finish with 11 tackles in his NFL regular-season debut, as well as two pass breakups and an impressive tackle for a loss where he wrapped Jeanty up behind the line of scrimmage on the Raiders' first offensive drive.

 Dolphins players and coaches have also pushed back on the notion that Johnson was "targeted" by the veteran Cousins. Johnson said the number of targets he saw was a by-product of him playing multiple cornerback positions, while defensive coordinator Sean Duggan said Cousins "put the ball where we allowed him to."

 "Some of that's a little overblown. I don't think necessarily the quarterback was looking his way," Brooks said. "Some of that stuff wasn't his fault -- that was a breakdown in the defense as a whole. And so I'm not worried about a guy like Chris. Chris is the ultimate confidence guy, very sure of himself. I think he's going to be great. He's got all the ability and he's got the want to.

 "You get hit in a game, that's what the NFL is. You make plays, you miss plays. It is what it is. And so he'll bounce back and we'll get it rolling from there."

 The Dolphins have been clear since draft weekend of their intentions for Johnson to be a pivotal part of their defense. He cross-trained at the outside cornerback and nickel cornerback positions, and coaches said his football intelligence and overall feel for the game have allowed him to play both.

 Hafley said he isn't concerned about the highs and lows from the Dolphins' 14 rookies this season -- the "rookie moments" are going to happen. But especially at high-visibility positions such as cornerback, it's important for his staff to remain consistent with its messaging.

 "You got to keep coaching them, you got to tell them the truth, and we got to develop these guys," Hafley said. "How you treat the game film should not be indicative of the wins or losses. How you treat the game film is you go play by play regardless of the result, and was the process right? Did they execute? Did they line up right? Was their footwork right? Did they do their job the best that they could? And if they didn't, we got to get them better. And if they did, you show them why and you move on.

 "I'm not going to waver and lose confidence and ride this up and down wave; I think having a consistent mindset of growing day by day and play by play is going to be really important for all these guys."

title: Cam Skattebo reclaims role as Giants' feature back
summary: Just like that, it's business as usual for the bruising running back as he dominated the field in Week 1 against the Cowboys.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- It wasn't long after getting emotional during last Sunday's national anthem that the  New York Giants ' Cam Skattebo raced around the left end untouched and into the end zone before launching immediately into a cartwheel and his trademark backflip. The second-year running back had scored the Giants' first touchdown of the season 10-plus months after a gruesome leg injury against the Dallas Cowboys .

 He was back. So was the backflip, despite some offseason controversies .

 "I've been saying it for about a month I was gonna do a backflip when I scored my first touchdown," Skattebo said after the 28-20 win over the Cowboys. "I might do it here or there throughout the year. You won't see if every single time, but I'm gonna make up something else now. Give the kids something else to do."

 Just like that, it's business as usual for the bruising running back. Skattebo rushed for 81 yards on 18 carries and played his usual physical brand of football. He ran over Cowboys linebacker DeMarvion Overshown on multiple occasions and had the game-clinching run late in the fourth quarter.

 Watching him run Sunday night, it was almost as if Skattebo had never suffered an open tibia fracture and ruptured ligament in his dislocated right ankle. New coach John Harbaugh was impressed.

 "I think it probably started with [Skattebo]. I mean, he was running really, really hard. Really, really well," Harbaugh said. "Set the tempo, brought the energy, juice."

 This is what he worked so hard to get back for. He's a football player.

 Not that it was all so easy. Skattebo was stuck on his couch for the first few months of his rehab. He admitted contemplating retirement . But the 24-year-old was back on the field practicing in the spring and full-go for the start of training camp this summer.

 "It was tough. It was tough because I had a lot of uncertainty and each process that happened, when one thing was hurting and it started feeling better, something else would start hurting," Skattebo said. "And over time, it got better and better, and different things popped up. So, depending on what I did in rehab, something else was going to pop up and bother me.

 

 "I had to work through all those little kinks and make sure that everything was feeling good. And I still have a little bit of soreness here and there with certain cutting and over time. But I mean, I feel great, man. I feel like what I've done in the PT room has put me in a good, successful position to be able to continue to play this game."

 Skattebo looked great in Week 1. He was the Giants' feature back, starting the game and handling a majority of the workload. When they needed a big play late, they turned to him.

 The 2025 fourth-round pick played 41 of 63 offensive snaps. He handled 69% of the rushing workload for the running backs.

 "I was pleased. It was physical. It was downhill. I enjoyed it," Skattebo said. "I'm not too sore."

 Skattebo did his best to downplay it all afterward. All the attention in the lead-up to the game was on wide receiver Malik Nabers , who was returning from a torn ACL suffered four weeks before Skattebo's injury last year.

 It was the first game back from serious injury for both. It shouldn't be taken lightly what they overcame to return.

 "I mean, I got a little emotional during the national anthem, but I think the big thing was [Nabers'] injury," Skattebo said. "Obviously, mine was gruesome. But his was such a long process and such a process because of an ACL. It's a little harder to come back from that. And all props to him for grinding this whole offseason.

 "We were alongside each other in the training room, and I started to get a lot better faster because of the different injury. And his was a little bit slower of an incline. I used to tell him all the time, me and [quarterback] Jaxson [Dart] would tell him, we'll meet you in Week 1. ... I look back at my injury like I was supposed to come back and I was supposed to play Game 1, so it was really cool to see him come back and actually do it."

 Now the Giants look to build on it in a Week 2 "Monday Night Football" matchup with the Los Angeles Rams (8:15 p.m. ET, ESPN). Skattebo as the Giants' feature running back. Nabers as the No. 1 receiver.

 Their workloads should increase as they get back to full strength. That was Nabers' first game since the injury. Skattebo appeared in one preseason game this summer.

 But this was different. This was the final hurdle cleared.

 "I felt like myself again," Skattebo said. "And the guys, the training staff, the coaches, they've understood where I've been at. They understand who I am. They take my words for what they take them for. They trust who I am. If I'm sore one day, they cut me some slack. So I appreciate them and am going to continue to kick ass and work my ass off."

full_text:
The second "Monday Night Football" game of the 2026 NFL season features two teams that got off to vastly different starts in Week 1.

 Fresh off their season-opening win against the Dallas Cowboys , John Harbaugh and the New York Giants head west to take on Sean McVay and the Los Angeles Rams . The Rams look to bounce back after opening their campaign with a divisional loss to the San Francisco 49ers  in Melbourne, Australia.

 The Giants hope to delay Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford 's climb up the record books. The reigning NFL MVP enters Monday night with 423 career passing touchdowns, two shy of tying Philip Rivers for sixth most in NFL history.

 Here are key facts about the Week 2 "Monday Night Football" matchup:

 What is the schedule?

 Monday

 8:15 p.m.: Giants at Rams on ESPN and ABC

 8:15 p.m.: "Monday Night Football with Peyton and Eli" -- the "ManningCast" -- on ESPN2

 How can fans watch?

title: Eagles' new perspective for '26: Don't 'let anyone steal our joy'
summary: It's no coincidence the mood inside Philly's locker room was at its most sullen in 2023 and '25, two seasons following Super Bowl runs.
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA -- The  Philadelphia Eagles  beat the Washington Commanders 24-22 in the season opener and were consciously making an effort in the game's aftermath to let that be enough.

 "Last year, I know everyone [would] try to make something of, we won by two points. We're not getting on that this year. And that's a beautiful thing," running back Saquon Barkley said. "We come out with a win, we're going to be happy, we're going to celebrate and we're going to flush it and move on and get ready for next week."

 That was the core of coach Nick Sirianni's postgame message to the team, players said: that, as receiver/returner Britain Covey put it, "We're not going to let anyone steal our joy from the wins."

 Philadelphia has felt like Whoville at times in recent years, with inflated expectations and over analysis swiping the gift of victory with a Grinch-like harshness.

 

 Such an environment -- where there's such angst over a four-year stretch in which the team has gone 51-18, reached two Super Bowl and won one -- is only possible when outsized standards are enforced by members of the organization and its city alike. And it's no coincidence that the mood inside the locker room and out was at its most sullen in 2023 and '25, two seasons following Super Bowl runs when good was in the shadows of great.

 Barkley said he tried his best not to compare his more-than-respectable 2025 campaign (1,140 rushing yards, 7 TDs) to '24, when he became just the ninth back ever to eclipse 2,000 yards in the regular season, but "human nature" sometimes got the better of him.

 He credits the team psychiatrist, Dr. Jody Foster, for helping to shift his mindset. Barkley told ESPN that the pivotal conversation with Foster occurred on the bus ride from the hotel to Gillette Stadium in front of the Eagles' preseason game against the New England Patriots on Aug. 22. She encouraged him to recognize the small wins during the course of a game or a season and to focus on three or four short-term goals within his control instead of overly concerning himself with the big picture.

 "She's really just trying to get me focused on just getting back to the process and falling in love with the process. It's so easy in this business and who I am as a person to get motivated or pushed by results," he said, "but in reality, that's not what it's about."

 Winning, Sirianni reminded the gathered media Wednesday, is hard, and he used a "Seinfeld" reference to illustrate his point.

 He noted the Paul O'Neill episode, in which Kramer promises a child in the hospital that the Yankees slugger will hit two home runs for him in one game. "It's hard to hit home runs, and where did you get two from?" O'Neill asks Kramer, who snuck into the clubhouse.

 In other words, winning is hard enough; there's no need to throw qualifiers on top of it when seeking satisfaction.

 "You have to enjoy it because you know you're going to go right back to work, win or lose. We're going to sit here and we're all going to take ownership of the tape. Naturally as humans, you tend to look at the negatives more than you look at the positives, but there are so many positives and it's so important that joy comes after every time," Sirianni said.

 

 It's not as easy when you're talking about a room full of ultra-high achievers -- players who have come to expect both team and personal success and know their legacy rides on it.

 This time last year, it wasn't unusual for wins to be followed by cryptic messages from a clearly disenchanted A.J. Brown , now in New England. He's a player who cared about creating both a dynasty and a Hall-of-Fame résumé. The inefficiencies in the Eagles' passing game were a threat to both. He was not alone in his frustrations but the frequency in which he made his displeasure known helped put a cloud over things, as did the lack of progress on the offensive front.

 "It's a combination of everything," Covey said. "One, it's playing in Philadelphia, it's loud. And you always want to feel like you're improving throughout the season so when you keep seeing the same problems appear in games, it can feel frustrating."

 Some of the players are taking their cues from quarterback Jalen Hurts , who has "a confidence and aura to him," Covey said, stemming from being singularly focused on winning.

 "That's always been my perspective, that's always been the MO is to go out there and find a way to win," Hurts said. "Because it's a hard thing to do. Winning is hard and it requires what it requires so we try to focus on the work, try to focus on the process and I think Coach has been really good with leading that."

 New offensive coordinator Sean Mannion was brought in from Green Bay to help get the arrow pointing upwards once again. As expected, there were plenty of imperfections as the players took the new scheme for its first test drive during Week 1.

 Barkley had four runs for negative yards. He acknowledged afterwards that those plays were top of mind and that last year, he "probably would have sat on this game too long." Now, though, he was trying to package it as a learning experience.

 "It's going to be really good. We're going to just continue to build. I know how the media is and how Philly is and we like to overreact a little bit but it's not a finished product," Barkley said.

 "We're going to keep working, we're going to keep trusting in Sean, we're going to keep trusting the system. We're going to find ways to just continue to get better. That's the goal and it's easier to do when you've got a win."

title: Who is Commanders' special teams ace Tyler Owens?
summary: J.J. Watt called Owens' play against the Eagles 'legitimately one of the greatest football plays I've ever seen.'
full_text:
ASHBURN, Va. -- The play, viewed more than 18 million times on one social media platform, went like this: Washington Commanders special-teamer Tyler Owens , ready to cover a punt, stepped outside then cut back inside and ripped through a double-team at the line of scrimmage. He flung one blocker to the side then stiff-armed the other as he raced downfield. When the other blocker caught back up to Owens, he shoved him to the ground then did the same to the second one.

 Owens looked like a man chasing someone stealing his car.

 And then Owens reached the returner, who decided to leap. Bad decision. Owens corralled him and body-slammed him to the ground. Owens then got up and casually walked to the sideline, as if he had just clocked out of work for the day.

 "It was just a good rep," he said.

 

 Others begged to differ. Former Pro Bowl defensive end J.J. Watt called it "legitimately one of the greatest football plays I've ever seen." It has been viewed more than 11.6 million times on the NFL's X feed and another 6.9 million times on the NFLmemes feed. More than 40,000 people liked it on the NFL's Instagram page.

 "I was just out there playing football," Owens said. "It never really stood out to me until after."

 And though it introduced Owens to the sporting world, his teammates needed no introductions. They already knew what he could do -- and has done. They might have been impressed by the play, but they were not surprised.

 There's a reason Owens made the Commanders as an undrafted free agent in 2024; he made two plays that summer to stand out. Those plays also prompted coach Dan Quinn to make an unusual announcement in a team meeting about Owens. His special teams coach at Texas Tech, Kenny Perry, could point to plays in college that prompted him to tell Owens he would make a long living in the NFL.

 "That's what he's been doing," said Washington safety  Jeremy Reaves , a special teams Pro Bowler after the 2022 season. "He's done that over and over and over again. That's who he is."

 Commanders punter  Tress Way , who has been in the league since 2014, said he gets the same question from coordinators or assistant coaches on other teams.

 "Just about every team we play, they're like, 'What do you guys feed 18?'" Way said. "I tell them punt returners."

 Three days after the play, after he had become a teaching tool for special teams coaches at every level and after seeing the reaction and appearing on "The Pat McAfee Show," Owens knows it was more than "just a good rep."

 And though other plays stand out in his mind, this one vs. the Eagles vaulted to the top.

 "I would say this is my favorite," Owens said. "Just because of the physicality. ... It's just rewarding. You put in all this work, finally get to see something come out of it."

 What he saw was a viral reaction.

 "Just all the GOATS retweeting it and stuff like that. It's pretty dope," Owens said. "I like it."

 But he admitted that he ran downfield angry, perturbed, because he said the Eagles' jammers had been holding him during the first three punts, grabbing his jersey and even his hair. Owens made it tougher on him on the fourth one by taking an outside release after going inside on the previous punts. It created a space to turn back inside and split the double-team.

 One of the players he shoved to the ground was  Jonathan Jones  -- a teammate in 2025. Jones wasn't shocked by the play either: He knows Owens has size (6-foot-2, 213 pounds) and speed (he ran the 100-meter dash in 10.35 seconds in high school). Owens' broad jump of 12 feet 2 inches at the NFL combine in 2024 fell 1 inch short of tying the event's record -- and was 10 inches better than any other defensive player that year.

 On Owens' first sprint downfield to cover a punt Sunday, he was clocked at 21.19 mph. Owens made the tackle for a 1-yard loss. On Washington's final punt -- after Owens had returned from an ankle injury -- he was clocked at 21.31 mph as he beat the double-team to the outside, was 3 yards ahead of his blockers and forced a fair catch.

 "He's aggressive. He's athletic," Jones said of Owens. "He's basically a linebacker and a safety."

 Eagles returner  Britain Covey  discovered what that combination can do. He also regretted leaping as Owens approached.

 

 "I have no idea what I was doing. It was the dumbest thing I've ever done in my life," said Covey, who gained 12 yards on the return. "There was a moment in the air where time stopped and I was like, 'Oh my gosh, I'm taller than [6-foot-8 teammate]  Jordan Mailata . Right now, I'm going to die.'"

 But Covey didn't mind his role in Owens' stardom.

 "I feel honored to be part of that play, even though I was on the not-so-good end," Covey said. "Anytime you see great football like that, you tip your hat. It was a really cool play to watch and shoutout to him. He's a menace. We double-teamed him, and it was like a fly to him."

 Reaves was at the bottom of that pile. "He actually slammed him on me," Reaves said. "I didn't know what happened until after the play. I looked back and I'm like, 'Somebody just f---ed him up. My expectation was it was him or [Percy] Butler [Washington's other gunner]. I expect [Owens] to make everything."

 Quinn said it was "awesome" to see the effort and speed result in this moment. He said Owens reacted like, "Thanks, man, that's what I do. ... It was no big deal."

 "And [I'm] like, 'Man, this is a really big deal,'" Quinn said. "It was one of my favorite plays in a long time on special teams for sure."

 Ditto for special teams coach Larry Izzo, who pointed out that the Commanders' other gunner, Butler, is equally accomplished. But Izzo knew Owens' play was unique.

 "When you combine that mindset and that play style with the freakish skill-set he has, that's what you're left with," Izzo said, "which is an exceptional play, one that in 30 years in the NFL I don't know if I've seen a better demonstration of just a dude whupping people's asses.

 "That was just a sheer ass whupping. Pretty cool play."

 In Washington, Owens' ascension started with his first preseason game in 2024. Lined up on the left side, he beat solo blocking and sprinted downfield. Because it was a windy day, the returner let the 55-yard punt hit at the 35-yard line; he caught the bounce at the 28 -- just as Owens arrived and decked him.

 The punt was the first Owens had covered in the NFL.

 "It was like all of a sudden, he just gained 12 yards of speed and took this guy out," Way said. "I remember thinking, how did that happen so fast?"

 Then, a week later vs. Miami, Owens knocked the man blocking him 5 yards backward and directly into the path of the returner, who then flipped over his teammate.

 "You look at the Miami game, that's how he made the team," Reaves said. "He put the guy on his ass."

 After that Miami game, in which Owens also de-cleated a Dolphins gunner, Quinn told Izzo after reviewing the film that this effort is what he wanted as the Commanders' identity.

 Izzo said Owens was just "crushing dudes on kickoff." So, several days after that Dolphins game, Quinn told Owens in a team meeting that he had made the 53-man roster.

 While playing for Miami in 1996, Izzo enjoyed the same words from then-coach Jimmy Johnson, who told the team that he knew of two players who were locks: quarterback Dan Marino and Izzo.

  "It's a pretty cool deal," Izzo said.

 That came as no surprise to Perry, who coached Owens for two seasons at Texas Tech after he had transferred from Texas. Perry saw it in practice and in games.

 "When we got here, I saw him and I'm like, 'Holy s---, this kid's a freak,'" Perry said. "Nobody could ever block him. I kept telling him, 'You're going to make a lot of money in the NFL doing this.' And he's like, 'You really think so?' I'm like, 'Hell yes.' I'd tell all my dudes that I knew in the NFL, there's a guy here that he's going to play a long time doing this in the NFL. And I wasn't wrong."

title: Inside the saga around Joey Porter Jr.'s future with Steelers
summary: The future of Pittsburgh's No. 1 cornerback with the team he grew up around remains unclear. Here's what we know.
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- After navigating through nearly two feet of snow dumped on the city by Winter Storm Fern, cornerback Joey Porter Jr . slipped in the PNC Champions Club at Acrisure Stadium through a side door on Jan. 27 and took a seat next to his dad, Joey Porter Sr., facing the stage.

 In front of the pair, the Pittsburgh Steelers  introduced Mike McCarthy as the team's next head coach, two central figures in the organization's future staring at each other face to face as the past looked on.

 A legacy player and the team's first 2023 second-round pick, Porter was the perfect bridge for the organization as it transitioned from Mike Tomlin to McCarthy.

 Nine months later, Porter's future with the team he grew up around is unclear and becoming less certain by the day. After lengthy and contentious negotiations, ones that continued until just hours before kickoff against the visiting Atlanta Falcons in Week 1, the Steelers and Porter's side failed to agree to a contract extension prior to the start of the 2026 regular season.

 

 Porter, meanwhile, was inactive for the season opener, instead watching the game from the sideline in a gray sweatshirt and gray Steelers shorts. McCarthy decided to hold Porter out against the Falcons because he hadn't completed the ramp-up period in his return to practice. The cornerback was placed on the physically unable to perform list and missed all of training camp with an aggravated back injury he reported to the team following a mobility workout on the first day on July 28.

 While the plan was to increase Porter's workload this week, the cornerback left Thursday's practice with an athletic trainer during the media viewing window. Before his early exit, Porter stretched with the team and did a rep of a ball-security drill. Unlike Wednesday's practice report in which he was listed as a limited participant with "Not Injury Related -- conditioning" as his official injury, Thursday's report listed a back injury. Porter, the team said, was cleared of the previous back injury earlier in the week, though McCarthy declined to give specifics on Porter's timeline or availability for Sunday's Week 2 game at the New England Patriots (1 p.m. ET, CBS).

 "I'm with Joe, whatever he's doing -- whether it's injury, whether it's contract, whatever it is, I respect it," Steelers linebacker Patrick Queen said after Thursday's practice. "I'm behind him 100%. I tell him every single time, 'I respect how you go about your business every single day.'"

 Thursday night, some close to the situation sensed a fracture in the relationship between Porter and the organization.

 "I don't know if he ever puts on a Steelers uniform again," a source with knowledge of the situation told ESPN.

 That leaves the Steelers and their homegrown talent in limbo, a place that seemed unlikely when Porter arrived at Acrisure Stadium to greet his new coach in January.

 The two sides have been here because of a significant difference between the Steelers' view of Porter's value and how Porter values himself. The core issue is the structure of the contract, sources told ESPN, and the Steelers' organizational precedent that doesn't fully guarantee a healthy portion of the contract was considered a sizable hurdle.

 Many of the Steelers past deals for key players fully guarantee only the first year. That was the case for Porter's draft mates, Keeanu Benton , Darnell Washington  and Nick Herbig , whose four-year extensions this summer guaranteed 2027 for injury only. Porter wants stronger guarantees, sources said. Pittsburgh has broken precedent in the past. For example, Pittsburgh guaranteed $108 million for T.J. Watt in the summer of 2025. While Porter doesn't have the megastar cachet of Watt, he's still a high-level cover corner.

 The sides simply did not get close to bridging that guaranteed gap, which sources say made any talks about a per-year average on a deal moot. "It never even got that far," a source said.

 Porter believes that he deserves a contract commensurate with his impressive skill set. However, Porter hasn't been voted to a Pro Bowl or All-Pro team during his three seasons, and each of the 10 highest-paid corners on a per-year average have at least one Pro Bowl or All-Pro nod. All but one ( Dallas ' DaRon Bland ) are former first-round picks.

 

 As a second-round selection, Porter isn't in the same boat as Christian Gonzalez and Devon Witherspoon , who have reset the market with their own extensions this offseason. Though the pair were drafted in the same class as Porter in 2023 and are also up-and-coming cornerbacks, Gonzalez and Witherspoon already had their fifth-year options picked up, a contract clause attached only to first-round picks. While Porter has the opportunity to hit free agency a year earlier, the Patriots and Seattle Seahawks were motivated to get extensions done to alleviate the 2027 cap hit that comes with the fifth-year guarantees.

 With a year still left on his rookie deal, Porter also isn't in the same position as Le'Veon Bell was in 2018, when the running back held out and refused to sign his second consecutive franchise tag with Pittsburgh. Unlike Bell, Porter is still under contract. Not only do the Steelers have control of Porter's rights this season, but the team could also franchise tag him before he's able to hit free agency in 2027.

 The emergence of cornerback Asante Samuel Jr . is a factor, too. With Porter out, the Steelers are comfortable with Samuel as a starter.

 A 2021 Los Angeles Chargers second-round pick, Samuel landed with the Steelers late last season once he was cleared to return to football activities following spinal fusion surgery. He gave the secondary an immediate boost in 2025, leading to him signing a one-year, $4 million deal to return to the Steelers. He was a standout during training camp and the preseason. Listed as a co-starter alongside Porter on the depth chart, he played all 60 defensive snaps in Porter's absence against the Falcons on Sunday.

 The Steelers could trade Porter, though the team has neither made nor received any serious inquiries about the cornerback. One NFL executive believes the Steelers could get a second-round pick in exchange for Porter and a quality Day 3 draft selection.

 Before the season opener, Porter was hopeful that his future remained with the organization. But sources have described Porter as "disappointed" a deal couldn't be made and "frustrated" by the situation. Because of that, Porter requested a trade, per ESPN senior NFL insider Adam Schefter and NFL Network national insider Ian Rapoport , a possibility that seemed inconceivable nine months ago. The notion of a trade was not surprising to multiple sources who first brought up the possibility to ESPN in August, when the Steelers hadn't made a formal offer and gave the full impression they wanted Porter to play out his rookie deal.

 Adding to that emotion is Porter's history with the Steelers.

 "I'm from here," Porter said on Sept. 1. "My family lives here. My cousin went to high school here, so they know I'm a hometown kid."

 Porter's dad was a linebacker for the Steelers from 1999 to 2006 and had 98 sacks in 13 seasons. He eventually returned as a defensive assistant in 2014 and remained as a coach with the team through 2018. Last year, Porter was inducted into the team's Ring of Honor, and he's a constant presence at games and occasionally pops into some practices at the team facility.

 

 Though he was born in California, Porter grew up running around the Southside practice facility with Tomlin's sons and went to high school at North Allegheny in Wexford, Pennsylvania -- a suburb of Pittsburgh. As a 5-year-old wearing his dad's jersey, Porter was hoisted up by his father as confetti rained down on Ford Field after the Steelers celebrated their Super Bowl XL title in Detroit on Feb. 5, 2006.

 As a teenager, Porter was a ball boy at Steelers training camp, scrubbing footballs after…

title: How the 49ers are readjusting after weeklong Australia trip
summary: On their 16-hour flight home from Australia, the 49ers chose sleep over celebration. That kick-started a long week of getting back into routine.
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- After a convincing 27-7 win over a division rival, the San Francisco 49ers boarded their buses and headed to the Melbourne airport with visions of a victory party dancing in their heads.

 The Niners knew they couldn't take off before the  Los Angeles Rams ' departed, but they still had every intention of making the most of the 16-hour flight home. But by the time they boarded the plane, all of those plans stayed on the ground, as adrenaline gave way to the fatigue from their weeklong trip down under.

 "We're all like, dude, we're going to fall asleep and then we're going to wake up and we're going to celebrate," fullback Kyle Juszczyk said. "We're going to have our team party that we didn't get to have. And then I woke up like an hour before we got there, and everyone was still sleeping. I don't think anybody celebrated."

 While they had every reason to celebrate in the moment, the fact that they didn't should only help them overcome the final obstacle of the Australia trip: reacclimating to Pacific time and a normal workweek.

 

 Asked this week whether it was more difficult to adjust to Australian time or readjusting to Pacific time, there were players on both sides of the fence. But they all agreed there was at least a little bit of an adjustment period.

 "Speaking for myself, I felt like crap all weekend," coach Kyle Shanahan said. "We had two days off and I did not feel right. Took a couple of days. I think I was good by Monday. Talking to some of the guys, some guys felt fine right away. Some went through the same stuff, but I think we're definitely all good by now."

 Much like they did for the flight to Melbourne, the Niners had recovery plans for their players that began as soon as they stepped back on the Qantas A380 plane . Dustin Perry, the team's vice president of player health and performance, and his staff provided players with instructions on how much water to drink on the plane, how long to stay up before falling asleep and when to wake up.

 Right tackle Colton McKivitz said the objective was to stay up for a couple of hours (an easy enough task with so much adrenaline still pumping from the game), go to sleep in their lie-flat seats, and then wake up for the final few hours of the flight.

 McKivitz estimated he slept for about seven hours. Running back Christian McCaffrey said he was out for about 13 hours, which was about the same as rookie defensive tackle Gracen Halton . Defensive end Nick Bosa was in the same range.

 "I actually felt it worse on the way back," Bosa said. "Going out, you just kind of power through a few hours and then go to bed early and then just stay on a little earlier wake-up is what I did. And then when I came back, it's been kind of hard to get to bed, but [Tuesday] night I got to bed nice and early."

 

 The 49ers landed at San Francisco International Airport on Friday night around 5 p.m., took a bus to Santa Clara, and then went their separate ways for the rest of the weekend. Perry's training staff offered further instructions on when to sleep and not, when to take in sunlight, and even the best times to consume caffeine. Shanahan gave the team Saturday and Sunday off, with the only schedule modification coming Monday.

 Coming off a normal Thursday game, the Niners routinely have a more normal "bonus" practice on Monday, but Shanahan tweaked it into something easier this week. Shanahan said the team met for its normal postgame film session before Perry and his staff put the players through a workout.

 Tuesday was a normal day off, and then the regular workweek began with practices at their normal early afternoon times Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. While the travel required some adjusting, Shanahan's message to the team was to ignore it as much as possible and maintain the same mindset that led to a win in Australia.

 "I thought one of the reasons we played so well is just because of the focus that we had," Shanahan said. "We can talk about the travel and all that, but that's whatever. Our whole team was locked into that game. I could tell from the first practice all the way to the night before the game, to pregame, to the end of the game. Nothing ever changed with them. That's the goal to do that same thing this week."

 Like Shanahan, it took varying amounts of days for his players to feel normal. McCaffrey said it took a couple of days before he felt like himself. It was the same for McKivitz and Halton. Linebacker Fred Warner , ever the overachiever, said it was "about a day" before he was "ready to rock."

 

 When the 49ers first agreed to play in Melbourne in Week 1, they asked the league to play on "Monday Night Football" in Week 2, according to Shanahan. The NFL denied that request but awarded them three consecutive home games, starting Sunday against the Miami Dolphins .

 On paper, it's a favorable matchup against a team with a new QB, head coach and general manager . But it's understood that an upset loss to the Dolphins -- the Niners are 13.5-point favorites on DraftKings -- would wipe away the momentum built in Week 1.

 "We loved the outcome of last week, but there's things to clean up all across the board," Warner said. "We're trying to see how we can get a little bit better going into this week to give ourselves a chance to win one more."

title: Titans remain patient with Cam Ward despite 'rough' opener
summary: Tennessee didn't score a touchdown until its last drive in coach Robert Saleh's debut.
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- When Robert Saleh signed to become the next coach of the Tennessee Titans in January, one thing was clear:  Cam Ward 's development into a franchise quarterback was the key to his success.

 There was optimism for Ward after he showed growth over the final six games of his rookie season last year, with 10 of his 15 touchdowns and only one of his seven interceptions coming over that stretch.

 But Ward's season debut under Saleh on Sunday against the New York Jets  wasn't what they imagined in the 23-10 loss , but Saleh is still confident in the Titans' plans to get the best out of the second-year quarterback.

 "I thought he did a lot of good things in the game early that showed the progress that he's been making," Saleh said of Ward, who finished the game 19 of 32 passing for 140 yards and was sacked three times. "He had a rough game, but it's not all on him. There were opportunities where we've got to be better for him as a staff; his teammates have got to be better for him, and then obviously he's got to be better for his teammates with regards to delivering a football."

 

 The Titans wanted to see improved pocket presence and accuracy from Ward as he entered his second season, but both issues surfaced Sunday. 

 "I'm sure there are times where Cam says he wishes he would have stood in there, just like there are times he feels he could gotten out," quarterback coach Shea Tierney said. "It's a feel thing. You just continue educating him and have him make the best decision. We do drills every day for that."

 Ward missed throws to  Wan'Dale Robinson  on a screen and Tyjae Spears on a swing route. Rookie receiver Carnell Tate was wide open on a crossing route, but Ward was unable to find him either. Ward still believes he's a "very good quarterback." But he isn't running from the fact he needs to play better to prove it.

 "I'm very critical of myself. I want to be a great player," Ward said. "That comes whether it's from myself or the coaching staff, it's what can I do to be the best I want to be and for the team for us to be the best. There are key plays that myself and the staff think that I helped, but there are plays where I could have helped even more. That means continuing to take coaching from myself and from [offensive coordinator Brian Daboll] and [Tierney] and getting back to the drawing board and making something happen."

 The Titans staff believes Ward's improvement will come with more time on task. Allowing Ward to accumulate more practical experience will require patience the organization hasn't shown in the past. This is the same franchise that has fired a general manager or coach every year since 2022.

 That patience is going to be tested considering the success of fellow second-year quarterbacks Tyler Shough , who won Offensive Rookie of the Year with the New Orleans Saints last season, and Jaxson Dart , who had three passing touchdowns in Giants' season-opening win over the Dallas Cowboys last Sunday night. Sure, they're in different situations, but it's natural for team ownership to get frustrated that quarterbacks selected after Ward have had a higher degree of statistical success.

 

 Saleh is committed to allowing time for the process to carry out. He pointed out how Ward has had seven coordinators over the last seven years and stressed the importance of building a foundation for the young quarterback with stability around him. Despite Sunday's performance, Saleh is fully committed to Ward and feels the quarterback's growth is going to happen throughout the year.

 "We're fully committed to Cam because we believe in him," Saleh told ESPN. "You've got to let these young men grow. You would hate to be on the other side of it where you give up on a young man, and he goes to another team, and he wins a Super Bowl. We believe he has the right mindset, and we're going to give him every opportunity to grow."

 Saleh has seen this movie before. The Jets selected Zach Wilson with the second overall pick in the 2021 draft when he was the head coach. Wilson, like Ward, led his team to three wins as a rookie. The Jets gave Wilson two seasons to show he can develop into a franchise quarterback. His 18 interceptions to 15 touchdowns and 4,022 passing yards in 22 starts didn't cut it, so the Jets acquired future Hall of Famer Aaron Rodgers in a trade with the Green Bay Packers .

 Unlike when he was in New York, Saleh has a proven quarterback developer in Daboll, but the Ward and Daboll duo failed the first test in the opener.

 When asked to assess the performance, Daboll refused to place all of the blame on Ward either.

 "It takes all 11," Daboll said. "There's certainly plays that I wish I had back. I'm sure there's plays that Cam wishes he had back -- and the 10 other guys out there as well. So we got to do a better job with that. That starts with me."

 

 The Titans have done a lot to create a launching pad for Ward. They selected Tate with the No. 4 overall pick in the draft. They signed Robinson in free agency. Titans general manager Mike Borgonzi also signed veteran quarterback Mitchell Trubisky to be Ward's backup and a veteran presence to help him grow.

 Trubisky has experienced what Ward is going through, having been the No. 2 overall pick by the Chicago Bears in 2017. He spent four seasons in Chicago as a starter before signing with the Buffalo Bills  as a backup, where he first played for Daboll.

 Trubisky mentioned how this era is different than the old-school days when quarterbacks were given time to develop and grow into the franchise role. A highly-drafted quarterback is usually thrown into the fire and asked to produce right away. Trubisky's advice to Ward is to focus on what he can control and not lose sight of who he is.

 "You've got to go back to what made you get drafted that high and know that you're a talented quarterback," Trubisky told ESPN. "Continue to believe in yourself and just know that it's a process. This is not an easy league. There are no easy games. There's going to be bumps along the way."

 There were plenty of bumps for Ward and the Titans in the opener, where their lone touchdown came on their ninth and final drive trailing 23-3.

 "I'm just continuing to try and get better," Ward said. "How can I get better from last Sunday to this Sunday? It's going to be a process." 

 Ward's next opportunity will come against last year's NFC East champions in the  Philadelphia Eagles  on Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, FOX ) at Nissan Stadium. 

 "I have great coaches around me who continue to push me to that level that I want to play at," Ward said. "And when the tide turns, I'm pretty sure it's going to be a different story."

title: Commanders rule out Frankie Luvu, Chig Okonkwo vs. Cowboys
summary: The Commanders have ruled out linebacker Frankie Luvu, and tight end Chig Okonkwo for Sunday's road game against Dallas, coach Dan Quinn said.
